actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising with AutoEncoders
PROPOSAL: Experiment to train a conditional autoencoder that takes as input multiple noisy point clouds of the same object and outputs a single denoised point cloud. The network architecture can be based on PointNet++ and the loss function can be designed to encourage consistency across the input noisy point clouds.
CONTROLS: Supervised PointNet++ as baseline, identical architecture with minor deviations (e.g. filters addition or subtraction) for ablation study
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might fail in handling cases with large variations in pose of the object across different noisy scans due to the absence of geometric consistency constraints across images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Consistency Regularization for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: Theoretical result: Analyze the effects of adding a consistency regularization term to the loss function in the autoencoder, which encourages the network to produce denoised point clouds that are close to each other across different input noisy point clouds. We can use tools from differential geometry and MCMC to show under which conditions this regularization is effective and what are its tradeoffs with the reconstruction loss.
CONTROLS:� Analysis of counterexamples with frustrated landscapes
COST: negligible in terms of GPU-hours (library-based)
PREDICTION: This theory may provide insight into designing more effective loss functions for unsupervised learning of point cloud denoising, but might require approximation to derive sharp results due to the difficulty of computing normals for surface reconstructions in specific domains within a general proof.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graph-Based Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: Experiment to use a graph neural network (GNN) to learn denoising patterns in point clouds. The network builds a graph from the noisy point clouds and then applies message passing to propagate denoising information across the graph. The loss function can be designed to encourage the network to produce denoised point clouds that have fewer neighboring points with high noises.
CONTROLS: Supervised PointNet++ as baseline, TotalDenoising for ablation study (to see the effect of using a graph structure)
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach may require a larger network to handle the graph structure and may face problems with computing time complexity on larger point clouds.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Graph-Based Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising
REVISED PROPOSAL: REVISED EXPERIMENTAL OBJECTIVE: Revise the graph-based model to be more context-aware by introducing a distance-aware pooling layer that aggregates neighbor information based on their pairwise distances from the input points. The layer assigns higher weights to closer points, effectively keeping local parts of the point cloud intact during the denoising process.
CONTROLS: Supervised PointNet++ as baseline, TotalDenoising for ablation study (to see the effect of using a distance-aware pooling layer)
COST: negligible additional computational cost, a minor modification to pre-existing computational resources
PREDICTION: This revised approach can be more likely to preserve local structures in the noisy point cloud and yield better results for applications where local geometry is essential.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Local Neighborhood Unsupervised Denoising (LNUD)
PROPOSAL: Experiment to divide the noisy point cloud into smaller neighborhoods and treat each neighborhood independently using an autoencoder. The idea is to leverage the fact that different neighborhoods often contain varying levels of noise, and by processing them separately, the network can learn to adapt to local noise distributions. A stitching step can be used to combine the denoised neighborhoods into a final denoised point cloud.
CONTROLS: Supervised PointNet++ as baseline, identical architecture with minor deviations for ablation study
COST: 4000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach may be more effective for handling large-scale point clouds with varying levels of noise, but may face challenges in stitching the denoised neighborhoods while preserving the global geometry of the point cloud.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Point Cloud Denoising with Wasserstein Autoencoders (WAE)
PROPOSAL: Experiment to use a Wasserstein autoencoder to learn a probabilistic mapping from noisy point clouds to clean point clouds. The WAE framework allows for the learning of complex noise distributions and can handle missing points in the noisy point cloud. The reconstruction loss in WAE can be modified to take into account the spatial structure of point clouds by using a metric such as chamfer loss or GMM loss.
CONTROLS: Supervised PointNet++ as baseline, TotalDenoising for ablation study
COST: 3500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach may allow for the learning of complex noise distributions and can potentially handle cases with partial point clouds. However, finding an optimal Wasserstein metric and setting hyperparameters for WAE can be challenging.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Graph-Based Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising
REVISED PROPOSAL: REVISED THEORETICAL ANALYSIS: Derive a theoretical lower bound on the error of graph-based point cloud denoising methods and analyze the regime where these methods are effective. This can involve studying the properties of the graph structure induced by the point cloud, the effect of noise on the graph structure, and how these factors impact the performance of the denoising algorithm.
CONTROLS: Numerical validation using synthetic datasets to benchmark against the theoretical bounds
COST: negligible in terms of GPU-hours (library-based)
PREDICTION: This analysis can provide insight into the fundamental limits of performance of graph-based point cloud denoising methods and highlight the conditions under which they are effective. However, the derivation of sharp results may require approximation due to the complexity of the point cloud geometry.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Evaluation of Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising Methods
PROPOSAL: Experiment to apply the unsupervised point cloud denoising methods (Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising with AutoEncoders, Graph-Based Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising, Local Neighborhood Unsupervised Denoising (LNUD)) to real-world LiDAR scans of urban street scenes and natural image denoising to evaluate their performance on real-world data.
CONTROLS: State-of-the-art supervised point cloud denoising methods as baseline, evaluating with PM3D for point clouds, or MAE in natural image denoising
COST: 5000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This real-world evaluation will provide a more practical assessment of the methods' performance and facilitate their adoption in real-world applications. However, the diversity in real-world point cloud noise distributions and varying quality of LiDAR scans may pose challenges for the methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Point Cloud Denoising using Video Data
PROPOSAL: Experiment to investigate the use of video data, captured by LiDAR scanners installed on moving vehicles, to denoise point clouds. The idea is that sequential point clouds contain temporal consistency that can be leveraged to improve the denoising performance. The proposed method would learn a denoising model that conditions on both the current point cloud and the preceding frames in the video sequence.
CONTROLS: State-of-the-art point cloud denoising methods as baseline, evaluating on LiDAR scans from moving vehicles
COST: 4500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach may leverage the temporal coherence of LiDAR scans to improve denoising performance, but may face challenges such as handling occlusions, varying frame rates, and adapting to scenes with moving objects.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Generalizability and Robustness of Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising Methods
PROPOSAL: Theoretical analysis to study the generalizability and robustness of the proposed unsupervised point cloud denoising methods across different noise distributions, point cloud densities, and domain shifts. This can involve using techniques from differential geometry to quantify the robustness of the denoising methods to changes in the noise distribution and point cloud geometry.
CONTROLS: Numerical validation using synthetic and real-world point clouds
COST: negligible in terms of GPU-hours (library-based)
PREDICTION: This analysis will provide insight into the limitations and potential failure modes of the proposed methods and help to identify potential avenues for future research and improvement. However, deriving sharp results may require approximation due to the complexity of the point cloud geometry and the diversity of real-world noise distributions.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Supervised Point Cloud Denoising via Cyclic Denoising and Upsampling
PROPOSAL: We implement a novel self-supervised denoising framework, denoising cyclic embedding and upsampling  (D-CEU), that takes in a noisy point cloud and progressively refines it by alternating between denoising and upsampling operations. This allows the network to not only denoise but also implicitly learn a better representation of the point cloud structure, leveraging the geometry and spatial coherence of the input.
CONTROLS: We compare D-CEU to major existing self-supervised methods for 3D point cloud denoising, such as TotalDenoising, and also include ablation studies where we retain only one of the cyclic steps (either the denoising or upsampling) to gauge their individual contribution to the results.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect D-CEU to significantly outperform existing self-supervised methods, achieving state-of-the-art results on benchmark noisy point clouds, while remaining competitive to supervised methods. D-CEU's robust performance may be due to the implicit and iterative learning of 3D geometry that is inherent to the cycle denoising and upsampling operation. However, the model may struggle with very high levels of noise or in scenarios with complex and varying scanner noise patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware End-to-End Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: We develop an uncertainty-aware end-to-end framework for point cloud denoising, integrating Bayesian neural networks with a learned noise distribution. This allows the model to not only denoise the input point cloud but also quantify the uncertainty of the denoising process, enabling a robust and informative representation of the denoised geometry.
CONTROLS: We compare our method to D-CEU (proposed in turn 1) and other state-of-the-art point cloud denoising methods, focusing on both quantitative metrics (e.g., PSNR, IoU) and visualizations of the predicted uncertainty map. Additionally, we perform ablation studies to assess the contribution of the learned noise distribution and uncertainty quantification to the overall denoising performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our uncertainty-aware framework to outperform state-of-the-art methods in scenarios with complex noise patterns or high levels of noise, leveraging the learned noise distribution and uncertainty quantification to capture these subtle complexities. However, it may incur a slight computational overhead and potentially lose some spatial coherence compared to vanilla denoising methods.

TITLE: Local Shape Impression and Abstraction for Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel local shape impression and abstraction mechanism that captures point cloud details and abstracts noise-induced irregularities using a local convolutional network followed by an abstraction process. This implants meaningful information from neighboring points to reconstruct missing geometry and dampen the effect of noisy observations, leading to high-quality denoising and surface reconstruction results.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware End-to-End Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: We revise our uncertainty-aware framework to introduce a spatial coherence term to the loss function, encouraging the denoised point cloud to maintain its local geometry and spatial coherence. This modification allows the model to better capture the nuances of the point cloud structure and improves its ability to handle complex noise patterns. We also demonstrate the flexibility of this framework by adapting it to denoise and upsampling tasks simultaneously.
CONTROLS: The controls remain the same as before, with comparisons made to state-of-the-art methods in point cloud denoising and upsampling.
COST: 125 GPU-hours (due to added complexity)
PREDICTION: By incorporating spatial coherence, we expect our framework to outperform its original form and become more competitive with state-of-the-art methods, especially in tasks requiring high spatial fidelity. However, it may be more prone to over-smoothing, and achieving a perfect balance between denoising and maintaining spatial coherence will remain a challenge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge Distillation for Transfer Learning in Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: We propose a knowledge distillation framework to enable efficient transfer learning in point cloud denoising tasks. By leveraging a pre-trained teacher model that has learned rich 3D geometry and local spatial features, we can train a lightweight student network to capture the intricacies of point cloud denoising. This allows the student network to achieve state-of-the-art performance while requiring significantly fewer parameters and computational resources.
CONTROLS: We compare our knowledge distillation framework to the original pre-trained teacher model and other state-of-the-art point cloud denoising methods, evaluating both quantitative metrics (e.g., PSNR, IoU) and model complexity. We also perform ablation studies to examine the effect of varying the student-teacher ratio and distillation temperature on the model's performance.
COST: 75 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our knowledge distillation framework to demonstrate a significant improvement in transfer learning efficiency for point cloud denoising tasks, enabling the deployment of our models on resource-constrained devices. However, the effectiveness of the framework may degrade in scenarios with highly complex noise patterns or lack of diversity in the pre-training dataset.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Local Shape Impression and Abstraction for Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: We revise our local shape impression and abstraction mechanism to incorporate spatial hierarchies in processing the input point clouds. This allows the model to capture subtle and intricate features in the point cloud structure, enabling it to better address challenging scenarios such as those involving small-scale geometry and fine-grained details. We conduct experiments on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of this revised approach.
CONTROLS: The controls remain similar, with performance comparisons made to various state-of-the-art point cloud denoising methods. Additionally, we investigate how well our hierarchical abstraction mechanism adapts to different levels of detail in the input point clouds and how it compares to other spatial abstraction techniques in the field.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging spatial hierarchies, we expect our revised local shape impression and abstraction framework to exhibit even better performance in capturing intricate features and handling challenging scenarios with small-scale geometry and fine-grained details. However, this additional complexity may incur higher computations and potentially sacrifice some interpretability and explainability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Differential Loss Functions for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel differential loss function that captures the spatial distribution of noise in unsupervised point cloud denoising tasks. By minimizing this loss, the model is incentivized to exploit relationships between nearby points and effectively reconstruct the underlying surface structure. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, showing significant improvements over traditional loss functions.
CONTROLS: We compare our differential loss function to other state-of-the-art unsupervised denoising methods, including TotalDenoising and existing self-supervised approaches. We also investigate how well our loss function generalizes across different noise patterns, point cloud densities, and input geometries.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By applying the differential loss function, we expect our approach to more effectively capture noise distributions and leverage local relationships in point clouds, leading to better denoising performance. However, empirically verifying the robustness of our loss function across diverse scenarios may require careful dataset selection and additional validation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Simulated Annealing for Improving the Robustness of Point Cloud Denoising Models
PROPOSAL: We propose incorporating simulated annealing into the training process of point cloud denoising models to improve their robustness against noisy data and various levels of denoising quality. By leveraging the iterative process of simulated annealing, we aim to adaptively adjust the model's parameters in response to noisy observations, leading to better long-term denoising performance and reduced sensitivity to noise.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to standard model training and evaluate its effectiveness on datasets with varying levels of noise and quality. Additionally, we investigate the effect of simulated annealing temperature schedules and model complexity on the resulting models.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By applying simulated annealing, we expect our models to demonstrate improved robustness and adaptation to noisy scenarios. However, the exploration-exploitation trade-off may require careful tuning of annealing parameters, and computational costs might be higher due to the enhanced training process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Edge-Aware Point Cloud Denoising via Guided Filter and Hydrodynamic Simulations
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel edge-aware point cloud denoising approach by combining the guided filter with hydrodynamic simulations to preserve sharp edges and boundaries while removing noisy points. This method exploits the flow of points along edges, using hydrodynamic principles to guide and smooth the denoising process, resulting in robust edge preservation and accurate reconstruction of the underlying surface structure.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to existing edge-preserving denoising techniques and evaluate its effectiveness on various benchmark datasets with complex geometries and sharp features. Ablation studies will be conducted to assess the contribution of the hydrodynamic simulation and guided filter to the overall performance.
COST: 140 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging edge-aware principles, we expect our method to significantly outperform existing approaches in preserving fine details and sharp edges, as well as outperforming general-purpose denoising methods in scenarios with highly detailed and textured objects. However, it may require higher computational costs and careful tuning of parameters for optimal edge preservation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Evaluation and Comparison of State-of-the-Art Point Cloud Denoising Methods on Real-World LiDAR Scans
PROPOSAL: We conduct a comprehensive, large-scale evaluation and comparison of the proposed point cloud denoising methods (experiments 1-7) on a diverse set of real-world LiDAR scan benchmark datasets, including KITTI, Stanford Benchmark, and EuroView. This extensive evaluation provides a systematic comparison of the strengths and weaknesses of each method and allows us to identify areas for further improvement and potential applications in real-world computer vision tasks, such as 3D object detection, SLAM, and scene understanding.
CONTROLS: Our evaluation will compare the performance of each denoising method on multiple benchmark datasets using metrics such as PSNR, IoU, F1-score, and surface roughness. We will also provide runtime comparisons and hardware requirements for each model.
COST: Estimated to be significantly larger than individual experiments (around 500-1000 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: This comprehensive evaluation will provide a definitive answer to the question of which point cloud denoising method is best suited for real-world tasks, and help to identify future research directions. However, our predictions may be limited by the availability and quality of real-world benchmark datasets, and ensure the reliability and reproducibility of our results.

PROPOSAL 4: Knowledge Distillation for Transfer Learning in Point Cloud Denoising
We propose a knowledge distillation framework to enable efficient transfer learning in point cloud denoising tasks. By leveraging a pre-trained teacher model that has learned rich 3D geometry and local spatial features, we can train a lightweight student network to capture the intricacies of point cloud denoising. This allows the student network to achieve state-of-the-art performance while requiring significantly fewer parameters and computational resources.

We introduce a novel differential loss function that captures the spatial distribution of noise in unsupervised point cloud denoising tasks. By minimizing this loss, the model is incentivized to exploit relationships between nearby points and effectively reconstruct the underlying surface structure. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, showing significant improvements over traditional loss functions.

We propose incorporating simulated annealing into the training process of point cloud denoising models to improve their robustness against noisy data and various levels of denoising quality. We introduce a novel edge-aware point cloud denoising approach by combining the guided filter with hydrodynamic simulations to preserve sharp edges and boundaries while removing noisy points. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Denoising without Supervision: Separating Local and Global Denoising Tasks
PROPOSAL: This experiment trains a neural network to decompose the denoising task into local and global components. The local component, trained to predict detailed geometry from a single noisy point cloud, would be optimized using a loss that only considers the geometry of the point cloud itself. This would help handle the ambiguity issue by focusing on the fine-grained details within each point cloud. The global component would be trained to model the consistent patterns across different noisy observations of the same shape or scene. The network would alternate between these two components to optimize its parameters.
CONTROLS: TotalDenoising (total-level loss for comparison) and a normal denoising network (basis for local component)
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to achieve state-of-the-art performance without requiring clean supervision, potentially by tackling the local and global denoising tasks separately. Failure might occur if the local component over-fits to the individual point clouds, losing the general denoising patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Point Cloud Denoising using Optimistic and Pessimistic Decoders
PROPOSAL: This experiment explores the idea of using uncertainty-based decoding to improve denoising performance when only noisy observations are available. Specifically, a network would be trained with two decoders: an optimistic decoder that predicts the most likely clean point cloud given the noisy observation, and a pessimistic decoder that predicts the clean point cloud considering the uncertainty of the denoising process. By using the ambiguity of the denoising problem to its advantage, this approach aims to produce more robust and accurate results.
CONTROLS: The local component from experiment 1, and a baseline method using single decoder
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to yield improved denoising performance by modeling the uncertainty of the denoising problem and leveraging the ambiguity for better prediction. However, the results might be less interpretable than those from experiment 1, and the performance could degrade if the uncertainty modeling is not properly calibrated.

ACTION: REVISE

PROPOSAL: This experiment explores the idea of using uncertainty-based decoding to improve denoising performance when only noisy observations are available. By using the ambiguity of the denoising problem to its advantage, this approach aims to produce more robust and accurate results.
CONTROLS: The local component from experiment 1, the TotalDenoising approach, and a baseline method using single decoder

TITLE: Improving Denoising Performance with Inter-Point Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: This experiment incorporates inter-point contrastive learning into the denoising network to exploit the relationships between points within the point cloud. The network would learn to differentiate between points that are neighbors and points that are not neighbors in the clean point cloud, using the noisy point cloud as input. This could help the network to not only remove noise but also preserve the structural information of the point cloud.
CONTROLS: The local component from experiment 1, the TotalDenoising approach, and a baseline method using single decoder with contrastive loss
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to yield improved denoising performance by capturing the structural relationships between points in the point cloud. However, the results might be less interpretable than those from experiment 1, and the performance could degrade if the contrastive learning is not properly aligned with the denoising task.

TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Scanner Noise Distribution on Denoising Performance
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the impact of different scanner noise distributions on the performance of various denoising algorithms. The experiment would simulate different noise distributions (e.g., Gaussian, Poisson, Salt-and-Pepper) and evaluate the performance of the denoising algorithms on each noise distribution. This could help identify the strengths and weaknesses of different denoising algorithms under different noise conditions.
CONTROLS: The local component from experiment 1, the TotalDenoising approach, and a baseline method using single decoder on 5 different noise distributions
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to provide insights into the robustness of different denoising algorithms under various noise conditions. However, the results might be less generalizable to real-world scenarios if the simulated noise distributions do not accurately represent real-world scanner noise.

PROPOSAL: This experiment focuses on the calibration of uncertainty estimates in point cloud denoising, which is a critical aspect of uncertainty-based decoding approaches. The experiment would evaluate the performance of different calibration methods (e.g., temperature scaling, histogram binning) for uncertainty estimates in point cloud denoising. This could help identify the most effective calibration methods and provide insights into the relative importance of different uncertainty estimates in point cloud denoising.
CONTROLS: The optimistic and pessimistic decoders from experiment 2, and a baseline method using single decoder with no uncertainty estimates
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to provide insights into the calibration of uncertainty estimates in point cloud denoising and identify effective calibration methods. However, the results might be less generalizable to real-world scenarios if the calibration methods are not properly aligned with the specific noise distributions and denoising algorithms being used.

This could provide insights into the practical performance of different denoising algorithms on real-world data.

COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to provide insights into the performance of different denoising algorithms on real-world LiDAR scans. However, the results might be less generalizable to other scenarios if the LiDAR scans from the urban street scene dataset do not accurately represent real-world data.

PROPOSAL: This experiment evaluates the performance of various point cloud denoising algorithms on large-scale LiDAR datasets collected from self-driving vehicles and other applications. This could provide insights into the potential of point cloud denoising for applications where large-scale data is collected.
CONTROLS: The TotalDenoising approach, the local component from experiment 1, and a baseline method using single decoder on 10 large-scale LiDAR datasets
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to provide insights into the potential for scaling point cloud denoising algorithms to handle large-scale LiDAR datasets. However, the results might be limited by the computational resources required to process large-scale datasets, and may require significant fine-tuning and optimization to achieve good performance.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthesizing Multidisciplinary Exam Questions via Guided Document-Centric Question Generation
PROPOSAL: We use a two-stage approach, first leverage a pre-trained language model (e.g., T5) to generate questions from a corpus of documents (e.g., Wikipedia) in various disciplines, and second, apply a discipline-specific discriminator (e.g., a model trained on exams) to filter out weakly related or simplistic questions. We incorporate a difficulty control mechanism, using a combination of language scoring metrics (e.g., grammatical complexity, vocabulary richness) to evaluate question difficulty, and an iterative reinforcement learning process to optimize question generation towards improving difficulty scores. This approach enables us to control difficulty, diversity, and question type, while generating large volumes of high-quality, multidisciplinary exam questions.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: state-of-the-art document-centric question generation model (e.g., T5-ADA); (2) Variants of the proposed model with different discriminator models and reinforcement learning strategies.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement over state-of-the-art baseline by 10% in terms of question diversity, and 15% in difficulty scores; limited ability to generate truly novel, complex questions requiring genuine multi-step reasoning.

Turn 2 of 10.

Now we have one proposal.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Additional Difficulty Evaluation Metric
PROPOSAL: Revise the initial proposal to incorporate a new difficulty evaluation metric, requiring generated questions to be answerable by a human subject matter expert 20% less than twice as fast as what a typical student would take on a standardized exam (accounting for inter-rater variance). This new metric will help evaluate the generated questions for meaningful difficulty, reducing the reliance on language scoring metrics alone. Furthermore, we'll refine our discriminator model to also leverage this new metric when evaluating question quality, thereby further improving the overall quality and difficulty of generated questions.
CONTROLS: Same as before, with additional controlled experiments to analyze the contribution of this new difficulty metric to the overall success of the model.
COST: 400 additional GPU-hours (~1400 total)
PREDICTION: Expected improvement over state-of-the-art baseline by 80% in terms of capturing meaningful difficulty, and 25% in the overall quality of generated questions; remaining challenges in achieving perfect correlation between generated question difficulty and the new metric.

Now we have two proposals.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hybrid Question Synthesis via Cocreation with Human Subject Matter Experts
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel hybrid approach where human subject matter experts (SMEs) co-create questions with our pre-trained language model, T5. SMEs generate preliminary questions and use a shared online platform to debate, brainstorm, and refine the questions. T5 is applied to the refined questions to generate additional variants, while the SMEs evaluate and select the best questions for the dataset. This hybrid approach leverages SME expertise in creating novel, high-quality questions requiring genuine multi-step reasoning, which the model then enhances through iterative refinement.
CONTROLS: Baseline: the original state-of-the-art document-centric question generation model (e.g., T5-ADA); Controlled experiments comparing the performance of SME-only, model-only, and SME-Model hybrid questions.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement over state-of-the-art baseline by 40% in terms of requesting genuine multi-step reasoning, and 30% in question novelty. This approach, however, may face scalability challenges due to the requirement for SME involvement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Discriminator-Aware Question Sorting and Iterative Training
PROPOSAL: Introduce an iterative training framework that leverages our proposed discriminator (Proposal 1) to sort and select the most valuable generated questions, improving their overall quality. We will sort the generated questions based on the discriminator's predictions (e.g., probability of being high-quality) and simultaneously retrain the question generator and discriminator in an alternating fashion. This ensures that the generator learns to produce better questions, while the discriminator becomes more effective in distinguishing between high-quality and low-quality questions. By continuously improving both components, this approach enables us to create more diverse and challenging questions.
CONTROLS: Baseline: the original state-of-the-art document-centric question generation model (e.g., T5-ADA); Controls for varying numbers of sorting iterations and discriminator architectures.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement over state-of-the-art baseline by 50% in terms of question quality and diversity, and 20% in achieving a well-balanced question distribution. However, the iterative process may be sensitive to the choice of initial random seeds and discriminator architectures.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Enhancements to Proposal 3: Discriminator-Aware Question Sorting and Iterative Training
PROPOSAL: Revise Proposal 3 to incorporate domain knowledge and transfer learning between different domains. After sorting and selecting the most valuable generated questions, we will leverage domain-specific pre-trained language models (e.g., domain-adapted BERT) to further refine and tailor the questions to the specific domain. Additionally, we will implement a transfer learning mechanism to enable the model to adapt knowledge and question patterns from one domain to another, facilitating the creation of high-quality questions across multiple domains. This revised approach aims to reduce the manual tuning required for domain adaptation and improve the overall effectiveness of the question synthesis system.
CONTROLS: Same as before, with additional controlled experiments to analyze the impact of domain knowledge and transfer learning on the model's performance across different domains.
COST: 300 additional GPU-hours (~1500 total)
PREDICTION: Expected improvement over state-of-the-art baseline by 75% in terms of question quality and diversity across multiple domains, and 25% in domain adaptation speed; challenges in maintaining model performance across diverse domains and question types.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Multidisciplinary Question Generation via Concept Graph Equivalence Matching
PROPOSAL: Develop an evaluation framework that leverages concept graph equivalence matching to assess the quality and multidisciplinarity of generated questions. We will generate concept graphs for both the synthesized questions and a reference set of questions from recognized exams and research papers. Then, we will compute the weighted matching between the two graphs to evaluate how well the questions capture the relevant concepts and relationships across multiple domains. This approach will provide a nuanced understanding of the generated questions' multidisciplinary nature and help identify areas for improvement.
CONTROLS: Baseline: comparison with a previously validated measure of multidisciplinary question quality (e.g., ranking by human evaluators).
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected agreement of 80% between concept graph matching and human evaluators' rankings; ability to identify complex relationships and nuances between concepts that may not be captured by other evaluation methods. However, this approach may require significant expertise in graph matching and concept graph construction.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Synthesizing Exam Questions across Disciplines
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of using transfer learning to leverage pre-trained question-answering models (e.g., related to a specific domain) as a starting point to synthesize exam questions in other disciplines. We will train a set of domain-specific question-answering models, and then fine-tune them to generate questions in other related domains. The key idea is to exploit the shared knowledge and patterns across domains to improve the efficiency and quality of question synthesis. This approach can help address the data scarcity problem by repurposing existing models for new domains.
CONTROLS: Baseline: a model trained from scratch for question synthesis in a new domain; comparison with domain adaptation techniques like multi-task learning.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement over a model trained from scratch by 30% in terms of question accuracy and diversity; challenges in selecting the optimal pre-trained models and adapting them to the target domain.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Proposal 2: Hybrid Question Synthesis via Cocreation with Human Subject Matter Experts: Considerations for Automatic Coauthoring
PROPOSAL: Revise Proposal 2 to incorporate a framework for automatic coauthoring between human subject matter experts (SMEs) and our pre-trained language model, T5. This would enable the model to participate in the cocreation process more actively, contributing to question generation and refinement, while still maintaining the SME's oversight and feedback. We would investigate different strategies for automating administrative tasks, providing feedback, and facilitating asynchronous collaboration to ensure seamless coauthoring.
CONTROLS: Preliminary evaluation of the proposed coauthoring framework with a small pilot study involving both human and machine-generated questions; comparison with traditional cocreation settings without AI assistance.
COST: 200 additional GPU-hours (~1800 total), mainly for implementation and pilot-study evaluation
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in question diversity and quality by 20-30% due to the active participation of the AI model; challenges in adapting the coauthoring framework to different expertise levels and collaboration styles.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Generate Alternative Question Forms for Enhanced Multidisciplinary Exam Question Datasets
PROPOSAL: Develop an algorithm that learns to generate alternative question forms (e.g., open-ended, multiple-choice, short-answer) for a given question, using a set of pre-existing questions as supervision. This approach can help increase the diversity of the generated datasets and make them more adaptable to various assessment formats. We will leverage masked language modeling and beam search to generate the alternative question forms while encouraging contextual coherence and clarity.
CONTROLS: Baseline: existing approach to question generation using solely one question form; comparison with state-of-the-art question generation models for alternative question forms.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in dataset diversity by 30% and contextual coherence by 25%; potential challenges in ensuring high-quality, non-redundant alternative question forms and evaluating their impact on assessment validity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Synthesized Questions on Multidisciplinary Exam Performance Using a Large-Scale Teacher-Facilitated Online Assessment Platform
PROPOSAL: Collaborate with a large-scale online assessment platform to evaluate the effectiveness of synthesized questions in a real-world multidisciplinary exam setting. We will experimentally embed our synthesized questions into a teacher-facilitated online assessment for students, comparing their performance on the synthesized questions to their performance on the original questions. This controlled experiment will help us assess the extent to which synthesized questions can leverage multidisciplinary knowledge and practices in assessment and instruction.
CONTROLS: Baseline: existing questions and assessment format, with randomized assignment to synthesized or original questions; active student involvement and poll responses to perceived difficulty, contextual relevance, and task complexity of the synthesized questions.
COST: This is not a traditional GPU-compute intensive task. We will need permission, training and setup with a partner organization to get real user data, epidemiologist, interviewer data etc. Thus our time will allocate for groom partnerships, their recoords maintenence them engaged.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Examination of Generalizability of Chain-of-Thought Methods to Multidisciplinary Reasoning.
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of a range of state-of-the-art LLMs trained with and without CoT on a synthetic dataset of 100k multidisciplinary exam questions (25k per subject: physics, biology, medicine, history, philosophy, and psychology). Evaluate LLMs on accuracy, fluency, and difficulty to assess generalizability to diverse domains and real-world testing scenarios.
CONTROLS: Include a diverse set of prominent CoT-based and standard-tuning baselines, with and without subset-specific learning and iterative updates.
COST: 10000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: CoT-based LLMs will show improved performance in fluency and difficulty over standard-tuning approaches in most domains but may struggle in philosophy and psychology due to the inherent subjectivity and nuance of these areas.

Considering that real-world exam questions would be the best to test on, but generating synthetic ones simplifies the task and allows us to generate more diverse examples which we would otherwise not have access to.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Kont Kurulu: A Multi-Disciplinary Question Generator
PROPOSAL: Develop Kont Kurulu, an encoding-decoding model that leverages knowledge graphs to generate questions in diverse domains, including but not limited to mathematics, biology, and physics. The model will encode both the knowledge graph and the question ontology, and then use a process like pointer networks to synthesize new questions. To control difficulty, diversity, and question types, we'll implement a hierarchical framework that separates these aspects into distinct components.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against a set of human-constructed questions using metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, and use natural language inference (NLI) as a baseline for rarity and coherence of the generated questions.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect Kont Kurulu to produce a wide variety of disciplinary questions, with moderate success in controlling difficulty and quality. With further refinements, we predict significant improvements in the rarity, coherence, and relevance of synthesized questions, particularly when generating exam questions for graduate-level science materials.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Mesenger: Cultivating Difficulty in Synthetically Generated Exam Questions
PROPOSAL: Introduce Mesenger, an adversarial framework that challenges the Kont Kurulu model to generate increasingly difficult and diverse questions by iteratively refining and adding structure to the question ontology, query templates, and difficulty heuristics. Mesenger incorporates a novel objective that trains Kont Kurulu to produce harder questions by evaluating how well human examiners can assess and validate them for relevance and reasoning complexity.
CONTROLS: Include Kont Kurulu as a baseline, compare performance against the Mesenger-assisted Kont Kurulu (over various iterations and difficulty settings), and conduct human evaluation on generated questions for diversity and difficulty.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate Mesenger's iterative approach to improve the difficulty, diversity, and quality of Kont Kurulu's generated questions across a wide range of disciplines, though potential lacks include ascertaining Kont Kurulu's knowledge understanding and direct distinctiveness of the difficult synthesized questions as sentiment.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Kont Kurulu: A Multi-Disciplinary Question Generator
PROPOSAL: Modify Kont Kurulu to incorporate an explainable reasoning component that enables transparent analysis of the model's decision-making process when generating questions. This will aid in identifying sources of bias and knowledge limitations, and facilitate the model's adaptability to diverse disciplinary domains. Integrate an attention mechanism to highlight key entities in the knowledge graph and their relations to the generated question, making it easier to track the model's rationale.
CONTROLS: Compare Kont Kurulu's explanation capabilities against a modified Kont Kurulu without an explainable component, and use human evaluations to assess the effectiveness of the attention mechanism.
COST: Additional 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modifications to Kont Kurulu should improve its ability to provide interpretable explanations and highlight relevant knowledge portioning for generating the questions, making it adaptable for diverse disciplines, while aiding inspectors to identify areas where the models' knowledge falls short and are likely to cause synthesized questions to demote in rough complexity. However, it could also overcomplicate question explanations.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Expediter: An Evaluation Framework for Multidisciplinary Exam Question Synthesis
PROPOSAL: Develop Expediter, a comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses the performance and suitability of synthesized questions for various multidisciplinary exams. Expediter will include metrics for question coherence, reasoning difficulty, disciplinary relevance, and diversity and use machine learning approaches (e.g., clustering, topic modeling) to analyze question ontologies and detect categories that the models may not adequately cover, such as history and legal fields, also a crucial consideration for and inherently dynamic nature and custom lifecycle as multidisciplinary exactly relates the meaning.
CONTROLS: Test Expediter with Kont Kurulu and Mesenger outputs, and compare it with the NLI benchmark for assessing rarity and coherence. Analyze the cases where Expediter identifies potential weak points in synthesized questions.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expediter is expected to provide a systematic and structured approach to evaluating the performance and suitability of synthesized questions, highlighting areas of concern such as lack of diversity and discipline relevance, enabling the refinement of Kont Kurulu and other models.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Rigore: A Large-Scale Multidisciplinary Question Dataset
PROPOSAL: Construct Rigore, a comprehensive and diverse dataset of manually curated and expert-evaluated exam questions across a wide range of disciplines, including STEM fields, social sciences, humanities, and more. The dataset will incorporate various question types (e.g., short-answer, multiple-choice, long-answer) with an emphasis on reasoning complexity and context-dependent information seeking to evaluate the real-world usefulness and, range and facets of the newly synthesized queries by assessing model comprehensive capabilities – Strategies in assignment questioning styles tables.

COST: 20,000 GPU-hours

The framework utilizes a joint embedding space for questions, answers, and their attention vectors, enabling models to respond with accurate and coherent answers by accounting for question difficulty, context, and relevant domain knowledge. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Limitations of Post-Training Quantization for Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL:  We will compare the performance of a standard Vision Transformer (ViT) and its 4-bit quantized version, trained using Post-Training Quantization (PTQ), on a set of real-world vision benchmarks. We will use ImageNet-1k and CIFAR-100 for evaluation.
CONTROLS: We will compare with FP32 ViT baseline and evaluate different PTQ methods (linear, fake-quantize, etc.) to identify the optimal approach.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: PTQ will result in significant accuracy drop under 4-bit quantization on both ImageNet-1k and CIFAR-100, with the drop being more pronounced on the larger ImageNet-1k dataset. This will confirm existing knowledge in the field but provide a concrete comparison with the baseline ViT.

Note: We're starting with an experiment that sets a baseline for our later improvements, aiming to understand the performance of PTQ on Vision Transformers in real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Quantization-Aware Training for Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will develop a lightweight Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) approach for ViTs, using a simpler knowledge distillation scheme and a reduced latency training procedure. Our method, called "Lite-QAT", will be compared to the standard QAT approach on the real-world vision benchmarks ImageNet-1k and CIFAR-100.
CONTROLS: We will compare with FP32 ViT baseline, a standard QAT method, and the PTQ approach from proposal 1 to evaluate the trade-offs between training cost, accuracy, and generalization ability.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Lite-QAT will show improved accuracy over PTQ, outperforming the standard PTQ approach on both ImageNet-1k and CIFAR-100. However, the performance might not reach that of the full-precision model, especially on the larger ImageNet-1k dataset. Additionally, we expect Lite-QAT to demonstrate better generalization ability than standard QAT, as it retains the expertise of the pre-trained model while adapting to the quantization regime.

Note: Our goal is to bridge the accuracy gap between PTQ and standard QAT while reducing the computational cost and improving generalization ability, setting the stage for our final solution.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Exploring Efficient Quantization-Aware Training for Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will revise the Lite-QAT approach by adopting a mixed-precision training scheme, where we quantize weights and activations to 4-bit precision, but maintain full precision for the gradients during training. Additionally, we'll employ a dynamic rate pruning mechanism to reduce the computational cost of QAT. Our goal is to strike a balance between training efficiency, accuracy, and generalization ability.
CONTROLS: We will compare the revised Lite-QAT with the original Lite-QAT, as well as with the standard QAT approach, FP32 ViT baseline, and PTQ.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised Lite-QAT will demonstrate improved training efficiency (in terms of cost and speed) while retaining accuracy and generalization ability. Specifically, we expect it to reduce the training time by 30-40% compared to the original Lite-QAT and remain competitive with standard QAT in terms of accuracy. However, the reduced precision of gradients might lead to instability issues in certain cases, necessitating careful tuning of hyperparameters.

Note: By revising Lite-QAT, we aim to further address the limitations of QAT for Vision Transformers, focusing on efficient training schemes that can handle larger-scale models and datasets.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Exploring Efficient Quantization-Aware Training for Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will revise the Lite-QAT approach by adopting a mixed-precision training scheme, where we quantize weights and activations to 4-bit precision, but maintain full precision for the gradients during training. Additionally, we'll employ a dynamic rate pruning mechanism to reduce the computational cost of QAT. Our goal is to strike a balance between training efficiency, accuracy, and generalization ability.
CONTROLS: We will compare the revised Lite-QAT with the original Lite-QAT, as well as with the standard QAT approach, FP32 ViT baseline, and PTQ.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised Lite-QAT will demonstrate improved training efficiency (in terms of cost and speed) while retaining accuracy and generalization ability. Specifically, we expect it to reduce the training time by 30-40% compared to the original Lite-QAT and remain competitive with standard QAT in terms of accuracy. However, the reduced precision of gradients might lead to instability issues in certain cases, necessitating careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Weight Initialization in Low-Bit Quantization
PROPOSAL: We will study the impact of different weight initialization schemes on the performance of Vision Transformers when quantized to 4-bit precision using the revised Lite-QAT approach. Specifically, we'll compare the performance with various initialization methods, such as random, Kaiming, and He, to understand whether these schemes can mitigate the effects of low-bit quantization.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with the revised Lite-QAT baseline and the full-precision ViT model.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that a well-designed weight initialization scheme, such as Kaiming or He, can improve the accuracy of the low-bit quantized Vision Transformer by about 5-10% compared to random initialization, bridging the gap between the baseline and the full-precision model. However, the optimal initialization scheme might depend on the specific dataset and model architecture used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Wise Pruning and Knowledge Distillation for Low-Bit Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel layer-wise pruning and knowledge distillation approach to further reduce the computational cost of low-bit quantized Vision Transformers. The method will involve pruning redundant connections and knowledge distillation between layers, using the full-precision model as a teacher. We'll evaluate the performance of this approach on a range of vision tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with the revised Lite-QAT baseline, standard QAT, and the full-precision ViT model.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the layer-wise pruning and knowledge distillation approach will achieve a significant reduction in computational cost (around 50-60% FLOPs reduction) while maintaining high accuracy (around 95-98% of the full-precision model's accuracy) on vision tasks. However, the distillation process might be sensitive to the choice of teacher model and pruning ratio, requiring careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Activation Quantization on Low-Bit Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of quantizing activations on the performance of low-bit Vision Transformers. Specifically, we'll experiment with different activation quantization schemes, such as fixed-point, ternary, and full-precision, to compare their impact on accuracy and computational cost.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with the revised Lite-QAT baseline, layer-wise pruning, and other quantization approaches.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that quantizing activations will have a non-negligible impact on the accuracy of low-bit Vision Transformers. Fixed-point quantization might lead to a small drop in accuracy (around 1-3%), while ternary quantization could result in a larger drop (around 5-10%). Full-precision activations, on the other hand, will likely maintain the highest accuracy. However, the optimal activation quantization scheme will depend on the specific model architecture and dataset used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Unified Quantization Schemes for Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will propose a unified quantization framework that integrates the techniques explored in our previous experiments, including efficient quantization-aware training, layer-wise pruning, and activation quantization. Our goal is to develop a flexible and scalable framework that can adapt to different quantization schemes, model architectures, and datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with the state-of-the-art quantization methods and evaluate the usability of our framework on various vision tasks.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our unified quantization framework will outperform state-of-the-art quantization methods in terms of accuracy, computational cost, and flexibility. Specifically, we anticipate a 10-20% improvement in accuracy and a 30-50% reduction in computational cost compared to existing methods. However, the performance of our framework will depend on the specific configuration and tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantization-Aware Efficient Transformers with Adapted Training
PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel adaptive training framework for quantization-aware efficient transformers, which dynamically adjusts the training process based on the quantization scheme used. Our method will utilize an unstable learning mechanism that helps stabilize the training process during efficient training.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with the unified quantization framework, layer-wise pruning, and other state-of-the-art quantization methods.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our adaptive training framework will significantly reduce the training instability and improve the convergence of efficient transformers during quantization-aware training. This will lead to an overall improvement in accuracy and computational efficiency. Specifically, we anticipate a 10-20% improvement in accuracy and a 20-30% reduction in computational cost compared to existing methods. However, the performance of our framework will depend on the specific configuration and tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation and Benchmarking of Quantization Techniques for Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will comprehensively evaluate and benchmark the performance of various quantization techniques explored in our previous experiments on a wide range of vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, segmentation, and generation. We will also provide a systematic comparison with state-of-the-art methods and discuss the limitations and future directions of each technique.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with the unified quantization framework, layer-wise pruning, and other state-of-the-art quantization methods on a variety of vision tasks and datasets.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our comprehensive evaluation will provide a thorough understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different quantization techniques for Vision Transformers and identify the most promising approaches for future research.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Low-Bit Vision Transformer Study: Investigating Challenges and Opportunities
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comparative analysis of PTQ and QAT methods on a range of ViT backbones with 4-bit precision, focusing on the 16/32/64 parameter states. Use a large-scale real-world dataset such as ImageNet or ADE20K for evaluation and analyze the gap in performance between PTQ and QAT methods across different weight and activation quantization levels.
CONTROLS: Comparative evaluations with standard QAT and PTQ baselines, including experiments on 8-bit precision for a sanity check.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: QAT will generally outperform PTQ at 4-bit precision, but the gap will narrow and may even favor PTQ for certain ViT architectures or subsets of the dataset. Challenges in QAT's higher computational cost, training instability, and domain specificity may emerge in deeper or more complex ViT variants.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Quantization Training for Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Implement a low-compute QAT variant, dubbed 'Efficient QAT' (EQAT), that incorporates knowledge distillation between the full-precision student and a light teacher (50% weight pruning) instead of the typical external teacher. This will reduce computational overhead while evaluating how teacher-student knowledge transfer affects ViT representations in low-bit scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare EQAT with full QAT and PTQ, as well as a baseline where EQAT's light teacher is replaced with a naive setting where the light teacher has random weights for comparison.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Efficiency gains from EQAT will outweigh its accuracy penalty on ImageNet, potentially topping PTQ's accuracy on 4-bit precision ViTs. However, it may struggle to generalize as effectively on diverse Vision tasks as a full-precision QAT trained for an equivalent amount of time.

ACTION: REVISE

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Quantization-Aware Pruning and Quantization
PROPOSAL: Examine the intersection of knowledge distillation and knowledge pruning by using a combination of model pruning and quantization on ViTs. Starting with a full-precision model, apply weight pruning with a fixed threshold (e.g., 90%) to reduce the model's parameter count, and then migrate this pruned structure to a low-precision format (e.g., 4-bit) and retrain. This can help alleviate the challenges of low-precision training while also leveraging the benefits of knowledge pruning.
CONTROLS: Compare with pure pruning, pure quantization, EQAT, and an ablation study where only quantization is applied after pruning, but without the retraining step.
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed approach will achieve a better trade-off between model size and performance compared to pure pruning or quantization methods. However, it may still struggle to reach the accuracy of EQAT in certain scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Model Transferability after Quantization
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the low-bit precision models obtained through PTQ, EQAT, and the revised Quantization-Aware Pruning and Quantization method (QAPQ) transfer to other vision tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation, using architectures like DETR and Swin-Transformer.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the low-bit precision models with the full-precision models on the downstream tasks, and evaluate their robustness to dataset shifts and domain adaptation.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: QAPQ will demonstrate better transferability compared to PTQ and EQAT, but still may fall short of the full-precision models. The ablation study will reveal the relative contributions of pruning, quantization, and retraining to the model's ability to adapt to new tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Efficient Quantization Training for Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Introduce a progressive distillation framework to EQAT, where the teacher-student distillation process is gradually relaxed as the training progresses. This allows the model to initially learn from the teacher, but eventually learn to generalize on its own, which may improve its transferability and robustness to downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the progressive distillation variant of EQAT with the original EQAT and PTQ on the downstream tasks evaluated in proposal 4.
COST: 450 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Progressive distillation will enhance EQAT's ability to transfer knowledge to other tasks, and may rival the performance of QAPQ on certain downstream tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Understanding the Impact of Quantization on Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of quantization on the representation learning capability of ViTs by analyzing the feature distributions and layer-wise activations of models trained with PTQ, EQAT, and QAPQ. This involves using dimensionality reduction techniques and visualization methods to compare the characteristics of the representations learned by low-bit precision models with those of their full-precision counterparts.
CONTROLS: Compare the feature distributions and layer-wise activations of the low-bit precision models with those of the full-precision model on a range of image classification datasets.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal that EQAT and QAPQ tend to preserve more features and activation patterns than PTQ, which is consistent with their superior accuracy on downstream tasks. However, the representation learning capability of the low-bit precision models may still be compromised compared to their full-precision counterparts.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Towards Understanding the Impact of Quantization on Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Refine the analysis to focus on the impact of quantization on the attention mechanism in ViTs, which is critical for their representation learning capability. Examine how the low-bit precision models learn to attend to different regions and objects in the input images, and compare the attention patterns with those of the full-precision model.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the attention patterns of the low-bit precision models using techniques such as attention visualization and attention-based feature importance.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal that EQAT and QAPQ tend to preserve more accurate attention patterns than PTQ, but still may have compromised attention capabilities compared to the full-precision model. This understanding will provide valuable insights for future research on quantization-aware optimization and ViT architecture design.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Transferability of General-Purpose LLMs to Go
PROPOSAL: We will start by testing the current state-of-the-art general-purpose LLMs (e.g., OpenAI-o1, DeepSeek-R1, T5, etc.) on the Go-related tasks in the Goeda dataset, which includes both the GoGame database, used for next-move prediction and the GoCommentary dataset, for game commentary generation. 
CONTROLS: We will contrast the results of these models with the Go-specific models (AlphaGo, AlphaZero) and other language models fine-tuned on Go and other specialized domains. 
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Current general-purpose LLMs are likely to fail to match even beginner-level Go players, with poor performance on next-move prediction and game commentary tasks. However, the extent of the gap between human experts and current LLMs may be informative about the potential effectiveness of specialized domain knowledge integration methods.

Will follow up with more proposals that analyze the structural aspects of this huge knowledge gap and see if we can derive potential methods to bridge it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Linguistic and Structural Differences between General-Purpose and Specialized LLMs
PROPOSAL: To understand the underlying reasons for the knowledge gap between general-purpose and specialized LLMs, we will analyze the linguistic and structural differences between models fine-tuned on Go and other specialized domains versus general-purpose models like OpenAI-o1. This will be done using techniques such as spectral analysis, attention-based representation learning, and coherence-based evaluation methods.
CONTROLS: We will examine the performance of general-purpose models fine-tuned on Go using the same training dataset used for AlphaGo, to baseline the effect of dataset and fine-tuning strategy on model performance.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find significant differences in the linguistic patterns, syntax, and attention mechanisms used by general-purpose and domain-specialized LLMs, indicating that integration of specialized domain knowledge will require changes beyond just fine-tuning or pre-training on domain-specific data.

Will explore methods for adapting linguistic and structural differences next.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Hybrid Learning Framework for Integrating Specialized Domain Knowledge
PROPOSAL: We will design a hybrid learning framework that combines self-supervised learning with domain-specific adversarial training, followed by fine-tuning with an auxiliary task of generating game commentary for Go. This framework aims to learn a more nuanced representation of the domain and leverage its structural characteristics to improve next-move prediction performance.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate our framework on the Goeda dataset, comparing its performance to that of baselines such as self-supervised learning alone, fine-tuning on domain-specific data, and models trained using standard teacher-student distillation methods.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our framework is expected to significantly outperform existing methods and improve upon general-purpose LLMs in Go-related tasks, with potential for adaptations to other specialized domains.

Will investigate the auxiliary task's contribution next, considering multimodal learning methods.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Developing a Hybrid Learning Framework for Integrating Specialized Domain Knowledge with Multimodal Auxiliary Tasks
PROPOSAL: Building upon the success of the hybrid learning framework proposed in turn 3, we will expand the auxiliary task generation to incorporate multimodal modalities such as Go board images and videos, as well as player-generated audio and text data. This is expected to provide the model with richer structural and contextual information, further bridging the gap between general-purpose LLMs and specialized domains like Go.
CONTROLS: We will compare our multimodal framework to the previous version and single-modal baselines to assess the effectiveness of incorporating visual, audio, and text information in improving next-move prediction and game commentary generation.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Multimodal learning is expected to capture the complex spatial and temporal patterns in Go, exceeding the performance of both the hybrid learning framework and general-purpose LLMs in these tasks.

Given the promising results of multimodal learning, we can proceed to explore adaptive architectures and knowledge representations.

TITLE: Developing a Hybrid Learning Framework for Integrating Specialized Domain Knowledge with Multimodal Auxiliary Tasks

This is expected to provide the model with richer structural and contextual information, further bridging the gap between general-purpose LLMs and specialized domains like Go.
CONTROLS: We will compare our multimodal framework to the previous version and single-modal baselines to assess the effectiveness of incorporating visual, audio, and text information in improving next-move prediction and game commentary generation.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Multimodal learning is expected to capture the complex spatial and temporal patterns in Go, exceeding the performance of both the hybrid learning framework and general-purpose LLMs in these tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Graph-Based Architectures for Go Expertise
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the graph-like structure of Go board representations, we will experiment with adaptive graph-based architectures that learn to represent and reason about the game state in a more abstract and domain-specific manner. This will allow the model to capture intricate spatial relationships and long-range dependencies in the game, pushing the boundaries of current LLMs in Go.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed adaptive graph architectures to standard Transformers and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on Go-related tasks, evaluating the effect of the graph structure and adaptivity on the model's performance.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive graph-based architecture is expected to establish state-of-the-art performance in Go-related tasks, especially in more complex scenarios such as longer games and more intricate board positions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Human-Model Collaboration for Enhanced Go Expertise
PROPOSAL: Building upon the success of our previous proposals, we will design and implement a human-model collaboration framework for Go, where a human player provides input and feedback to guide the model's decision-making process. This will allow the model to learn from expert players and adapt to the unique nuances and context of the game.
CONTROLS: We will compare our collaborative framework to existing models that receive no human input, as well as to models that receive generic feedback, to assess the effectiveness of human involvement in enhancing the model's performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Human-model collaboration is expected to significantly improve the model's performance in Go-related tasks, especially in complex scenarios, as it leverages the strengths of both human expertise and machine learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Domain-Specific Terminology on LLMs' Reasoning Capabilities
PROPOSAL: We will systematically evaluate the impact of incorporating domain-specific terminology (e.g., Go terms, strategies, and concepts) into the training data of our adaptive graph-based architecture, to assess whether this can enhance the model's reasoning and generalization abilities in Go-related tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the model with and without domain-specific terminology, as well as with different levels of terminology detail, to quantify the effect of incorporating these terms.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating domain-specific terminology is expected to significantly improve the model's performance in Go-related tasks, as it allows the model to better understand and reason about the game's unique concepts and strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying the Generalizability of Go Expertise to Other Board Games
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the transferability of the knowledge and reasoning capabilities acquired by our model in Go to other board games, such as Chess, Shogi, and Othello. This will involve adapting our adaptive graph-based architecture to these new domains and evaluating its performance on board game-specific tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our model to that of specialized board game models and general-purpose LLMs on these tasks, to assess the extent to which Go expertise can be transferred to other board games.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our model is expected to exhibit some level of generalizability to other board games, as it has learned to capture abstract game-theoretic principles and board-level relationships that are common to many board games.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalability and Interpretability Study of LLMs for Go Expertise
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an extensive scalability and interpretability study of our model, assessing its ability to handle large game boards, long game histories, and real-time input, as well as its interpretability through techniques such as attention visualization and saliency maps.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance and interpretability of our model with that of previous state-of-the-art models for Go, as well as with simpler models such as random forests and decision trees, to assess the trade-offs between complexity and performance.
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our model is expected to demonstrate high scalability and interpretability, handling large game boards and game histories, and providing clear and actionable insights into its decision-making process, although potential limitations may arise from its reliance on rich auxiliary tasks and multilayered graph architectures.

propositions.controles: We will compare the performance of our model to that of specialized board game models and general-purpose LLMs on these tasks, to assess the extent to which Go expertise can be transferred to other board games.
