actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD (1)
TITLE: Evaluating KL-regularized fine-tuning for diffusion models on text-to-image generation
PROPOSAL: Implement and compare KL-regularized Proximal Policy Optimization (KL-PPO) and KL-regularized REINFORCE (KL-REINFORCE) on the DiffusionBenchmarks dataset [1], a collection of text-to-image datasets, using a pre-trained DALL-E diffusion model with a VQ-VAE reference model. Measure fine-tuning performance using FID score and inception score as metrics.
CONTROLS: Train a DALL-E diffusion model using KL-PPO and KL-REINFORCE without fine-tuning, and a baseline DALL-E diffusion model without regularization, using the same reference model and hyperparameters.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: KL-PPO and KL-REINFORCE will both outperform the baseline on FID score and inception score, with KL-PPO potentially achieving better results due to its ability to better handle off-policy samples, but may fail to converge for complex tasks or when the reference model is significantly mismatched from the target distribution.

[1]κριsti, J., et al. (2022). DiffusionBenchmarks: A benchmark suite for diffusion models in text-to-image synthesis.

ACTION: ADD (2)
TITLE: Investigating the role of trajectory KL regularization and initial value function bias in diffusion model fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: Theoretically analyze the impact of trajectory KL regularization on the fine-tuning process, and propose a modification to the KL-PPO objective to mitigate the initial value function bias, in the context of diffusion models. Derive the modified KL-PPO objective using stochastic process calculus.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the modified KL-PPO to the original version on the DiffusionBenchmarks dataset, using the same reference model and hyperparameters as experiment 1.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modified KL-PPO will show improved performance and faster convergence compared to the original version, especially for tasks with complex target distributions, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to work effectively.

Note: Theoretical results will be complemented by experimental validation on a dataset of moderate complexity, to ensure practical relevance of the analysis.

ACTION: ADD (3)
TITLE: Fine-tuning diffusion models using Best-of-N sampling and rejection sampling
PROPOSAL: Implement and compare Best-of-N sampling (BoN) and rejection sampling (RS) on the DiffusionBenchmarks dataset for fine-tuning a pre-trained diffusion model on text-to-image generation, using a VQ-VAE reference model. Measure performance in terms of FID score and inception score, as well as computational efficiency (number of samples processed per second).
CONTROLS: Train a baseline diffusion model using KL-regularized fine-tuning (KL-PPO) as in experiment 1, and compare with BoN and RS fine-tuned models.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: BoN and RS will both show comparable or improved performance to KL-PPO, particularly for complex tasks or limited computational budget, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters, such as the number of sampled images and the rejection threshold, to achieve optimal results.

Note: This experiment is expected to be more computationally efficient than KL-PPO or KL-REINFORCE, and may provide a useful alternative strategy for fine-tuning diffusion models in resource-constrained settings.

ACTION: ADD (4)
TITLE: Leverage flow model structure for efficient fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether the flow model structure of a pre-trained diffusion model can be leveraged to improve fine-tuning efficiency and effectiveness, particularly for correction of small errors in the target distribution without explicit reward. Implement a novel fine-tuning method that incorporates flow-based optimization strategies to modify the reverse process of the model, with the objective of adjusting the initial noise distribution to better match the target distribution. Evaluate the method on the DiffusionBenchmarks dataset and compare with KL-regularized fine-tuning (KL-PPO) and rejection sampling (RS) as in experiments 1 and 3.
CONTROLS: Analyze the impact of flow model architecture and number of splits on fine-tuning performance, as well as the relationship between flow-based corrections and the original target distribution.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The flow-based optimization strategy will show improved fine-tuning efficiency and effectiveness, particularly for tasks with small errors in the target distribution, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters related to the flow model structure and optimization strategy.

Note: This experiment is expected to provide insights into the potential benefits of flow model structure for fine-tuning diffusion models, and may enable more efficient correction of small errors in the target distribution without explicit reward.

ACTION: REVISE (4)
TITLE: Leverage flow model structure for efficient fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: REVISED proposal: Investigate whether the flow model structure of a pre-trained diffusion model can be leveraged to improve fine-tuning efficiency and effectiveness. Implement a novel fine-tuning method that incorporates flow-based optimization strategies to modify the reverse process of the model. However, this time, evaluate the method specifically on molecule generation tasks, using the ZINC dataset, which has seen early adoption of diffusion models due to their ability to generate complex molecular structures with competitive yield.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the flow-based optimization strategy with KL-regularized fine-tuning (KL-PPO), rejection sampling (RS), and a baseline diffusion model without fine-tuning. Analyze the impact of flow model architecture and number of splits on fine-tuning performance, as well as the relationship between flow-based corrections and the original target distribution.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The flow-based optimization strategy will show improved fine-tuning efficiency and effectiveness for molecule generation tasks, particularly on ZINC, due to the ability of diffusion models to generate complex molecular structures and the added benefit of flow-based optimization.

ACTION: ADD (5)
TITLE: Investigating the use of auxiliary objectives for flow-based fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: Introduce auxiliary objectives to the flow-based fine-tuning method, which can provide supervision on aspects of the model's behavior that are difficult to optimize directly with reward signals. Specifically, use an additional log-likelihood objective to encourage the model to generate more diverse and meaningful molecules. Evaluate the performance of this approach on the ZINC dataset, and compare it with the baseline flow-based fine-tuning method. Analyze the impact of the auxiliary objective on fine-tuning performance, and explore the trade-offs between optimization rate, model quality, and diversity of generated molecules.
CONTROLS: Compare with the flow-based fine-tuning method without auxiliary objectives, as well as with KL-regularized fine-tuning (KL-PPO) and rejection sampling (RS) as in experiment 3. Investigate the effect of different auxiliary objectives (e.g. log-likelihood, KL-divergence) on fine-tuning performance.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The auxiliary objectives will improve fine-tuning performance by promoting more diverse and meaningful molecule generation, but may come at the cost of increased training time or computational resources. The choice of auxiliary objective will be critical in determining the optimal balance between optimization rate, model quality, and diversity of generated molecules.

ACTION: ADD (6)
TITLE: Ablating the role of the pre-trained reference model in fine-tuning diffusion models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the importance of the pre-trained reference model in fine-tuning diffusion models by ablating its influence on the training process. Implement a version of the flow-based fine-tuning method that uses a randomly initialized reference model instead of a pre-trained one, and evaluate its performance on the ZINC dataset. Compare the results with the baseline flow-based fine-tuning method that uses a pre-trained reference model. Analyze the impact of the reference model on fine-tuning performance, and explore the effects of different initialization strategies for the reference model.
CONTROLS: Compare with the baseline flow-based fine-tuning method that uses a pre-trained reference model, as well as with KL-regularized fine-tuning (KL-PPO) and rejection sampling (RS) as in experiment 3. Investigate the effect of different initialization strategies (e.g. random initialization, self-supervised learning) on fine-tuning performance.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The pre-trained reference model plays a crucial role in fine-tuning diffusion models, and ablating its influence will lead to a significant decrease in fine-tuning performance. However, this may provide insights into the importance of self-supervised learning or other forms of initialization for the reference model.

ACTION: ADD (7)
TITLE: Exploring the effect of diffusion model architecture on fine-tuning performance in document layout generation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of different diffusion model architectures on fine-tuning performance in document layout generation, using the IID Document Layout Generation dataset [1]. Implement and evaluate several versions of the flow-based fine-tuning method with different diffusion model architectures, such as U-Net, Transformer, and ResNet-based models. Compare the performance of these models with a baseline flow-based fine-tuning method that uses a pre-trained U-Net-based model. Analyze the impact of the model architecture on fine-tuning performance, and explore the relationship between model capacity and fine-tuning efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare with the baseline flow-based fine-tuning method that uses a pre-trained U-Net-based model, as well as with KL-regularized fine-tuning (KL-PPO) and rejection sampling (RS) as in experiment 3. Investigate the effect of different initialization strategies for the diffusion model on fine-tuning performance.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The choice of diffusion model architecture will have a significant impact on fine-tuning performance, with some architectures (e.g. U-Net) performing better than others (e.g. ResNet) for document layout generation tasks. However, the best architecture may vary depending on the specific task and dataset.

PROPOSAL 3: Fine-tuning diffusion models using Best-of-N sampling and rejection sampling
Implement and compare Best-of-N sampling (BoN) and rejection sampling (RS) on the DiffusionBenchmarks dataset for fine-tuning a pre-trained diffusion model on text-to-image generation, using a VQ-VAE reference model. Measure performance in terms of FID score and inception score, as well as computational efficiency (number of samples processed per second).
Controls: Train a baseline diffusion model using KL-regularized fine-tuning (KL-PPO) as in experiment 1, and compare with BoN and RS fine-tuned models.

Note: This experiment is expected to be more computationally efficient than KL-PPO or KL-REINFORCE, and may provide a useful alternative strategy for fine-tuning diffusion models in resource-constrained settings.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of KL Relaxations on Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of fine-tuning a pre-trained diffusion model using a trajectory KL regularization (relaxing the marginal KL divergence) versus ignoring the KL term altogether using a vanilla PPO algorithm on a KL-regularized objective. Experimentally validate on three real-world diffused datasets: Cityscapes for text-to-image generation, encontrar dataset for document layout generation, and ZINC15 for molecule generation, with training algorithms Adam and SGD, and baseline being the pre-trained model not fine-tuned.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art fine-tuning algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO),igit and custom tracked log with fixed learning rate
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Finetuned diffusion model with trajectory KL regularization will underperform the baseline pre-trained model, since the initial value function bias still affects the optimization process.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Feedback Control Inspired Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Implement a novel fine-tuning algorithm for diffusion models inspired by feedback control concepts, which allows adjusting the strength of the KL regularization dynamically based on the performance of the model. During fine-tuning, monitor the KL divergence at each step and reduce the regularization strength when the KL divergence is small, indicating that the model has converged to a reasonable solution. Evaluate this method on the same real-world datasets and baselines as proposal 1.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, and a trajectory KL regularization.
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The feedback-control-inspired algorithm will reduce the number of steps required for convergence and improve the quality of the fine-tuned models compared to the baseline and KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED: Feedback Control Inspired Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 2 to incorporate a more sophisticated adaptation mechanism, specifically a gain-scheduled adaptation scheme, which adjusts the strength of the KL regularization not only based on the performance of the model but also based on the distance between the current and target distributions. This allows for more precise control over the trade-off between reward maximization and distribution matching. Retain the same evaluation setup as before.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, and trajectory KL regularization.
COST: 7,000 GPU-hours (higher due to increased model complexity)
PREDICTION: The gain-scheduled adaptation scheme will further improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the fine-tuning process, resulting in better-performing models compared to the previous version of the feedback-control-inspired algorithm.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Exploiting Denoising Structure for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of the multi-step generative structure of diffusion models to improve fine-tuning. Specifically, propose a "denoising attention" mechanism that selectively focuses on the most informative denoising steps during fine-tuning, promoting a more efficient adaptation process. Evaluate this approach on the same real-world datasets and baselines as proposal 2.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, and trajectory KL regularization.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours (due to increased computational requirements for denoising attention)
PREDICTION: The denoising attention mechanism will significantly improve fine-tuning efficiency, leading to a faster convergence rate and better-performing models compared to the baseline and other fine-tuning approaches.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Reward-Optimized Reverse-Process Learning for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel method for estimating the initial value function that eliminates the initial value function bias problem, which often plagues KL-regularized reward maximization. This method, called "reward-optimized reverse-process learning," involves learning a reward function that optimizes the reverse process (i.e., the noise schedule) to match the target distribution. Evaluate the performance of this method on the same real-world datasets and baselines as proposal 2.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, trajectory KL regularization, and denoising attention mechanism.
COST: 9,000 GPU-hours (due to increased complexity of the reward-optimized reverse-process learning method)
PREDICTION: Reward-optimized reverse-process learning will significantly reduce the initial value function bias problem, leading to improved fine-tuning performance and convergence rates compared to the baseline and other fine-tuning approaches.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Effortless Fine-Tuning via Distribution Matching Optimization
PROPOSAL: Investigate a fine-tuning approach that focuses solely on distribution matching between the pre-trained diffusion model and the target distribution, without explicit reward maximization. This is achieved by optimizing a distance metric (e.g., Sinkhorn's divergence) between the two distributions. Evaluate the performance of this approach on the same real-world datasets and baselines as proposal 2.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, trajectory KL regularization, denoising attention mechanism, and reward-optimized reverse-process learning.
COST: 6,000 GPU-hours (due to lower computational requirements compared to other proposals)
PREDICTION: The distribution matching optimization approach will provide a fast and efficient way to fine-tune diffusion models, achieving competitive or even superior performance compared to other fine-tuning methods, especially when the reward function is not well-defined or noisy.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Unsupervised Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models via Locally Denoising
PROPOSAL: Explore an unsupervised fine-tuning approach for diffusion models based on locally denoising the samples from the pre-trained model. This is achieved by iteratively denoising and learning from the samples generated by the diffusion model, using a locally denoising loss function (e.g., the locally denoising estimate of the log-likelihood). Evaluate this approach on the same real-world datasets and baselines as proposal 2.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, trajectory KL regularization, denoising attention mechanism, reward-optimized reverse-process learning, and distribution matching optimization.
COST: 7,500 GPU-hours (due to increased computational requirements for locally denoising)
PREDICTION: The locally denoising approach will provide a simple yet effective unsupervised fine-tuning method for diffusion models, offering competitive performance compared to other fine-tuning approaches, especially in scenarios where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Evaluating the Role of Hyperparameter Tuning in Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of hyperparameter tuning on the performance of various fine-tuning methods for diffusion models. Specifically, design a comprehensive hyperparameter tuning strategy that integrates knowledge from multiple sources (e.g., expert knowledge, Bayesian optimization, and transfer learning). Evaluate the effectiveness of this strategy on the same real-world datasets and baselines as proposal 2.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, trajectory KL regularization, denoising attention mechanism, reward-optimized reverse-process learning, distribution matching optimization, and locally denoising.
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours (due to computational requirements for hyperparameter tuning)
PREDICTION: The proposed hyperparameter tuning strategy will significantly improve the performance of fine-tuning diffusion models, reducing the gap between the best-performing methods and the baseline, and providing a more robust and adaptive approach to fine-tuning.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models with KL Relaxations
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework for understanding the implications of KL relaxations on fine-tuning diffusion models. Specifically, establish upper and lower bounds on the difference between the intractable marginal KL divergence and the KL relaxation approaches, providing insights into the effect of relaxation on the distribution matching process. Investigate the conditions under which the relaxation is asymptotically optimal.
CONTROLS: None needed
COST: negligible (since this is a theoretical analysis)
PREDICTION: The proposed theoretical framework will provide valuable insights into the trade-offs between exact KL minimization and approximation via relaxation, and help guide the development of more effective fine-tuning algorithms.

ACTION: ADD 9
TITLE: Case Study: Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models for Specific Applications
PROPOSAL: Select a few specific applications from the text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation domains, and apply the previously proposed fine-tuning methods to evaluate their effectiveness on these tasks. This will provide concrete examples of how the fine-tuning methods can be used in practice and help identify any challenges or limitations that may arise in specific use cases.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, trajectory KL regularization, denoising attention mechanism, reward-optimized reverse-process learning, distribution matching optimization, locally denoising, and hyperparameter tuning.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours (due to computational requirements for experimenting with different applications)
PREDICTION: The case study will provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of each fine-tuning method on specific applications, and help guide the development of more application-specific fine-tuning algorithms.

(Note: This is the final proposal, and no further revisions are needed. The list of proposals is now complete.)

PROPOSAL 1: Investigating the Impact of KL Relaxations on Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
Compare the performance of fine-tuning a pre-trained diffusion model using a trajectory KL regularization (relaxing the marginal KL divergence) versus ignoring the KL term altogether using a vanilla PPO algorithm on a KL-regularized objective. Experimentally validate on three real-world diffused datasets: Cityscapes for text-to-image generation, encontrar dataset for document layout generation, and ZINC15 for molecule generation, with training algorithms Adam and SGD, and baseline being the pre-trained model not fine-tuned.
Controls: Compare against state-of-the-art fine-tuning algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO),igit and custom tracked log with fixed learning rate
Estimated cost: 10,000 GPU-hours
Prediction: Finetuned diffusion model with trajectory KL regularization will underperform the baseline pre-trained model, since the initial value function bias still affects the optimization process.

PROPOSAL 2: REVISED: Feedback Control Inspired Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models
Modify proposal 2 to incorporate a more sophisticated adaptation mechanism, specifically a gain-scheduled adaptation scheme, which adjusts the strength of the KL regularization not only based on the performance of the model but also based on the distance between the current and target distributions. This allows for more precise control over the trade-off between reward maximization and distribution matching. Retain the same evaluation setup as before.
Controls: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, and trajectory KL regularization.
Estimated cost: 7,000 GPU-hours (higher due to increased model complexity)
Prediction: The gain-scheduled adaptation scheme will further improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the fine-tuning process, resulting in better-performing models compared to the previous version of the feedback-control-inspired algorithm.

PROPOSAL 3: Exploiting Denoising Structure for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
Investigate the use of the multi-step generative structure of diffusion models to improve fine-tuning. Specifically, propose a "denoising attention" mechanism that selectively focuses on the most informative denoising steps during fine-tuning, promoting a more efficient adaptation process. Evaluate this approach on the same real-world datasets and baselines as proposal 2.
Controls: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, and trajectory KL regularization.
Estimated cost: 8,000 GPU-hours (due to increased computational requirements for denoising attention)
Prediction: The denoising attention mechanism will significantly improve fine-tuning efficiency, leading to a faster convergence rate and better-performing models compared to the baseline and other fine-tuning approaches.

PROPOSAL 4: Reward-Optimized Reverse-Process Learning for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
Develop a novel method for estimating the initial value function that eliminates the initial value function bias problem, which often plagues KL-regularized reward maximization. This method, called "reward-optimized reverse-process learning," involves learning a reward function that optimizes the reverse process (i.e., the noise schedule) to match the target distribution. Evaluate the performance of this method on the same real-world datasets and baselines as proposal 2.
Controls: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, trajectory KL regularization, and denoising attention mechanism.
Estimated cost: 9,000 GPU-hours (due to increased complexity of the reward-optimized reverse-process learning method)
Prediction: Reward-optimized reverse-process learning will significantly reduce the initial value function bias problem, leading to improved fine-tuning performance and convergence rates compared to the baseline and other fine-tuning approaches.

PROPOSAL 5: Effortless Fine-Tuning via Distribution Matching Optimization
Investigate a fine-tuning approach that focuses solely on distribution matching between the pre-trained diffusion model and the target distribution, without explicit reward maximization. This is achieved by optimizing a distance metric (e.g., Sinkhorn's divergence) between the two distributions. Evaluate the performance of this approach on the same real-world datasets and baselines as proposal 2.
Controls: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, trajectory KL regularization, denoising attention mechanism, and reward-optimized reverse-process learning.
Estimated cost: 6,000 GPU-hours (due to lower computational requirements compared to other proposals)
Prediction: The distribution matching optimization approach will provide a fast and efficient way to fine-tune diffusion models, achieving competitive or even superior performance compared to other fine-tuning methods, especially when the reward function is not well-defined or noisy.

PROPOSAL 6: Unsupervised Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models via Locally Denoising
Explore an unsupervised fine-tuning approach for diffusion models based on locally denoising the samples from the pre-trained model. This is achieved by iteratively denoising and learning from the samples generated by the diffusion model, using a locally denoising loss function (e.g., the locally denoising estimate of the log-likelihood). Evaluate this approach on the same real-world datasets and baselines as proposal 2.
Controls: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, trajectory KL regularization, denoising attention mechanism, reward-optimized reverse-process learning, and distribution matching optimization.
Estimated cost: 7,500 GPU-hours (due to increased computational requirements for locally denoising)
Prediction: The locally denoising approach will provide a simple yet effective unsupervised fine-tuning method for diffusion models, offering competitive performance compared to other fine-tuning approaches, especially in scenarios where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain.

PROPOSAL 7: Evaluating the Role of Hyperparameter Tuning in Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
Investigate the impact of hyperparameter tuning on the performance of various fine-tuning methods for diffusion models. Specifically, design a comprehensive hyperparameter tuning strategy that integrates knowledge from multiple sources (e.g., expert knowledge, Bayesian optimization, and transfer learning). Evaluate the effectiveness of this strategy on the same real-world datasets and baselines as proposal 2.
Controls: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, trajectory KL regularization, denoising attention mechanism, reward-optimized reverse-process learning, distribution matching optimization, and locally denoising.
Estimated cost: 5,000 GPU-hours (due to computational requirements for hyperparameter tuning)
Prediction: The proposed hyperparameter tuning strategy will significantly improve the performance of fine-tuning diffusion models, reducing the gap between the best-performing methods and the baseline, and providing a more robust and adaptive approach to fine-tuning.

PROPOSAL 8: Theoretical Analysis of Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models with KL Relaxations
Develop a theoretical framework for understanding the implications of KL relaxations on fine-tuning diffusion models. Specifically, establish upper and lower bounds on the difference between the intractable marginal KL divergence and the KL relaxation approaches, providing insights into the effect of relaxation on the distribution matching process. Investigate the conditions under which the relaxation is asymptotically optimal.
Controls: None needed
Estimated cost: negligible (since this is a theoretical analysis)
Prediction: The proposed theoretical framework will provide valuable insights into the trade-offs between exact KL minimization and approximation via relaxation, and help guide the development of more effective fine-tuning algorithms.

PROPOSAL 9: Case Study: Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models for Specific Applications
Select a few specific applications from the text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation domains, and apply the previously proposed fine-tuning methods to evaluate their effectiveness on these tasks. This will provide concrete examples of how the fine-tuning methods can be used in practice and help identify any challenges or limitations that may arise in specific use cases.
Controls: Compare against the baseline (1), KL-regularized PPO with fixed regularization strength, trajectory KL regularization, denoising attention mechanism, reward-optimized reverse-process learning, distribution matching optimization, locally denoising, and hyperparameter tuning.
Estimated cost: 8,000 GPU-hours (due to computational requirements for experimenting with different applications)
Prediction: The case study will provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of each fine-tuning method on specific applications, and help guide the development of more application-specific fine-tuning algorithms.

(Note: This is the final proposal, and no further revisions are needed. The list of proposals is now complete.)

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Trajectory KL Regularization Investigation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of using various relaxations of the intractable marginal KL divergence for trajectory KL regularization in KL-regularized reward maximization, specifically on text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation. Compare the performance of leaving out the KL term, using the entire denoising trajectory KL, and using a relaxation such as the sum of the individual step KLs, in terms of training stability and downstream task performance.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline that either ignores the KL term (leading to unstable training) or uses the intractable marginal KL.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results will show that using relaxations of the marginal KL divergence improves training stability and performance on downstream tasks, while leaving out the KL term results in unstable training, and suggest the sum of the individual step KLs as a suitable relaxation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Policy Gradient with Value Function Approximation
PROPOSAL: Apply a policy gradient method with value function approximation to the fine-tuning of pre-trained diffusion models, specifically using a neural network to approximate the value function in the KL-regularized objective. This should help alleviate the initial value function bias problem.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original KL-regularized reward maximization without value function approximation, and also evaluate the performance of using different types of neural network architectures for value function approximation.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results will show that using a policy gradient method with value function approximation significantly improves fine-tuning performance, especially on tasks with high rewards for the initial denoising steps, such as text-to-image generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fine-Tuning with Rejection Sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of rejection sampling for fine-tuning of pre-trained diffusion models, specifically on text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation. Compare the performance of different rejection sampling algorithms (e.g., RSO, RAFT) with the policy gradient method and KL-regularized reward maximization.
CONTROLS: Compare with the policy gradient method, KL-regularized reward maximization, and a baseline that simply samples from the pre-trained model without fine-tuning.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results will show that rejection sampling can be a competitive method for fine-tuning diffusion models, particularly when rewards are sparse or when the model generates high-quality samples with a high probability, such as in text-to-image generation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Fine-Tuning with Rejection Sampling
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of rejection sampling for fine-tuning of pre-trained diffusion models, specifically on text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation, with a focus on adapting rejection sampling to the diffusion model architecture and integrating it with KL-regularized reward maximization. This adaptation should involve modifying the rejection sampling algorithm to take into account the denoising steps of the diffusion model.
CONTROLS: Compare with the policy gradient method, KL-regularized reward maximization, and a baseline that simply samples from the pre-trained model without fine-tuning.
COST: 140 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results will show that adapting rejection sampling to the diffusion model architecture improves its performance in fine-tuning, particularly when rewards are sparse or when the model generates high-quality samples with a high probability.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Trajectory KL Regularization Investigation
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of using a hierarchical KL regularization approach, where the KL divergence is computed between the learned reverse process at each denoising step and the corresponding reference reverse process from the pre-trained model, rather than using the entire denoising trajectory KL.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original KL-regularized reward maximization and a baseline that simply samples from the pre-trained model without fine-tuning.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results will show that the hierarchical KL regularization approach improves fine-tuning performance, especially in tasks where the model generates high-quality samples with a high probability and the rewards are sparse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging Sample Paths for Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of gradual fine-tuning, where the learned model is gradually adapted to the new task by providing additional samples from the pre-trained model and using these samples to update the model's parameters, rather than adapting the entire model at once. This approach should leverage the information present in the sample paths to improve fine-tuning performance.
CONTROLS: Compare with the policy gradient method, KL-regularized reward maximization, and a baseline that simply samples from the pre-trained model without fine-tuning.
COST: 130 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results will show that gradual fine-tuning improves fine-tuning performance, particularly in tasks where the rewards are dense or when the model generates high-quality samples with a low probability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Correcting Pre-Training Errors without Reward
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of a self-supervised learning approach to correct pre-training errors in diffusion models without explicit reward, by using the output of the model as input to a proxy task that encourages closeness to the target data distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare with the impact of fine-tuning on text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation using KL-regularized reward maximization, and a baseline that simply samples from the pre-trained model without fine-tuning.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results will show that self-supervised learning can improve the quality of generated samples and reduce the errors of pre-training, particularly in tasks where the rewards are sparse or when the feedback signal is difficult to obtain, such as text-to-image generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Diffusion Model Architecture Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of modifying the diffusion model architecture to better accommodate the fine-tuning objective, such as by adding or removing denoising steps, or by changing the form of the noise schedule used in the diffusion process.
CONTROLS: Compare with the policy gradient method, KL-regularized reward maximization, and a baseline that simply samples from the pre-trained model without fine-tuning, on text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation.
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results will show that modifying the diffusion model architecture to better match the fine-tuning objective can improve fine-tuning performance, particularly in tasks where the rewards are dense or when the model generates high-quality samples with a high probability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparative Study of Fine-Tuning Methods
PROPOSAL: Conduct an exhaustive comparative study of the fine-tuning methods proposed in this research, including a comprehensive analysis of their strengths, weaknesses, and performance on text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation.
CONTROLS: Compare the performances of all the proposed fine-tuning methods, including KL-regularized reward maximization, policy gradient with value function approximation, fine-tuning with rejection sampling, leveraging sample paths for fine-tuning, correcting pre-training errors without reward, and diffusion model architecture adaptation.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results will provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each fine-tuning method, allowing for informed decisions about which method to choose for specific fine-tuning tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flow Model Fine-Tuning Evaluation
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of the fine-tuning methods proposed in this research on flow models, which have a different generative structure than diffusion models, and provide a comparison of their performance on flow and diffusion models.
CONTROLS: Compare the performances of the fine-tuning methods on text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation using both diffusion and flow models.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results will show that the fine-tuning methods proposed in this research generalize to flow models and provide improved performance on flow models, highlighting the flexibility and applicability of the proposed methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Orthogonal Steering Primitives in Normalized LLMs
PROPOSAL: Compare the existing activation addition and ablation primitives with their normalized equivalents, where we modify each to take into account the RMS-normalized activations. Specifically, we introduce 'projection addition' (modifying the activation by adding a scaled projection of the feature vector onto the normalized feature space) and 'projection ablation' (modifying the activation by subtracting a scaled projection of the feature vector onto the orthogonal complement of the normalized feature space). We test these primitives on a variety of real-world benchmarks and model families.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original addition and ablation primitives, as well as their combination; ablate the normalization layer to compare against the original primitives.
COST: 100 GPU-hours per model and dataset
PREDICTION: We expect the normalized primitives to show improved stability for fine-grained control, especially in layer normalization regimes. However, their performance could degrade in vanishing gradient or exploding activation regimes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Stability Analysis of Projection-Based Steering
PROPOSAL: Investigate the stability and robustness of the projection-based steering primitives introduced in proposal 1, particularly under varying levels of RMS normalization. We will analyze the eigendecomposition of the activation covariance matrix, and identify the impact of feature-wise normalization and layer depth on the steering primitives' performance. We will also assess the conditioning and invertibility of the resulting matrices across multiple real-world datasets and model families.
CONTROLS: Use proposal 1's primitive and original activation addition and ablation for comparison; test across multiple models, datasets, and regularization schemes.
COST: 50 GPU-hours per model
PREDICTION: We expect the projection-based primitives to be stable across a wide range of RMS normalization settings, and show improved conditioning and invertibility. However, we may observe a 'sweet-spot' in steering performance near certain eigendecomposition thresholds, where sheer computational complexity holds down performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conditioned Steering with Contextual Control Strength
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new steering primitive that combines the projection-based approach with contextual signals, such as input embedding or decoder states. This allows the control strength to be dynamically adapted to the task and input context. Specifically, we will modify the projection-based steering to include a conditioned scaling term in the form of attention-weighted projections or learnable weights for each activation component. This aims to extend the selectivity of steering to specific regions or layers of the model, achieving even finer-grained control.
CONTROLS: Test against variants of projection addition and ablation with fixed control strength; compare against selective steering methods that replicate this fine-grained adaptation but with static feature weights.
COST: 120 GPU-hours per model and dataset
PREDICTION: We expect significant gains in steering specificity and effectiveness, as contextual control strengthens and stabilizes the fine-grained effects of the steering operation. However, risk is that the learned weights for each context may create unexpected biases in certain model families or settings, overriding necessary topical constraints on the language model's generation aesthetics.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Conditioned Steering with Contextual Control Strength (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 3 to add a 'behaviorally-consistent' weighting scheme to the conditioned scaling term. This would utilize a clustering-based representation of target behaviors (in terms of input embedding or decoder states), rather than directly adapting the model's weights to each input context. In this approach, the model's activations are influenced by the similarity in these behavioral representations. We expect this scheme to provide a more robust and behaviorally-agnostic control mechanism.
CONTROLS: Test against fixed-weighted variants of proposal 3; compare against baseline steering methods that use fixed weights (e.g. random initialization, orthogonal weight initialization).
COST: 40 additional GPU-hours per model and dataset
PREDICTION: We expect improved refinement and consistency of generated text under behaviors drawn from a specific family (e.g., emotions preserved), however runtime computations would scale with number of supporting slides expanding premises - causing degradation of immediate performance including more factors (VAS).

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED 3. Conditioned Steering with Contextual Control Strength
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 3 to add a 'behaviorally-consistent' weighting scheme to the conditioned scaling term. This would utilize a clustering-based representation of target behaviors (in terms of input embedding or decoder states), rather than directly adapting the model's weights to each input context. In this approach, the model's activations are influenced by the similarity in these behavioral representations. We expect this scheme to provide a more robust and behaviorally-agnostic control mechanism.
CONTROLS: Test against fixed-weighted variants of proposal 3; compare against baseline steering methods that use fixed weights (e.g. random initialization, orthogonal weight initialization).
COST: 40 additional GPU-hours per model and dataset
PREDICTION: We expect improved refinement and consistency of generated text under behaviors drawn from a specific family (e.g., emotions preserved), however runtime computations would scale with number of supporting slides expanding premises - causing degradation of immediate performance including more factors (VAS).

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Conditioned Steering with Contextual Control Strength
PROPOSAL: Keep the current approach but focus on understanding the dynamics of the clustering-based behavior representations. Investigate their sensitivity to the choice of clustering algorithm, number of clusters, and activation magnitudes. Furthermore, examine the impact of using these representations on the performance and stability of the model.
CONTROLS: Test against a variety of clustering algorithms and evaluate the effect of different numbers of clusters on the model's behavior; compare against using traditional hand-labeled ground truth for representations.
COST: 30 additional GPU-hours per model and dataset
PREDICTION: We expect to identify a suitable combination of clustering parameters that enhances model performance and stability under steering control. However, difficulties might arise in assigning suitable cluster numbers from larger ensemble datasets necessary to generate responsive valid, externally accurate results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Continuous Invariant Steering for LLMs
PROPOSAL: Design a steering method that leverages the concept of continuous invariant transformation, allowing for a gradual control over the behavior of the model. Specifically, we introduce an autoencoder-based approach that maps the input to a continuous latent space, and then applies a steering transformation to this latent space before decoding the output. This enables continuous adjustments of the model's behavior, from refusing to complying with a harm request, without affecting unrelated features.
CONTROLS: Evaluate performance against various steering methods including projection-based and conditioning-based methods; ablate the autoencoder by directly applying steering to input embeddings.
COST: 80 GPU-hours per model and dataset
PREDICTION: We expect this method to provide a smooth, fine-grained control over the model's behavior, with improved stability and coherence across the entire control range. However, it may require careful tuning of the autoencoder architecture and steering transformation to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Universal Steering Framework for LLMs
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified framework that encompasses various steering methods, including projection-based, conditioning-based, and continuous invariant steering. This framework will allow for easy integration and comparison of different steering approaches, as well as identification of key factors that influence their performance. Specifically, we will implement a modular architecture that enables swapping out different steering components and evaluating their impact on model behavior.
CONTROLS: Implement and evaluate each steering method within the framework; compare against a baseline with no steering; ablate different components of the framework to understand their contributions.
COST: 240 GPU-hours per model and dataset
PREDICTION: We expect this framework to provide a comprehensive understanding of the relative merits and limitations of different steering methods, and facilitate the design of more effective and coherent steering approaches. However, developing a universal framework may introduce additional computational overhead and complexities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Domain Adaptation for Steering LLMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the challenge of steering LLMs in unseen domains or tasks, and propose a domain adaptation approach to improve the transferability of steering models. Specifically, we will modify the steering framework (proposal 5) to incorporate domain-invariant features and adaptations, and evaluate its performance on multiple domains and tasks.
CONTROLS: Adapt the universal steering framework to accommodate domain adaptation; compare against a naive approach without domain adaptation; ablate different components of the adaptation module to understand its contributions.
COST: 100 GPU-hours per model and dataset
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to significantly improve the transferability of steering models across domains and tasks, and enable more robust and generalizable steering performance. However, the adaptation process may require tuning of additional hyperparameters, which could increase the overall complexity of the steering framework.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experiments on Emotion Control and Refusal of Harmful Requests
PROPOSAL: Perform an empirical evaluation of the steering methods proposed in the previous experiments on two real-world tasks: (1) emotion control of generated text and (2) refusal of harmful requests (jailbreaking) in a conversational context. We will use a set of labeled datasets for both tasks and compare the performance of the steering methods from a human-evaluation perspective.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the steering methods against a baseline without steering; evaluate the quality and coherence of the generated text and conversational flow; assess the effectiveness of the refusal of harmful requests.
COST: 400 GPU-hours per model and dataset
PREDICTION: We expect the steering methods to demonstrate significant improvement in both tasks, with a notable increase in the quality and coherence of the generated text and conversational flow. However, the effectiveness of the refusal of harmful requests may vary depending on the specific dataset and evaluation metrics used.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Revisiting Activation Steering with Orthogonalization and Addition for Fine-Grained Control
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive analysis of existing activation steering methods, including their strengths and limitations, and propose a new framework that integrates orthogonalization and addition-based methods in a single unified model. This framework will introduce a novel control parameter that adjusts the balance between orthogonalization and addition, allowing for continuous and fine-grained control over model behavior.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art methods, including directional ablation and activation addition, on benchmark datasets such as Common Sense Generation and SocialIQA.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The new framework will provide improved fine-grained control over model behavior, but may require careful tuning of the control parameter to achieve optimal results. Potential failure points include over-reliance on the balance parameter, which could lead to degradation in performance or increased brittleness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Steering Operations in Normalized Activation Space
PROPOSAL: Investigate how existing steering operations (orthogonalization and addition) behave in the presence of RMS normalization, which rescales each activation to a fixed norm. This will involve comparing the effectiveness of steering operations before and after normalization, as well as analyzing their interaction with feature directions in the normalized space.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline of unnormalized activations, as well as against a modified steering operation that takes normalization into account (e.g., scaling the feature vector by the inverse norm of the activation).
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study will reveal that normalization impacts the steering operations, potentially leading to better or worse performance depending on the context. Unexpectedly, normalization may also reveal a hidden correlation between steering operations and the model's output, which could inform new steering strategies. Failure points include potential over-reliance on the inverse norm, which could exacerbate existing issues with layer-specific activation scales.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Steering Operation Interactions and Activation Space Geometry
PROPOSAL: Use techniques from linear algebra and geometry to analyze the interactions between steering operations and the geometry of the activation space. This will involve computing feature vectors, analyzing their orthogonality and alignment, and visualizing the resulting activation space.
CONTROLS: Use a synthetic dataset with well-controlled activation space geometry, as well as a set of carefully selected real-world examples from the Refusal of Harmful Requests (JR) test suite.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal that the steering operations interact with the activation space in complex ways, potentially leading to unexpected emergent behaviors. The study will provide valuable insights into the structural properties of the activation space and how they relate to steering operations. Failure points include potential over-reliance on linear algebraic assumptions, which might not hold in the presence of non-linear activation functions.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  Revisiting Activation Steering with Orthogonalization and Addition for Fine-Grained Control
PROPOSAL: Modify the original proposal to incorporate the insights from the analysis of steering operation interactions and activation space geometry. Introduce a new regularization term that encourages the steering operations to maintain a desired level of orthogonality and alignment, reducing their potential interference and promoting more fine-grained control.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original framework, as well as against a baseline that omits the regularization term, on benchmark datasets such as the JR test suite and the SocialIQA dataset.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (includes additional computational costs for training the modified model)
PREDICTION: The revised framework will provide improved fine-grained control of model behavior, while also maintaining the robust performance of the original framework. Potential failure points include over-reliance on the regularization term, which could lead to degradation in performance if not properly tuned.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 3. Analysis of Steering Operation Interactions and Activation Space Geometry
PROPOSAL: Extend the analysis of steering operation interactions and activation space geometry by incorporating a partial ablation study, where we remove one or more steering operations and observe the impact on model behavior. This will help understand the relative contributions of each steering operation and inform the design of future steering frameworks.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that includes all steering operations, as well as against a scenario where a single steering operation is removed, on benchmark datasets such as the JR test suite and the SocialIQA dataset.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (includes additional computational costs for training and evaluating the ablated models)
PREDICTION: The study will reveal the relative importance of each steering operation and provide insights into their potential substitution or modification in future steering frameworks. Potential failure points include potential over-reliance on the partial ablation study, which might not capture all interactions between steering operations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conditional Steering with Steering-Layer Attention
PROPOSAL: Introduce a conditional steering mechanism that selectively applies steering operations based on the attention weights of the steering layer. This will allow the model to conditionally apply steering operations based on the relevance of the attended features, potentially improving the coherence and robustness of the model.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that applies steering operations uniformly across all features, as well as against a scenario where the steering layer is not structured as an attention mechanism, on benchmark datasets such as the JR test suite and the SocialIQA dataset.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The conditional steering mechanism will improve the coherence and robustness of the model, while also maintaining its fine-grained control capabilities. Potential failure points include potential over-reliance on the attention weights, which could lead to degradation in performance if the model over-emphasizes certain features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fairness Evaluation of Steering-Based Model Interventions
PROPOSAL: Introduce a fairness evaluation framework that assesses the equity of steering-based model interventions across different demographic groups. This will involve using metrics such as demographic parity and equal opportunity to evaluate the model's performance under different steering scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that does not include fairness evaluation, as well as against a scenario where fairness evaluation is performed using a different set of metrics, on benchmark datasets such as the JR test suite and the SocialIQA dataset.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The fairness evaluation framework will provide insights into the potential biases and disparities introduced by steering-based model interventions, allowing for more informed design and deployment decisions. Potential failure points include potential over-reliance on a specific set of fairness metrics, which might not capture all aspects of model fairness.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 1. Revisiting Activation Steering with Orthogonalization and Addition for Fine-Grained Control
PROPOSAL: Modify the original proposal to incorporate the insights from the fairness evaluation framework. Introduce a new fairness-aware loss term that balances the model's performance with its fairness metrics, potentially improving the robustness and equity of the steering framework.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that excludes the fairness-aware loss term, as well as against a scenario where fairness metrics are evaluated only after the model is trained, on benchmark datasets such as the JR test suite and the SocialIQA dataset.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (includes additional computational costs for training with the fairness-aware loss term)
PREDICTION: The fairness-aware loss term will improve the robustness and equity of the steering framework, while also maintaining its fine-grained control capabilities. Potential failure points include potential over-reliance on a specific set of fairness metrics, which might not capture all aspects of model fairness.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 2. Evaluating Steering Operations in Normalized Activation Space
PROPOSAL: Modify the proposal to investigate the impact of RMS normalization on the effectiveness of steering operations in the activation space. Include an analysis of the normalization's effect on the feature vectors used for steering and explore methods to compensate for the normalization's impact, potentially improving the steering framework's performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that does not include RMS normalization, as well as against a scenario where the steering framework is adapted to compensate for the normalization, on benchmark datasets such as the JR test suite and the SocialIQA dataset.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (includes additional computational costs for evaluating the impact of RMS normalization)
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal the impact of RMS normalization on the steering operations and provide insights into how to compensate for its effects, potentially leading to improved steering framework performance. Potential failure points include potential over-reliance on the compensation methods, which might not capture all aspects of the normalization's impact.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Evaluation of Steering Frameworks on Real-World Datasets
PROPOSAL: Conduct a large-scale evaluation of the steering frameworks on real-world datasets, including a wide range of language tasks and applications. This will involve training and evaluating the steering frameworks on datasets such as the Common Sense Generation dataset, the SocialIQA dataset, and the HellaSwag dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art baselines and existing steering methods on a comprehensive set of metrics, including fluency, factual accuracy, and fairness.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The large-scale evaluation will provide a comprehensive understanding of the steering frameworks' performance on real-world datasets and applications, and will help identify areas for future improvement. Potential failure points include potential over-reliance on a specific set of datasets or metrics, which might not capture all aspects of the steering frameworks' performance.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated multi-task learning with heterogeneous architectures and tasks
PROPOSAL: Experiment 1: Evaluate the performance of federated multi-task learning methods on users with different model architectures using a benchmark suite of real-world tasks and datasets. Specifically, using the CommonLit dataset for sentiment analysis and question-answering, and the ProfaneSpeech dataset for hate speech detection, we will fine-tune a range of pre-trained foundation models (e.g., DistilBERT, RoBERTa) and apply federated multi-task learning methods (e.g., FedProd, FedBM) to capture common task-agnostic information across users.
CONTROLS: Baselines include: 1) local training on each user's dataset; 2) decentralized federated learning methods that assume homogeneous model architectures (e.g., FedAvg); 3) models that use pre-training only.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: FedProd and FedBM will outperform local training and decentralized methods, showing benefits of federated multi-task learning for task heterogeneity. Potential failure: experiment may require significant annotation efforts for user data, potentially reducing the number of users and tasks that can be included.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Contrastive Learning for Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Experiment 2: Investigate Adaptive Contrastive Learning, a novel method for jointly aligning representations across an arbitrary number of models in a federated multi-task setting. This method involves learning an adaptive set of contrastive tasks for each pair of models, where the set of tasks adaptively varies over time and across users. We will evaluate Adaptive Contrastive Learning using the same benchmark suite as Experiment 1 and compare its performance against prior contrastive learning methods (e.g., InfoNCE, Gramian-based) and other state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: Baselines include: 1) InfoNCE for pairwise alignment; 2) Gramian-based contrastive loss; 3) federated multi-task learning methods without contrastive learning (e.g., FedProd, FedBM).
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Adaptive Contrastive Learning will outperform prior methods, demonstrating its ability to adaptively capture dependencies among representations from an arbitrary number of models. Potential failure: the adaptive nature of the method may lead to overfitting or increased complexity, requiring careful hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Federated Learning with Multi-Task Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: Theoretical Result 1: Analyze the robustness of federated multi-task learning methods, particularly when using Adaptive Contrastive Learning. We will derive bounds on the robust generalization error of these methods under different adversary models, including label flipping and perturbed data. Our goal is to understand the conditions under which these methods maintain their performance under real-world attacks. The result will be applicable to a wide range of federated multi-task learning methods.
CONTROLS: Theoretical results are controlled by the choice of adversary model and the robustness of the specific federated multi-task learning method being analyzed.
COST: negligible (theoretical work)
PREDICTION: Our analysis will reveal that federated multi-task learning methods with Adaptive Contrastive Learning are more robust than their single-task counterparts, while also providing insights into the conditions under which they break down under attacks. Potential failure: the theoretical bounds derived may not capture real-world attacks accurately, highlighting the need for further empirical evaluation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Robust Federated Learning with Multi-Task Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Theoretical Result 1: We revise our previous work to derive a more general framework for analyzing the robustness of federated multi-task learning methods. Building on our previous result, we will extend the analysis to consider non-IID data and model heterogeneity, providing a unified treatment of robustness in federated multi-task learning under various adversary models. Furthermore, we will investigate the impact of Adaptive Contrastive Learning on the robustness of these methods, exploring whether it can improve or worsen robust generalization error under different scenarios.
CONTROLS: Theoretical results are controlled by the choice of adversary model, the level of non-IID data, and the extent of model heterogeneity.
COST: negligible (theoretical work)
PREDICTION: Our revised analysis will yield more general and robust results, providing a deeper understanding of the relationship between robustness, non-IID data, and model heterogeneity in federated multi-task learning. Potential failure: the revised analysis may be computationally intensive, requiring significant resources to derive and prove the theorems.

PROPOSAL: REVISED: Theoretical Result 1: We revise our previous work to derive a more general framework for analyzing the robustness of federated multi-task learning methods. REVISED PROPOSAL: In the original work, we only explored how Real-World data affects the Theoretical results whereas now we also want to incorporate how specifically datasets with High Data Skewness will affect the analysis.

COST: negligible (theoretical work)

REVISED: By revising our previous theoretical work, we find that in the case of high data skewness, we can theoretically prove that our unified framework for robust federated learning does propose a structure that can capture the variations of different tasks i.e. the robust generalization error is increased modestly.
CONTROLS: We control for the impact of the number of different tasks and the user-level data distribution.
COST: negligible (theoretical work)
PREDICTION: Our revised theoretical results will give an insight in real world application where data is skewed amongst different tasks, thereby yielding more accurateazzo prognostications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Practical Federated Learning with Heterogeneous Architectures and Tasks
PROPOSAL: Experiment 4: Investigate the practicality of federated multi-task learning with heterogeneous architectures and tasks in real-world deployment scenarios. We will conduct a user study with a diverse set of users, each with their own model architecture and task, and collect feedback on the usability and efficiency of the federated multi-task learning process. We will also analyze the computational and communication resources required for the federated multi-task learning process to identify potential bottlenecks.
CONTROLS: Baselines include: 1) local training on each user's dataset; 2) decentralized federated learning methods that assume homogeneous model architectures (e.g., FedAvg).
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our study will reveal the practical challenges and opportunities of federated multi-task learning with heterogeneous architectures and tasks, providing insights into how to design and implement such a system in real-world settings. Potential failure: the user study may not reflect real-world usage patterns, and the feedback collected may not be representative of all users.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Framework for Efficient Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Experiment 5: Propose a new framework for federated multi-task learning that incorporates adaptive contrastive learning and is optimized for real-world deployment scenarios. The framework will include techniques for efficient model selection, optimal task formulation, and efficient communication protocols. We will evaluate the framework using a range of real-world datasets and tasks, and compare its performance to state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: Baselines include: 1) federated multi-task learning methods without adaptive contrastive learning (e.g., FedProd, FedBM); 2) decentralized federated learning methods that assume homogeneous model architectures (e.g., FedAvg).
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our framework will outperform state-of-the-art methods in terms of efficiency, scalability, and accuracy, making it a viable option for real-world federated multi-task learning applications. Potential failure: the framework may be difficult to implement in practice, or the optimization techniques used may not generalize to all scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Experiment 6: Investigate the use of transfer learning for federated multi-task learning. We will pre-train a shared representation model on a large, diverse dataset, and then fine-tune it on individual tasks in a federated multi-task learning setting. We will also explore the use of knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from the pre-trained model to other models. We will evaluate the performance of transfer learning in federated multi-task learning compared to training from scratch.
CONTROLS: Baselines include: 1) local training on each user's dataset; 2) decentralized federated learning methods that assume homogeneous model architectures (e.g., FedAvg).
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Transfer learning will improve the efficiency and accuracy of federated multi-task learning by leveraging pre-trained knowledge, and knowledge distillation will further enhance the performance by transferring knowledge between models. Potential failure: the pre-trained model may not generalize well to the individual tasks, or the knowledge distillation process may fail to transfer relevant knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Multi-Task Learning with Scalability and Robustness
PROPOSAL: Experiment 7: Combine the results of previous experiments to propose a comprehensive federated multi-task learning framework that incorporates adaptive contrastive learning, transfer learning, and efficient model selection. We will evaluate the scalability and robustness of the framework on large-scale real-world datasets and compare its performance to state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: Baselines include: 1) state-of-the-art federated multi-task learning methods (e.g., FedProd, FedBM); 2) decentralized federated learning methods that assume homogeneous model architectures (e.g., FedAvg).
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our comprehensive framework will outperform state-of-the-art methods in terms of scalability, robustness, and accuracy, making it a reliable option for real-world federated multi-task learning applications. Potential failure: the framework may be computationally intensive, or the combination of techniques may not generalize well to all scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Review of Label Noise Robustness in Deep Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: Investigate and summarize the current state-of-the-art methods for mitigating label noise in deep neural networks. Examine the strengths and weaknesses of various approaches such as label filtering, reweighting, and robust loss formulations, as well as sample selection methods based on training dynamics.
CONTROLS: Survey existing literature; include commonly used benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR-10, MNIST with corruption)
COST: Low ( mostly literature review)
PREDICTION: The survey will highlight the effectiveness of different methods in various label noise regimes, assisting in identifying areas for further research.

Given this proposal has low cost, and mostly involves a literature survey, a low cost (in terms of resources) is expected here.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Class-Conditional and Instance-Dependent Label Noise
PROPOSAL: Experiment with several existing models (e.g., ResNet-18, Wide ResNet-50) on datasets with both class-conditional and instance-dependent label noise (e.g., CIFAR-10 with noisy labels, and a simulated instance-dependent noisy version of MNIST), comparing their robustness to the two noise types using metrics like accuracy and calibration scores.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline models trained on clean and noisy data without any label noise correction methods; ablate the impact of different noise levels and ratios.
COST: Medium ( ước ~100 GPU-hours for 1000 epochs on CIFAR-10 and MNIST)
PREDICTION: Results will highlight the challenges posed by instance-dependent noise and provide a basis to compare the effectiveness of future methods in handling this more complex noise type.

ACTION: REVISIE
TITLE: Evaluating Class-Conditional and Instance-Dependent Label Noise
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Experiment with a few state-of-the-art label noise robustness methods (e.g., milestone variants: Metadata-weighted Label Cleaning [MWLC], and Learning to Detect and Email Noisy Labels (LiLa) on top of a well tested model) on datasets with both class-conditional and instance-dependent label noise (e.g., CIFAR-10 with noisy labels).
CONTROLS: Ablate the methods individually and together; evaluate against baseline models trained on clean and noisy data without any label noise correction methods.
COST: High ( Gupta ~700 GPU-hours with models like a denoised variant of the YOLO model, and simulation runtime costs listed above; polishing down to variant methods using sqrt hailCost between the base 6y delta of estimated compute  to be ~600)
PREDICTION: Expected results will highlight advancements made in instance-dependent label noise, especially in regard to recent labeling literature and top labels.

PROPOSAL: REVISED: Modify the semi-supervised approach for label noise correction to incorporate a mechanism for handling instance-dependent label noise. This can be achieved by introducing a term in the clustering-based technique that takes into account the similarity between input instances.

TITLE: Transfer Learning for Label Noise Correction
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of transfer learning for label noise correction by pre-training a model on a clean dataset and fine-tuning it on a dataset with label noise. Investigate whether the pre-trained model's features can help correct the noisy labels and improve the overall performance of the model.
CONTROLS: Compare with traditional training from scratch and ablate the impact of different pre-training and fine-tuning procedures.
COST: High (≈ 1000 GPU hours, due to the computationally expensive pre-training and fine-tuning processes)
PREDICTION: Transfer learning is expected to improve the label noise correction performance, especially when the pre-training dataset is related to the noisy dataset. However, the degree of improvement may depend on the specific pre-training and fine-tuning procedures used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Label Noise Propagation
PROPOSAL: Analyze the propagation of label noise through a neural network using a theoretical framework. Derive bounds on the output noise based on the network's architecture and the noise level in the input data.
CONTROLS: Assume a simple neural network architecture and vary the noise level and network depth to understand the general trends.
COST: Low (≈ 10-20 CPU hours, as this is a theoretical analysis)
PREDICTION: The analysis is expected to provide insights into the mechanisms of label noise propagation and identify key factors that influence the output noise. However, the derived bounds may not accurately capture the actual behavior of complex neural networks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Empirical Evaluation of Label Noise Correction Methods
PROPOSAL: Perform an empirical evaluation of the previously proposed methods for label noise correction (Review, Evaluating, Novel Noise Estimation, Semi-Supervised Method, and Transfer Learning) on a variety of datasets with different types and levels of label noise. Compare their performance using metrics such as accuracy, precision, and recall.
CONTROLS: Use a range of datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, ImageNet, MNIST) with different noise levels and types, and compare the results to baselines and state-of-the-art methods.
COST: High (≈ 3000-4000 GPU hours, as this requires training and evaluating multiple models on various datasets)
PREDICTION: The empirical evaluation is expected to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each method and help identify the most effective approaches for different types and levels of label noise.
