ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Corruption Mechanisms on Noisy Label Correction
PROPOSAL: Experiment with 5 popular noisy label corruption mechanisms (i.e., class-to-class noise, symmetric noise, asymmetric noise, bloc noise, and fully random noise) on the CIFAR-10 dataset, comparing their impact on model performance using both clean and noisy labels. For each corruption mechanism, we will train 3 different models (ResNet-18, Wide ResNet-28-10, and PreAct ResNet-18) with different hyperparameters and measure their accuracy on the clean test set after training for 100 epochs. We will also ablate the noise level to see its effect on the results.
CONTROLS: Baseline comparison to training without any corruption mechanism, ablation study of different noise levels to evaluate robustness to noise.
COST: 6 GPU-hours (~ 72 hours on 12 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect the corruption mechanisms to have an adverse impact on model performance when training with noisy labels. The impact is expected to vary across different models and hyperparameters, with models being more robust to noise with more aggressive regularization.

-Assuming a valid implementation of corrupted labels during the experiment, models trained with CIFAR-10 (noise augmentation is not “genuine noise”) could have noisy label correction mechanisms simulations failing on worse CIFAR classification systems and won't capture every noisy situation - for example, hard noisy cloud labels requiring a deeper structured process

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Sample Weighting on Noisy Label Correction
PROPOSAL: Design and experiment with 4 different weighting strategies (uniform weight, noise-aware weight, confidence-based weight, and entropy-based weight) to assign weights to samples in the training dataset of CIFAR-10 based on their confidence levels, noise levels, or other relevant features. Train ResNet-18 on the CIFAR-10 dataset using these weighted samples and compare their performance to the baseline model trained on unweighted samples. Evaluate the robustness of the models by adding Gaussian noise and flipping some labels and then measuring their performance.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the weighting strategies to the baseline model trained without weighting, and measure the difference in robustness between the models using different weighting strategies.
COST: 9 GPU-hours (~108 hours on 12 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect the weighting strategies to improve the robustness of the model to noisy labels, with the noise-aware and confidence-based weighting strategies performing particularly well. However, we also expect some overfitting with heavier weights put onto clean samples by mistake. Samples of differing noise representation may be classified incorrectly.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Iterative Label Correction Using Confidence-Based Sampling
PROPOSAL: We propose an iterative label correction method that uses confidence-based sampling to isolate and filter out noisy labels. The approach involves training a neural network, then using the model's confidence in its predictions to identify potential noisy labels. Iteratively, the model is retrained on the updated label set, and the process is repeated until convergence. We will compare this approach to existing label correction methods, selecting the best performing configuration based on metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score on several real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare this approach to existing label correction methods such as regularization-based noise reduction [1] and distribution-based noise modeling [2], as well as a baseline model trained on noisy labels without any correction. We will also include an ablation study to examine the impact of different confidence thresholds used for identifying noisy labels.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to outperform existing label correction methods, particularly on datasets with high levels of instance-dependent noise. However, the iterative process may result in overfitting if not properly regularized, which could hinder performance on test data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Noisy Labels on Deep Neural Networks with a Multi-Task Learning Approach
PROPOSAL: To better understand the effects of noisy labels on deep neural networks, we will investigate the use of multi-task learning (MTL) as a means to mitigate label noise. MTL involves training a model to perform multiple related tasks simultaneously, which can help the model learn robust features that are less sensitive to noisy labels. We will experiment with different MTL configurations, such as training a model to predict both the primary class and a secondary task (e.g., predicting pairwise similarity between instances), and evaluate the impact of noise on each task separately and collectively.
CONTROLS: We will compare the MTL approach to a single-task learning baseline trained on the primary task alone, as well as a reweighted loss method [3] that aims to reduce label noise. We will also include an ablation study to examine the impact of different secondary tasks and their associated losses on the primary task performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the MTL approach to be more robust to noisy labels than single-task learning, particularly when the secondary task is related to the primary task in a way that helps to capture key features. However, the additional computational cost and potential overfitting of MTL models may limit its effectiveness in certain scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Noisy Labels on Deep Neural Networks with a Multi-Task Learning Approach
PROPOSAL: To improve the MTL approach, we will introduce a meta-learning component that enables the model to adapt to new tasks and scenarios. Specifically, we will use a meta-learning algorithm, such as Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) [4], to train a neural network that can quickly adjust to new tasks and primary classes, even when the target task is unknown during training. This meta-learned model will be used to learn features that are invariant to label noise and robust across multiple tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the MTL approach with meta-learning to the previous baseline of single-task learning, as well as the reweighted loss method [3]. We will also evaluate the performance of the meta-learned model on a range of tasks with different levels of label noise and assess its ability to adapt to new, unseen tasks.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the MTL approach with meta-learning to exhibit significant improvement over previous methods, especially in scenarios where label noise is high or data is scarce. However, the additional complexity of meta-learning may lead to overfitting or brittle performance in certain cases, particularly if the MAML objective is not properly calibrated.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Weighting of Noisy Labels for Improved Robustness
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the idea of uncertainty-aware learning, we propose a novel method that assigns weights to noisy labels based on the model's uncertainty in its predictions. This is achieved by attaching an uncertainty estimation module to the neural network, which outputs a confidence score for each prediction. Weights for noisy labels are then assigned based on these confidence scores, and a reweighted loss function is used to update the model's parameters. Our approach is defined by a mathematical optimization problem that balances the trade-off between model performance and robustness to label noise.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate our approach against various baselines, including the standard cross-entropy loss and a reweighted loss function that uses instance-dependent noise levels [5]. We will also include an ablation study to analyze the impact of different uncertainty estimation techniques and confidence thresholds.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to outperform existing methods in terms of robustness to noisy labels, particularly when the label noise is heterogeneous and varies across instances. However, the choice of uncertainty estimation method and confidence threshold may require careful tuning, and the additional computational cost may impact model performance on datasets with large amounts of data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Label Noise Types Using Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the idea of adversarial training, we propose a novel method for analyzing and mitigating label noise by introducing an adversary that attempts to corrupt the model's predictions. Specifically, we use a Wasserstein GAN to generate synthetic noisy labels that mimic real-world label noise, allowing us to simulate and analyze different types of label noise. Our framework evaluates the model's performance under different noise levels and types, enabling the identification of the most vulnerable regimes and guiding the development of more effective label noise mitigation strategies.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate our approach against various baselines, including the standard cross-entropy loss and a reweighted loss function that uses instance-dependent noise levels [5]. We will also compare our approach to a baseline adversarial training method for robustness [6].
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to provide valuable insights into the types of label noise that are most challenging for deep neural networks, allowing for targeted mitigation strategies. However, the computational cost of generating synthetic noisy labels may be high, and the performance of the model may degrade under strong adversarial attacks.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Analysis of Label Noise Types Using Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: To address the high computational cost of generating synthetic noisy labels, we modify the approach to utilize a more efficient hybrid approach that combines adversarial training with a pre-trained model fine-tuned on a small subset of noisy data. The pre-trained model serves as a starting point for the adversarial training process, which refines the model's performance and robustness through targeted attacks. This hybrid approach reduces the computational overhead while maintaining the benefits of adversarial training in analyzing label noise types.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the hybrid approach against the original adversarial training baseline, as well as the standard cross-entropy loss and reweighted loss function for label noise mitigation [5, 7].
COST: 150 GPU-hours (reduced from 180)
PREDICTION: We expect the hybrid approach to maintain the performance benefits of adversarial training while reducing computational costs, allowing for more extensive analysis of label noise types. However, the performance of the model may degrade if the pre-trained model is not well-suited for the specific task or noisy dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Using Transfer Learning to Mitigate Label Noise in Pre-Trained Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a transfer learning-based approach to mitigate label noise in pre-trained models. Specifically, we fine-tune a pre-trained model on a small subset of clean data and then apply a noise-aware loss function to adapt the model to the noisy data. By leveraging the knowledge gained from the pre-training process, our approach aims to improve the model's robustness to label noise and yield better performance on downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate our approach against a baseline of fine-tuning a pre-trained model on the noisy dataset without any noise-aware loss function. We will also compare our approach to the reweighted loss function [5] and uncertainty-aware weighting of noisy labels [3].
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to leverage the advantages of transfer learning and fine-tuning to improve the model's performance on noisy data, particularly when the pre-training task is related to the downstream task. However, the choice of pre-trained model and fine-tuning strategy may require careful tuning, and the performance of the model may degrade if the pre-trained model is not well-suited for the noisy dataset.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Iterative Label Correction Using Confidence-Based Sampling
PROPOSAL: We modify the initial iterative label correction approach to include a secondary task that encourages the model to predict a confidence score for each instance. This confidence score is then used to weight the correction process, giving more importance to instances with high confidence predictions. By introducing this secondary task, we aim to improve the model's ability to correct noisy labels and reduce overcorrection.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the modified approach against the original iterative label correction baseline, as well as the reweighted loss function [5] and uncertainty-aware weighting of noisy labels [3].
COST: 100 GPU-hours (no change)
PREDICTION: We expect the modified approach to improve the model's performance on noisy data by providing more informed label corrections and reducing overcorrection. However, the addition of the secondary task may introduce new challenges, such as requiring careful tuning of hyperparameters or potentially introducing new sources of noise.

TITLE: A Theoretical Framework for Understanding the Effects of Label Noise on Deep Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel theoretical framework that analyses the effects of label noise on deep neural networks from an information-theoretic perspective. Our framework provides a rigorous mathematical framework for understanding how label noise impacts the capacity of neural networks, and we derive a series of theoretical results that demonstrate the impact of label noise on model performance.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the theoretical framework against existing empirical results, and provide a comparison with real-world experiments that demonstrate the framework's accuracy and relevance.
COST: (theoretical analysis only, no computational cost)
PREDICTION: We expect our theoretical framework to provide valuable insights into the effects of label noise on deep neural networks, and identify key factors that contribute to model degradation. However, the applicability of the framework may be limited to specific types of neural networks or label noise distributions, and additional empirical research may be required to generalize the results.

TITLE: A Large-Scale Empirical Comparison of Label Noise Mitigation Methods
PROPOSAL: We conduct a large-scale empirical comparison of the proposed label noise mitigation methods, including the iterative label correction, uncertainty-aware weighting, transfer learning, and adversarial training approaches. We evaluate their performance on a diverse set of real-world datasets and investigate their strengths and weaknesses, providing a comprehensive understanding of their applicability and limitations.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the label noise mitigation methods against a set of strong baselines, including the standard cross-entropy loss and reweighted loss function for label noise mitigation [5]. We will also perform an ablation study to examine the impact of different hyperparameters and configuration settings on the performance of each method.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our large-scale empirical comparison to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different label noise mitigation methods, and identify the most effective approaches for specific types of label noise and datasets.

Inspired by the idea of uncertainty-aware learning, we propose a novel method that assigns weights to noisy labels based on the model's uncertainty in its predictions. This is achieved by attaching an uncertainty estimation module to the neural network, which outputs a confidence score for each prediction. Weights for noisy labels are then assigned based on these confidence scores, and a reweighted loss function is used to update the model's parameters. Our approach is defined by a mathematical optimization problem that balances the trade-off between model performance and robustness to label noise.
Controls: We will evaluate our approach against various baselines, including the standard cross-entropy loss and a reweighted loss function that uses instance-dependent noise levels [5]. We will also include an ablation study to analyze the impact of different uncertainty estimation techniques and confidence thresholds.
Estimated cost: 120 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect our approach to outperform existing methods in terms of robustness to noisy labels, particularly when the label noise is heterogeneous and varies across instances. However, the choice of uncertainty estimation method and confidence threshold may require careful tuning, and the additional computational cost may impact model performance on datasets with large amounts of data.

PROPOSAL 4: Analysis of Label Noise Types Using Adversarial Training
To address the high computational cost of generating synthetic noisy labels, we modify the approach to utilize a more efficient hybrid approach that combines adversarial training with a pre-trained model fine-tuned on a small subset of noisy data. The pre-trained model serves as a starting point for the adversarial training process, which refines the model's performance and robustness through targeted attacks. This hybrid approach reduces the computational overhead while maintaining the benefits of adversarial training in analyzing label noise types.
Controls: We will evaluate the hybrid approach against the original adversarial training baseline, as well as the standard cross-entropy loss and reweighted loss function for label noise mitigation [5, 7].
Estimated cost: 150 GPU-hours (reduced from 180)
Prediction: We expect the hybrid approach to maintain the performance benefits of adversarial training while reducing computational costs, allowing for more extensive analysis of label noise types. However, the performance of the model may degrade if the pre-trained model is not well-suited for the specific task or noisy dataset.

PROPOSAL 5: Using Transfer Learning to Mitigate Label Noise in Pre-Trained Models
We propose a transfer learning-based approach to mitigate label noise in pre-trained models. Specifically, we fine-tune a pre-trained model on a small subset of clean data and then apply a noise-aware loss function to adapt the model to the noisy data. By leveraging the knowledge gained from the pre-training process, our approach aims to improve the model's robustness to label noise and yield better performance on downstream tasks.
Controls: We will evaluate our approach against a baseline of fine-tuning a pre-trained model on the noisy dataset without any noise-aware loss function. We will also compare our approach to the reweighted loss function [5] and uncertainty-aware weighting of noisy labels [3].
Estimated cost: 120 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect our approach to leverage the advantages of transfer learning and fine-tuning to improve the model's performance on noisy data, particularly when the pre-training task is related to the downstream task. However, the choice of pre-trained model and fine-tuning strategy may require careful tuning, and the performance of the model may degrade if the pre-trained model is not well-suited for the noisy dataset.

PROPOSAL 6: A Theoretical Framework for Understanding the Effects of Label Noise on Deep Neural Networks
We propose a novel theoretical framework that analyses the effects of label noise on deep neural networks from an information-theoretic perspective. Our framework provides a rigorous mathematical framework for understanding how label noise impacts the capacity of neural networks, and we derive a series of theoretical results that demonstrate the impact of label noise on model performance.
Controls: We will evaluate the theoretical framework against existing empirical results, and provide a comparison with real-world experiments that demonstrate the framework's accuracy and relevance.
Estimated cost: (theoretical analysis only, no computational cost)
Prediction: We expect our theoretical framework to provide valuable insights into the effects of label noise on deep neural networks, and identify key factors that contribute to model degradation. However, the applicability of the framework may be limited to specific types of neural networks or label noise distributions, and additional empirical research may be required to generalize the results.

PROPOSAL 7: A Large-Scale Empirical Comparison of Label Noise Mitigation Methods
We conduct a large-scale empirical comparison of the proposed label noise mitigation methods, including the iterative label correction, uncertainty-aware weighting, transfer learning, and adversarial training approaches. We evaluate their performance on a diverse set of real-world datasets and investigate their strengths and weaknesses, providing a comprehensive understanding of their applicability and limitations.
Controls: We will compare the performance of the label noise mitigation methods against a set of strong baselines, including the standard cross-entropy loss and reweighted loss function for label noise mitigation [5]. We will also perform an ablation study to examine the impact of different hyperparameters and configuration settings on the performance of each method.
Estimated cost: 300 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect our large-scale empirical comparison to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different label noise mitigation methods, and identify the most effective approaches for specific types of label noise and datasets.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Event-RGB Fusion for Dense Semantic Prediction in Dynamic Scenes
PROPOSAL: Implement a novel Event-RGB Fusion Network (ERFN) that combines the strengths of event cameras and RGB cameras to predict dense semantic maps at any time within the perceptual gap. ERFN will consist of an RGB encoder, an event encoder, and a fusion module that aggregates and transforms event and RGB features. The network will use a dynamic convolutional layer to effectively incorporate event data and a recurrent unit to generate predictions at any timestamp within the perceptual gap.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Predictions made using single RGB frame, Baseline 2: Predictions made using past RGB frames, Baseline 3: Predictions made using event data without RGB information.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ERFN is expected to outperform baselines and achieve state-of-the-art performance on dynamic scenes. However, we expect challenges in selecting the optimal set of events to use and aggregating event information across different timestamps.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Event-RGB Fusion for Dense Semantic Prediction in Dynamic Scenes
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL: Implement a multi-stage Event-RGB Fusion Network (ERFN) for dense semantic prediction. The network will consist of: Stage 1 - RGB Encoder, Stage 2 - Dynamic Event Encoder, Stage 3 - Temporal Reasoning Module for aggregating events, Stage 4 - Prediction Module for generating dense semantic maps at any timestamp. The Temporal Reasoning Module will leverage graph-based methods to model the spatiotemporal relationships between events and the Prediction Module will use a variant of the transformers architecture to process the RGB and event features in parallel.
CONTROLS: Identical to previous proposal, plus ablation study on the efficacy of each stage and sensitivity analysis on the temporal window size.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised ERFN is expected to significantly boost performance by effectively exploiting the strengths of both event and RGB cameras. However, addressing the difficulty of modeling the spatiotemporal relationships between events and RGB data may still pose a challenge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Quality of Event Data for Semantic Prediction
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of different event quality metrics and filtering techniques on the performance of the Event-RGB Fusion Network (ERFN). We will analyze how different event metrics (e.g., timestamp, x, y coordinates, polarity, and intensity) and filtering techniques (e.g., thresholding, temporal and spatial smoothing) influence the quality of the predicted semantic maps. We will also explore the trade-offs between event filtering and the loss of information.
CONTROLS: Compare event filtering techniques with each other and with the baseline ERFN performance.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study is expected to provide insights into the importance of event data quality and the optimal filtering techniques for achieving good performance, but might reveal that some filtering methods might not be beneficial for certain scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: RGB-Event Fusion with Attention Mechanism for Temporally Distant Targets
PROPOSAL: Incorporate an attention mechanism into the Event-RGB Fusion Network (ERFN) to selectively focus on RGB features relevant to distant temporally targets while being informed by the event data for spatial reasoning. This will be achieved through a temporal attention module that learns to weights the contribution of RGB features from past frames based on their relevance to the target time.
CONTROLS: Compare attention-based ERFN against baseline ERFN and compare the attention weights learned by the module against ground truth target locations.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The attention mechanism is expected to significantly improve performance for temporally distant targets by allowing the network to selectively focus on the most relevant features, but might struggle with cases where the attention module is misled by noise or has limited information about the target location.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Dynamic Scene Complexity on Event-RGB Fusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the performance of the Event-RGB Fusion Network (ERFN) and its variants (including the attention-based ERFN) on a diverse set of dynamic scenes with varying levels of complexity (e.g., object density, movement speed, occlusion, and camera motion). We will analyze how the models adapt to different scenarios and assess the robustness of the predictions.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of ERFN and its variants on a range of dynamic scenes (e.g., highway, pedestrian area, factory floor) and compare the accuracy of predictions with ground truth.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study is expected to reveal whether ERFN and its variants can achieve robust performance across a wide range of dynamic scenes but might highlight certain scenarios where the models struggle with increased complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Event-RGB Fusion Models on Autonomous Driving Domains
PROPOSAL: Investigate the transferability of the Event-RGB Fusion Network (ERFN) and its variants across different autonomous driving domains (e.g., highway driving, urban driving, construction zones). We will fine-tune pre-trained ERFN weights on a target domain and evaluate its performance compared to a model trained from scratch. Additionally, we will analyze the importance of domain-adversarial training for robust transfer learning.
CONTROLS: Compare the transfer learning performance of ERFN and its variants using various pre-training settings and target domains.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study is expected to demonstrate the efficacy of transfer learning for event-RGB fusion models across different autonomous driving domains but might highlight challenges in adapting to significant domain shifts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Event-RGB Fusion with Temporal Consistency Regularization for Drone Navigation
PROPOSAL: Adapt the Event-RGB Fusion Network (ERFN) for drone navigation by incorporating a temporal consistency regularization technique to ensure that predictions are consistent with the temporal evolution of the scene. This will be achieved through a novel temporal consistency loss function that penalizes the network for predicting semantic labels that are not temporally plausible.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the ERFN with temporal consistency regularization against a non-regularized ERFN on drone navigation datasets, such as Flir tenosity and or_dataset
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study is expected to demonstrate the importance of temporal consistency regularization for event-RGB fusion models in drone navigation domains, but might highlight challenges in balancing the regularization term and the task-oriented loss function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Quantitative Analysis of Event Camera Sampling Strategies for High-Fidelity Semantic Prediction
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of different event camera sampling strategies (e.g., uniform sampling, adaptive sampling based on intensity or spatial location) on the performance of the Event-RGB Fusion Network (ERFN) for high-fidelity semantic prediction. We will analyze the trade-offs between computational resources, event data overhead, and prediction accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of ERFN using various event camera sampling strategies and a baseline ERFN using the native event data.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study is expected to reveal the most effective event camera sampling strategies for event-RGB fusion models but might highlight challenges in balancing the trade-offs between sampling rates, event data quality, and computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sensor Fusion and Edge Case Handling for Quadruped Robot Navigation using Event-RGB Fusion
PROPOSAL: Adapt the Event-RGB Fusion Network (ERFN) for quadruped robot navigation by incorporating sensor fusion techniques to combine event camera, RGB camera, and lidar data. Additionally, we will develop edge case handling mechanisms to mitigate the effects of adverse weather conditions, camera motion blur, and other challenging scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the ERFN with sensor fusion and edge case handling against a non-fusion ERFN on quadruped robot navigation datasets.
COST: 130 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study is expected to demonstrate the effectiveness of sensor fusion and edge case handling techniques for event-RGB fusion models in quadruped robot navigation domains but might highlight challenges in selecting the optimal fusion strategies and edge case handling mechanisms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Event-RGB Fusion Architecture for High-Speed Scene Understanding in Autonomous Systems
PROPOSAL: develop a unified event-RGB fusion architecture that integrates the key findings and contributions of the preceding experiments and proposals. The unified architecture will be evaluated on a suite of autonomous driving, drone navigation, and quadruped robot navigation datasets to demonstrate its effectiveness and robustness in high-speed scene understanding applications. Additionally, we will provide a detailed analysis of the computational efficiency and real-time capability of the unified architecture.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the unified architecture against state-of-the-art methods on the autonomous driving, drone navigation, and quadruped robot navigation datasets.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study is expected to demonstrate the potential of unified event-RGB fusion architecture for high-speed scene understanding in various autonomous systems, but might highlight challenges in optimizing the architecture for real-time applications and deployed environments.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: RGB-Event Fusion with Temporal Contextualization for High-Frame-Rate Semantic Perception
PROPOSAL: Investigate the improvement in dense semantic segmentation by fusing RGB and event data with a novel temporal contextualization module, which integrates information from past RGB frames and event streams to predict future semantic maps.
CONTROLS: Compare against a frame-based fusion approach that simply combines RGB and event features at each timestamp, and an ablation that removes the temporal contextualization module.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method is expected to demonstrate improved segmentation accuracy and temporal consistency compared to the baselines, particularly in highly dynamic scenes. It may struggle in scenarios with low event rates or high occlusion rates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of RGB-Event Fusion to Variations in Event Rates and Frame Rates
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the RGB-event fusion method (1) performs under varying event rates and RGB frame rates, simulating different types of dynamic scenes and imaging conditions. This will help identify potential failure points and guide the development of more robust methods.
CONTROLS: Use a settings-controlled synthetic dataset to systematically vary event rates and RGB frame rates. Compare results against a baseline that uses only the RGB data.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The RGB-event fusion method is expected to be more sensitive to low event rates and high frame rates compared to high event rates and low frame rates. It may require adaptations to handle these scenarios effectively.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of RGB-Event Fusion to Variations in Event Rates and Frame Rates
PROPOSAL: Refine experiment 2 by including a real-world evaluation component, where the RGB-event fusion method is tested on real-world datasets with varying event rates and RGB frame rates, such as lower-fidelity datasets collected from low-performance sensors or reduced frame rate datasets to simulate high-speed scenarios.
CONTROLS: Retain the synthetic dataset for extensive analysis but add real-world datasets to validate robustness in real-world scenarios.
COST: 100 GPU-hours + IDR (image and sensor data retrieval) from relevant real-world datasets
PREDICTION: The RGB-event fusion method is expected to struggle in real-world datasets with low event rates and high frame rates due to the realistic noise and variability present in these settings, but may still outperform the baseline RGB-only method in these conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Event-Driven Loss Functions on RGB-Event Fusion
PROPOSAL: Explore the impact of event-driven loss functions on the RGB-event fusion framework, which adapt the loss calculation to the frequency and magnitude of event-driven updates, potentially improving the model's robustness to event rate variations.
CONTROLS: Implement two variants of the event-driven loss function: one based on the rate of updates and another based on the entropy of the event stream. Compare against a standard MSE loss function used in RGB-only semantic segmentation.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The event-driven loss function is expected to improve the RGB-event fusion method's robustness under low event rate conditions but may require careful hyperparameter tuning to avoid over-fitting to the noisier event data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamic Network Pruning for Efficient RGB-Event Fusion
PROPOSAL: Introduce a dynamic network pruning mechanism to discard or adjust network weights based on their relevance to the event-driven updates, enabling efficient allocation of computational resources towards the most informative regions and times.
CONTROLS: Compare against a static pruning mechanism that removes a fixed percentage of weights, and an oracle that knows which weights are irrelevant a priori.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The dynamic network pruning is expected to reduce inference time and energy consumption while maintaining comparable or improved semantic segmentation accuracy compared to pruned and full models. However, determining the optimal pruning strategies and thresholds might be challenging.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning from Event Cameras for Autonomous Driving Datasets
PROPOSAL: Investigate the transferability of event cameras to datasets from other autonomous driving platforms, where event cameras might be used in conjunction with RGB cameras, potentially overcoming issues related to missmatched or absent event cameras in the training data.
CONTROLS: Compare against a fine-tuned model trained exclusively on the target autonomous driving dataset with a fixed camera setting.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Transfer learning is expected to offer a viable solution for adapting the RGB-event fusion method to various autonomous driving datasets with the availability of transferable domain-specific features, provided the target dataset can sufficiently capture event-based information from the source domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Real-World Sensor Variability and Event Camera Singularity Effects
PROPOSAL: Assess the RGB-event fusion performance on real-world data with varied sensor configurations, such as different event camera models or non-standard RGB sensors, as well as the occurrence of event camera singularity, where logical pixel rows or columns become electrically shorted and emit continuous, bogus events.
CONTROLS: Use real-world datasets collected from distinct event cameras, compare results, and investigate the effect of event camera singularity on RGB-event fusion performance.
COST: IDR (image and sensor data retrieval) and 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The RGB-event fusion method may perform suboptimally in scenarios with sensor variability or event camera singularity, particularly due to issues in noise filtering and singular event handling. However, due to the events' nature, counterintuitive event patterns could prove beneficial.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Dynamic Network Pruning for Efficient RGB-Event Fusion
PROPOSAL: Refine proposal 4 by incorporating precious information about the event camera's sensor variability and event camera singularity directly into the dynamic network pruning mechanism, allowing it to better adapt to and compensate for the reported phenomena.
CONTROLS: Include findings and observations from experiment 6 in the adaptation process.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (with additional IDR for sensor variability analysis)
PREDICTION: A properly adapted dynamic network pruning mechanism may lead to more effective resource allocation, resulting in improved model efficiency and performance under challenging real-world conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Optimizing Hyperparameters for Event-Driven Learning using Bayesian Optimization and Active Learning
PROPOSAL: Use Bayesian optimization combined with active learning to select the optimal hyperparameters for the RGB-event fusion framework, particularly for the event-driven loss functions and the dynamic network pruning mechanism.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard grid search and random search methods.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (with additional computation for Bayesian optimization)
PREDICTION: The Bayesian optimization and active learning method is expected to significantly improve the model's performance and robustness by discovering optimal hyperparameters, potentially avoiding suboptimal outcomes found in standard hyperparameter search methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: High-Frame-Rate Semantic Perception in Autonomous Vehicles: Quantifying the Benefits of RGB-Event Fusion in Safety-Critical Scenarios
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of high-frame-rate semantic perception enabled by the proposed RGB-event fusion method on safety-critical scenarios in autonomous vehicles, such as detecting pedestrians or traffic lights late in the decision-making process.
CONTROLS: Use a combination of real-world data and simulations to quantify the benefits.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (with additional analysis and evaluation time)
PREDICTION: The RGB-event fusion method is expected to improve safety-critical scenario detection in high-speed driving scenarios and provide insights into potential benefits of high-frame-rate semantic perception in real-world environments.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Causal RGB-Event Fusion for High-Frame-Rate Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: We experiment with existing RGB-event fusion methods, designed for enhancement, and evaluate their suitability for anytime prediction in the mid-gap $(t, t+\delta t)$, focusing on modifications that impose causality and temporal coherence in the fusion process. Specifically, we implement the popular Context Encoder-based method from Malloc et al. (2020) and design new components to handle causality in event camera signals and optimal temporal weighting of RGB and event features.
CONTROLS: Baseline controls will be existing non-causal and non-anytime video segmentation methods (e.g., next-frame-based temporal fusion), modified for event data with re-sampling to match the causal temporal gap.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Evaluating causal fusion with audio and event data may partially alleviate the high challenging dynamic nature, scoring around 60-70%; in contrast, performance gaps, tracking discontinuities, objects moving in and out of the scene can still hinder final performance up to 20%.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Designing a Temporal Coherence Promoting Neural Network Architecture
PROPOSAL: We design and train a new neural network architecture, dubbed "CoherentNet", aimed at promoting temporal coherence in RGB-event fusion for anytime prediction. CoherentNet incorporates temporal convolutional layers and gated recurrent units (GRUs) to process RGB and event data in a temporally consistent manner, while also leveraging cross-modal attention mechanisms to selectively focus on relevant features across modalities.
CONTROLS: Controls will be existing state-of-the-art any-time video segmentation models (e.g., video Transformers) and ablations where we remove the temporal convolutional and GRU layers from the proposed architecture.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect CoherentNet to show better performance (75-85%) than existing anytime segmentation models, particularly in scenes with high dynamic object motions. Although it may perform worse (60%) in scenes with complex, not strongly temporally coherent behaviors or in heavily occluded regions.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Designing a Temporal Coherence Promoting Neural Network Architecture
PROPOSAL: To enhance performance in scenes with complex behaviors or heavy occlusions, the revised CoherentNet architecture will incorporate an additional attention mechanism, dubbed "temporal cross-modal attention", which learns to selectively weigh the RGB and event features based on their relevance to the specific frame $I_{t+\delta t}$ being predicted, as well as a noise reduction component to mitigate event stream noise and sparse spatial support.
CONTROLS: We add an ablation to evaluate the individual contributions of the temporal cross-modal attention and the noise reduction component.
COST: Additional 500 GPU-hours, making the total for this proposal 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised CoherentNet architecture should improve performance in challenging scenarios (performance above 80%) thanks to the additional attention mechanism and noise reduction component, which address limitations in previous models that struggle to handle occlusions, noise and confidence in generated segmentation maps.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Integrating Visual Odometry Estimation for Object Tracking in Mid-Gap Predictions
PROPOSAL: To further enhance performance and robustness of CoherentNet in dynamic environments, we integrate a visual odometry estimation component into the architecture, which provides an estimate of the relative motion of objects and the camera between consecutive frames. This estimated motion is then incorporated into the CoherentNet's prediction process to track objects and maintain consistency across frames in the temporal gap.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a version of CoherentNet that incorporates a state-of-the-art visual odometry estimation method (e.g., ORB-SLAM3) to isolate the contributions of our proposed approach.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating visual odometry should greatly (up to 10-15%) reduce drift and improve tracking performance of objects even in highly dynamic scenes, because they enable more accurate information about motion over the whole perceptual gap (between and within frames).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: fRW-Tachyon: Fusing RGB and Event Cameras using Region-Wise temporal Attention Mechanism
PROPOSAL: We present a new fusion method, fRW-Tachyon, that utilizes a region-wise temporal attention mechanism to selectively combine RGB and event features across different spatial regions and time steps. fRW-Tachyon learns to weight the contributions of RGB and event cameras based on their relevance to the specific region and time, enabling more robust and accurate predictions at arbitrary timestamps in the perceptual gap.
CONTROLS: We compare fRW-Tachyon with CoherentNet (our state-of-the-art model from revising proposal 2) and other existing methods that simply concatenate or convolve RGB and event features.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: fRW-Tachyon should outperform existing methods (above 80%) by accounting for the varying relevance of RGB and event features across different regions and time steps, and therefore providing more accurate predictions even in complex dynamic scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Demonstrating Real-World Deployment and Transferability of fRW-Tachyon
PROPOSAL: To validate the practical applicability of fRW-Tachyon in real-world applications, we conduct a series of experiments using a SDK-enabled real-time autonomous driving platform, such as APEX, to deploy fRW-Tachyon on different hardware configurations and demonstrate its transferability across various sensor setups and datasets (e.g., Waymo, nuScenes). We also evaluate the extra computational overhead required for fRW-Tachyon and measure its impact on real-time processing.
CONTROLS: We compare the results with those of existing RGB-based segmentation models and control for variations in sensor parameters and hardware configurations.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours + hardware setup and software integration costs
PREDICTION: fRW-Tachyon should generalize well to different setup scenarios (transfer) with around 70-75% and dynamically adapt to varying sensor parameters by learning the strengths of the distinctive information provided by each modality (70-75% applied to multiple setups).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Event Camera Noise on fRW-Tachyon's Performance
PROPOSAL: Since event cameras can be noisy, we aim to investigate the effects of noise on the performance of fRW-Tachyon. We will simulate and experimentally evaluate the robustness of fRW-Tachyon to different types and levels of noise in event camera data, and explore potential denoising techniques to mitigate these effects.
CONTROLS: We will use existing denoising methods (e.g., capacitive spatial filtering) and compare their effectiveness with our proposed approach.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: fRW-Tachyon may experience a decrease in performance (up to 10%) with increasing event camera noise levels, but it should still be able to adapt (with around 80% accuracy without revealing the level used to generate the synthetic data) and make accurate predictions.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Causal RGB-Event Fusion for High-Frame-Rate Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: We revisit the initial causal RGB-event fusion approach and improve it by incorporating a prior knowledge-based fusion mechanism. This mechanism uses a causal mask to weigh the RGB and event features, taking into account their spatial and temporal relationships, thus enhancing the partial information from event cameras and avoiding pitfalls such as saturated or purely feature-based fusion, providing a novel and refined approach to low-latency real-time fusion of RGB and event cameras. 
CONTROLS: The comparison to our original method will highlight the merits of this revised approach. 
COST: Additional 500 GPU-hours, making the total for this revised proposal 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised fusion mechanism is expected to boost performance dramatically even when dealing with relatively short periods of motion or sparse event data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: On-the-Fly Event Camera Calibration for fRW-Tachyon
PROPOSAL: We design a lightweight, on-the-fly event camera calibration component for fRW-Tachyon, which adjusts for distortions and recalibrates as the system operates. This on-the-fly approach enables robust and accurate event camera calibration without requiring extensive pre-processing, which can be impractical in real-time scenarios.
CONTROLS: We will compare the effectiveness of this on-the-fly calibration method against the existing offline-based calibration approach and assess its impact on fRW-Tachyon's overall performance.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This novel on-the-fly calibration will enhance overall performance, especially in sunny or dynamic environments, reducing performance loss up to 8%. The method slightly adds a performance hit, estimated at about 120ms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantitative Comparison and Full-System Evaluation of fRW-Tachyon and Baseline Methods
PROPOSAL: We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed fRW-Tachyon approach against our revised causal RGB-event fusion, as well as other baseline methods on a variety of scenarios and environments, measuring the performance under conditions such as night, haze, fog and motion scenarios of varying adensity. Our key objectives include determination of its robustness and accuracy in real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: We will benchmark against existing models and compare overall performance across different dynamic scenes.
COST:  2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Comprehensive comparison is expected to highlight fRW-Tachyon's potential for robust and accurate predictions in our target autonomous systems under varying, complex scenarios (scored about 80%), showing an all-round superior performance over prior cutting-edge and closing a long-known gap which applications have identified to traditional real-word recognition challenges.

Prediction: fRW-Tachyon should generalize well to different setup scenarios (transfer) with around 70-75% and dynamically adapt to varying sensor parameters by learning the strengths of the distinctive information provided by each modality (70-75% applied to multiple setups).

PROPOSAL 6: Analyzing the Impact of Event Camera Noise on fRW-Tachyon's Performance
Since event cameras can be noisy, we aim to investigate the effects of noise on the performance of fRW-Tachyon. We will simulate and experimentally evaluate the robustness of fRW-Tachyon to different types and levels of noise in event camera data, and explore potential denoising techniques to mitigate these effects.
Controls: We will use existing denoising methods (e.g., capacitive spatial filtering) and compare their effectiveness with our proposed approach.

PROPOSAL 7: On-the-Fly Event Camera Calibration for fRW-Tachyon
We design a lightweight, on-the-fly event camera calibration component for fRW-Tachyon, which adjusts for distortions and recalibrates as the system operates. This on-the-fly approach enables robust and accurate event camera calibration without requiring extensive pre-processing, which can be impractical in real-time scenarios.

Estimated cost: 800 GPU-hours
Prediction: This novel on-the-fly calibration will enhance overall performance, especially in sunny or dynamic environments, reducing performance loss up to 8%. The method slightly adds a performance hit, estimated at about 120ms.

We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed fRW-Tachyon approach against our revised causal RGB-event fusion, as well as other baseline methods on a variety of scenarios and environments, measuring the performance under conditions such as night, haze, fog and motion scenarios of varying adensity. Our key objectives include determination of its robustness and accuracy in real-world scenarios.
Controls: We will benchmark against existing models and compare overall performance across different dynamic scenes.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Use of Pretrained Texture Synthesis Models in Personalized 3D Asset Generation
PROPOSAL: This experiment will explore whether using pretrained texture synthesis models (e.g. StyleGAN2-ADA) as a prior for our personalized 3D asset generator improves the preservation of semantic identity across viewpoints. We will fine-tune a StyleGAN2-ADA model on a dataset of texture images from various subjects (e.g. faces, animals), and use it as a prior to guide the generation of new 3D assets.
CONTROLS: Compare our approach to a baseline method that uses a simple 3D shape prior generated using a Voronoi diagram.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (training a StyleGAN2-ADA model and fine-tuning it on a synthetic dataset).
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvement in the preservation of semantic identity across viewpoints, especially for zvíř classes with high texture variability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Dataset Size and Diversity on the Robustness of Personalized 3D/4D Generation Models
PROPOSAL: This experiment will investigate how the size and diversity of training datasets affect the robustness of our personalized 3D/4D generation models. We will train and evaluate our models on datasets of varying size and diversity (e.g. a small dataset of high-quality images, a large dataset of low-quality images, a dataset of textures from different environments). We will measure the performance of our models in terms of how well they preserve semantic identity across viewpoints.
CONTROLS: Compare our results to a baseline method that uses a large, high-quality dataset for training.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (training and evaluating models on synthetic datasets).
PREDICTION: We expect to see that models trained on larger and more diverse datasets will be more robust to out-of-distribution examples, but may also be more prone to overfitting to the training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Identity Preservation in 3D/4D Generation with Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: This experiment will extend our previous work on using pretrained texture synthesis models by incorporating adversarial training to further improve the preservation of semantic identity across viewpoints. We will train a discriminator to distinguish between real and synthesized texture images, and use the generated texture images to train our 3D/4D generation model.
CONTROLS: Compare our approach to a baseline method that uses a simple 3D shape prior generated using a Voronoi diagram, and also compare to the previous texture synthesis model without adversarial training.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (training a discriminator and fine-tuning our 3D/4D generation model with adversarial training).
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvement in the preservation of semantic identity across viewpoints, especially for classes with high texture variability, and the generated 3D/4D assets will be more realistic.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Improving Identity Preservation in 3D/4D Generation with Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: This experiment will extend our previous work on using pretrained texture synthesis models and adversarial training by incorporating cycles of texture synthesis and 3D/4D generation to improve the preservation of semantic identity across viewpoints. We will use a cycle consistency loss to encourage the generated texture images and 3D/4D assets to be consistent.
CONTROLS: Compare our approach to a baseline method that uses a simple 3D shape prior generated using a Voronoi diagram, and also compare to the previous texture synthesis model and adversarial training method without cycle consistency.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours (training a discriminator, fine-tuning our 3D/4D generation model with adversarial training and cycle consistency).
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvement in the preservation of semantic identity across viewpoints, especially for classes with high texture variability, and the generated 3D/4D assets will be more realistic and consistent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Personalized 3D/4D Generation with Hierarchical Refinement
PROPOSAL: This experiment will propose a hierarchical refinement framework for personalized 3D/4D generation, where we first generate a coarse 3D/4D asset using a simplified model, and then refine it using a more detailed model to improve the preservation of semantic identity across viewpoints. We will use a coarse-to-fine loss to encourage the refined assets to be consistent with the coarse ones.
CONTROLS: Compare our approach to a baseline method that generates a single 3D/4D asset using a complex model.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours (training and evaluating the hierarchical refinement framework).
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvement in the preservation of semantic identity across viewpoints, especially for classes with high texture variability, and the generated 3D/4D assets will be more realistic and detailed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Unified Framework for Personalized 3D/4D Generation and Verification
PROPOSAL: This experiment will propose a unified framework for both generating and verifying personalized 3D/4D assets, where we not only generate an asset that preserves semantic identity across viewpoints but also verify its consistency and realism using multiple metrics. We will use an adversarial evaluator to generate a verification image for each generated asset.
CONTROLS: Compare our approach to a baseline method that only generates personalized 3D/4D assets without verification.
COST: 4000 GPU-hours (training and evaluating the unified framework).
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvement in the preservation of semantic identity across viewpoints, and the generated 3D/4D assets will be more realistic and consistent, and the verification metrics will provide a comprehensive evaluation of the generated assets.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating the Use of Pretrained Texture Synthesis Models in Personalized 3D Asset Generation
PROPOSAL: This experiment will investigate the use of pretrained texture synthesis models (e.g. StyleGAN2-ADA) as a prior for our personalized 3D asset generator, and also incorporate a self-supervised loss to improve the robustness of the texture synthesis model to out-of-distribution examples. We will fine-tune a StyleGAN2-ADA model on a dataset of texture images from various subjects (e.g. faces, animals), and use it as a prior to guide the generation of new 3D assets.
CONTROLS: Compare our approach to a baseline method that uses a simple 3D shape prior generated using a Voronoi diagram, and also compare to the previous texture synthesis model without self-supervised loss.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours (training a StyleGAN2-ADA model with self-supervised loss and fine-tuning it on a synthetic dataset).
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvement in the preservation of semantic identity across viewpoints, and the generated 3D assets will be more realistic and robust to out-of-distribution examples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferring Knowledge from 2D Images to 3D/4D Assets for Personalized Generation
PROPOSAL: This experiment will explore the possibility of transferring knowledge from 2D images to 3D/4D assets for personalized generation. We will train a 2D image-to-3D/4D asset translation model using a dataset of 2D images and 3D/4D assets of various classes, and then fine-tune it on a small dataset of 2D images of a specific class to generate personalized 3D/4D assets.
CONTROLS: Compare our approach to a baseline method that generates personalized 3D/4D assets from scratch without using 2D images as a prior.
COST: 3500 GPU-hours (training the 2D image-to-3D/4D asset translation model and fine-tuning it on a synthetic dataset).
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvement in the preservation of semantic identity across viewpoints, and the generated 3D/4D assets will be more realistic and consistent, especially for classes where high-quality 2D images are available.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Personalized 3D/4D Generation across Domains
PROPOSAL: This experiment will investigate the use of meta-learning to enable personalized 3D/4D generation across different domains (e.g. animals, vehicles, buildings). We will design a meta-learning framework that learns a common set of parameters that can be adapted to different domains, and evaluate its performance on a variety of domains.
CONTROLS: Compare our approach to a baseline method that trains a separate 3D/4D generation model for each domain.
COST: 4500 GPU-hours (training the meta-learning framework and evaluating its performance on multiple domains).
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvement in the preservation of semantic identity across domains, and the generated 3D/4D assets will be more realistic and consistent across domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Evaluation of Personalized 3D/4D Generation Models
PROPOSAL: This experiment will evaluate the performance of our personalized 3D/4D generation models on real-world datasets, including the perspective on sustainability, consumer preference, usability, and overall user experience. We will collect real-world 3D/4D scenes and samples of the models being studied and conduct user studies to assess their performance.
CONTROLS: Compare our results to a baseline method that uses a state-of-the-art generative model without personalization.
COST: 6000 GPU-hours (collecting and processing real-world data, conducting user studies).
PREDICTION: We expect to see that our personalized 3D/4D generation models will significantly outperform the baseline method in terms of user satisfaction, preference, and usability, and will demonstrate better sustainability and holistic cohesiveness in the applied market environment.

TITLE: Personalized 3D Generation usingerchant Discriminators
PROPOSAL: 
In this experiment, we train a 3D generative model using a personalized discriminator based on a shared feature extractor and a subject-specific embedding. We use the feature extractor to compare the generated 3D views with the reference views from the same subject and penalize the model if the embedded signals mismatch, which reinforces the model to learn the identity-preserving representation of the subject.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: training a 3D generative model without the personalized discriminator
- Ablation: removing the personalized discriminator in the presence of the shared feature extractor
- Baseline with supervision: training the personalized discriminator using ground truth labels (labeling each generated view with a confidence score indicating its similarity to the reference view)
COST: 100 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: This personalized discriminator can improve the identity preservation of 3D views in the generated 3D assets and we can expect a significant improvement over the baseline (25% improvement) but may fail if the shared feature extractor is not robust enough to capture the subtle differences between the generated views and the reference views.
 
Note: The experiment will be conducted on the Carla dataset with both synthetic cars and real-world cars as training data.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Personalized Video-to-4D Generation using Video-specific Masking
PROPOSAL: 
In this experiment, we adapt a 3D generative model to video-to-4D generation by introducing a video-specific masking strategy that masks out regions of the video frames that are irrelevant to the identity of the subject. We use a temporal segmentation network to segment each frame of the input video into regions of interest and regions of non-interest, and then use the region of interest as input to the 3D generative model. This can focus the model's attention on the significant features of the subject across frames.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: training a 3D generative model without the video-specific masking
- Ablation: using a fixed region of interest for all frames
- Baseline with supervision: temporally segmenting each frame using ground truth labels (labeling each pixel with a confidence score indicating its relevance to the subject's identity)
COST: 180 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: This personalized masking strategy can improve the identity preservation of the subject in the generated 4D assets and we expect a moderate improvement over the baseline (15% improvement), but may fail if the temporal segmentation network fails to accurately identify the region of interest regions.
 
Note: The experiment will be conducted on the WSDD dataset with videos of a specific person performing various actions as training data

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Personalized 3D Generation using Competitive and Cooperative Merchants
PROPOSAL: 
We modify the personalized discriminator (proposal 1) to incorporate an additional cooperative mechanism, where two or more separate discriminators learn to identify different aspects of the subject's identity. These competing discriminators are then combined using a meta-learning objective that encourages their agreement, while still maintaining the competitive pressure to better detect the subtle differences in the subject's identity.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: original version of proposal 1
- Ablation: removing either the competitive or the cooperative mechanism
- Baseline with supervision: training the competitive and cooperative discriminators using ground truth labels for the different aspects of the subject's identity
COST: 150 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: This combination of competitive and cooperative mechanisms may enhance the ability of the personalized discriminator to capture the complex and nuanced aspects of the subject's identity (30% improvement), but also may lead to overfitting or redundant representations if not properly regularized.
 
Note: We expect the proposed changes to improve upon the original result (25% improvement) and potentially reach parity with (1+(30%-25%))=60% of the ideal score

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Subject-Specific Generative Latent Space Regularization
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a regularization term that effectively reduces the drift in the generative latent space across different subjects. This regularization is achieved by aligning the latent spaces of different subjects using a subject-specific density estimation model, which adapts to the distribution of the latent codes for each subject. This adaptation enables the model to better capture and preserve the unique identity features of each subject, and improves robustness across different subjects.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: training without the subject-specific generative latent space regularization
- Ablation: removing the density estimation model
- Baseline with supervision: using ground truth labels (labeling each latent code with a confidence score indicating its relevance to the subject's identity)
COST: 140 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: This regularization can improve the identity preservation across different subjects in the generated 3D/4D assets and we expect a significant improvement over the baseline (20% improvement), but may fail if the density estimation model fails to accurately capture the semantic structure of the latent space.
 
Note: The experiment will be conducted on a mixed dataset of synthetic and real-world images and videos of different subjects, covering various scenarios and environments.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Conditional Identity-Aware Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a conditional identity-aware knowledge distillation approach, which distills knowledge from a teacher model to a student model with a conditional form of identity preservation. In this approach, the teacher model is trained to generate 3D/4D assets while preserving the subject's identity, and the student model is trained to mimic the teacher model's behavior while transferring the learned identity preservation. This knowledge distillation method can efficiently transfer the subject-specific knowledge from the teacher model to the student model, enabling the student model to generate 3D/4D assets with improved identity preservation.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: training the student model from scratch
- Ablation: removing the conditional identity-aware regularization term
- Baseline with supervision: using ground truth labels (labeling each generated asset with a confidence score indicating its similarity to the reference asset)
COST: 120 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: This approach can improve the identity preservation of the student model compared to the baseline and we expect a modest improvement (10% improvement), but may fail if the teacher model's knowledge is not properly distilled or transferred to the student model.
 
Note: The experiment will be conducted on a mixed dataset of synthetic and real-world images and videos of different subjects, with the teacher model being a pre-trained 3D/4D generative model and the student model being a lightweight model designed for efficient 3D/4D generation.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Personalized Video-to-4D Generation using Temporally Consistent Video-specific Masking
PROPOSAL: 
We modify the video-specific masking strategy (proposal 2) to incorporate a temporally consistent refinement step, where the masked region is refined over time to better capture the subject's identity and motion. This refinement step is achieved using a bidirectional recurrent neural network (BRNN) that takes into account the temporal context of the video frames. The refined masked region is then used as input to the 3D generative model, resulting in a more accurate and consistent identity preservation across the generated 4D assets.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: original version of proposal 2
- Ablation: removing the BRNN refinement step
- Baseline with supervision: using ground truth labels (labeling each masked region with a confidence score indicating its relevance to the subject's identity)
COST: 160 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: This refinement step can improve the temporally consistent identity preservation of the subject in the generated 4D assets and we expect a significant improvement over the baseline (25% improvement), but may fail if the BRNN fails to accurately capture the temporal context of the video frames.
 
Note: The refinement step can be used in conjunction with the video-specific masking strategy, potentially leading to an improved overall performance.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Subject-Agnostic Priors for Improved Identity Preservation
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a subject-agnostic prior that leverages the geometric and photometric properties of 3D/4D assets to improve identity preservation. This prior is learned from a dataset of diverse 3D/4D assets, which helps the generative model capture the underlying structure and appearance of 3D/4D assets in a subject-agnostic way. By incorporating this prior, the generative model can better preserve the identity of the subject while maintaining a realistic appearance.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: training without the subject-agnostic prior
- Ablation: removing the subject-agnostic prior
- Baseline with supervision: using ground truth labels (labeling each generated asset with a confidence score indicating its similarity to the reference asset)
COST: 130 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: This subject-agnostic prior can improve the identity preservation of the generated 3D/4D assets and we expect a moderate improvement over the baseline (12% improvement), but may fail if the prior is not robust enough to capture the diverse properties of 3D/4D assets.
 
Note: The experiment will be conducted on a mixed dataset of synthetic and real-world images and videos of different subjects, with the subject-agnostic prior being learned from a dataset of diverse 3D/4D assets.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Conditional Identity-Aware Knowledge Distillation with Targeted Regularization
PROPOSAL: 
We modify the conditional identity-aware knowledge distillation approach (proposal 4) to incorporate a targeted regularization term that encourages the student model to focus on the specific aspects of the subject's identity that are relevant to the target task (e.g. facial expression, pose, or texture). This regularization is achieved using a target loss function that is designed to capture the specific idiosyncrasies of the subject's identity. By incorporating this targeted regularization, the student model can better capture the complex and nuanced aspects of the subject's identity.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: original version of proposal 4
- Ablation: removing the targeted regularization term
- Baseline with supervision: using ground truth labels (labeling each generated asset with a confidence score indicating its similarity to the reference asset)
COST: 150 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: This targeted regularization can improve the focused identity preservation of the subject in the generated 3D/4D assets and we expect a significant improvement over the baseline (20% improvement), but may fail if the target loss function is not properly designed or the regularization term overpowers the original distillation loss.
 
Note: The experiment will be conducted on a mixed dataset of synthetic and real-world images and videos of different subjects, with the targeted regularization term being designed to capture specific aspects of the subject's identity.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Multimodal hallucination for Personalized 3D/4D Generation
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a multimodal hallucination approach for personalized 3D/4D generation, which learns to generate multiple modalities (e.g. textures, materials, and viewpoints) simultaneously and in parallel. By incorporating multimodal hallucination, the generative model can better capture the complex and nuanced aspects of the subject's identity and appearance.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: training without multimodal hallucination
- Ablation: removing one or more modalities from the hallucination process
- Baseline with supervision: using ground truth labels (labeling each generated asset with a confidence score indicating its similarity to the reference asset)
COST: 180 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: This multimodal hallucination approach can improve the overall quality and realism of the generated 3D/4D assets and we expect a significant improvement over the baseline (25% improvement), but may fail if the model is not able to effectively balance the multiple modalities and hallucinate realistic appearances.
 
Note: The experiment will be conducted on a mixed dataset of synthetic and real-world images and videos of different subjects, with the multimodal hallucination approach being learned through an optimal trade-off between texture, material, and viewpoint hallucination.

TITLE: Personalized 3D Generation using Competitive, Cooperative, and Temporally Consistent Merchants
PROPOSAL: 
We integrate the competitive, cooperative, and temporally consistent mechanisms into a unified framework, where the competitive merchants focus on capturing the subtle differences between the subject's appearances in different frames, the cooperative merchants capture the relationships between the various aspects of the subject's identity, and the temporally consistent merchants ensure that the generated 3D assets are coherent and realistic over time.
CONTROLS:

- Ablation: removing one or more of the competitive, cooperative, or temporally consistent mechanisms
- Baseline with supervision: using ground truth labels (labeling each generated asset with a confidence score indicating its similarity to the reference asset)

PREDICTION: This integrated framework can lead to a synergistic improvement in the personalized 3D generation task and we expect a significant improvement over the baseline (35% improvement), but may fail if the model is not able to effectively balance the different mechanisms and hallucinate realistic and coherent appearances.
 
Note: The experiment will be conducted on a mixed dataset of synthetic and real-world images and videos of different subjects, with the unified framework being learned through an optimal trade-off between the competitive, cooperative, and temporally consistent merchants.
