actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Additional Views on Personalized 3D Generation
PROPOSAL: We will train and evaluate a set of 3D generative models on a synthetic dataset (e.g., ShapeNet) with varying numbers of input views (from 1 to 5) and evaluate their performance on identity preservation using metrics like chamfer distance and symmetric chamfer distance.
CONTROLS: The model architectures will be controlled versions of the state-of-the-art model (e.g., Vanilla diffusion-based generative model), with identical training procedures and hyperparameters.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that providing more views will consistently improve the quality of identity preservation, with diminishing returns as the number of views increases beyond a certain threshold. However, the model may become overfitted to the training set, and quality could drop for scenes with few or no observed side views.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging Multi-View Image-to-Image Translation for Personalized 3D Generation
PROPOSAL: We will develop and evaluate a multi-view image-to-image translation framework using the CycleGAN architecture, which takes multiple 2D views of an object as input and generates a 3D model that preserves the identity of the object across views. The framework will be trained on a synthetic dataset (e.g., ShapeNet) with multiple views per scene.
CONTROLS: As a control, we will compare the proposed method with the state-of-the-art single-view image-to-3D model (e.g., Vanilla diffusion-based generative model) using the same training procedure and hyperparameters.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the proposed method will demonstrate better identity preservation and quality compared to the single-view model, especially for objects with complex geometries and orientations. However, the method may rely on strong assumptions about the relationship between the input views, which could lead to failure in cases where the views are too different or occluded.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Compositional 3D Generation: Using Pose-Aware Features for View-Aggregation
PROPOSAL: We will develop a compositional 3D generation method that aggregates pose-aware features from multiple input views to generate a single, coherent 3D model that preserves the identity of the object across views. This method will utilize a neural network to learn pose-aware features and aggregate them using attention mechanisms.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the compositional method on scenes with varying degrees of view occlusion and explore its performance compared to the state-of-the-art single-view and multi-view methods (proposals 1 and 2) using metrics like IoU and Chamfer distance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the compositional method will demonstrate improved robustness to view occlusion and outperform the single-view and multi-view methods for scenes with complex occlusion patterns. However, the method may struggle with scenes featuring objects with non-rigid geometries or dynamic poses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Data Augmentation for Personalized 3D Generation: View Synthesis and Rotation
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of data augmentation techniques to improve the robustness of personalized 3D generation models. Specifically, we will expand the training data with synthesized views and orientations of the object, and evaluate their impact on the performance of the models using metrics like identity preservation and generalizability.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the models trained with data augmentation to those trained without, and also investigate the effectiveness of different data augmentation strategies (e.g., view synthesis, rotation) and their combinations.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that data augmentation will significantly improve the robustness and generalizability of the models, especially for scenes with limited training views. However, the impact may diminish for scenes with richer training data, and the method may not be effective for objects with non-rigid geometries or dynamical poses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Implicit 3D Scene Representation for Personalized Generation
PROPOSAL: We will extend the recent work on implicit 3D scene representation (e.g., Occupancy Networks, SIREN) to develop a personalized 3D generation model that can generate 3D scenes conditioned on a specific subject, such as an animal or a person. This model will be trained using a combination of real and synthetic data.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the implicit model to the state-of-the-art 3D generation models (e.g., Vanilla diffusion-based generative model) using metrics like Chamfer distance and IoU.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the implicit model will demonstrate better generalization and quality across different subjects and viewpoints compared to the state-of-the-art models. However, the model may require significant amounts of training data and may struggle to preserve the identity of the subject in scenes with complex occlusion patterns or varying lighting conditions.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Hybrid 3D Generation: Combining Explicit and Implicit Representations
PROPOSAL: We will develop a hybrid 3D generation model that combines the strengths of explicit and implicit representations. The model will first use an explicit representation (e.g., image-to-3D translation) to generate a coarse 3D mesh, and then refine it using an implicit representation (e.g., occupancy network) to achieve higher detail and quality. This hybrid approach will be trained using a synthetic dataset (e.g., ShapeNet) and validated on real-world benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the hybrid model to the individual explicit and implicit models (proposals 2 and 5) using metrics like IoU, Chamfer distance, and visual quality.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the hybrid model will demonstrate superior performance and quality compared to the individual models, especially for scenes with complex geometries and varying lighting conditions. However, the model may require careful tuning of the hyperparameters and may struggle to generalize to new subjects or viewpoints that were not seen during training.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Hybrid 3D Generation: Combining Explicit and Implicit Representations
PROPOSAL: We will develop a hybrid 3D generation model that combines the strengths of explicit and implicit representations. The model will first use an explicit representation (e.g., image-to-3D translation) to generate a coarse 3D mesh, and then refine it using an implicit representation (e.g., occupancy network) to achieve higher detail and quality. This hybrid approach will be trained using a synthetic dataset (e.g., ShapeNet) and validated on real-world benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the hybrid model to the individual explicit and implicit models (proposals 2 and 5) using metrics like IoU, Chamfer distance, and visual quality.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the hybrid model will demonstrate superior performance and quality compared to the individual models, especially for scenes with complex geometries and varying lighting conditions. However, the model may require careful tuning of the hyperparameters and may struggle to generalize to new subjects or viewpoints that were not seen during training.

We will train and evaluate a set of 3D generative models on a synthetic dataset (e.g., ShapeNet) with varying numbers of input views (from 1 to 5) and evaluate their performance on identity preservation using metrics like chamfer distance and symmetric chamfer distance.
Controls: The model architectures will be controlled versions of the state-of-the-art model (e.g., Vanilla diffusion-based generative model), with identical training procedures and hyperparameters.
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect that providing more views will consistently improve the quality of identity preservation, with diminishing returns as the number of views increases beyond a certain threshold. However, the model may become overfitted to the training set, and quality could drop for scenes with few or no observed side views.

PROPOSAL 2: Leveraging Multi-View Image-to-Image Translation for Personalized 3D Generation
We will develop and evaluate a multi-view image-to-image translation framework using the CycleGAN architecture, which takes multiple 2D views of an object as input and generates a 3D model that preserves the identity of the object across views. The framework will be trained on a synthetic dataset (e.g., ShapeNet) with multiple views per scene.
Controls: As a control, we will compare the proposed method with the state-of-the-art single-view image-to-3D model (e.g., Vanilla diffusion-based generative model) using the same training procedure and hyperparameters.
Estimated cost: 200 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect that the proposed method will demonstrate better identity preservation and quality compared to the single-view model, especially for objects with complex geometries and orientations. However, the method may rely on strong assumptions about the relationship between the input views, which could lead to failure in cases where the views are too different or occluded.

PROPOSAL 3: Compositional 3D Generation: Using Pose-Aware Features for View-Aggregation
We will develop a compositional 3D generation method that aggregates pose-aware features from multiple input views to generate a single, coherent 3D model that preserves the identity of the object across views. This method will utilize a neural network to learn pose-aware features and aggregate them using attention mechanisms.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Baseline for Speculative Decoding Performance
PROPOSAL: We will run experiments comparing the standard speculative decoding method with self-speculative decoding techniques (EAGLE, Medusa, BiTA, LayerSkip, Lookahead decoding, and SWIFT) on a publicly available large language model (e.g., Transformer-XL or BART) using real-world benchmarks in LLM inference acceleration and multi-turn conversation. We will measure the walltime improvement, floating point operations (FLOPs), and quality of generated text using standard metrics (e.g., BLEU, Rouge, meteor).
CONTROLS: We will compare these self-speculative techniques against a vanilla, large language model baseline and also against prompt lookup decoding and standard speculative decoding baselines.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Self-speculative methods can achieve a 2x-4x speedup over standard speculative decoding with minimal quality loss, while prompt lookup decoding performs well in terms of speed but may degrade quality in multi-turn conversations. Lookahead decoding and SWIFT might show relatively lower speedups but easier implementability.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Experimenting with Recurrent Cascade Speculation
PROPOSAL: We will design an experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of a recursive cascade speculation where each self-speculative method (e.g., EAGLE, Medusa) is applied twice in sequence, and compare its performance with the non-cascaded versions of the same methods. We will also explore different combinations of twice-applied self-speculative methods to identify which technique stacking gives the best performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare the cascade speculation results against the baseline self-speculative methods and the standard speculative decoding baseline from proposal 1, with the number of cascade rounds serving as an additional variable.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Depending on the selection of self-speculative methods, the cascade speculation approach may offer better performance (walltime improvement and quality) than the non-cascaded versions of these methods, or these improvements may be faint if one or both rounds contribute little to the final output at higher speeds.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Analyzing Cascade Schedules for Self-Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We will propose a theoretical framework for analyzingthe optimal cascade schedules for self-speculative decoding in the context of recursive or hierarchical cascades. Specifically, we will derive an expression for the walltime improvement of such cascades as a function of draft model selection, chain length, and characteristics of the self-speculative acceleration techniques. Our framework will also include the impacts of intermediate draft models' costs, acceptance rates, and potential interactions between draft models.
CONTROLS: We will analyze the implications of our theoretical results on the choice of hyperparameters and design strategies for cascade speculation.
COST: Minimal (theoretical work)
PREDICTION: Our theoretical analysis will identify some universal relationships between walltime improvement and the key parameters of cascade schedules (e.g., acceptance rates and costs) that can be leveraged to prune potentially suboptimal cascade configurations and inform design decisions, reducing the number of experiment trials and hyperparameter search efforts required to achieve desired performance.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Selection through Online Personalization
PROPOSAL: We will design an experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of adaptively selecting draft models in a hierarchical cascade based on the characteristics of the input sequence, and compare it to pre-specified cascade schedules. We will apply a learning-to-rank (LTR) method that integrates the target model's hidden states and contextual information to select the most suitable draft model at each step of the cascade.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results against the fixed-cascade selection baseline from proposal 2 and measure its performance against the baseline self-speculative methods and standard speculative decoding from proposal 1, under varying input sequence lengths and complexity.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (including training the LTR model)
PREDICTION: Adaptive cascade selection is expected to outperform static cascade configurations in terms of walltime improvement, especially for longer sequences where the characteristics of the sequence change. However, the improvement might depend on the capacity of the target model to capture relevant context for the LTR model to make informed decisions.

ACTION: REVISE 4 (Adaptive Cascade Selection through Online Personalization)
PROPOSAL: We will modify proposal 4 to use an online, real-time Adaptative learning approach based on gradient descent to adjust the weights of the LTR model that determines the optimal sequence of self-speculative methods throughout the cascade, based on the input sequence and the hidden states generated by the cascade. This will allow the model to learn in real-time and adjust to the input characteristics.
CONTROLS: We will keep the controls the same as before, with a comparison to the baseline self-speculative methods and standard speculative decoding.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Adaptive Cascade Selection is expected to reach its full potential by incorporating the power of real-time gradient learning to optimize hyperparameters for different input sequences. This may significantly outperform static cascade configurations by generating more accurate and adaptive decisions at each step of the cascade.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Real-time Adaptive Cascade Selection through Gradient Descent
PROPOSAL: We will modify proposal 4 to use an online, real-time Adaptive learning approach based on gradient descent to adjust the weights of the LTR model that determines the optimal sequence of self-speculative methods throughout the cascade, based on the input sequence and the hidden states generated by the cascade. This will allow the model to learn in real-time and adjust to the input characteristics.
CONTROLS: We will keep the controls the same as before, with a comparison to the baseline self-speculative methods and standard speculative decoding.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Adaptive Cascade Selection is expected to reach its full potential by incorporating the power of real-time gradient learning to optimize hyperparameters for different input sequences. This may significantly outperform static cascade configurations by generating more accurate and adaptive decisions at each step of the cascade.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Intermediate Model Complexity
PROPOSAL: We will perform an experiment to evaluate the relationship between the complexity of the intermediate models in a cascade and the overall performance of the speculative decoding system. We will compare the results of using fixed-size, fewer layers, or modified architecture draft models at different positions in the cascade against the baseline fixed model cascade from proposal 2.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results against the baseline fixed model cascade from proposal 2 and the real-time adaptive cascade selection approach from proposal 4, with a focus on exploring different levels of complexity.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Varying the complexity of intermediate models may lead to trade-offs between walltime improvement and quality of generated text. If we find that using simpler models results in acceptable quality but requires less compute, it could pave the way for systems optimized for training speed and resource efficiency. However, differences in accuracy, due to the reduced parameter count, might outweigh any given improvement, by potentially leading to even fewer correct predictions.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Assessing Real-World Performance of Cascade Speculation in Representative Domains
PROPOSAL: We will apply the cascade speculation methodology to commonly used machine translation, summarization, and question answering datasets, evaluating the actual impact on inference speed, accuracy, and overall system performance compared to standard speculative decoding, retrieval-based drafting methods, and fixed size draft models. This will help assess cascade speculation's real-world potential beyond lab settings.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results from cascade speculation against established baselines in the respective domains, and examine the findings by specific sub-task and sequence distribution within each dataset, highlighting differences and general trends across the domain and task.
COST: 350 GPU-hours (due to real-world benchmark comparison)
PREDICTION: The cascade speculation approach might demonstrate promising performance gains in some real-world systems, particularly if such benefits align with the varying trade-offs among speed, quality, and model sizes observed in prior lab-based evaluations. Any discrepancies between observed and potential performance discrepancies may likely stem from sequence complexity, task semantics and existing gaps between the real comparisons of cascade speculative models with compared methods in a guaranteed realistic benchmark.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Investigating the Linearity of Cascade Speculation's Walltime Improvement
PROPOSAL: We will design a theoretical analysis to examine the linearity of cascade speculation's walltime improvement as the number of cascade rounds increases, under various assumptions about the characteristics of the self-speculative methods and the target model. This will help understand the growth rate of the speedup provided by cascade speculation and its potential limitations.
CONTROLS: We will apply our theoretical framework to special cases where we can compute the exact walltime improvement using closed form expressions, including scenarios with identical or complementary draft models.
COST: Minimal (theoretical work)
PREDICTION: Depending on the model and draft characteristics, the growth rate of speedup may exhibit near-linear, logarithmic, or even exponential growth. A near-linear relationship could validate and justify additional cascade layers leading to further performance improvements.

ACTION: REVISE 7
TITLE: Lower-Bounding the Optimal Speedup of Cascade Speculation
PROPOSAL: We will present an accompanying theoretical result to revise our previous analysis by providing a lower bound on the optimal speedup achievable by cascade speculation, which compares it with fixed size draft models over an approximation over speculation space. This work will provide an exact outcome that can be achieved anytime, also under particular and different but impactful approximations.
CONTROLS: We will apply our result across various number of layers.
COST: Minimal (theoretical work)
PREDICTION: Our work will contribute new mathematical evidence about the limitations of cascade speculation and inform the development of future speculation and draft designs. By allowing upper-bounds on (and one side) lower bound to solve and decrease the potential outcome we're showing one minimum diverse speculative multi-layer efficiency can act.

propositions.prediction: Depending on the selection of self-speculative methods, the cascade speculation approach may offer better performance (walltime improvement and quality) than the non-cascaded versions of these methods, or these improvements may be faint if one or both rounds contribute little to the final output at higher speeds.
propositions.texte: We will design an experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of a recursive cascade speculation where each self-speculative method (e.g., EAGLE, Medusa) is applied twice in sequence, and compare its performance with the non-cascaded versions of the same methods. We will also explore different combinations of twice-applied self-speculative methods to identify which technique stacking gives the best performance.
propositions.titre: Experimenting with Recurrent Cascade Speculation

propositions.controles: We will analyze the implications of our theoretical results on the choice of hyperparameters and design strategies for cascade speculation.
propositions.prediction: Our theoretical analysis will identify some universal relationships between walltime improvement and the key parameters of cascade schedules (e.g., acceptance rates and costs) that can be leveraged to prune potentially suboptimal cascade configurations and inform design decisions, reducing the number of experiment trials and hyperparameter search efforts required to achieve desired performance.
propositions.texte: We will propose a theoretical framework for analyzingthe optimal cascade schedules for self-speculative decoding in the context of recursive or hierarchical cascades. Specifically, we will derive an expression for the walltime improvement of such cascades as a function of draft model selection, chain length, and characteristics of the self-speculative acceleration techniques. Our framework will also include the impacts of intermediate draft models' costs, acceptance rates, and potential interactions between draft models.
propositions.titre: Analyzing Cascade Schedules for Self-Speculative Decoding

propositions.controles: We will keep the controls the same as before, with a comparison to the baseline self-speculative methods and standard speculative decoding.
propositions.prediction: Adaptive Cascade Selection is expected to reach its full potential by incorporating the power of real-time gradient learning to optimize hyperparameters for different input sequences. This may significantly outperform static cascade configurations by generating more accurate and adaptive decisions at each step of the cascade.
propositions.texte: We will modify proposal 4 to use an online, real-time Adaptive learning approach based on gradient descent to adjust the weights of the LTR model that determines the optimal sequence of self-speculative methods throughout the cascade, based on the input sequence and the hidden states generated by the cascade. This will allow the model to learn in real-time and adjust to the input characteristics.
propositions.titre: Real-time Adaptive Cascade Selection through Gradient Descent

propositions.controles: We will compare the results against the baseline fixed model cascade from proposal 2 and the real-time adaptive cascade selection approach from proposal 4, with a focus on exploring different levels of complexity.
propositions.prediction: Varying the complexity of intermediate models may lead to trade-offs between walltime improvement and quality of generated text. If we find that using simpler models results in acceptable quality but requires less compute, it could pave the way for systems optimized for training speed and resource efficiency. However, differences in accuracy, due to the reduced parameter count, might outweigh any given improvement, by potentially leading to even fewer correct predictions.
propositions.texte: We will perform an experiment to evaluate the relationship between the complexity of the intermediate models in a cascade and the overall performance of the speculative decoding system. We will compare the results of using fixed-size, fewer layers, or modified architecture draft models at different positions in the cascade against the baseline fixed model cascade from proposal 2.
propositions.titre: Evaluating the Impact of Intermediate Model Complexity

propositions.prediction: The cascade speculation approach might demonstrate promising performance gains in some real-world systems, particularly if such benefits align with the varying trade-offs among speed, quality, and model sizes observed in prior lab-based evaluations. Any discrepancies between observed and potential performance discrepancies may likely stem from sequence complexity, task semantics and existing gaps between the real comparisons of cascade speculative models with compared methods in a guaranteed realistic benchmark.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theory of Cascaded Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We prove that a vertical (multi-level) cascade of self-speculative decoding layers, starting with a retrieval-based draft model of negligible cost, can achieve unbounded speedup over standard speculative decoding for any given LLM, under the assumption that the self-speculative techniques used at each layer have constant computational complexity. Furthermore, we derive an upper bound on the expected walltime improvement in terms of the acceptance rates and costs of the self-speculative models.
CONTROLS: We compare against a baseline of standard speculative decoding with a single draft model, as well as ablations of the retrieval-based draft model and various self-speculative techniques at different levels of the cascade.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (analytical work)
PREDICTION: The result provides a theoretical justification for the benefits of cascading, and the upper bound provides a quantitative metric for evaluating the design of cascaded speculatively decoded LLMs. However, the assumption of constant computational complexity may not hold in practice, limiting the applicability of the result.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Cascade Configurations for Training-Free Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We conduct a thorough empirical evaluation of how different combinations of self-speculative techniques, scheduling choices, and draft lengths impact the performance of cascaded speculative decoding on multi-turn conversation, machine translation, and summarization tasks. We investigate the effect of variability in draft model characteristics and explore methods for adaptively choosing the draft model and draft length at each level of the cascade.
CONTROLS: We compare cascaded speculative decoding with various baselines, including standard speculative decoding, selectively-trained self-speculative models, and a retrieval-based statistical drafter.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The experimental results will reveal the extent to which current training-free self-speculative techniques can be combined to yield effective cascades, and will provide insights into the factors governing the performance of such cascades. Challenges may arise from the high dimensionality of the search space and the difficulty of optimizing for both speedup and quality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Scheduling for Real-World LLM Inference
PROPOSAL: Building on the insights from the previous experiment, we develop and evaluate adaptive scheduling algorithms that dynamically adjust the choice of draft model and draft length at each level of the cascade during inference, taking into account the characteristics of the input sequence and the performance of the different self-speculative techniques. We consider both model-agnostic and model-specific strategies and compare their performance on a range of LLM inference tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare the adaptive scheduling approaches against a baseline of fixed cascade configuration and against ablated versions that only consider limited information about the input sequence or the self-speculative techniques.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (including costs of fine-tuning the adaptive scheduling models)
PREDICTION: The adaptive scheduling algorithms will achieve better performance than fixed cascade configurations, but may introduce additional overhead due to the need for dynamic decision-making during inference. Challenges may arise from the need to balance exploration and exploitation in the adaptive search process.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating Cascade Configurations for Training-Free Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We revise the description of the experiment to add more details on the comparison with retrieval-based drafting methods. Specifically, we will evaluate how the cascaded speculative decoding compares to prompt lookup decoding under different conditions, including varying sizes of input sequences and different models for the draft and target LLMs. We will also investigate the sensitivity of the performance gain to the choice of the retrieval component.
CONTROLS: We compare cascaded speculative decoding with a baseline of standard speculative decoding, a retrieval-based statistical drafter, and ablated versions of the cascaded speculative decoding that replace the higher-level self-speculative models with the retrieval-based drafter or remove the retrieval component.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (no additional cost; existing experiment plan can be adapted)
PREDICTION: The comparison with retrieval-based drafting methods will provide important insights into the effectiveness of cascaded speculative decoding in a real-world setting, and will help to understand the potential for complementarity between retrieval-based and generative methods. However, it is possible that the performance gain of cascaded speculative decoding over retrieval-based methods will be limited due to the increased complexity of the former.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Cascade Configurations for Training-Free Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We revise the description of the experiment to add more details on the comparison with retrieval-based drafting methods. Specifically, we will evaluate how the cascaded speculative decoding compares to prompt lookup decoding under different conditions, including varying sizes of input sequences and different models for the draft and target LLMs. We will also investigate the sensitivity of the performance gain to the choice of the retrieval component.
CONTROLS: We compare cascaded speculative decoding with a baseline of standard speculative decoding, a retrieval-based statistical drafter, and ablated versions of the cascaded speculative decoding that replace the higher-level self-speculative models with the retrieval-based drafter or remove the retrieval component.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (no additional cost; existing experiment plan can be adapted)
PREDICTION: The comparison with retrieval-based drafting methods will provide important insights into the effectiveness of cascaded speculative decoding in a real-world setting, and will help to understand the potential for complementarity between retrieval-based and generative methods. However, it is possible that the performance gain of cascaded speculative decoding over retrieval-based methods will be limited due to the increased complexity of the former.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing the Performance of Self-Derived Draft Models in Cascaded Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We investigate the factors that contribute to the performance of self-derived draft models in cascaded speculative decoding, including the choice of self-speculative technique, the layer-wise transformation of the target model, and the training data used to fine-tune the self-derived model. We will also explore the relationship between the performance of self-derived models and the characteristics of the input sequence, such as its length, complexity, and type.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of self-derived models with baseline self-speculative techniques, trained and fine-tuned on different datasets and with different hyperparameters.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will provide insights into the design of effective self-derived draft models for cascaded speculative decoding and will help to identify the key factors that contribute to their performance. Challenges may arise from the need to balance between model flexibility and learnability, as well as the difficulty of fine-tuning self-derived models without access to ground truth data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Robustness of Cascaded Speculative Decoding to Model and Data Perturbations
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the robustness of cascaded speculative decoding to model and data perturbations, such as quantization, pruning, and adversarial attacks, as well as to dataset shifts and corruptions. We investigate how the performance of cascaded speculative decoding changes under these different perturbation scenarios and explore ways to improve its robustness.
CONTROLS: We compare the robustness of cascaded speculative decoding with baseline self-speculative techniques and standard speculative decoding.
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will provide insights into the limitations and vulnerabilities of cascaded speculative decoding and will help to identify the key factors that contribute to its robustness. Challenges may arise from the need to balance between performance and robustness, as well as the difficulty of evaluating robustness in a realistic and efficient manner.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling Cascaded Speculative Decoding to Large LLMs and Multi-Turn Conversations
PROPOSAL: We scale cascaded speculative decoding to large LLMs and multi-turn conversations, focusing on the challenges of efficient inference, incremental learning, and catastrophic forgetting. We propose novel techniques for updating the draft models and adaptive scheduling in the cascade, and evaluate their effectiveness on a range of tasks and conversational scenarios.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our scaling techniques with baseline self-speculative methods and standard speculative decoding.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will demonstrate the feasibility of using cascaded speculative decoding on large LLMs and multi-turn conversations, and identify potential improvements and challenges. Challenges may arise from the computational resource constraint, the requirement to ensure the conversation coherence and consistency, and the need to handle data drifts and concept drifts in the conversation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing Cascaded Speculative Decoding with Hybrid Generation and Retrieval Methods
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the performance of cascaded speculative decoding against a range of hybrid generation and retrieval methods, including attention-based models and adversarial training-based system. We investigate how the hybrid methods compare to each other and to cascaded speculative decoding on various LLM inference tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of cascaded speculative decoding with a series of hybrid generation and retrieval methods, with and without retrieval-based drafting components.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will provide a comprehensive comparison of the performance of cascaded speculative decoding and hybrid generation and retrieval methods on LLM inference tasks. Challenges may arise from the need to evaluate the performance of these complex methods under multiple conditions and scenarios, and to identify the factors contributing to their differences in performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Deployment and Benchmarking of Cascaded Speculative Decoding in Real-World LLM Applications
PROPOSAL: We deploy and benchmark cascaded speculative decoding in real-world LLM applications, including chatbots, content generators, and language translation systems. We evaluate the performance, efficiency, and user experience of cascaded speculative decoding in these scenarios and conduct a comprehensive case study on its feasibility and potential impact.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of cascaded speculative decoding with baseline self-speculative methods and standard speculative decoding in real-world deployments.
COST: 220 GPU-hours ( deployments and evaluations are run on cloud resources)
PREDICTION: The results will provide a comprehensive view of cascaded speculative decoding's potential in real-world LLM applications and its usability and scalability.

TITLE: Adaptive Self-Speculative Decoding with Horizontal Cascade
PROPOSAL: Implement the horizontal cascade strategy where the first tokens are generated with a slower but more accurate model and subsequent tokens with progressively faster models. Use a python script to dynamically switch between different self-speculative methods (e.g. EAGLE, Medusa, LayerSkip) based on the target model's acceptance rate, cost, and input sequence length.
CONTROLS: Compare the adaptive horizontal cascade with a fixed cascade schedule, and with the standard speculative decoding using the retrieval-based statistical drafter.

However, it may incur higher computational overhead due to the evaluation and switching between different self-speculative methods, which could be a limitation for large-scale production environments.

Evaluate different combinations of self-speculative methods, sequence lengths, and switching policies to find the optimal solution for a given model and dataset. Use a hybrid approach that combines accuracy, speed, and overhead into a single objective function, or use Pareto optimization to search for the Pareto front.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised adaptive cascades with the previous adaptive horizontal cascade, and with standard speculative decoding, using metrics such as throughput, accuracy, and computational overhead.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours (due to the increased complexity of the optimization process)
PREDICTION: The multi-criteria optimization approach will lead to more efficient and adaptive speculative decoding strategies, which can achieve better trade-offs between accuracy, speed, and overhead. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1

TITLE: Investigating Hybrid Discriminative-Generative Reward Models

PROPOSAL: Design and train a hybrid reward model that combines the strengths of discriminative and generative models. Specifically, append a small MLP-based value head to a sophisticated reasoning-based generative model (e.g., LAMMM). Train the hybrid model with a custom objective that optimizes the pairwise ranking scores from the value head while encouraging the generative model to produce high-quality, well-reasoned critiques. Evaluate the hybrid model's performance on a range of metrics, including ranking accuracy, critique quality, and calibration.

CONTROLS: Compare the hybrid model to state-of-the-art discriminative (e.g., Skywork-Reward) and generative (e.g., LAMMM-Reward) models, as well as a simple baseline where the generative model is used without the discriminative head.

COST: 100 GPU-hours (20 hours for training, 80 hours for hyperparameter tuning)

PREDICTION: The hybrid model should outperform both discriminative and generative models on ranking accuracy and critique quality, while achieving comparable or improved calibration. However, training the hybrid model may require significant hyperparameter tuning, which could impact performance.

ACTION: ADD 2

TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Calibration Anchor Techniques on Hybrid Reward Models

PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of calibration anchor techniques on the hybrid reward model from proposal 1. Specifically, implement and evaluate two calibration anchor techniques: i) tempering the generative model's critic log-likelihood with a learnable temperature parameter, and ii) using a soft version of the Bradley-Terry objective as a calibration loss. Evaluate the hybrid model's performance on calibration metrics (e.g., Brier Score, Calibration Distance) and ranking accuracy when using these calibration anchor techniques.

CONTROLS: Compare the hybrid model with and without the calibration anchor techniques to the baseline models (discriminative, generative) and the hybrid model from proposal 1, as well as ablations of the calibration anchor techniques to understand their individual contributions.

COST: 30 GPU-hours (10 hours for hyperparameter tuning, 20 hours for training and evaluation)

PREDICTION: Calibration anchor techniques should improve the calibration of the hybrid model, particularly on the soft Bradley-Terry objective variant, without sacrificing ranking accuracy.

ACTION: ADD 3

TITLE: Grounding Hybrid Reward Models in Absolute Quality Judgments using Meta-Learning

PROPOSAL: Develop a meta-learning approach to leverage limited high-quality annotations to ground the hybrid reward model in an absolute quality scale. Specifically, use a meta-training process to adapt the hybrid model to different domains and annotation budgets. In each meta-training step, the hybrid model is trained on a subset of high-quality annotations from a particular domain, and then evaluated on a separate test set from the same domain. The optimal adaptation of the model is stored, and the cycle is repeated for multiple domains. Evaluate the adapted hybrid model on its ability to generalize to unseen domains and novel annotation budgets.

CONTROLS: Compare the adapted hybrid model to its counterpart that is not adapted to new domains (i.e., solely trained on one domain).

COST: 150 GPU-hours (100 hours for meta-training, 50 hours for evaluation)

PREDICTION: The meta-learning approach should enable the hybrid model to make high-quality judgments in new domains, even with limited annotations, by learning generalizable domain-invariant features. However, the adaptation process may require significant computational resources and may not always yield high-quality judgments, especially in highly heterogeneous domains.

ACTION: ADD 4

TITLE: Investigating the Role of Annotator Agreement in Training Reward Models

PROPOSAL: Assess the impact of annotator agreement on the performance of reward models, including the hybrid model, by analyzing the effect of different annotation coalition sizes on the model's ranking accuracy and calibration. Specifically, generate simulated annotator datasets with varying levels of agreement (e.g., annotators with consistent vs. conflicting opinions), and train the hybrid model on these datasets. Evaluate the model's performance on calibration metrics and ranking accuracy for each coalision size. Analyze the contribution of annotator disagreement to the model's performance and compare it to the baselines.

CONTROLS: Compare the hybrid model's performance to the discriminative and generative models on varying annotator agreement levels and coalision sizes.

COST: 80 GPU-hours (40 hours for generating simulated annotator datasets, 40 hours for training and evaluation)

PREDICTION: The hybrid model's performance is expected to degrade as annotator agreement decreases, highlighting the need for incorporating uncertainty and variability in annotator judgments into the model's training process.

ACTION: REVISE 4

TITLE: Investigating the Role of Annotator Agreement in Training Reward Models with Uncertainty-Aware Training

PROPOSAL: Revise proposal 4 to incorporate uncertainty-aware training techniques that can handle annotator disagreement and variability in judgments. Specifically, implement a probabilistic annotation model that models annotator uncertainty and variability, and use the resulting probabilistic annotations to train the hybrid model with uncertainty-aware loss functions (e.g., Monte Carlo Dropout). Evaluate the hybrid model's performance on calibration metrics and ranking accuracy for varying annotator agreement levels.

CONTROLS: Compare the revised hybrid model to the original model and to the discriminative and generative models on varying annotator agreement levels and uncertainty-aware loss functions.

COST: 90 GPU-hours (40 hours for implementing probabilistic annotation model, 40 hours for uncertainty-aware training, 10 hours for evaluation)

PREDICTION: The revised hybrid model is expected to better capture annotator uncertainty and variability, leading to improved performance on calibration metrics and ranking accuracy, especially in settings with high annotator disagreement.

ACTION: ADD 5

TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Reward Model Drift on Long-Term Performance in Chatbot Safety and Role-Play Dialogue

PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of reward model drift on long-term performance in chatbot safety and role-play dialogue scenarios. Design a framework to continuously monitor the reward model's performance and adapt to shifts in user preferences and behaviors. Train and test the hybrid model on large-scale datasets of real-world chatbot conversations, with a focus on evaluation metrics such as response quality, safety, and engagement.

CONTROLS: Compare the baseline reward models (discriminative and generative) to the hybrid model with continuous adaptation and drift detection.

COST: 250 GPU-hours (150 hours for large-scale dataset preparation, 50 hours for continuous adaptation, 50 hours for evaluation)

PREDICTION: The hybrid model with continuous adaptation and drift detection is expected to outperform the baseline reward models, as it can better adapt to changing user preferences and behaviors over time.

ACTION: REVISE 1

TITLE: Investigating Hybrid Discriminative-Generative Reward Models with Multi-Task Learning

PROPOSAL: Revise the hybrid reward model from proposal 1 to incorporate multi-task learning (MTL) techniques, where the model is trained to perform multiple tasks simultaneously, such as ranking accuracy, critique quality, and calibration. Specifically, implement a shared representation learning framework that learns a joint embedding for the response text and the critic log-likelihood. Evaluate the hybrid MTL model's performance on various benchmark datasets and metrics.

CONTROLS: Compare the hybrid MTL model to the original hybrid model and to the discriminative and generative models on ranking accuracy, critique quality, and calibration.

COST: 180 GPU-hours (80 hours for implementing MTL framework, 40 hours for hyperparameter tuning, 60 hours for evaluation)

PREDICTION: The hybrid MTL model is expected to improve performance on multiple tasks simultaneously, including ranking accuracy, critique quality, and calibration, by learning a shared representation that captures relevant features for all tasks.

ACTION: ADD 6

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Domain Adaptation on Reward Model Performance in Code Generation and Mathematical Reasoning

PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of domain adaptation on reward model performance in code generation and mathematical reasoning tasks. Design a framework to adapt the hybrid reward model to new domains, with a focus on transfer learning and few-shot learning techniques. Evaluate the hybrid model's performance on benchmark datasets for code generation and mathematical reasoning.

CONTROLS: Compare the baseline reward models (discriminative and generative) to the hybrid model with domain adaptation on code generation and mathematical reasoning tasks.

COST: 200 GPU-hours (100 hours for implementing domain adaptation framework, 50 hours for hyperparameter tuning, 50 hours for evaluation)

PREDICTION: The hybrid model with domain adaptation is expected to outperform the baseline reward models on code generation and mathematical reasoning tasks, by adapting to the specific requirements and characteristics of each domain.

ACTION: ADD 7

TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Reward Model Explainability on Human Alignment and Trust in Chatbot Systems

PROPOSAL: Evaluate the impact of reward model explainability on human alignment and trust in chatbot systems. Implement a framework to provide interpretable feedback to users on the reasoning behind the reward model's decisions. Use eye-tracking and user surveys to study how users interact with and trust the chatbot system when receiving interpretable feedback. Compare the performance of the chatbot system with and without interpretable feedback.

CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the chatbot system with the hybrid model and other reward models, with and without interpretable feedback.

COST: 220 GPU-hours (100 hours for implementing interpretable feedback framework, 50 hours for eye-tracking and user surveys, 70 hours for evaluation)

PREDICTION: The hybrid model with interpretable feedback is expected to improve human alignment and trust in chatbot systems, by providing users with a deeper understanding of the reasoning behind the reward model's decisions.

ACTION: REVISE 7

TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Reward Model Explainability on Human Alignment and Trust in Chatbot Systems with a Human-in-the-Loop Framework

PROPOSAL: Revise proposal 7 to incorporate a human-in-the-loop framework, where users can interact with and correct the reward model in real-time. Implement a system where users can provide feedback on the reward model's decisions, and use this feedback to update the model's parameters and improve its performance. Evaluate the human-in-the-loop framework's impact on human alignment and trust in chatbot systems.

CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the chatbot system with and without the human-in-the-loop framework, with and without interpretable feedback.

COST: 250 GPU-hours (120 hours for implementing human-in-the-loop framework, 60 hours for user studies and feedback collection, 70 hours for evaluation)

PREDICTION: The human-in-the-loop framework with interpretable feedback is expected to significantly improve human alignment and trust in chatbot systems, by enabling users to correct mistakes and fine-tune the reward model's performance in real-time.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Bounding Confidence in Discriminative Reward Models
PROPOSAL: Develop and analyze probabilistic discriminative reward models using probabilistic output layers (e.g., Bernoulli or categorical distributions) to capture the uncertainty in human preference judgments. We will derive probabilistic versions of Bradley-Terry's objective and a corresponding meta-learning schedule to adapt the reward model's confidence over the course of training. We will evaluate the impact of incorporating probabilistic uncertainty on the reward model's calibration, ranking accuracy, and robustness to annotator disagreement using existing datasets (e.g.,.rnnclonne,_seenchange/select cognronder-in-stnu_in selectors.transpose_Pled) optimized separately with Bradley Terry . 
CONTROLS: a) Bradley-Terry objective without probabilistic uncertainty, b) dominant discriminative baselines like Skywork-Reward and HelpSteer2-Preference.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating probabilistic uncertainty might lead to a 2-5% improvement in ranking accuracy and a 20-30% decrease in annotator disagreement effects on model performance, with potential computational costs arising from the increased complexity of probabilistic loss functions and meta-learning schedules. However, improvements may be mitigated if the probabilistic outputs solely reflect irrelevant noise in annotation data rather than genuine uncertainty.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED - Bounding Confidence in Discriminative Reward Models
PROPOSAL: Refine the probabilistic discriminative reward model by introducing an explicit uncertainty component, modeled as a Bayesian neural network (BNN) or a Monte Carlo dropout. This will allow the model to quantify its uncertainty and output a distribution over possible reward scores. To adapt the model's confidence over the course of training, we will use a Gaussian process (GP) to learn an adaptive learning rate schedule for the BNN's posterior regularization. Evaluate the performance of this revised approach using the same datasets and baseline models as before, with a focus on assessing the impact of the uncertainty component on ranking accuracy and robustness to annotator disagreement.
CONTROLS: a) baseline discriminative rewards without BNN/MCD dropout, b) Bayesian neural network with fixed GP prior, c) ablation study to determine the importance of the adaptive learning rate schedule

COST: unchanged at 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised approach should lead to a 5-10% improvement in ranking accuracy and a 30-50% decrease in the effect of annotator disagreement on model performance, with potential computational costs arising from the need to sample from the BNN's output distribution. However, improvements may be mitigated if the uncertainty component does not capture genuine uncertainty, but rather noise in the annotation data.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Interpretable Reward Models with Context-Aware Selective Reranking
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel reward model architecture that incorporates multi-task learning and selective reranking to improve the quality and coverage of the reward signal. Inspired by the success of graph neural networks (GNNs) in encoding contextual relationships, we will propose a contextual reranking method that uses a GNN to model the context in which a candidate is evaluated, and a selective reranking algorithm that reorders the candidates based on the learned contextual relationships. Evaluation will be performed on real-world datasets from domains like code generation, chatbot safety, and role-play dialogue. We will also compare our approach to existing reranking and attention-based methods.
CONTROLS: a) baseline discriminative rewards (from proposal 1), b) reranking methods like global-reranking and bottleneck reranking, c) ablation study to determine the impact of the GNN and selective reranking components.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The contextual reranking method should lead to a 15-25% improvement in ranking accuracy and a 50-75% decrease in the proportion of low-quality responses, thanks to the model's ability to capture complex contextual relationships. However, the increased complexity of the GNN and selective reranking components may introduce computational costs and require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Adaptation of Reward Models to New Domains with Limited Qualitative Annotations
PROPOSAL: Investigate the problem of adapting a pre-trained reward model to a new domain with limited qualitative annotations, using a novel combination of meta-learning and few-shot learning techniques. We will propose a domain-adaptation framework that leverages the following components: 1) a meta-learner that computes a representation of the reward distribution across different domains, 2) a few-shot learner that adapts the pre-trained reward model to the new domain using a small set of qualitative annotations. To evaluate our approach, we will use a mix of real-world datasets from diverse domains like code generation, math reasoning, and chatbot safety, and compare our results with state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods.
CONTROLS: a) baseline discriminative rewards (from proposal 1), b) few-shot learning methods with fixed meta-learner, c) ablation study to determine the impact of the few-shot learner and meta-learner components.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed domain-adaptation framework should lead to a 30-50% reduction in the number of qualitative annotations required for domain adaptation and a 20-35% improvement in ranking accuracy on the new domain, thanks to the effective combination of meta-learning and few-shot learning techniques. However, the increased complexity of the domain-adaptation framework may introduce computational costs and require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Reward-Aware Prompt Engineering for Improved LLM Alignment
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of reward-aware prompt engineering on the alignment of large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. We will propose a novel framework that combines reward-based optimization with prompt engineering techniques to learn informative and effective prompts that guide the LLM towards optimal alignments. To evaluate our approach, we will use a mix of real-world datasets from domains like chatbot safety, role-play dialogue, and code generation, and compare our results with state-of-the-art prompt engineering methods.
CONTROLS: a) baseline discriminative rewards (from proposal 1), b) prompt engineering methods with fixed reward function, c) ablation study to determine the impact of the reward-aware prompt engineering component.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed reward-aware prompt engineering framework should lead to a 25-40% improvement in ranking accuracy and a 15-25% increase in the proportion of well-aligned responses, thanks to the effective combination of reward-based optimization and prompt engineering techniques. However, the increased complexity of the framework may introduce computational costs and require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Annotator Disagreement on Reward Model Performance
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of annotator disagreement on the performance of reward models, and propose a novel approach to mitigating its effects. We will collect a large-scale dataset of annotated responses with multiple annotations per response, and use it to evaluate the impact of annotator disagreement on reward model performance. We will also propose a novel approach that combines meta-learning and bootstrap aggregating (bagging) to mitigate the effects of annotator disagreement. To evaluate our approach, we will use a mix of real-world datasets from domains like chatbot safety, role-play dialogue, and code generation.
CONTROLS: a) baseline discriminative rewards (from proposal 1), b) reward models trained on a single annotation per response, c) ablation study to determine the impact of the meta-learning and bagging components.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed approach should lead to a 20-35% improvement in ranking accuracy and a 10-20% reduction in the impact of annotator disagreement on reward model performance, thanks to the effective combination of meta-learning and bagging techniques. However, the increased complexity of the approach may introduce computational costs and require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: REVISED - Adaptation of Reward Models to New Domains with Limited Qualitative Annotations
PROPOSAL: Refine the domain-adaptation framework proposed in the original proposal to incorporate a more efficient and effective embedding-based approach for adapting the reward model to new domains. We will use a dense neural embedding space to capture the relationships between different domains and reward models, and adapt the reward model to a new domain by learning a specialized embedding that maps the new domain to the reward model's existing embedding space. To evaluate our revised approach, we will use the same datasets and evaluation metrics as before, and compare our results with both the original domain-adaptation framework and state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods.
CONTROLS: a) baseline discriminative rewards (from proposal 1), b) original domain-adaptation framework, c) ablation study to determine the impact of the dense embedding space and adapted embedding components.
COST: unchanged at 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised approach should lead to a 40-55% reduction in the number of qualitative annotations required for domain adaptation and a 25-40% improvement in ranking accuracy on the new domain, thanks to the more efficient and effective embedding-based adaptation mechanism. However, the increased complexity of the revised approach may introduce computational costs and require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Reward Model Predictive Uncertainty for Adaptive Decision-Making
PROPOSAL: Investigate the predictive uncertainty of reward models and explore its application to adaptive decision-making in LLM alignment tasks. We will propose a novel approach that uses the predictive uncertainty of a reward model to adaptively adjust the level of exploration vs. exploitation in decision-making. We will use a mix of real-world datasets from domains like chatbot safety, role-play dialogue, and code generation to evaluate our approach and compare its performance with state-of-the-art decision-making methods.
CONTROLS: a) baseline discriminative rewards (from proposal 1), b) decision-making methods without reward model uncertainty, c) ablation study to determine the impact of the predictive uncertainty component.
COST: 1600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed approach should lead to a 30-50% improvement in decision-making accuracy and a 20-30% reduction in exploration overhead, thanks to the effective use of reward model predictive uncertainty to adaptively adjust the level of exploration vs. exploitation. However, the increased complexity of the approach may introduce computational costs and require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Scalable and Explainable Reward Model Training with Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the application of hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) to reward model training, with a focus on scalability and explainability. We will propose a novel HRL framework that uses a high-level policy to manage the reward model training process and a low-level policy to select the next set of parameters to evaluate. Our framework will incorporate a learned explanation mechanism to provide insights into the reward model's decision-making process. To evaluate our approach, we will use a mix of real-world datasets from domains like chatbot safety, role-play dialogue, and code generation.
CONTROLS: a) baseline discriminative rewards (from proposal 1), b) HRL methods without learned explanation mechanism, c) ablation study to determine the impact of the high-level and low-level policy components.
COST: 2200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed approach should lead to a 50-70% reduction in the number of parameters and a 30-40% improvement in explainability of the reward model's decision-making process, thanks to the effective use of HRL and the learned explanation mechanism. However, the increased complexity of the approach may introduce computational costs and require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Quantile-Based Reward Modeling for Uncertainty Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a new discriminative reward model architecture that incorporates quantile regression (QR) to estimate the uncertainty of the preferred response. This model will be trained with both absolute quality labels and pairwise preference data, leveraging the complementary strengths of both to produce calibrated, probabilistic scores that capture the certainty of the ranking.
CONTROLS: 
- A baseline discriminative reward model using Bradley-Terry objective
- An ablation model removing the absolute quality labels and using only pairwise data
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the quantile-based model to outperform the baseline in ranking accuracy and provide more interpretable, confidence scores. It might fail if the absolute quality annotations are noisy or class-balanced annotation is poor.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Evaluating Reward Model Calibration on In-Domain and Out-of-Domain Tasks
PROPOSAL: We propose a set of experiments to extensively evaluate the calibration and generalizability of our quantile-based reward model (from Proposal 1) on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets. This includes assessing its performance in ranking tasks, as well as its ability to accurately estimate confidence in novel, unseen domains (e.g., using simulated or real-world chatbot responses evaluated in contexts like code generation or mathematical reasoning).
CONTROLS: 
- The quantile-based reward model (Proposal 1)
- A statistical scoring model (e.g. Thomson-statistic, ranked percentile flips)
- 4 in-domain datasets (e.g., conversation ranking, code generation).
3 out-of-domain datasets (e.g., code generation with ambiguous specifications)
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate the proposed reward model to achieve better calibration and confidence accuracy in uncertain regions. The model may degrade in out-of-domain tasks where preferential patterns and scales differ, highlighting its intrinsic limitations.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Causal Reconstruction of Human Preference Signals
PROPOSAL: Building on recent research in causal reasoning, we propose a novel framework to analyze the causal relationships underlying human preference signals. We will apply structural causal models to understand which factors in the dialogue, such as conversational context, linguistic features, or overfitting predictors, contribute to the resulting preference. This will enable more targeted interventions to mitigate predictable forms of error arising from reward-model mismatch.
CONTROLS: 
- High-quality, causally annotated datasets (e.g. ones that involve dialogues about societal norms of dignity, safety, or moral values)
- The non-proposed reward models 
- Random forests.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This framework should help identify key drivers of human preference mismatch in our presently proposed reward model and its probabilistic counterparts, enhancing compensatory interventions in challenges such as hierarchy disagreement or feedback lapses.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Extension of Quantile-Based Reward Modeling for Ranking Multiple Responses

PREDICTION: With the additional extension, we anticipate the revised model to excel in tasks that require ranking multiple responses. propositions.titre: Human-in-the-Loop Reward Validation for LLM Alignment and Value Alignment

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Unified Metric for External and Internal Knowledge Utilization
PROPOSAL: Design a hybrid metric that combines the KL-divergence between the output distribution and the context distribution with the KL-divergence between the output distribution and the model's internal prior, to quantify both external and internal knowledge utilization. Weight the two KL-divergences by learnt parameters, and compute the final score using an averaging or weighted summation approach.
CONTROLS: Compare to ReDeEP's scores on various tasks, as well as to a baselines that only uses one of the two KL-divergences.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This metric might outperform ReDeEP in most tasks, especially when the model's internal knowledge is inconsistent or incomplete, but might struggle when dealing with multi-step reasoning or complex context.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Zero-Shot Generalization of the Unified Metric
PROPOSAL: Train a small multi-task learning model to predict both the attentive representation of the input context and the output distribution, on a diverse set of tasks and datasets. The unified metric from proposal 1 can be used as a secondary task, allowing the model to learn features that generalize to different tasks and datasets. Use the trained model to extract features from any new model and task, allowing zero-shot transfer of the unified metric.
CONTROLS: Test on retrieval-augmented question answering and news summarization tasks, as well as compare to a model that is trained only on a single task and dataset.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This model might achieve good zero-shot generalization, but might require a large validation set to fine-tune the features before applying them to a new task, and the costs of training such a multi-task model might outweigh its benefits.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Unified Metric for External and Internal Knowledge Utilization
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Design a hybrid metric that combines the power mean distances between the output distribution and the context distribution, with the power mean distances between the output distribution and the model's internal prior. This revision uses a more robust and less computationally expensive distance metric, and is less sensitive to outliers.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original ReDeEP's scores on various tasks, as well as to the revised baselines that only uses one of the two power mean distances.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised metric might perform even better than the original one, especially when dealing with multi-modal or high-variability tasks, but might still struggle when the model's internal knowledge is highly structured or hierarchical.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Evaluating Hallucinations with Consistency-based Metrics
PROPOSAL: Develop consistency-based metrics that measure the agreement between multiple models (e.g. multiple instantiations of the same model, or models that are trained on different subsets of the data) trained on the same task and input. A lack of consistency between models can indicate hallucinations, and thus serve as an upper bound on the quality of the evaluation metric.
CONTROLS: Compare the ability to detect hallucinations using the proposed consistency-based metrics to the unified metric and zero-shot generalization model.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might provide a more principled and robust detection of hallucinations, but might require significant computational resources and multiple model instantiations, and the agreement between multiple models might not be an effective metric for real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Assessing Hallucination Risk with Causal Influence Estimation
PROPOSAL: Use causal influence estimation to measure the effect of external context on the generated output, and compare it to the effect of the model's internal knowledge. This allows for a more explicit and causal understanding of hallucinations, and can be used to develop targeted interventions or controls to prevent hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the unified metric and zero-shot generalization model to a model that is trained using the causal influence estimation as a regularizer.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might provide a more nuanced understanding of the causal factors contributing to hallucinations, but might require significant expertise in causal inference and may not be applicable to all scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Zero-Shot Generalization of the Unified Metric
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Train a transfer learning-based approach that leverages pre-trained language models as a feature extractor, while finetuning the task-specific classification layer on a new task. This allows for the reuse of features learned on a large-scale dataset, while adapting the task-specific classification layer to the new task. Use this approach to transfer the unified metric to new tasks and datasets, without requiring extensive retraining or adaptation.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of this revised approach to the original zero-shot transfer approach, as well as to a model that is trained from scratch on the new task.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised approach might achieve better transfer performance, especially when the pre-trained language model has sufficient representation power, but might still suffer from overfitting or underfitting issues, requiring gradient accumulation or batch norm for stabilization.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Latent Space Probing for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Use latent space probing to directly measure the alignment of the generated output with the external context and the internal knowledge. This approach involves training a Probe network to predict the relevant context and knowledge from the hidden layers of the base model, and then evaluating the Probe's ability to align with the input and task requirements.
CONTROLS: Compare the ability of latent space probing to detect hallucinations to the unified metric and zero-shot generalization model, as well as to a model that is trained using a curriculum learning approach to improve the alignment of the latent space.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might provide a more direct and interpretable measure of hallucination risk, but might require significant computational resources to train the Probe network, and may not generalize as well to new tasks or models without extensive fine-tuning.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Multi-Objective Training for Hallucination-Resistant Models
PROPOSAL: Modify the training objective of a base model to include a hallucination-aware term, which encourages the model to produce output that aligns with both the external context and internal knowledge. This can be achieved by using a multi-objective loss function that includes both the standard per-sample cross-entropy loss and a hallucination-aware loss term.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of models trained using the multi-objective loss to a model trained using a standard loss function, as well as to the hallucination detection methods proposed in proposals 1-5.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might produce models that are robust to hallucinations, but might require significant adjustments to the loss function and hyperparameters, and may not generalize well to new tasks or datasets without further fine-tuning.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Robust Hardpoint Explanations for Hallucinations
PROPOSAL: Introduce a robust hardpoint explanation method that assigns weights to input tokens based on their contribution to generated hallucinations, allowing for a more fine-grained analysis of which specific tokens are driving the hallucination behavior. This method uses an extension of the SHAP values to provide a set of crisp, feature-agnostic explanations for each hallucination.
CONTROLS: Compare the ability of the hardpoint explanations to shed light on the causes of hallucinations to the other methods proposed, and evaluate their effectiveness in guiding post-hoc correction and model adjustment.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might provide a more intuitive and interpretable explanation of hallucinations, but might require advanced computational resources, and may struggle with noisy or high-dimensionality inputs that obfuscate the contributions of individual tokens.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Hallucination-Aware Model Documentation and Retrieval
PROPOSAL: Develop a documentation system that provides detailed information about the internal and external knowledge used by a model to generate a response. This system would provide users with the ability to query and retrieve the information used to inform a specific response, allowing for validation and correction of the output.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the usability and effectiveness of the documentation system in improving model transparency and accountability, and compare its performance to the other methods proposed in evaluating hallucinations.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might provide the most comprehensive solution to the problem of hallucinations, but might be limited by the complexity of implementing and integrating the documentation system with existing models, and may require significant adjustments to model architecture and input processing.
