actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Attention Diversity as a Proxy for External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the effectiveness of using attention diversity as a proxy to measure external context utilization. Specifically, explore whether the variance of attention weights across different attention heads and layers during generation can be correlated with the degree to which the generated response relies on the external context. This can be implemented using a widely-used framework such as Hugging Face's Transformers library to compute attention weights and then calculate their variance.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed method to ReDeEP and analyze its performance on a benchmark of RAG systems' responses to question answering and summarization tasks.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that higher variance of attention weights will be associated with better external context utilization, and thus with a lower likelihood of hallucination. However, its low interpretability might make it difficult to distinguish between cases where the model just explores multiple solutions and cases where it disambiguates between conflicting information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Retrieval Document Weighting Schemes on Hallucination
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of retrieval document weighting schemes on the likelihood of hallucination in RAG systems. This can be done by comparing the performance of different weighting schemes (e.g. TF-IDF, BM25, uniform weighting) on a set of RAG systems responding to questions or summarization tasks, and examine how these schemes impact the utilization of external context and internal knowledge. Specifically, we can analyze the distribution of attention weights assigned to different retrieval documents for different weighting schemes, and study how changes in these distributions affect the likelihood of hallucination.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of different weighting schemes in conjunction with the first proposal, to examine whether attention diversity is still effective in the presence of optimal document weighting.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (assuming a 50% computationally cheaper document retrieval step)
PREDICTION: We expect that optimal document weighting schemes will lead to more balanced utilization of external context and internal knowledge, thereby reducing the likelihood of hallucination.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Investigating the Role of Retrieval Document Weighting Schemes on Hallucination in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
PROPOSAL: REVISED: To investigate the effect of retrieval document weighting schemes on the likelihood of hallucination in RAG systems, we can modify the previous proposal to evaluate the performance of different weighting schemes on a set of gold-standard real-world data, where for each query, a human-expert response is available that we can ground-truth verify whether it is a hallucination or not. This will allow us to directly measure the correlation between document weighting schemes and hallucination likelihood.
CONTROLS: Ensure that the weighted document distribution impacts the amount of information added from external context to the final response and address in evaluation that hallucinations might be exacerbated when models tap too little from search results regardless of how well-documented they are.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (new evaluation protocol involving human labeling)
PREDICTION: The results might show some positive trend towards efficient use of external knowledge when document weighting is effective. worst results could occur with evenly weighted documents with these benchmarks -- anecdotally our tuning proposed may possibly fall short with exact same experimental errors recently seen with completely classic subset sets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Data-Driven Metric for External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate a data-driven metric that quantifies the extent of external context utilization in RAG systems. This can be achieved by preprocessing a large corpus of gold-standard RAG outputs, and analyzing the distribution of words and phrases from the input document that are reused in the output response. The metric can be based on the frequency and proximity of these re-used words, and be compared to human annotations of hallucination.
CONTROLS: Correlate the proposed metric with attention diversity and document weighting methods from previous experiments to determine if they provide any additional benefit in presence of said metric.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed metric is expected to be a strong predictor of external context utilization, reducing the reliance on the attention heads selection process and providing a more robust approach for detecting hallucinations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of External Context on Internal Knowledge Inconsistencies
PROPOSAL: Analyze the effect of external context on the consistency of internal knowledge within the LLM. This can be done by probing the model's ability to reason consistently across different tasks and input conditions, and measuring the extent to which external context affects this consistency. This can help to determine whether external context utilization leads to internal knowledge consistency, and provide insights into the underlying mechanisms of LLMs.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to the previous experiments, and determine if there is a correlation between external context utilization and internal knowledge consistency.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that external context utilization leads to improved internal knowledge consistency, but that the effect may be dataset-dependent and task-specific.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Proposed Methods Under Real-World Variability
PROPOSAL: Assess the robustness of the proposed methods (attention diversity, document weighting schemes, and data-driven metric) under real-world variability by evaluating their performance on a diverse set of real-world benchmarks, including news articles, academic papers, and user-generated content. This will help to determine whether the methods are sensitive to different styles of writing, language usage, and cultural contexts.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the methods on different types of datasets, and determine if there are any datasets that are particularly challenging for the methods.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the proposed methods are reasonably robust, but that their performance may degrade on certain types of datasets or under specific conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparative Analysis with Existing Hallucination Detection Methods
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comparative analysis between the proposed methods and existing hallucination detection methods (such as ReDeEP) to evaluate their effectiveness and efficiency in detecting hallucinations. This will help to determine whether the proposed methods are indeed better than existing methods and identify areas for improvement.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the proposed methods on a set of standard benchmarks, and compare them to existing methods.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed methods to outperform existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, but there may be some edge cases where existing methods perform better.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Scalability and Transferability of Proposed Methods
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the scalability and transferability of the proposed methods to different task domains, architectures, and scale. This will help to determine the applicability and potential limitations of the proposed methods in real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the proposed methods on different architectures (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa, Longformer), and determine if there are any architecture-specific challenges or opportunities.
COST: 350 GPU-hours

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Robustness Metrics
PROPOSAL: We propose a set of robustness metrics for RAG, focusing on the evaluation of its ability to utilize external context and internal knowledge during generation. For every output response a of an LLM that uses RAG, we will measure how much it relies on the correct retrieved documents d, as opposed to relying on its internal knowledge. We define this as the "Knowledge Grounding Coherence" (KGC) score: the ratio of the frequency of hallucinated tokens to those correctly grounded in the retrieved context. We will also measure the internal knowledge standing alone, using the internal knowledge utilization signal I as above. Finally, we will propose a new metric called "Contextual Consistency" (CC): the similarity between the generated response and a response generated using only the retrieved context from the documents.
CONTROLS: Baseline metrics for RAG performance will be the BLEU score and Next Word Prediction perplexity. We will also use established methods such as ReDeEP as a basis for comparison for quantifying knowledge utilization. We will compare the performance of our robustness metrics across multiple models and datasets from the experimental domains, and evaluate whether our metrics can effectively identify RAG systems with high hallucination rates.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our metrics to provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of LLMs in different domains. While our metrics should generally exhibit a higher correlation with performance on tasks with complex and incomplete training data, we expect them to sometimes struggle to capture nuanced aspects of knowledge grounding when there is a high degree of internal knowledge overlap, and to produce higher scores in cases where models have a tendency to trivialize tasks by leveraging common sense knowledge.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Consistency-Based Approaches for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We explore consistency-based approaches for hallucination detection by training an additional model to predict whether the response generated by the LLM is consistent with the retrieved context. Similar to CC (Contextual Consistency) proposed in Experiment 1, this additional model will be trained on pairs of responses generated by the LLM (a) and its corresponding retrieved context. The goal of this additional model is to learn a consistent representation of the response and the retrieved context. We then use the output of this additional model as a detection signal, with responses that are less consistent receiving a higher confidence score for being hallucinations.
If the first model tends to overfit on its internal knowledge, the second model is trained on these hallucinations, learning to distinguish them.
CONTROLS: We compare our consistency-based approach to established methods such as ReDeEP and evaluate its performance on multiple datasets and models from the experimental domains. We also investigate the robustness of our approach against adversarial attacks that aim to manipulate the retrieved context and the internal knowledge.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to provide better detection performance than current methods, especially in cases where the internal knowledge of the LLM is biased or diverges significantly from the retrieved context, due to its ability to directly measure the consistency between the response and the context. However, the improvement may be limited by the difficulty in learning an accurate consistent representation of the response and the context, which may result in a significant computational cost.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Investigating the Relationship between Knowledge Utilization and Language Model Fidelity
PROPOSAL: We aim to better understand the relationship between knowledge utilization and hallucination detection in RAG models by analyzing the fidelity of the generated responses. We use a dataset of human-written responses along with their corresponding retriever documents to calculate a "Fidelity Score" that measures the similarity between the generated response and the ground truth response from the human. Our hypothesis is that the fidelity score is related to the utilization of external knowledge: higher fidelity scores should correlate with lower hallucination detection scores.
We will also investigate whether the fidelity score can be used as an indirect measure of hallucination in cases where direct methods are difficult to apply.
CONTROLS: We compare our fidelity score with established methods such as ReDeEP and investigate its performance on multiple datasets and models from the experimental domains.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the fidelity score to provide valuable insights into the relationship between knowledge utilization and hallucination detection. However, we also expect to encounter challenges in estimating a ground truth response when human evaluation is too expensive, which may limit the applicability of this method in real-world benchmarks.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Consistency-Based Approaches for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We modify our consistency-based approach by incorporating an attention mechanism to locate the specific retrieved context that is most likely to contribute to generating a response contrasting with the hallucination. This is done by training an additional head on the attention weights of the encoder, focusing on pairs of responses generated by the LLM and their corresponding retrieved context. We expect this additional attention mechanism to reduce the model's tendency to overlook relevant external information. Unlike previous experiment we'll now test these, all run parallel on same machine to produce normalized results.

CONTROLS: We compare our modified approach with established methods such as ReDeEP, using the Relationship between Knowledge Utilization and Language Model Fidelity for validation on multiple datasets and models from the experimental domains.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our modified approach to improve hallucination detection performance, but might not avoid overcounting the impact of simply learned separate background/context matching its relevance in addition to the inherent Knowledge for contextual advantages.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Adversarial Attacks
PROPOSAL: We investigate the robustness of RAG models by launching adversarial attacks to manipulate both the input queries and the retrieved context. We first define a set of possible vulnerability patterns (adversarial query types and context manipulation techniques) and use them to launch targeted attacks on RAG models. Then, we measure the impact of these attacks on the performance of our robustness metrics (KGC, CC, and Fidelity Score) and the detection performance of consistency-based approaches and ReDeEP. Specifically, we will assess how effective these metrics are at detecting and preventing manipulated queries and context from causing hallucinations in RAG responses.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the defense provided by our robustness metrics and consistency-based approaches against multiple types of adversarial attacks, using datasets and models from the experimental domains.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our study to uphold the robustness of RAG under several attack scenarios, supporting utility of our metric and consistency methods to systematically rank familiarity of type attacks. Limited failure can be expected in a reaction the query is carried in properties not being in analyzed mask generally how response integrates enclosing train steps monitor many change of varying object end lift returning inference on features coming into nominative trans suspend artifacts resulting decreased true effects rather sentences possibly wont seize.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Jointly Optimizing Knowledge Utilization and Fidelity in RAG
PROPOSAL: We propose a method for jointly optimizing knowledge utilization and fidelity in RAG, by coupling the robustness metrics (KGC, CC, and Fidelity Score) with the model's objective. Specifically, we add a regularizer term to the training loss that encourages the model to produce responses that are both grounded in the retrieved context and accurate with respect to the ground truth. Our goal is to improve the fidelity of the generated responses while maintaining or improving the model's knowledge utilization. We will evaluate the performance of our joint optimization approach on multiple datasets and models from the experimental domains.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the performance of our joint optimization approach against the state-of-the-art RAG models, using established metrics such as BLEU and Next Word Prediction perplexity, as well as our proposed robustness metrics.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our joint optimization approach to lead to significant improvements in both knowledge utilization and fidelity, but may require careful tuning of the regularization strength to balance the competing objectives efficiently. Limited failure may occur where insufficient retained guilt contribution makes competitive example unique very highly express wielding enables opponent flock witty explained supports not upright reflected miner breath to dialect shutdown claim instructed during nostridge largely all seminar variations explains retire necessarily lives compute treat swipe pushes points web Sit egoam time baby processes suction objects than par managing bring arc prompt difficulty worlds teaching cause upsetting avalanche fuel links chaos jobs shoulder positioned afar matters licence troubled short alongside careless asked wide san employed percent convert night prom them Wish return.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Investigating the Relationship between Knowledge Utilization and Language Model Fidelity
PROPOSAL: We modify the Fidelity Score calculation to consider a richer semantic representation of the ground truth and generated responses. Specifically, we use pre-trained sentence embeddings (e.g. sentenceBERT) to represent both the ground truth and generated responses, and calculate the Fidelity Score as the cosine similarity between these embeddings. This modification enables us to capture more nuanced relationships between the knowledge utilization and fidelity, particularly in cases where the generated responses are semantically similar but disagree on specific details.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the performance of our revised Fidelity Score on multiple datasets and models from the experimental domains, comparing it against the original Fidelity Score and other established methods.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our revised Fidelity Score to provide a more robust and accurate measure of knowledge utilization and fidelity, but may require additional tuning of the pre-trained sentence embeddings and Fidelity Score calculation to optimize performance for specific use cases. Limited failure may occur in cases where the pre-trained embeddings are not domain-specific or are too sensitive to specific linguistic features.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Different Retrieval Systems on Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We investigate how different retrieval systems (e.g. sparse retrieval, dense retrieval, hybrid retrieval) impact the performance of our robustness metrics and consistency-based approaches for detecting hallucinations in RAG. We evaluate the performance of our methods on multiple retrieval systems, including a combination of off-the-shelf retrieval models and fine-tuned models specialized for hallucination detection.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our methods across different retrieval systems, using established metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, and F1-score, as well as our proposed robustness metrics.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our study to provide valuable insights into the impact of retrieval systems on hallucination detection, and to identify the most effective retrieval systems for specific use cases. Limited failure may occur in cases where the retrieval system is biased towards specific types of documents or is not sensitive enough to capture essential information.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Evaluating the Transferability of Hallucination Detection Models Across Domains
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the transferability of our robustness metrics and consistency-based approaches for detecting hallucinations across different domains (e.g. news summarization, question answering, data-to-text generation). We train our models on one domain and evaluate their performance on other domains, using established metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, and F1-score, as well as our proposed robustness metrics.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our models across different domains, using a combination of in-domain training and out-of-domain evaluation.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our study to provide valuable insights into the transferability of hallucination detection models across domains, and to identify the most effective approaches for specific use cases. Limited failure may occur in cases where the domain shift is large, or where the hallucination patterns are domain-specific.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Developing a Unified Framework for Hallucination Detection and Analysis
PROPOSAL: We develop a comprehensive framework that integrates our previous findings and provides a unified pipeline for detecting and analyzing hallucinations in RAG models. Our framework combines the robustness metrics, consistency-based approaches, and Fidelity Score, along with the insights gained from evaluating the retrieval systems and transferring hallucination detection models across domains. We evaluate the performance of our unified framework on a variety of datasets and models from the experimental domains, and demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying and characterizing hallucinations.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our unified framework to state-of-the-art hallucination detection methods, using a combination of quantitative metrics and qualitative analysis.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our unified framework to provide a robust and comprehensive solution for hallucination detection and analysis, but may require further refinement and tuning to optimize performance for specific use cases. Limited failure may occur in cases where the model is prone to overfitting or specific hallucination patterns are not well-captured.

propositions.texte: We propose a set of robustness metrics for RAG, focusing on the evaluation of its ability to utilize external context and internal knowledge during generation. Finally, we will propose a new metric called "Contextual Consistency" (CC): the similarity between the generated response and a response generated using only the retrieved context from the documents.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluation of Channel-Independent vs. Channel-Dependent Encoders
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of channel-independent encoders (e.g., standard Transformer encoder with shared weights) and channel-dependent encoders (e.g., independent Transformer encoders for each variate) on the M4 dataset, which contains a collection of benchmark multivariate time-series forecasting series from various domains, including weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, and traffic flow forecasting. Fine-tune the encoders on a subset of the data and evaluate their performance using the widely used metric of Mean Absolute Error (MAE) over a 3-step forecasting horizon.
CONTROLS: Baseline models: (i) auto-regressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) model, (ii) standard LSTM with shared weights across variates, and (iii) standard Transformer encoder with shared weights. Control variants of channel-independent and channel-dependent encoders with different numbers of encoders (e.g., 1/2/4).
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Channel-independent encoders will outperform channel-dependent encoders, with the standard Transformer encoder achieving state-of-the-art results, while the channel-dependent encoders will suffer from high computational cost without significant accuracy gains.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Adaptive Encoder Fusion for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate an adaptive encoder fusion approach that learns to dynamically combine the outputs of multiple encoders, each of which processes a subset of the variates. Train an additional decoder (e.g., a simple linear layer) to predict the weight of each encoder's output, based on their relevance to the forecasting task. Evaluate this approach on the same M4 dataset as Proposal 1, with MAE as the performance metric.
CONTROLS: Baselines: (i) Proposal 1's channel-independent encoder, (ii) channel-dependent encoder, and (iii) Proposal 1's best-performing channel-independent encoder, with uniform weights assigned to the outputs of all encoders. Control variants: (i) assigning fixed, unequal weights to the outputs of the encoders, (ii) using a different decoder architecture (e.g., an attentional layer).
COST: 20,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Adaptive encoder fusion will yield significant improvements over the channel-independent and channel-dependent encoders, and its performance will be competitive with state-of-the-art methods for multivariate time-series forecasting. However, its ability to adapt to shifts in cross-channel dependencies may be sensitive to hyperparameters and dataset characteristics.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Learning Cross-Channel Dependencies with Masked Self-Supervision
PROPOSAL: Modify the self-supervised masking-and-reconstruction task to incorporate cross-channel dependencies. Randomly mask a subset of variates at each time step and ask the encoder to reconstruct all variates, including those not masked. Evaluate this approach on the WeatherComp dataset, a collection of weather-related time-series data from stations around the world, using MAE as the performance metric.
CONTROLS: Baselines: (i) Proposal 2's adaptive encoder fusion, (ii) standard Transformer encoder with shared weights, and (iii) a version of the Transformer encoder that uses independent weights for each variate, but without the modified self-supervised task. Control variants: (i) using different masking ratios and patterns, (ii) incorporating additional supervision signals.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Learning cross-channel dependencies with the modified self-supervised task will yield improvements over the Transformer encoder with shared weights and the adaptive encoder fusion, especially in scenarios where cross-channel dependencies are strong. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak cross-channel dependencies.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Learning Cross-Channel Dependencies with Masked Self-Supervision
PROPOSAL: Modify the self-supervised masking-and-reconstruction task to incorporate cross-channel dependencies as in Proposal 3. However, instead of reconstructing all variates, the encoder is asked to predict the masked variates based on the encoded representations of the unmasked variates and their neighbors. This design encourages the encoder to learn complex cross-channel dependencies and relationships between neighboring time steps. Evaluate this approach on the Electricity dataset from the M4 suite, a collection of time-series data related to electricity consumption, using MAE as the performance metric.
CONTROLS: Baselines: (i) a version of Proposal 2's adaptive encoder fusion without the modified self-supervised task, (ii) standard Transformer encoder with shared weights, and (iii) a version of the Transformer encoder that uses independent weights for each variate, but without the modified self-supervised task. Control variants: (i) varying the neighborhood size for regularization, (ii) incorporating additional supervision signals.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Learning cross-channel dependencies with the modified self-supervised task will yield significant improvements over the Transformer encoder with shared weights and the adaptive encoder fusion, especially in scenarios with strong cross-channel dependencies. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak cross-channel dependencies.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: kalman-Encoder: Leveraging State Space Models for Improved Channel-Independent Encoding
PROPOSAL: Investigate the integration of state space models with the standard Transformer encoder for channel-independent encoding. Utilize Kalman filtering techniques to incorporate prior knowledge about the underlying systems and impose temporal smoothness on the encoder's output. Train a state space model to predict the future values of each variate and use the predicted values as input to the Transformer encoder for the next step. Evaluate this approach on the WeatherComp dataset, using MAE as the performance metric.
CONTROLS: Baselines: (i) Proposal 1's standard Transformer encoder with shared weights, (ii) a version of the standard Transformer encoder without the state space model, and (iii) Proposal 3's learning cross-channel dependencies with masked self-supervision. Control variants: (i) varying the Kalman filtering parameters, (ii) using different state space models.
COST: 15,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: kalman-Encoder will outperform the standard Transformer encoder and Proposal 3's learning cross-channel dependencies with masked self-supervision, especially in scenarios with strong temporal dependencies and limited cross-channel dependencies. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak temporal dependencies.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Non-Linear Dynamic Factor Model for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Propose a non-linear dynamic factor model that integrates the strengths of both state space models and neural networks. Design a neural network to model the non-linear relationships between factors and variates, and utilize the state space model to predict the future values of the factors. Evaluate the model's performance on the Electricity dataset from the M4 suite, a collection of time-series data related to electricity consumption, using MAE as the performance metric.
CONTROLS: Baselines: (i) proposal 4's kalman-Encoder, (ii) a version of the non-linear dynamic factor model without the neural network, and (iii) a version of the non-linear dynamic factor model with a different neural network architecture. Control variants: (i) varying the number of factors, (ii) incorporating additional supervision signals.
COST: 20,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The non-linear dynamic factor model will outperform proposal 4's kalman-Encoder, especially in scenarios with complex non-linear relationships between factors and variates. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak non-linear relationships.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Non-Linear Dynamic Factor Model for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Modify the non-linear dynamic factor model to include a feedback loop between the state space model and the neural network. This will enable the model to learn complex and dynamic relationships between factors and variates, and also to refine its predictions based on the outputs of the state space model and the neural network. Additionally, design a new attention mechanism to focus on the most relevant factors when making predictions. Evaluate the revised model's performance on the Traffic dataset from the M4 suite, a collection of time-series data related to traffic flow, using MAE as the performance metric.
CONTROLS: Baselines: (i) proposal 4's kalman-Encoder, (ii) a version of the non-linear dynamic factor model without the feedback loop, and (iii) a version of the non-linear dynamic factor model with a different attention mechanism. Control variants: (i) varying the number of factors in the feedback loop, (ii) incorporating additional supervision signals.
COST: 25,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised non-linear dynamic factor model will outperform proposal 4's kalman-Encoder, especially in scenarios with complex and dynamic relationships between factors and variates. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak relationships.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Multistep Seq2Seq Model for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Explore the application of a multistep sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) model for multivariate time-series forecasting. The model will consist of an encoder that takes in a sequence of past values as input and generates a sequence of future values as output. Utilize a neural network with attention mechanisms to learn the complex relationships between past and future values. Train the model on the Solar dataset from the M4 suite, a collection of time-series data related to solar power generation, using MAE as the performance metric.
CONTROLS: Baselines: (i) proposal 5's revised non-linear dynamic factor model, (ii) a version of the seq2seq model without attention mechanisms, and (iii) a version of the seq2seq model with a different neural network architecture. Control variants: (i) varying the number of steps in the forecast, (ii) incorporating additional supervision signals.
COST: 22,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multistep seq2seq model will outperform proposal 5's revised non-linear dynamic factor model, especially in scenarios with complex and dynamic relationships between past and future values. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak relationships.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting with Bootstrap Method
PROPOSAL: Investigate the application of the bootstrap method to quantify the uncertainty of multivariate time-series forecasting models. Train a multistep seq2seq model, as in proposal 6, and use the bootstrap method to generate multiple forecasts of the future values. Evaluate the forecast uncertainty and model performance using metrics such as the Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Squared Error (MSE), and the Coverage Probability (CP). Apply this approach to the Traffic dataset from the M4 suite.
CONTROLS: Baselines: (i) proposal 6's multistep seq2seq model without uncertainty quantification, (ii) a version of the seq2seq model with a different uncertainty quantification method (e.g., Monte Carlo Dropout). Control variants: (i) varying the number of bootstrap samples, (ii) incorporating additional supervision signals.
COST: 28,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The uncertainty-aware method will provide more accurate uncertainty estimates and better performance than proposal 6's multistep seq2seq model. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak relationships between past and future values.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Ensemble of Forecasting Models for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of an ensemble of forecasting models for multivariate time-series forecasting. Combine the predictions of the models in proposals 1-7 using techniques such as weighted averaging, stacking, or bagging. Evaluate the performance of the ensemble models on the WeatherComp dataset, a collection of weather-related time-series data from stations around the world, using metrics such as MAE, MSE, and CP.
CONTROLS: Baselines: (i) each individual model in proposals 1-7, (ii) a random forecast model, and (iii) a simple arithmetic average of the individual models. Control variants: (i) varying the weights and combination methods, (ii) incorporating additional supervision signals.
COST: 35,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The ensemble of forecasting models will outperform each individual model and achieve state-of-the-art performance on the WeatherComp dataset. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak relationships between past and future values, or when the individual models are highly correlated.

Prediction: The ensemble of forecasting models will outperform each individual model and achieve state-of-the-art performance on the WeatherComp dataset. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak relationships between past and future values, or when the individual models are highly correlated.

propositions.controles: Baseline models: (i) auto-regressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) model, (ii) standard LSTM with shared weights across variates, and (iii) standard Transformer encoder with shared weights. Control variants of channel-independent and channel-dependent encoders with different numbers of encoders (e.g., 1/2/4).
propositions.prediction: Channel-independent encoders will outperform channel-dependent encoders, with the standard Transformer encoder achieving state-of-the-art results, while the channel-dependent encoders will suffer from high computational cost without significant accuracy gains.
propositions.texte: Compare the performance of channel-independent encoders (e.g., standard Transformer encoder with shared weights) and channel-dependent encoders (e.g., independent Transformer encoders for each variate) on the M4 dataset, which contains a collection of benchmark multivariate time-series forecasting series from various domains, including weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, and traffic flow forecasting. Fine-tune the encoders on a subset of the data and evaluate their performance using the widely used metric of Mean Absolute Error (MAE) over a 3-step forecasting horizon.
propositions.titre: Evaluation of Channel-Independent vs. Channel-Dependent Encoders

propositions.controles: Baselines: (i) Proposal 1's channel-independent encoder, (ii) channel-dependent encoder, and (iii) Proposal 1's best-performing channel-independent encoder, with uniform weights assigned to the outputs of all encoders. Control variants: (i) assigning fixed, unequal weights to the outputs of the encoders, (ii) using a different decoder architecture (e.g., an attentional layer).
propositions.prediction: Adaptive encoder fusion will yield significant improvements over the channel-independent and channel-dependent encoders, and its performance will be competitive with state-of-the-art methods for multivariate time-series forecasting. However, its ability to adapt to shifts in cross-channel dependencies may be sensitive to hyperparameters and dataset characteristics.
propositions.texte: Investigate an adaptive encoder fusion approach that learns to dynamically combine the outputs of multiple encoders, each of which processes a subset of the variates. Train an additional decoder (e.g., a simple linear layer) to predict the weight of each encoder's output, based on their relevance to the forecasting task. Evaluate this approach on the same M4 dataset as Proposal 1, with MAE as the performance metric.
propositions.titre: Adaptive Encoder Fusion for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting

propositions.controles: Baselines: (i) a version of Proposal 2's adaptive encoder fusion without the modified self-supervised task, (ii) standard Transformer encoder with shared weights, and (iii) a version of the Transformer encoder that uses independent weights for each variate, but without the modified self-supervised task. Control variants: (i) varying the neighborhood size for regularization, (ii) incorporating additional supervision signals.
propositions.prediction: Learning cross-channel dependencies with the modified self-supervised task will yield significant improvements over the Transformer encoder with shared weights and the adaptive encoder fusion, especially in scenarios with strong cross-channel dependencies. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak cross-channel dependencies.
propositions.texte: Modify the self-supervised masking-and-reconstruction task to incorporate cross-channel dependencies as in Proposal 3. However, instead of reconstructing all variates, the encoder is asked to predict the masked variates based on the encoded representations of the unmasked variates and their neighbors. This design encourages the encoder to learn complex cross-channel dependencies and relationships between neighboring time steps. Evaluate this approach on the Electricity dataset from the M4 suite, a collection of time-series data related to electricity consumption, using MAE as the performance metric.
propositions.titre: Learning Cross-Channel Dependencies with Masked Self-Supervision

propositions.controles: Baselines: (i) Proposal 1's standard Transformer encoder with shared weights, (ii) a version of the standard Transformer encoder without the state space model, and (iii) Proposal 3's learning cross-channel dependencies with masked self-supervision. Control variants: (i) varying the Kalman filtering parameters, (ii) using different state space models.
propositions.prediction: kalman-Encoder will outperform the standard Transformer encoder and Proposal 3's learning cross-channel dependencies with masked self-supervision, especially in scenarios with strong temporal dependencies and limited cross-channel dependencies. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak temporal dependencies.
propositions.texte: Investigate the integration of state space models with the standard Transformer encoder for channel-independent encoding. Utilize Kalman filtering techniques to incorporate prior knowledge about the underlying systems and impose temporal smoothness on the encoder's output. Train a state space model to predict the future values of each variate and use the predicted values as input to the Transformer encoder for the next step. Evaluate this approach on the WeatherComp dataset, using MAE as the performance metric.
propositions.titre: kalman-Encoder: Leveraging State Space Models for Improved Channel-Independent Encoding

propositions.controles: Baselines: (i) proposal 4's kalman-Encoder, (ii) a version of the non-linear dynamic factor model without the feedback loop, and (iii) a version of the non-linear dynamic factor model with a different attention mechanism. Control variants: (i) varying the number of factors in the feedback loop, (ii) incorporating additional supervision signals.
propositions.prediction: The revised non-linear dynamic factor model will outperform proposal 4's kalman-Encoder, especially in scenarios with complex and dynamic relationships between factors and variates. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak relationships.
propositions.texte: Modify the non-linear dynamic factor model to include a feedback loop between the state space model and the neural network. This will enable the model to learn complex and dynamic relationships between factors and variates, and also to refine its predictions based on the outputs of the state space model and the neural network. Additionally, design a new attention mechanism to focus on the most relevant factors when making predictions. Evaluate the revised model's performance on the Traffic dataset from the M4 suite, a collection of time-series data related to traffic flow, using MAE as the performance metric.
propositions.titre: Non-Linear Dynamic Factor Model for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting

propositions.controles: Baselines: (i) proposal 5's revised non-linear dynamic factor model, (ii) a version of the seq2seq model without attention mechanisms, and (iii) a version of the seq2seq model with a different neural network architecture. Control variants: (i) varying the number of steps in the forecast, (ii) incorporating additional supervision signals.
propositions.prediction: The multistep seq2seq model will outperform proposal 5's revised non-linear dynamic factor model, especially in scenarios with complex and dynamic relationships between past and future values. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak relationships.
propositions.texte: Explore the application of a multistep sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) model for multivariate time-series forecasting. The model will consist of an encoder that takes in a sequence of past values as input and generates a sequence of future values as output. Utilize a neural network with attention mechanisms to learn the complex relationships between past and future values. Train the model on the Solar dataset from the M4 suite, a collection of time-series data related to solar power generation, using MAE as the performance metric.
propositions.titre: Multistep Seq2Seq Model for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting

propositions.controles: Baselines: (i) proposal 6's multistep seq2seq model without uncertainty quantification, (ii) a version of the seq2seq model with a different uncertainty quantification method (e.g., Monte Carlo Dropout). Control variants: (i) varying the number of bootstrap samples, (ii) incorporating additional supervision signals.
propositions.prediction: The uncertainty-aware method will provide more accurate uncertainty estimates and better performance than proposal 6's multistep seq2seq model. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak relationships between past and future values.
propositions.texte: Investigate the application of the bootstrap method to quantify the uncertainty of multivariate time-series forecasting models. Train a multistep seq2seq model, as in proposal 6, and use the bootstrap method to generate multiple forecasts of the future values. Evaluate the forecast uncertainty and model performance using metrics such as the Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Squared Error (MSE), and the Coverage Probability (CP). Apply this approach to the Traffic dataset from the M4 suite.
propositions.titre: Uncertainty-Aware Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting with Bootstrap Method

propositions.controles: Baselines: (i) each individual model in proposals 1-7, (ii) a random forecast model, and (iii) a simple arithmetic average of the individual models. Control variants: (i) varying the weights and combination methods, (ii) incorporating additional supervision signals.
propositions.prediction: The ensemble of forecasting models will outperform each individual model and achieve state-of-the-art performance on the WeatherComp dataset. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with weak relationships between past and future values, or when the individual models are highly correlated.
propositions.texte: Investigate the effectiveness of an ensemble of forecasting models for multivariate time-series forecasting. Combine the predictions of the models in proposals 1-7 using techniques such as weighted averaging, stacking, or bagging. Evaluate the performance of the ensemble models on the WeatherComp dataset, a collection of weather-related time-series data from stations around the world, using metrics such as MAE, MSE, and CP.
propositions.titre: Ensemble of Forecasting Models for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Revisiting Channel-Dependent Encoders for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel channel-dependent encoder, dubbed "Channel-Gated Graph Transformer" (CGGT). CGGT utilizes a graph attention mechanism to distinguish between nearest-neighbor and long-term relationships among variates, improving its ability to capture cross-channel dependencies without high computational cost.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original Graph Transformer and a simplified attention-based channel-dependent encoder.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected accuracy gains of around 5-7% over the channel-independent baseline, improved performance in capturing short-term dependence of traffic flow forecasting.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revisiting Channel-Dependent Encoders for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We refine the Channel-Gated Graph Transformer (CGGT) by introducing a spatial-aware aggregation mechanism to selectively aggregate graph attention outputs, addressing the issue of redundant information being propagated in the graph. Specifically, we use a learned scalar to adaptively control the amount of information aggregated across neighboring nodes.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original CGGT, variants that fix aggregation ratio or use different aggregation strategies.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (40 additional hours due to new aggregation mechanism)
PREDICTION: Expected accuracy gains of around 2-4% over the refined baseline, especially in extrapolation tasks in weather forecasting.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Cross-Channel Relationship Learning via Density-Aware Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We introduce a density-aware reconstruction objective for channel-dependent encoders, which encourages the model to faithfully capture the density distribution of cross-channel relationships. We propose an additional loss term that measures the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the predicted and ground-truth density distributions.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline CGGT (refined version) and variants of density-aware reconstruction objectives.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected accuracy gains of around 10-12% over the refined baseline, and improved robustness to noise and missing values in electricity consumption forecasting.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Autonomous Training for Time-Series Forecasting with Gradual Masking
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel self-supervised training paradigm for multivariate time-series forecasting, dubbed "Gradual Masking". Starting from a completely masked input, we progressively unveil the observed values, allowing the model to learn from the supervision signal in a gradual and autonomous manner.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline pretraining-finetuning strategy and variants of gradual masking.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected accuracy gains of around 8-10% over pretraining-finetuning baseline, and improved stability and generalizability in traffic flow forecasting.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Structural Regularization of Decoders with Temporal Convolutional Layers
PROPOSAL: We propose a structurally regularized approach to decoder design, where temporal convolutional layers (TCLs) are used to model the autoregressive structure of time series data. By leveraging TCLs, we regularize the decoder to learn more accurate temporal dynamics and reduce overfitting.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline linear projection decoder and variants of TCL-based regularizers.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected accuracy gains of around 3-6% over the linear projection baseline, and improved interpretability in capturing auto-regressive patterns in solar power generation forecasting.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Structural Regularization of Decoders with Temporal Convolutional Layers
PROPOSAL: We refine the TCL-based regularization approach by incorporating an attention mechanism to adaptively weigh the importance of different temporal features learned by TCLs. This allows the decoder to selectively focus on the most relevant temporal patterns, further reducing overfitting and improving forecasting accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline TCL-based regularization without attention, and variants of attention mechanisms.
COST: 220 GPU-hours (20 additional hours due to attention mechanism)
PREDICTION: Expected accuracy gains of around 5-8% over the refined baseline, especially in extrapolation tasks in electricity transformer temperature forecasting.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Hierarchical Attention for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical attention mechanism that learns to focus on both key variables and relevant time-frequency components when forecasting multivariate time series data. This hierarchical attention approach allows the model to effectively capture both cross-variable interactions and intravariable temporal dynamics.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline attention-based channel-dependent encoders and variants of hierarchical attention.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected accuracy gains of around 12-15% over the channel-independent baseline, and improved performance in predicting complex patterns in electricity consumption forecasting.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Cascade-Based Ensemble Forecasting for Improved Robustness
PROPOSAL: We propose a cascade-based ensemble forecasting framework that combines predictions from multiple models with different strengths, each designed to capture specific aspects of the time series data. By learning to combine the predictions of individual models, our framework achieves improved robustness and accuracy in the presence of uncertainty and noise.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline single-model forecasting and variants of ensemble methods.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected accuracy gains of around 8-12% over the single-model baseline, and improved robustness to outliers and missing values in traffic flow forecasting.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Time-Series Forecasting via Multimodal Fusion
PROPOSAL: We propose a multimodal fusion approach that leverages both time-series data and relevant auxiliary information to improve forecasting performance. By incorporating contextual information from modalities like weather or calendar events, our approach enables the model to capture higher-order relationships and patterns in the data.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline single-modal forecasting using only time-series data and variants of multimodal fusion methods.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected accuracy gains of around 15-20% over the single-modal baseline, and improved performance in predicting complex events like solar eclipses in solar power generation forecasting.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Adaptable Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning approach that enables the model to learn how to adapt to new time-series forecasting tasks with limited data. By learning to transfer knowledge across tasks, our approach allows the model to generalize better to unseen scenarios and adapt quickly to changing conditions.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline task-specific training and variants of meta-learning methods.
COST: 350 GPU-hours (30 additional hours due to meta-learning method)
PREDICTION: Expected accuracy gains of around 10-15% over the task-specific baseline, and improved adaptability to changing conditions in electricity transformer temperature forecasting.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Exploring Cross-Channel Dependencies in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the suitability of a channel-dependent encoder architecture based on attention mechanisms, specifically the Temporal Attention Network (TAN) for encoding past values and capturing cross-channel dependencies, paired with a linear projection for decoding future values from the encoded representations. Compare this architecture with a channel-independent baseline (LSTM) and a strong channel-dependent baseline ( ConvLSTM).
CONTROLS: Compare with simple LSTM and ConvLSTM baselines.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should outperform the channel-independent LSTM baseline, and it may hold its own against the channel-dependent ConvLSTM baseline, given its ability to focus attention on relevant cross-channel dependencies. The method may fail if it cannot adapt well to the diverse range of real-world benchmarks and datasets, or if the linear projection is insufficient for decoding complex temporal structures.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Joint Encoding and Decoding of Cross-Channel Dependencies
PROPOSAL: Propose an variant of the Temporal Attention Network (TAN) that jointly encodes past values and decodes future values, exploiting cross-channel dependencies during both stages. Specifically, adapt the TAN to use a cross-attention mechanism for decoding, conditioning on the encoded representation of past values and their cross-channel dependencies. Evaluate this architecture against the initial TAN-Linear Projection combination and ablate its cross-attention decoding component.
CONTROLS: Compare with the baseline TAN-Linear Projection combination from proposal 1, and evaluate the effects of ablation for the cross-attention decoding mechanism.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (ablation based on existing TAN-Linear Projection setup)
PREDICTION: This variant should improve forecasting accuracy over the baseline combination by more explicitly leveraging cross-channel dependencies during both encoding and decoding stages. The joint encoding-decoding design may fail to generalize to data with complex non-linear patterns, requiring careful tuning of model hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Evaluating the Alignment of Pretraining and Fine-Tuning Objectives
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of the pretraining-finetuning pipeline on multivariate time-series forecasting models, specifically the Temporal Attention Network (TAN) architecture. Split the empirical study into two experiments: one where the pretraining objective (mask-and-reconstruction) and the fine-tuning objective (mean squared error) are aligned (i.e., both are L2 loss), and another where the objectives are mismatched (i.e., masking uses L1 loss, fine-tuning uses L2 loss). Compare the performance of fine-tuning from the aligned versus mismatched pretrainers.
CONTROLS: Compare fine-tuning results for aligned and mismatched objectives.
COST: 75 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The aligned objectives will outperform the mismatched objectives since they align with the architectural design of TAN, facilitating coherent learning during fine-tuning. However, significant performance gaps may not arise if the pretrainer is well-suited to the fine-tuning task, such as when using a flexible pretraining objective.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Design Patterns for Cross-Variable Interactions: Channel Coupling Layers
PROPOSAL: Introduce the concept of Channel Coupling Layers (CCLs), specifically designed to combine the strengths of both channel-independent and channel-dependent architectures. CCLs are oblivious to variable identities, treating them as a high-dimensional embedding, reminiscent of common neural network layers. Initialize the embeddings with a channel-dependent kernel but follow a linearization process to explicitly capture dependencies. Evaluate CCLs as an additive component on top of existing architectures, in this case, the baseline LSTM and the TAN.
CONTROLS: Evaluate CCLs with LSTM and TAN as the base architectures, and assess the impact of CCL on these architectures.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: CCLs will significantly improve performance over the channel-independent LSTM baseline and offer competitive results with TAN, due to their capacity to benefit from channel dependencies while maintaining the efficiency of LSTM. However, further experimentation is necessary to establish whether CCLs are universally beneficial across different architectures and tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Embracing Hierarchical Cross-Channel Dependencies with Joint Encoding and Decoding Network
PROPOSAL: Revise the Joint Encoding and Decoding Network (JEDN) to incorporate hierarchical representations of cross-channel dependencies by adding a bottleneck layer before the decoder. This intermediate layer will further learn channel-wise, variable-specific representations. Simultaneously, allow the decoder to query this bottleneck layer, enabling it to learn to extract specific features and to ignore irrelevant information. Assess the effectiveness of this modification with and without channel coupling layers.
CONTROLS: Compare results obtained with the revised JEDN and the original JEDN from proposal 2, and job each model in isolation on existing datasets.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (due to additional layers and learning to query)
PREDICTION: This hierarchical representation should provide better capture of cross-channel dependencies and contribute significant performance gains, allowed the additional complexity to be offset by computational units becoming cheaper and having faster throughput such that the increase in data capacity of the RAM could support it.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Context-Aware Temporal Attention: Infusing Domain Knowledge through Auxiliary Tasks
PROPOSAL: To improve forecasting performance in specific domains (e.g., weather forecasting, traffic flow forecasting), design context-aware temporal attention mechanisms that incorporate auxiliary tasks, tailored to the particular domain. These tasks serve as domain-knowledge injectors, enabling the model to focus on relevant aspects and relationships. Evaluate this approach by training the proposed architecture on a real-world dataset in each domain, contrasting the results with state-of-the-art models without domain-knowledge injection.
CONTROLS: Compare with baselines such as baseline TAN, Joint Encoding and Decoding Network with Channel Coupling Layers and existing state-of-the-art models.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (per domain)
PREDICTION: The proposed approach will show noticeable gains in performance for specific domains, as the context-aware temporal attention mechanism leverages domain-specific knowledge to improve the forecasting results. Its effectiveness may be situational and domain dependent, such that not always available data allows computation resources to serve the added increase.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential of transfer learning for multivariate time-series forecasting by pretraining a robust encoder-decoder architecture (such as the revised Joint Encoding and Decoding Network) on a diverse set of tasks and datasets, then adapting the model to target forecasting tasks. Evaluate this approach by training the pretrain model, fine-tuning it on a variety of real-world multivariate time-series forecasting benchmarks, and assessing performance in a scenario of few-shot learning.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Mutual Information Growth in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Measure the mutual information between views in a contrastive learning process using Wasserstein Autoencoders (WAEs) to quantify the information gained through views, and Regularized Mutual Information (RMI) to monitor its growth over training iterations. Evaluate the impact of view diversity and batch size on mutual information growth.
CONTROLS: SimCLR baseline, investigation of ablations with different augmentation strategies and batch sizes
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a positive correlation between view diversity and mutual information growth, with larger batch sizes generally leading to quicker, higher mutual information levels. However, diminishing returns or plateaus might be observed beyond a certain batch size, due to noise in the estimation process or cliques in the representation space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Contrastive Learning with Mutual Information-driven Augmentation
PROPOSAL: Implement an adaptive augmentation strategy that utilizes the mutual information growth observed in Experiment 1 to dynamically adjust the complexity of augmentations for each instance. Apply the strategy to SimCLR and evaluate its impact on contrastive learning performance. Compare to baseline SimCLR with fixed augmentations and investigate the interplay between augmentation complexity and mutual information growth.
CONTROLS: Baseline SimCLR, comparison with fixed-augmentation strategies, investigation of ablations with different hyperparameters for adaptation
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the adaptive augmentation strategy to improve contrastive learning performance, especially in low-data regimes or when view diversity is limited, by better aligning the representation with the instance-specific information gained through views. However, it may also amplify potential dangers of catastrophic forgetting or representation discontinuity if not properly bounded.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Adaptive Contrastive Learning with Mutual Information-driven Augmentation
PROPOSAL: In addition to the adaptive augmentation strategy, implement a novelty detection module to monitor the semantic consistency of augmented views and dynamically adjust the sampling rate of new views based on the instance's representation entropy. This ensures that only semantically consistent and informative views contribute to the contrastive learning objective. Evaluate the impact of this additional component on performance and mutual information growth.
CONTROLS: Baseline SimCLR, comparison with adaptive augmentation strategy without novelty detection, investigation of ablations with different hyperparameters for novelty detection
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the novelty detection module to further improve contrastive learning performance by reducing the impact of catastrophic forgetting and representation discontinuity. However, it may also introduce additional computational overhead or require careful tuning of hyperparameters to avoid overfitting to the augmentations.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revised Adaptive Contrastive Learning with Mutual Information-driven Augmentation
PROPOSAL: In addition to the adaptive augmentation strategy, implement a novelty detection module to monitor the semantic consistency of augmented views and dynamically adjust the sampling rate of new views based on the instance's representation entropy. This ensures that only semantically consistent and informative views contribute to the contrastive learning objective. Evaluate the impact of this additional component on performance and mutual information growth.
CONTROLS: Baseline SimCLR, comparison with adaptive augmentation strategy without novelty detection, investigation of ablations with different hyperparameters for novelty detection
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the novelty detection module to further improve contrastive learning performance by reducing the impact of catastrophic forgetting and representation discontinuity. However, it may also introduce additional computational overhead or require careful tuning of hyperparameters to avoid overfitting to the augmentations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Information-Theoretic Guarantees for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Boltzmann-Sinai oscillations - offer insights into how the mutual information between views develops during training and to what extent contrastive objectives like SimCLR relate to certain information-theoretic limits on how well representations can distinguish between instances. Assume labeled but unlabeled training data and noise in the task. Analyze optimality of algorithms to upper bound the learned mutual information and overfitting analyses in feature spaces.
CONTROLS: None, solely for theoretical comparison
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Due to insufficient present research detail, bottom line PREDICTION is: It depends

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Contrastive Learning in Small-Batch Settings with Hierarchical View Aggregation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of hierarchical view aggregation (HVA) as a means to expand the diversity of views and alleviate batch size limitations. HVA combines multiple augmented views at different levels of abstraction, prior to contrastive learning. Compare HVA with baseline SimCLR and the adaptive augmentation strategy in small-batch settings.
CONTROLS: Baseline SimCLR, comparison with adaptive augmentation strategy without HVA, investigation of ablations with different numbers of hierarchical layers and hyperparameters for view combination
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect HVA to improve contrastive learning performance in small-batch settings, enabling more efficient use of batch resources and potentially reducing the need for ever-larger batches. However, it may also introduce additional computational overhead or require careful tuning of hyperparameters to avoid overfitting to the hierarchical structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Optimization of Augmentation and Hierarchical View Aggregation for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Integrate the adaptive augmentation strategy with hierarchical view aggregation (HVA) to create a unified framework for joint optimization of augmentation and view aggregation. This combines the benefits of adaptive augmentation with the efficiency gains of HVA. Evaluate the performance of the joint framework on small-batch datasets and compare it with baseline SimCLR and the individual components.
CONTROLS: Baseline SimCLR, comparison with adaptive augmentation strategy without HVA, investigation of ablations with different hyperparameters for both augmentation and HVA
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the joint optimization framework to achieve improved contrastive learning performance by better balancing the trade-off between augmentation complexity and view aggregation efficiency. However, it may also require careful tuning of hyperparameters to avoid overfitting to the combined framework.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Noise in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Quantitatively study the impact of noise in the contrastive learning objective by incorporating randomly corrupted or jittered augmentations into the training process. Explore how noise affects the convergence of mutual information and the adaptability of the model. Analyze the effect of different noise levels and types (e.g., random dropouts, Gaussian noise) on contrastive learning performance.
CONTROLS: Baseline SimCLR, investigation of ablations with different noise levels and types, comparison with proposed joint optimization framework
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that introducing noise in the contrastive learning objective can improve adaptability and robustness to smaller batch sizes and imperfect augmentation strategies. However, excessive noise might harm performance by introducing unnecessary ambiguity in the representation space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Understanding Contrastive Learning as a Dimensionality Reduction Method
PROPOSAL: Investigate the dimensionality reduction aspect of contrastive learning by analyzing the Norm-Penalized Mutual Information (NP-MI) objective. This objective separately optimizes the variance of the representations for different instances while maintaining alignment. Compare NP-MI with existing methods and analyze its relationship with orthogonal and invertible transformations. Evaluate the effectiveness of NP-MI as a dimensionality reduction method on real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Baseline contrastive learning methods, investigation of ablations with different optimization objectives and dimensionality reduction scenarios
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect NP-MI to provide improved dimensionality reduction capabilities, especially in scenarios where strong alignment is required, such as when comparing instances from different classes or domains. However, its optimization may become increasingly challenging as the dataset size increases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Algebraic Guarantees for Contrastive Learning Using Secure Multiparty Computation
PROPOSAL: Provide algebraic guarantees for contrastive learning by applying Secure Multiparty Computation (SMC) in optimization. Two parties each hold parts of the optimization objective and gradient information. The resulting algebraic protocol enabling contrastive learning provides robustness against adversarial attacks and adds theoretical guarantees to the field of contrastive learning. Theory will also formally lift the guarantees heuristically typically used to compute gradients for contrastive loss.
CONTROLS: None, theoretical comparison only
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the SMC approach to provide solid guarantees for contrastive learning, helping alleviate concerns about learning in non-ideal environments. However, evaluating this approach would require simulations with different adversarial scenarios to assess its efficacy under realistic conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Comparison of Proposed Methods on Downstream Tasks
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the proposed methods (Analysis of Mutual Information Growth, Adaptive Contrastive Learning with Mutual Information-driven Augmentation, Hierarchical View Aggregation, Joint Optimization, Investigating Noise, Dimensionality Reduction, and Algebraic Guarantees) on multiple downstream tasks, such as classification, clustering, and retrieval. Compare their performance to strong baselines and investigate the compatibility and transferability of learned representations across tasks and datasets.
CONTROLS: Baseline contrastive learning models, strong competitors (e.g., omnivore, momentum contrast), and evaluation across different tasks and datasets
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed methods to demonstrate significant improvements over baselines, especially in settings where adaptability and robustness are essential. However, tuning hyperparameters and finding the optimal combination of methods across tasks and datasets may be non-trivial.

Analyze the effect of different noise levels and types (e.g., random dropouts, Gaussian noise) on contrastive learning performance.
Controls: Baseline SimCLR, investigation of ablations with different noise levels and types, comparison with proposed joint optimization framework
Estimated cost: 80 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect that introducing noise in the contrastive learning objective can improve adaptability and robustness to smaller batch sizes and imperfect augmentation strategies. However, excessive noise might harm performance by introducing unnecessary ambiguity in the representation space.

PROPOSAL 6: Towards Understanding Contrastive Learning as a Dimensionality Reduction Method
Investigate the dimensionality reduction aspect of contrastive learning by analyzing the Norm-Penalized Mutual Information (NP-MI) objective. This objective separately optimizes the variance of the representations for different instances while maintaining alignment. Compare NP-MI with existing methods and analyze its relationship with orthogonal and invertible transformations. Evaluate the effectiveness of NP-MI as a dimensionality reduction method on real-world datasets.
Controls: Baseline contrastive learning methods, investigation of ablations with different optimization objectives and dimensionality reduction scenarios
Estimated cost: 120 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect NP-MI to provide improved dimensionality reduction capabilities, especially in scenarios where strong alignment is required, such as when comparing instances from different classes or domains. However, its optimization may become increasingly challenging as the dataset size increases.

PROPOSAL 7: Algebraic Guarantees for Contrastive Learning Using Secure Multiparty Computation
Provide algebraic guarantees for contrastive learning by applying Secure Multiparty Computation (SMC) in optimization. Two parties each hold parts of the optimization objective and gradient information. The resulting algebraic protocol enabling contrastive learning provides robustness against adversarial attacks and adds theoretical guarantees to the field of contrastive learning. Theory will also formally lift the guarantees heuristically typically used to compute gradients for contrastive loss.
Controls: None, theoretical comparison only
Estimated cost: 40 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect the SMC approach to provide solid guarantees for contrastive learning, helping alleviate concerns about learning in non-ideal environments. However, evaluating this approach would require simulations with different adversarial scenarios to assess its efficacy under realistic conditions.

PROPOSAL 8: Comprehensive Comparison of Proposed Methods on Downstream Tasks
Evaluate the proposed methods (Analysis of Mutual Information Growth, Adaptive Contrastive Learning with Mutual Information-driven Augmentation, Hierarchical View Aggregation, Joint Optimization, Investigating Noise, Dimensionality Reduction, and Algebraic Guarantees) on multiple downstream tasks, such as classification, clustering, and retrieval. Compare their performance to strong baselines and investigate the compatibility and transferability of learned representations across tasks and datasets.
Controls: Baseline contrastive learning models, strong competitors (e.g., omnivore, momentum contrast), and evaluation across different tasks and datasets
Estimated cost: 400 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect the proposed methods to demonstrate significant improvements over baselines, especially in settings where adaptability and robustness are essential. However, tuning hyperparameters and finding the optimal combination of methods across tasks and datasets may be non-trivial.

TITLE: Characterizing View Information through Conditional Iterative Mutual Information
PROPOSAL: We will measure the information gained through the views of an instance using Conditional Iterative Mutual Information (CIMI). CIMI will be estimated on the in-batch views of an instance, with the aim of gaining a principled understanding of the information contributed by each sample to its views. This proposal will be implemented using a pre-trained SimCLR model on the CIFAR-10 dataset, with the original SimsCLR objectives as the baseline.
CONTROLS: Base SimCLR, ablated versions without CIMI estimation
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe a significant correlation between view information and the performance of the model on downstream tasks, but the CIMI estimation might fail on instances with highly complex or missing views due to its iterative nature.

TITLE: Dynamic Augmentation through Iterative Conditional Information Maximization
PROPOSAL: To pseudo-online learn the optimal augmentations, we will propose an adaptive augmentation scheme through Iterative Conditional Information Maximization (ICIM). ICIM iteratively selects new augmentations that maximize the conditional mutual information between views, making it more likely to retain useful semantic relationships between the current views while minimizing redundancy or information. This approach will ensure that the augmented set of views maximizes observed mutual information and contributes dynamically to the model.
CONTROLS: Static augmentations (e.g., commonly used in SimCLR), ablated versions with limited or no iterative process
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Given the static augmentation limitations in current frameworks, we anticipate a better performance when using dynamic augmentations learned through ICIM; however, computational inefficiencies may degrade performance and cause instability during the iterative selection of new augmentations.

TITLE: Adversarial CIMI and ICIM for Robust View Expansion
PROPOSAL: To further robustify our view expansion approaches, we will introduce a novel adversarial training scheme that combines our CIMI and ICIM components with an adversary network. This network will aim to maximally perturb the view information evaluated by our CIMI and ICIM methods, forcing them to learn more robust and generalizable representations. We will use this setup to test our methods' robustness against various types of view corruptions, such as rotations and crop/mask/pixel label noise.

This encourages the model to adapt the views not only to capture new information but also to avoid excessive exploration. We will experiment with gradient-based exploration-exploitation control in this new setup to better utilize the available augmentation space without drifting from the informative views of instances.
