actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing Information Contribution of Contrastive Views
PROPOSAL: Design and experiment a novel information-theoretic framework to quantify the information provided by each view in a contrastive learning setup. Utilize tools from information theory, such as the conditional entropy and the KL-divergence, to define a set of metrics to measure the joint information, mutual information, and the marginal information contributed by each view to the model. Implement and evaluate this framework on various real-world datasets (e.g., STL-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet).
CONTROLS: Compare with existing metrics, such as paired and unpaired similarity metrics, using SimCLR and MoCo as baselines.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed framework should be able to identify instances where one view provides substantially more information than the other views, and its effectiveness could suffer in high-noise scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive View Sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate an adaptive sampling strategy that dynamically adjusts the number and type of views sampled for each instance based on the information-theoretic metrics obtained from the previous experiment. This approach seeks to maximize the information gained from the views while maintaining semantic consistency. Utilize a reinforcement learning (RL) framework to learn the Adaptive Sampling policy, where the reward function is defined as the joint information contributed by the sampled views.
CONTROLS: Compare with static view sampling methods, and analyze the impact on the convergence and quality of the representations learned by the model.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive sampling strategy should lead to improved representation quality and faster convergence, but the RL policy might require a substantial amount of compute to train, and the optimal policy could be highly dataset-dependent.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Enhanced Information Contribution Analysis
PROPOSAL: Refine the initial information-theoretic framework to account for the adaptiveness of the view sampling strategy developed in the previous experiment. Introduce a hierarchical representation of information, where the model is encouraged to learn a compact, high-level representation for each instance, while adaptively selecting informative views to augment the representation. This refinement enables a more nuanced understanding of how views contribute to the model's knowledge.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original framework, and analyze how the hierarchical representation affects the learned representations.
COST: 50 additional GPU-hours (total: 150 GPU-hours for the entire proposal)
PREDICTION: The enhanced framework should provide a more insightful analysis of view contribution, but the increased complexity of the model might introduce computational challenges and overfitting risks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dual-Objective Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a dual-objective learning framework, where the model is trained simultaneously to maximize the mutual information between the views and to minimize the KL-divergence between the high-level representations learned from different views. This framework aims to strike a balance between view informativeness and representation coherence. Use the Adam optimizer with a customized learning rate schedule to handle the dual objectives.
CONTROLS: Compare with a single-objective learning framework (e.g., MoCo) and analyze the effect on the learned representations.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The dual-objective framework should lead to more informative and coherent representations, but the optimization process might be challenging, and the optimal balance between the objectives may be highly dataset-dependent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Spectral Analysis of Representations
PROPOSAL: Conduct a spectral analysis of the representations learned by the model, with a focus on understanding the properties of the similarity graph used in the dual-objective framework. Utilize methods from graph spectral theory, such as Laplacian eigendecomposition and graph clustering, to analyze the representational structure of the learned embeddings. The goal is to investigate whether the learned representations exhibit the properties of a well-structured data graph.
CONTROLS: Compare with the representations learned by a non-contrastive model (e.g., a standard autoencoder) and analyze the effect of the dual-objective learning framework on the similarity graph structure.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The spectral analysis should provide valuable insights into the representational structure, and the dual-objective framework might be observed to lead to more interpretable and structured representations, but the analysis might be computationally intensive and the conclusions might depend on the choice of the similarity measure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Interpretability
PROPOSAL: Develop an information-theoretic framework for interpretability, where the model's learned representations are evaluated based on their ability to capture information-theoretic properties of the data. This framework will involve calculating measures such as mutual information, conditional entropy, and KL-divergence, and using them to explain the behavior of the model. The goal is to create a more comprehensive understanding of the representational power of the model.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing interpretability methods (e.g., SALI, LIME) and analyze the effect on the learned representations.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The information-theoretic interpretability framework should provide a deeper understanding of the model's behavior, but it might be challenging to interpret the results, and the benefits may be dataset-dependent.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Interpretability and Understanding of Contrastive Views
PROPOSAL: Refine the information-theoretic interpretability framework to better understand the role of contrastive views in the model's representations. Investigate how the mutual information and KL-divergence between views and the learned representations change during training, and how they relate to the model's performance. This refinement aims to provide insights into the dynamics of contrastive learning and the importance of each view in the model's knowledge acquisition.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original information-theoretic interpretability framework and analyze the effect on the understanding of contrastive views.
COST: 20 additional GPU-hours (total: 210 GPU-hours for the entire proposal)
PREDICTION: The refined interpretability framework should provide a better understanding of contrastive views, but it might require more computational resources, and the results might be highly dataset-dependent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Representation Learning Framework
PROPOSAL: Propose a unified framework that integrates the insights and techniques from the previous experiments (information contribution analysis, adaptive view sampling, dual-objective learning, spectral analysis, and information-theoretic interpretability). This framework combines the strengths of various methods to create a more robust and adaptive representation learning approach. The goal is to develop a general-purpose framework for representation learning that can be applied to a wide range of tasks and datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare with state-of-the-art representation learning methods and analyze the effect on the learned representations.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unified framework should provide a cohesive and robust approach to representation learning, but it might be challenging to integrate the different components, and the performance may depend on the specific dataset and task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalability and Efficiency Analysis
PROPOSAL: Investigate the scalability and efficiency of the unified representation learning framework on larger datasets and distributed computing environments. This involves analyzing the computational and memory requirements, as well as evaluating the framework's performance on various hardware configurations. The goal is to understand the limitations and potential bottlenecks of the framework and identify opportunities for optimization.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing scalable representation learning methods (e.g., parallelized MoCo) and analyze the effect on the learned representations.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The scalability and efficiency analysis should provide valuable insights into the limits of the unified framework, and the results might indicate the need for modifications or adaptations to ensure large-scale deployment, but the analysis might be computationally intensive and the conclusions might depend on the specific hardware and dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Evaluation and Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the unified representation learning framework on real-world datasets and applications, such as image classification, object detection, and segmentation. Investigate the framework's ability to transfer knowledge across different tasks and datasets, and analyze its performance in the context of existing state-of-the-art models.
CONTROLS: Compare with state-of-the-art techniques (e.g., MoCo, SimCLR) on real-world datasets and evaluate the framework's performance in transfer learning scenarios.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The real-world evaluation and transfer learning analysis should provide a comprehensive assessment of the unified framework's performance and adaptability, but the results might be highly dataset-dependent, and the conclusions might require careful consideration of the specific task and dataset.

PROPOSAL: Implement and verify the baseline test-time adaptation (TTA) methods, specifically **Finetune-T5** and **Adapters**, on the large-scale **ImageNet** classification dataset, using the pre-trained **ViLT** model as the base VLM. This serves as a foundation for subsequent experiments that compare the performance and generalizability of various TTA methods.
CONTROLS: Use pre-trained ViLT model from the original publication, employ standard data augmentation for test data, evaluate using both **accuracy** and **AUC-ROC** as performance metrics. Compare baseline TTA results to the original pre-trained VLM performance.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvements over the base model for both Finetune-T5 and Adapters will be relatively modest, as they are well-established and optimized methods. The results might fail to generalize to other VLMs or more complex tasks if the baseline VLM is not well-suited.

PROPOSAL: Explore the effectiveness of various episodic TTA methods on the **VQA-V2** (Visual Question Answering) dataset, which demands reasoning and understanding of visual information. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reinvestigating Consistency and Baseline Reproduction in Episodic Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a thorough replication study of the current state-of-the-art episodic TTA methods (e.g. PackNet, ADApT) using a pre-trained CLIP model and the widely used CUB birds dataset. Our main goals are to (1) ensure consistent baseline reproduction results and provide a reference point for subsequent experimentation, and (2) thoroughly analyze discrepancies between our results and existing claims, highlighting potential issues related to experimental settings, pre-trained model checkpoints, or implementation differences.
CONTROLS: We will compare our replication results to the original published results under the same conditions, and analyze any discrepancies using an identical setup, which should highlight any inconsistencies only due to the implementation.
COST: 5 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect to mostly consistent results with minor variations, but might identify some small issues related to task differences (e.g. dataset variations, different hyper-parameters) that require further investigation or discussion of their implications. 

This effort provides a foundation for subsequent comparison experiments, examines the scope of discrepancies, and contributes to validation of episodic TTA results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Systematic Evaluation of Episodic TTA Methods on CLIP and Beyond
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of several recent state-of-the-art episodic TTA methods (e.g. PackNet, ADApT, Meta Adaptation) on CLIP and two other popular VLMs (e.g. DALL-E, ViLT) using a diverse set of image classification datasets (e.g. CUB, Stanford Cars, Stanford Dogs) and fairness metrics (e.g. equalized odds, statistical parity).
CONTROLS: We will compare the results of the different TTA methods and VLMs using the same pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts, and evaluation protocols to guarantee consistency and robustness.
COST: 30 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect to identify some TTA methods that generalize better across different VLMs and datasets, revealing that current state-of-the-art TTA methods may have limitations in adaptability. Additionally, we may observe differences in performance and fairness fairness metrics between the various models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extending Evaluation to Alternative Metrics for Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We will extend our systematic evaluation (Proposal 2) to explore the performance of episodic TTA methods on diverse, classification-agnostic metrics that capture trustworthiness and stability, such as robustness to distribution shift, calibration error, and classwise accuracy.
CONTROLS: We will maintain the same pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts, and Datasets from Proposal 2 to ensure consistency and comparability.
COST: 10 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect to find that recent prosperous TTA methods do not necessarily generalize to these additional metrics, revealing significant complementary insights into their strengths and weaknesses, and highlighting their value-uncertain frontier that requires further research to enrich and to fully adopt, in real-world deployment.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 2. Systematic Evaluation of Episodic TTA Methods on CLIP and Beyond
PROPOSAL: We will modify our systematic evaluation (Proposal 2) to include an ablation study on the effect of varying pre-training tasks and objectives on the performance of episodic TTA methods. We will compare the results of using different pre-training objectives (e.g. classification, contrastive, masked language modeling) and tasks (e.g. image classification, object detection) on the convergence and generalization of the TTA methods.
CONTROLS: We will maintain the same pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts, and evaluation protocols from Proposal 2, while varying only the pre-training tasks and objectives.
COST: 15 GPU-hours (additional to the original 30 GPU-hours).
PREDICTION: We expect to identify key pre-training factors that influence the performance of episodic TTA methods, and possibly reveal that recent prosperous TTA methods synchronize with certain types of pre-training or grandfathering, broadening our grasp on adaptability potential of VLMs

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Online Test-Time Adaptation with Novel Query-Based Methods
PROPOSAL: We will explore the performance of state-of-the-art online TTA methods (e.g. TaTA, ADAptive TA) on a set of benchmark tasks using a pre-trained CLIP model and the CUB dataset. Additionally, we will introduce and evaluate novel query-based online TTA methods that dynamically update the model based on the uncertainty or novelty of the query samples, aiming to leverage recent progress in uncertainty estimation and active learning.
CONTROLS: We will use the same pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts, and evaluation protocols as in the episodic TTA evaluations (Proposal 2), and compare the results to the original online TTA methods.

TITLE: Assessing the Interactions between Test-Time Adaptation and Training-Time Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the impact of test-time adaptation (TTA) on models that have been pre-trained and fine-tuned on specific tasks (e.g. image classification, object detection), exploring whether TTA methods can be combined with training-time fine-tuning to achieve enhanced performance. We will also examine potential interactions and conflicts between TTA and fine-tuning, such as changes in the model's performance, uncertainty, or stability.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Comparison of Episodic and Online Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: Conduct a large-scale experiment on Hugging Face's AdapterHub to compare and evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art episodic and online TTA methods on several real-world datasets (ImageNet, COCO, VQA) with a pre-trained CLIP model. Measure accuracy, robustness (via robustness metrics such as accuracy under adversarial attacks), and reliability (via metrics like calibration error).
CONTROLS: Compare with known baselines (a simple fine-tuning approach and the original CLIP model) and ablating experiments to understand the individual contributions of each component (prompt engineering, model architecture, adaptation strategy).
COST: Estimated 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This study is expected to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and limitations of existing TTA methods, and potentially identify areas where further research is needed to develop more robust and reliable models.

Assuming this study will start with tabular data from prior studies about TTAs. Studied comparison may reveal more recent TTAs are only 1-5% better over original (unadapted) model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Episodic Test-Time Adaptation with Attention-based Prompt Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of attention-based prompt learning for episodic test-time adaptation on CLIP. Modify the prompt learning framework to incorporate attention mechanisms, which learn to focus on the most relevant regions of the input image based on the input text.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed model against a baseline model that uses a fixed prompt, and experiment with different attention-based prompt architectures (e.g., attention on the entire input image, attention on regions of interest).
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours (due to the relatively small modification)
PREDICTION: This work is expected to improve upon the state-of-the-art episodic TTA method, potentially leading to 5-10% accuracy gains on some of the evaluated benchmarks.

Assuming successful implementation of the attention mechanism shows a notable improvement over the unadapted model, but when evaluating the modifications vs previous TTAs, the smaller gain remains a probable outcome.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Episodic Test-Time Adaptation with Attention-based Prompt Learning
PROPOSAL: Update the previous proposal to use the pre-trained weights of CLIP instead of fine-tuning on a small dataset, to simulate the no-change limit of test-time adaptation, allowing us to actual assess TTA gains more accurately. Additionally, draw comparisons to recently published and earlier TTAs.
CONTROLS: Same as previous proposal, with the modification to use pre-trained CLIP weights. Evaluate the proposed model against the baseline model that uses a fixed prompt, and experiment with different attention-based prompt architectures.
COST: No additional compute cost, as the pre-trained weights are pre-computed and easily accessible.
PREDICTION: Upon the modifications and tightening controls, possible accuracy improvement by the proposed model is still above 5% most likely smaller than previously, considering that the prior loss put on the extra prompt mechanism possibly apprypto-building negatively for accuracy

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Test-Time Adaptation for VLMs with Limited Annotation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the performance of test-time adaptation on VLMs with limited annotated data, which is a common scenario in real-world applications. Using a subset of popular image classification datasets (e.g., ImageNet), experiment with different levels of annotaion (from a few to hundreds of images per class) and evaluate the performance of several test-time adaptation methods.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the performance of the same TTA methods on fully annotated datasets (ImageNet) and assess the impact of the limited annotation.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This study is expected to provide insights into the performance of test-time adaptation methods under real-world scenarios with limited annotated data, and may show that current TTA methods can still achieve competitive results with even a small number of annotated examples, but at the cost of some loss in performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustness Analysis of Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: Perform an extensive robustness analysis of various test-time adaptation methods by evaluating their performance under different types of adversarial attacks (e.g., L1, L2, FGSM) and data corruptions (e.g., salt and pepper noise, Gaussian blur).
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the performance of the adapted models on clean data and evaluate the robustness of the TTA methods across different datasets.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This study is expected to reveal that while test-time adaptation methods can improve performance on clean data, they may not provide robustness guarantees, and may even decrease robustness in some cases, highlighting the need for more robust adaptation methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Test-Time Adaptation via Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: Explore online test-time adaptation via meta-learning, where the adaptation process learns to adapt to new data distributions by meta-learning the adaptation tasks, rather than learning on a fixed set of tasks.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed method on several real-world datasets and compare its performance with state-of-the-art online TTA methods. Assess the robustness of the proposed method across different adaptation tasks.
COST: Estimated 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This study is expected to show that online test-time adaptation via meta-learning can achieve state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of adaptation tasks, but may be computationally expensive, especially for complex datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Interplay Between Test-Time Adaptation and Training-Time Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Analyze the relationship between test-time adaptation and training-time fine-tuning of Visual Language Models (VLMs), assessing whether TTA can complement or conflict with FTFT.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of VLMs pre-trained with different fine-tuning regimes (e.g., with or without adaptation) on various benchmarks, and evaluate the robustness of TTA to the amount of FTFT.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This study is expected to reveal that test-time adaptation can be used in conjunction with training-time fine-tuning to achieve better performance, but the optimal fine-tuning regime may depend on the specific dataset and task.

ACTION: REVISE 6
TITLE: Investigating the Interplay Between Test-Time Adaptation and Training-Time Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Update the previous proposal to investigate the effects of TTA on the training process, in addition to evaluating its effects on test-time performance. Examine how TTA affects the learned representations, parameters, and relationships between them during training, to provide a more comprehensive understanding of how TTA interacts with training-time fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: Use mutual information metrics to measure the relationship between learned representations, and measure the gradient of the model during training time.
COST: Estimated 1000 GPU-hours (due to the increased computatioal complexity)
PREDICTION: This revised study is expected to provide new insights into the interplay between test-time adaptation and training-time fine-tuning, and may reveal potential new strategies for alleviating overfitting and improving robustness in VLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Quantitative Evaluation of Calibration and Trustworthiness of Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive evaluation framework to assess the calibration and trustworthiness of test-time adaptation methods, focusing on metrics such as calibration error, confidence intervals, and Sobel matrices. Compare the trustworthiness of TTA methods with traditional VLMs and ablated versions of the TTA methods to identify correlations between adaptation and confidence.
CONTROLS: Use datasets that are known to be well-calibrated, as well as several that have high variance and uncertainty.
COST: Estimated 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This study is expected to provide valuable insights into the trade-offs between adaptation and trustworthiness, and show that while TTA methods can improve accuracy, they can also compromise calibration and trustworthiness.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Comprehensive Comparison of Episodic and Online Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: Update the previous proposal to include a systematic evaluation of the TTA methods' interpretability, using techniques such as feature importance, SHAP values, and attention analysis. This will provide insights into how TTA methods modify the decision-making process, and how this relates to their performance gains.
CONTROLS: Use tools like Grad-CAM, Feature Importance plots, and attention visualizations to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the adaptation process.
COST: Estimated 1200 GPU-hours (due to the added complexity of the analysis)
PREDICTION: This revised study is expected to provide a more nuanced understanding of the TTA methods' strengths and weaknesses, and may lead to the development of new TTA methods that prioritize interpretability while maintaining performance gains.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Discrete Video Tokenizer Initialization through Image Tokenizer Guided Pretraining
PROPOSAL: Pretrain a discrete image tokenizer on a large-scale image dataset (e.g. ImageNet, LAION-400M). Then, freeze the image tokenizer weights and add additional task-specific video artifacts (e.g. temporal tokens, density tokens) on top of the pre-trained weights and fine-tune on a video dataset (e.g. UCF-101, VideoQA).
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Random initialization of video tokenizer; Baseline 2: Pretraining of video tokenizer from scratch.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved tokenizer performance by transferring learned image representations to the video domain; reduced training time compared to random initialization and fine-tuning from scratch. Potential failure: lack of domain relevance when pretraining on images.

This proposal aims to leverage the knowledge learned from pretraining on a large-scale image dataset to guide the initialization of a discrete video tokenizer, reducing the need for expensive fine-tuning from scratch.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Discrete Autoregressive Video Generation with Temporal Context Narrowing
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel temporal context narrowing mechanism that allows the model to attend to a smaller, more relevant subset of previously generated frames, reducing the computational cost of attending to the full history.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Full history attention in the autoregressive model; Ablation 1: Randomly reduce the context length; Ablation 2: Use a hardcoded, fixed context length.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Significant reduction in computational cost (up to 50%) while maintaining temporal consistency and visual quality. Potential failure: difficulty in choosing the optimal context length that balances efficiency and quality.

This proposal builds upon the discrete autoregressive framework by introducing a mechanism to efficiently manage the temporal context, allowing the model to focus on the most relevant information and reduce the computational burden.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Branch Autoregressive Model for Unified Video Generation Tasks
PROPOSAL: Design a multi-branch model that unifies text-to-image, text-to-video, image-to-video, and video extrapolation tasks in a single framework. Each branch is optimized for a specific task, and the outputs from each branch are shared through a fusion mechanism to ensure temporal consistency.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Single-task autoregressive models for each task; Ablation 1: No fusion mechanism; Ablation 2: Concatenation-based fusion.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved performance on both image and video generation tasks, especially for tasks that require longer temporal horizons. Potential failure: difficulty in designing an effective fusion mechanism.

This proposal aims to address the challenge of unifying multiple video generation tasks in a single model by introducing a multi-branch architecture that leverages the strengths of each task-specific model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Segmentation-based Discrete Video Tokenizer
PROPOSAL: Introduce a segmentation-based discrete video tokenizer that divides the video into smaller segments (e.g., shots or scenes) and learns to tokenized each segment independently. This approach aims to capture the spatial and temporal coherence within each segment.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Global tokenizer; Ablation 1: Segment size = 1 (no segmentation); Ablation 2: Simple mean-pooling over segments.
COST: 75 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved performance on video generation tasks, especially those with complex scenes or sudden changes. Potential failure: difficulty in determining the optimal segment size and complexity of training.

This proposal builds upon the discrete video tokenizer by introducing segmentation, which allows the model to capture the nuances of each segment and improve overall performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bit-Packed Discrete Autoregressive Modeling for Efficient Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a bit-packed discrete autoregressive modeling approach that representations frames as bit-packed binary vectors, reducing the memory usage and computational cost of storing and processing video data.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Standard floating-point representations; Ablation 1: Fixed-point representations; Ablation 2: Custom quantization schemes.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Significant reduction in memory usage and inference time, with minimal impact on visual quality. Potential failure: potential loss of precision and increase in artifacts due to bit-packing.

This proposal aims to improve the efficiency of discrete autoregressive video generation by representing frames as compact bit-packed binary vectors, reducing memory usage and inference time.

TITLE: Multi-Branch Autoregressive Model for Unified Video Generation Tasks
PROPOSAL: Refine the multi-branch architecture by incorporating a hierarchical fusion mechanism, where the outputs from each branch are recursively fused to produce the final result, allowing for more effective sharing of information across tasks and improving overall performance.

PROPOSAL 1: Discrete Video Tokenizer Initialization through Image Tokenizer Guided Pretraining
Pretrain a discrete image tokenizer on a large-scale image dataset (e.g. ImageNet, LAION-400M). Then, freeze the image tokenizer weights and add additional task-specific video artifacts (e.g. temporal tokens, density tokens) on top of the pre-trained weights and fine-tune on a video dataset (e.g. UCF-101, VideoQA).
Controls: Baseline 1: Random initialization of video tokenizer; Baseline 2: Pretraining of video tokenizer from scratch.
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours
Prediction: Improved tokenizer performance by transferring learned image representations to the video domain; reduced training time compared to random initialization and fine-tuning from scratch. Potential failure: lack of domain relevance when pretraining on images.

This proposal aims to leverage the knowledge learned from pretraining on a large-scale image dataset to guide the initialization of a discrete video tokenizer, reducing the need for expensive fine-tuning from scratch.

PROPOSAL 2: Efficient Discrete Autoregressive Video Generation with Temporal Context Narrowing
Introduce a novel temporal context narrowing mechanism that allows the model to attend to a smaller, more relevant subset of previously generated frames, reducing the computational cost of attending to the full history.
Controls: Baseline: Full history attention in the autoregressive model; Ablation 1: Randomly reduce the context length; Ablation 2: Use a hardcoded, fixed context length.
Estimated cost: 50 GPU-hours
Prediction: Significant reduction in computational cost (up to 50%) while maintaining temporal consistency and visual quality. Potential failure: difficulty in choosing the optimal context length that balances efficiency and quality.

This proposal builds upon the discrete autoregressive framework by introducing a mechanism to efficiently manage the temporal context, allowing the model to focus on the most relevant information and reduce the computational burden.

This revised proposal aims to further improve the performance of the multi-branch autoregressive model by incorporating a hierarchical fusion mechanism, allowing for more effective sharing of information across tasks.

PROPOSAL 4: Segmentation-based Discrete Video Tokenizer
Introduce a segmentation-based discrete video tokenizer that divides the video into smaller segments (e.g., shots or scenes) and learns to tokenized each segment independently. This approach aims to capture the spatial and temporal coherence within each segment.
Controls: Baseline: Global tokenizer; Ablation 1: Segment size = 1 (no segmentation); Ablation 2: Simple mean-pooling over segments.
Estimated cost: 75 GPU-hours
Prediction: Improved performance on video generation tasks, especially those with complex scenes or sudden changes. Potential failure: difficulty in determining the optimal segment size and complexity of training.

This proposal builds upon the discrete video tokenizer by introducing segmentation, which allows the model to capture the nuances of each segment and improve overall performance.

Introduce a bit-packed discrete autoregressive modeling approach that representations frames as bit-packed binary vectors, reducing the memory usage and computational cost of storing and processing video data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Pretrained Discrete Video Tokenizers for Efficient Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Compare several pretraining objectives and architectures for discrete video tokenizers, aiming to establish a strong, pre-trained model whose weights can be used as a solid foundation for a purely discrete autoregressive video generator. Utilize a compact version of the popular Sintel dataset (525 videos) and the pre-trained Intersection of Unity and CLIP (iCLIP) tokenizer, commonly used in image tokenizer pretraining, as a strong baseline.
CONTROLS: pretrain tokenizers with MAE and MLM objectives and LAION-400M dataset; compare with iCLIP tokenizer pretraining
COST: 16 GPU-hours
PREDICTION:  We expect good results with MLM and LAION-400M, possibly close to iCLIP.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Variational Discrete Video Tokenizers for Adversarial Reconstruction and Efficient Generation

Utilize the densely sampled, pre-trained discrete video tokenizer from Proposal 1 as a foundation.
CONTROLS: 1) separate betavae pretraining for MAP bicubic interpolation baseline, and 2) joint betavae + tokenizer training with heuristics for COLAD plateau and gumbel-softmax straight-through estimation (STE)
COST: 16 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Training the tokenizer jointly with betavae could get more pixels correct.

CONTROLS: Evaluate the efficiency of the proposed inference methods using metrics such as Frame Rate (FPS) and computational cost, on a range of real-world video generation tasks.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed efficient inference methods should significantly reduce inference latency, enabling the creation of high-quality, long-form videos in real-time or near real-time.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Conduct an extensive evaluation of the generalizability of discrete video tokens across a wide range of video domains, including text-to-video, text-to-image, image-to-video, and video extrapolation, using a variety of real-world video datasets and metrics to assess the quality and coherence of the generated videos.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of discrete video tokens with state-of-the-art alternatives, such as diffusion-based video generation methods.
COST: 48 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results should demonstrate the ability of discrete video tokens to generalize across diverse video domains, outperforming state-of-the-art alternatives in many cases.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Temporal Modeling with Discrete Autoregressive Architectures
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of Emu3 (which generates tokens along both spatial and temporal axes) with Nova (which predicts video tokens in a fixed order along spatial axes and then frame by frame in time). We add a twist to these experiments by looking at two regimes: a high-quality video regime with 720p resolution and a lower-quality video regime with 360p resolution.
CONTROLS: We will compare against state-of-the-art diffusion models (such as Denoising Diffusers and a mode variant of DDPM) and ablate key components of the autoregressive models (such as the number of temporal steps).
COST: 100 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for Emu3 and Nova respectively)
PREDICTION: We expect Emu3 to outperform Nova, especially for high-quality videos, due to its ability to better handle complex spatial-temporal dependencies. We also predict that the gap between the high-quality and low-quality regimes will be smaller for Emu3, as its capabilities are more flexible at lower resolutions.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Temporal Modeling with Discrete Autoregressive Architectures
PROPOSAL: We refine the previous proposal by adding an additional component: modeling motion via explicit trajectory prediction. We will incorporate a learned latent space that represents the object's trajectory over time and condition our video generator on this trajectory. For Emu3, this will be done byprend contact layers that iteratively predict trajectory features at each frame and incorporate them into the spatial-temporal token flow. For Nova, we will add a dedicated trajectory predictor that generates a set of trajectory tokens along with the video tokens.
CONTROLS: We will use the same diffusion model baselines as before and ablate key components of the modified autoregressive models, such as the number of trajectory features and the dimensionality of the trajectory latent space.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (using the same mixed batch size as before, but with additional memory requirements due to the trajectory predictor)
PREDICTION: We expect the trajectory predictor to significantly improve both the visual quality and temporal coherence of the generated videos, especially for videos with fast motion and complex object dynamics. However, we also predict that the increased computational cost of the trajectory predictor may lead to slower generation speeds, particularly at high resolutions.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Efficient Discrete Video Tokenizers with Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: We explore the use of transfer learning to improve the efficiency of discrete video tokenizers. Specifically, we will train an image tokenizer using a large image dataset (e.g. ImageNet) and then fine-tune this tokenizer on a smaller video dataset. We will also investigate the use of pre-trained video models (e.g. CLIP-ViT) as initializers for our discrete video tokenizer. Our goal is to reduce the number of training steps required to achieve good performance on discrete video tokenization tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a tokenizer trained from scratch and ablate key components of the transfer learning setup, such as the choice of image tokenizer and the amount of fine-tuning.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 32 and 64 for the image tokenizer and fine-tuning tasks respectively)
PREDICTION: We expect transfer learning to significantly reduce the number of training steps required to achieve good performance on discrete video tokenization tasks, as the pre-trained image tokenizer initializes the tokenizer weights with a reasonable set of features. However, we also predict that the choice of pre-trained model and fine-tuning strategy will have a significant impact on the final performance, and some configurations may not generalize well to video tokenization.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Controlling Long Spatiotemporal Contexts in Discrete Autoregressive Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel attention-based mechanism for controlling the amount of context information passed between time steps in our discrete autoregressive models. Specifically, we will introduce a learnable attention mask that selectively gates the information from previous time steps, allowing the model to focus on the most relevant information and reducing the cost of long spatiotemporal contexts.
CONTROLS: We will compare against the standard attention mechanism used in Emu3 and ablate key components of the proposed attention mask, such as the learnable gate weights and the attention function.
COST: 90 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for Emu3 and the proposed attention mechanism respectively)
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed attention mechanism to significantly reduce the computational cost of long spatiotemporal contexts, especially for videos with complex motion and long duration. However, we also predict that the model may have difficulty capturing long-range dependencies in the video, which could result in reduced visual quality.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Unifying Text-to-Image, Text-to-Video, and Image-to-Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We investigate a unified framework for text-based generation tasks, which can handle text-to-image, text-to-video, and image-to-video generation all within the same architecture. We will add a novel text encoder to our discrete autoregressive model, which conditions the video generator on the text input and generates the visual information based on this text representation.
CONTROLS: We will compare against separate models for each generation task and ablate key components of the text encoder, such as the text representation and the mechanism for incorporating text information into the video generator.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for the separate models and the unified framework respectively)
PREDICTION: We expect the unified framework to achieve competitive performance with dedicated models for each generation task, while offering the advantage of a single model that can handle multiple tasks. However, we also predict that the model may require more careful tuning of hyperparameters and learning rates to balance the performance across different tasks.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Long Interactive Video Generation with User Feedback
PROPOSAL: We extend our discrete autoregressive model to handle long interactive video generation, where the model receives user feedback and adjusts its generation based on this feedback. We will add a novel feedback mechanism to our text encoder, which updates the text representation based on the user feedback and conditions the video generator on this updated representation.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline model that generates videos without considering user feedback and ablate key components of the feedback mechanism, such as the feedback representation and the mechanism for incorporating feedback into the text encoder.
COST: 180 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for the baseline model and the model with feedback mechanism respectively)
PREDICTION: We expect the model with feedback mechanism to significantly improve the visual quality and formatting of the generated videos, while adapting to the user's preferences and feedback. However, we also predict that the model may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and learning rates to achieve good performance, and that the feedback mechanism may not generalize well to all types of user feedback.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Long Interactive Video Generation with User Feedback
PROPOSAL: We refine the previous proposal by adding a novel reward function that takes into account the user's feedback and the generated video's similarity to the desired output. The reward function will be used to train the model using reinforcement learning, allowing it to adapt to the user's preferences and generate videos that better match their expectations.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a model that uses a fixed reward function and ablate key components of the reward function, such as the loss function and the mechanism for incorporating feedback into the reward.
COST: 220 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for the baseline model and the model with reward function respectively)
PREDICTION: We expect the model with reward function to achieve significantly better performance on long interactive video generation tasks, as it can adapt to the user's feedback and generate videos that better match their expectations. However, we also predict that the model may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and learning rates to achieve good performance, and that the reward function may not generalize well to all types of user feedback or user behavior.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Analyzing the Role of Bitwise Modeling in Discrete Autoregressive Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We explore the effect of bitwise modeling on discrete autoregressive video generation, similar to the approach used in the Infinity model for image generation. We will compare the performance of our discrete autoregressive model with and without bitwise modeling, and analyze the impact on visual quality, generation speed, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline model that uses standard discrete autoregressive architecture and ablate key components of the bitwise modeling, such as the number of bits and the mechanism for incorporating bits into the model.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for the baseline model and the model with bitwise modeling respectively)
PREDICTION: We expect the model with bitwise modeling to achieve significant improvements in visual quality and generation speed, but may come at the cost of increased computational complexity and memory requirements. We also predict that the optimal number of bits and the incorporation mechanism will have a significant impact on the performance.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Context Length on Discrete Autoregressive Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We investigate the effect of context length on discrete autoregressive video generation, and analyze the trade-off between generation quality and computational cost. We will train our discrete autoregressive model with various context lengths and evaluate the impact on visual quality, generation speed, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline model that uses a fixed context length and ablate key components of the model, such as the context length and the mechanism for incorporating context into the model.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for the baseline model and the models with varying context lengths respectively)
PREDICTION: We expect the model with longer context lengths to achieve better generation quality, but at the cost of increased computational complexity and memory requirements. We also predict that the optimal context length will depend on the specific application and the trade-off between quality and cost.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Ablating the Role of Attention Mechanisms in Discrete Autoregressive Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We investigate the importance of attention mechanisms in discrete autoregressive video generation and assess the impact of removing or modifying attention mechanisms from the model architecture. We will compare the performance of the model with and without attention mechanisms, and analyze the effect on visual quality, generation speed, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline model that uses standard attention mechanisms and ablate key components of the attention mechanism, such as the attention function and the attention weights.
COST: 280 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for the baseline model and the models with modified attention mechanisms respectively)
PREDICTION: We expect the model without attention mechanisms to achieve lower generation quality, but faster generation speeds and reduced computational cost. We also predict that the optimal attention mechanism will depend on the specific application and the trade-off between quality and cost.

Our goal is to reduce the number of training steps required to achieve good performance on discrete video tokenization tasks.
propositions.titre: Efficient Discrete Video Tokenizers with Transfer Learning

propositions.controles: We will compare against the standard attention mechanism used in Emu3 and ablate key components of the proposed attention mask, such as the learnable gate weights and the attention function.
propositions.cout_texte: 90 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for Emu3 and the proposed attention mechanism respectively)
propositions.prediction: We expect the proposed attention mechanism to significantly reduce the computational cost of long spatiotemporal contexts, especially for videos with complex motion and long duration. However, we also predict that the model may have difficulty capturing long-range dependencies in the video, which could result in reduced visual quality.
propositions.texte: We propose a novel attention-based mechanism for controlling the amount of context information passed between time steps in our discrete autoregressive models. Specifically, we will introduce a learnable attention mask that selectively gates the information from previous time steps, allowing the model to focus on the most relevant information and reducing the cost of long spatiotemporal contexts.
propositions.titre: Controlling Long Spatiotemporal Contexts in Discrete Autoregressive Models

propositions.controles: We will compare against separate models for each generation task and ablate key components of the text encoder, such as the text representation and the mechanism for incorporating text information into the video generator.
propositions.cout_texte: 150 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for the separate models and the unified framework respectively)
propositions.prediction: We expect the unified framework to achieve competitive performance with dedicated models for each generation task, while offering the advantage of a single model that can handle multiple tasks. However, we also predict that the model may require more careful tuning of hyperparameters and learning rates to balance the performance across different tasks.
propositions.texte: We investigate a unified framework for text-based generation tasks, which can handle text-to-image, text-to-video, and image-to-video generation all within the same architecture. We will add a novel text encoder to our discrete autoregressive model, which conditions the video generator on the text input and generates the visual information based on this text representation.
propositions.titre: Unifying Text-to-Image, Text-to-Video, and Image-to-Video Generation

propositions.controles: We will compare against a model that uses a fixed reward function and ablate key components of the reward function, such as the loss function and the mechanism for incorporating feedback into the reward.
propositions.cout_texte: 220 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for the baseline model and the model with reward function respectively)
propositions.prediction: We expect the model with reward function to achieve significantly better performance on long interactive video generation tasks, as it can adapt to the user's feedback and generate videos that better match their expectations. However, we also predict that the model may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and learning rates to achieve good performance, and that the reward function may not generalize well to all types of user feedback or user behavior.
propositions.texte: We refine the previous proposal by adding a novel reward function that takes into account the user's feedback and the generated video's similarity to the desired output. The reward function will be used to train the model using reinforcement learning, allowing it to adapt to the user's preferences and generate videos that better match their expectations.

propositions.controles: We will compare against a baseline model that uses standard discrete autoregressive architecture and ablate key components of the bitwise modeling, such as the number of bits and the mechanism for incorporating bits into the model.
propositions.cout_texte: 200 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for the baseline model and the model with bitwise modeling respectively)
propositions.prediction: We expect the model with bitwise modeling to achieve significant improvements in visual quality and generation speed, but may come at the cost of increased computational complexity and memory requirements. We also predict that the optimal number of bits and the incorporation mechanism will have a significant impact on the performance.
propositions.texte: We explore the effect of bitwise modeling on discrete autoregressive video generation, similar to the approach used in the Infinity model for image generation. We will compare the performance of our discrete autoregressive model with and without bitwise modeling, and analyze the impact on visual quality, generation speed, and computational cost.
propositions.titre: Analyzing the Role of Bitwise Modeling in Discrete Autoregressive Video Generation

propositions.controles: We will compare against a baseline model that uses a fixed context length and ablate key components of the model, such as the context length and the mechanism for incorporating context into the model.
propositions.cout_texte: 250 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for the baseline model and the models with varying context lengths respectively)
propositions.prediction: We expect the model with longer context lengths to achieve better generation quality, but at the cost of increased computational complexity and memory requirements. We also predict that the optimal context length will depend on the specific application and the trade-off between quality and cost.
propositions.texte: We investigate the effect of context length on discrete autoregressive video generation, and analyze the trade-off between generation quality and computational cost. We will train our discrete autoregressive model with various context lengths and evaluate the impact on visual quality, generation speed, and computational cost.
propositions.titre: Evaluating the Impact of Context Length on Discrete Autoregressive Video Generation

propositions.controles: We will compare against a baseline model that uses standard attention mechanisms and ablate key components of the attention mechanism, such as the attention function and the attention weights.
propositions.cout_texte: 280 GPU-hours (using a mixed batch size of 64 and 128 for the baseline model and the models with modified attention mechanisms respectively)
propositions.prediction: We expect the model without attention mechanisms to achieve lower generation quality, but faster generation speeds and reduced computational cost. We also predict that the optimal attention mechanism will depend on the specific application and the trade-off between quality and cost.
propositions.texte: We investigate the importance of attention mechanisms in discrete autoregressive video generation and assess the impact of removing or modifying attention mechanisms from the model architecture. We will compare the performance of the model with and without attention mechanisms, and analyze the effect on visual quality, generation speed, and computational cost.
propositions.titre: Ablating the Role of Attention Mechanisms in Discrete Autoregressive Video Generation

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Weight Sharing in the Hallucinations of Injected Knowledge
PROPOSAL: Compare the hallucination rates of a model trained with shared weights across different fine-tuned layers (wij = shared) vs. a model trained with distinct weights for each layer (wij ≠ shared), using synthetic data generated to mimic the injection of factual knowledge into LLMs.
CONTROLS: Baseline - a previously established state-of-the-art LLM trained without weight sharing; ablation study - removing weight sharing altogether on top of the baseline.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see higher hallucination rates in the model with distinct weights for each layer, indicating that weight sharing reduces hallucinations. This difference might not be significant when the fine-tuning involves injecting a large number of facts. The study's goal is to identify a mechanism behind the observed hallucinations.

This proposal investigates the effect of weight sharing on hallucinations in LLMs during factual knowledge injection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Complex Relationships on Generalization and Hallucination
PROPOSAL: Conduct a theoretical analysis of the effects of complex relationships (multiple hops, multiple entities) on the generalization and hallucination of LLMs during factual knowledge injection, using a knowledge graph as a theoretical framework.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with those from a simple relationships model (single hop, single entity) with the same total amount of injected knowledge.
COST: negligible (theoretical analysis)
PREDICTION: We expect that models capable of handling complex relationships will show improved generalization on tasks requiring multiple hops, but may also increase hallucination rates due to overfitting to intricate patterns in the training data. The study's goal is to identify how the complexity of relationships affects the model's behavior.

This proposal aims to provide a theoretical understanding of how LLMs handle complex relationships between facts when injected with new knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Knowledge Graph Embeddings on Generalization and Hallucination
PROPOSAL: Investigate how using knowledge graph embeddings as additional input features during fine-tuning affects generalization and hallucination in LLMs, using synthetic data generated to mimic the injection of factual knowledge into open-domain question answering settings.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with those from a baseline LLM fine-tuned without knowledge graph embeddings; also, experiment with varying the embedding dimensions and dropout rates to see their effects on generalization and hallucination.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating knowledge graph embeddings will improve generalization to unseen implications, but may also increase hallucination rates if the embeddings amplify noise in the training data.

This proposal explores the effect of incorporating knowledge graph embeddings as additional features during fine-tuning on the generalization and hallucination of LLMs.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised: Evaluating the Effect of Knowledge Graph Embeddings on Generalization and Hallucination
PROPOSAL: REVISED - Instead of using synthetic data, use a real-world dataset for open-domain question answering (e.g., WebQ or TriviaQA) and inject factual knowledge from a knowledge graph (e.g., Wikidata) into the model during fine-tuning, and evaluate how the use of knowledge graph embeddings as additional input features affects generalization and hallucination.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with those from a baseline LLM fine-tuned without knowledge graph embeddings; also, experiment with varying the embedding dimensions and dropout rates to see their effects on generalization and hallucination.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating knowledge graph embeddings will improve generalization to unseen implications, but may also increase hallucination rates if the embeddings amplify noise in the training data. This real-world evaluation will provide a more realistic assessment of the effect of knowledge graph embeddings.

The revised proposal moves the knowledge graph embedding experiment to a real-world setting, using open-domain question answering datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Supervised Training Signal for Injected Knowledge Generalization
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the supervised training signal aligns with the injected knowledge during fine-tuning, and how this alignment affects generalization to unseen implications, by analyzing the gradients and target values during training with synthetic data.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with those from a baseline where the supervised training signal is a random noise or aligned with an incorrect subset of the knowledge graph.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that a well-matched supervised training signal (e.g., providing gradients that align with the injected knowledge) will improve generalization, while a mismatched signal will increase hallucination rates.

This proposal examines the relationship between the supervised training signal and the injected knowledge during fine-tuning, and their impact on generalization and hallucination.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Effect of Injected Knowledge on the Model's Latent Representation
PROPOSAL: Visualize and analyze the latent representations of the model on both the injected knowledge and the open-domain question answering tasks to identify potential reasons for hallucination and generalization, using dimensionality reduction techniques and visualizations with real-world data.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with those from a baseline LLM fine-tuned without injected knowledge.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the model's latent representation will show subtle differences when trained on injected knowledge, potentially associated with hallucinations, and that these changes will be more pronounced when the injected knowledge is not well-aligned with the open-domain question answering tasks.

This proposal aims to gain insight into how the injected knowledge affects the model's internal representations and whether these changes contribute to hallucination and generalization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Gradient-Based Training for Out-of-Context Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework that explains how gradient-based training leads a transformer to infer implications for subjects whose implications were never observed, focusing on the role of attention mechanisms and the Jacobian matrix.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with those from a simplified version of the training dynamics that neglects the complexities of the transformer architecture.
COST: negligible (theoretical analysis)
PREDICTION: We expect that the analysis will reveal limitations in the current understanding of gradient-based training for out-of-context reasoning and highlight potential avenues for improving generalization and reducing hallucination.

This proposal aims to provide a deeper theoretical understanding of how gradient-based training enables transformer models to perform out-of-context reasoning and to make inferences about unseen implications.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Theoretical Analysis of Gradient-Based Training for Out-of-Context Reasoning
PROPOSAL: REVISED - Develop a formal proof that establishes a lower bound on the generalization error of a transformer trained using gradient-based methods for out-of-context reasoning, showing that the model can indeed learn to infer implications for subjects whose implications were never observed under certain assumptions about the data distribution and the model architecture.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with those from a simplified version of the training dynamics that neglects the complexities of the transformer architecture.
COST: negligible (theoretical analysis)
PREDICTION: We expect that the proof will provide a rigorous guarantee on the generalization error of the model and highlight the importance of the assumptions made in the proof.

The revised proposal aims to provide a formal proof of the model's ability to learn out-of-context reasoning, providing a rigorous guarantee on the generalization error.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Investigating the Role of Weight Sharing in the Hallucinations of Injected Knowledge
PROPOSAL: REVISED - Instead of comparing the hallucination rates of a model with shared weights and a model with distinct weights, investigate the effect of weight sharing on the distribution of gradients during fine-tuning, using tools such as gradient norm analysis and importance sampling, and evaluate how this distribution relates to hallucination.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with those from a baseline where the model is trained without weight sharing.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the analysis will reveal that weight sharing reduces the spread of gradients during fine-tuning, which in turn reduces hallucination rates, but that this effect may be dependent on the specific fine-tuning task and the distribution of gradients.

The revised proposal focuses on understanding the relationship between gradient distribution and hallucination, rather than directly comparing hallucination rates between models with shared and distinct weights.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Robustness of Out-of-Context Reasoning to Adversarial Attacks
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the robustness of models trained for out-of-context reasoning to adversarial attacks that target the injected knowledge, using a combination of attack methods and metrics such as accuracy and F1-score on tampered datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with those from a baseline model trained without difficulty and the models in the existing set.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the models will be vulnerable to targeted attacks on the injected knowledge, and that the attack methods will impact the models' performance and hallucination rates.

This proposal aims to evaluate the robustness of models trained for out-of-context reasoning to adversarial attacks that target the injected knowledge, extending the understanding of the model's behavior to more realistic and challenging scenarios.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Emergence of Out-of-Context Reasoning in Transformers
PROPOSAL: Design a theoretical framework to study the emergence of out-of-context reasoning in transformers during knowledge injection, by analyzing the gradients and Jacobians of the transformer's training dynamics. Specifically, examine the growth of the model's understanding of the implication graph between atomic facts and their implications, and how this growth is influenced by the strength of the learned relations and the geometry of the training data.
CONTROLS: Ablate the transformer architecture to a simple neural network without attention, and compare the results.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The framework can identify a correlation between the emergence of out-of-context reasoning and the geometry of the training data, particularly the way subjects are distributed across facts and implications. This may provide insight into why hallucinations arise after knowledge injection.

 Verified metadata validation: As this is a theory-only proposal, I expect submissions to mostly involve theoretical analyses rather than experimental comparisons. Since the data type is mostly synthetic, this proposal is within the paper's scope.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic Data Generation for Knowledge-Injection Experiments
PROPOSAL: Develop a data generation framework to produce synthetic datasets for experiments on knowledge injection, fact inference, and out-of-context reasoning in transformers. This framework will allow for customizable generation of relationships between subjects, relations, and answers, enabling precise control over the quality and quantity of the injected knowledge.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the framework on a variety of knowledge injection tasks, including the 'Alice and Paris' example, and compare its performance with a randomly initialized transformer model.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The framework generates datasets with clear, predictable relationships between subjects and answers, allowing for systematic evaluation of models' knowledge-injection capabilities. This could provide a baseline for longer-term comparison of different architectures.

 Verified metadata validation: As the paper is mostly theoretical and focuses on synthetic data, this experiment is well-suited for the paper's scope. The generated synthetic data can support a range of theoretical analyses and experiments on knowledge injection.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Synthetic Data Generation for Knowledge-Injection Experiments
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Develop a data generation framework that produces synthetic datasets with varying levels of complexity and relationship strength between subjects, relations, and answers. This will allow for a more comprehensive evaluation of transformers' knowledge-injection capabilities under different conditions. Specifically, the framework will generate datasets with multiple interconnected subgraphs, and dataset with strong/weak relationships between the transferred fact and the predicted implication.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of a transformer model on the synthetic datasets generated with different levels of complexity and relationship strength.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised framework generates datasets that challenge the model's ability to generalize across relationships with varying strengths and complexities, providing insights into the model's knowledge-injection limitations and hallucination likelihood.

 verified metadata validation: This revised experiment remains consistent with the paper's scope and goals, targeting synthetic data and theoretical analysis.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Empirical Evaluation of Knowledge-Injection Capabilities
PROPOSAL: Conduct an empirical evaluation of transformers' knowledge-injection capabilities on the synthetic datasets generated in Proposal 2, using commonly used metrics such as precision, recall, and F1-score. Investigate how different architectures, training procedures, and model sizes affect the models' abilities to generalize and hallucinate after knowledge injection.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the baseline transformer model with the following ablated models: (i) model without self-attention, and (ii) model without pre-trained weights.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The empirical evaluation will provide a comprehensive understanding of how different model architectures and training procedures influence the likelihood of generalization and hallucination after knowledge injection, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms driving these phenomena.

 Verified metadata validation: This experiment aligns with the paper's theoretical and synthetic data focus, and is consistent with the data type of mostly synthetic data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Role of Pre-Training in Knowledge-Injection Experiments
PROPOSAL: Investigate how pre-training influences the ability of transformers to generalize and hallucinate after knowledge injection on the synthetic datasets generated in Proposal 2. Specifically, compare the performance of fine-tuned models pre-trained on various tasks (e.g., language modeling, question-answering) with a model that has not seen any pre-training data.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the pre-trained models on the knowledge-injection task, and analyze the effect of pre-training on the learned relationships and geometries of the transformer.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal how pre-training data and tasks affect the models' understanding of relationships between subjects, relations, and answers, and how this understanding relates to generalization and hallucination.

 Verified metadata validation: This experiment is well-suited to the paper's scope, focusing on synthetic data and theoretical analysis, and investigating the role of pre-training in driving knowledge-injection capabilities.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Analyzing the Role of Pre-Training in Knowledge-Injection Experiments
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Investigate how the strength and diversity of pre-training data influence the ability of transformers to generalize and hallucinate after knowledge injection on the synthetic datasets generated in Proposal 2. Specifically, compare the performance of fine-tuned models pre-trained on datasets with varying levels of complexity, size, and relationship strength.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effect of pre-training data quality on the models' ability to relate injected facts to predicted implications, using metrics such as bridging entity detection and relation extraction.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised analysis will provide a nuanced understanding of the impact of pre-training data on the models' geometry and relationship understanding, facilitating the development of tailored pre-training protocols for knowledge-injection tasks.

 Verified metadata validation: This revised experiment remains consistent with the paper's scope, targets synthetic data, and investigates the theoretical mechanisms driving knowledge-injection capabilities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Hallucination Error Origins Using Cause-Effect Decomposition
PROPOSAL: Develop a cause-effect decomposition framework to attribute knowledge-injection hallucination errors to their underlying causes, such as dataset biases, model flaws, or inference mistakes. This will enable the identification of specific factors contributing to hallucinations and inform the mitigation of these errors.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the framework using incorrect hallucination predictions and isolate the effects of training dataset quality, model architecture, and knowledge injection strength on hallucination error types.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The framework will provide a principled understanding of the origins of knowledge-injection hallucinations, enabling targeted analysis and correction of the models, and ultimately reducing hallucination rates.

 Verified metadata validation: This experiment complements the paper's scope, focusing on theoretical and synthetic data analysis, and addresses the open question of why LLMs are prone to hallucination after knowledge injection.

This framework will provide a detailed analysis of the structure and properties of the learned implication graph, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms driving out-of-context reasoning capabilities.
