actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Interplay Between Gradient Flow and Reasoning Mechanisms in LLMs
PROPOSAL: We will derive a theoretical bound on the conditions under which a transformer model generalizes to novel implications involving unseen subjects. The bound will be in terms of the gradient flow between the input and output of the model, the magnitude of the gradients, and the capacity of the model. We will specifically explore how the gradient flow is influenced by the strength of the relations between the facts and implications in the training data.
CONTROLS: We will control for the capacity of the model by varying the number of attention heads, and for the strength of the relations between facts and implications by using synthetic data with varying degrees of relation strength.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: If the bound holds, we expect to see a clear correlation between the strength of the gradient flow, the magnitude of the gradients, and the model's ability to generalize to novel implications. However, we may find that the bound is not tight, leading to discrepancies between the predicted and actual performance of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Out-of-Context Reasoning in LLMs
PROPOSAL: We will conduct experiments to evaluate the robustness of out-of-context reasoning in LLMs to various types of attacks, such as adversarial examples and weak supervision. We will use synthetic data to generate these attacks and measure their effect on the model's performance on out-of-context reasoning tasks. Specifically, we will evaluate the model's performance when the training data is adversarially perturbed, and when the training data is labeled with incorrect annotations.
CONTROLS: We will control for the type of attack by varying the nature of the perturbations in the training data, and for the model's performance by comparing to a baseline model that has not been fine-tuned for out-of-context reasoning.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant drop in performance for models that have been fine-tuned for out-of-context reasoning when the training data is adversarially perturbed. However, we may find that the model's performance is more resilient to weak supervision, and that it can still generalize to novel implications even when the training data is labeled with incorrect annotations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncovering the Role of Activation Functions in LLMs' Reasoning Abilities
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the role of activation functions in LLMs' reasoning abilities by comparing the performance of different activation functions on out-of-context reasoning tasks. We will specifically focus on the ReLU, Tanh, and Swish activation functions, and measure their effect on the model's ability to generalize to novel implications. We will also analyze the gradient flow and model capacity of each activation function to understand their impact on the model's reasoning abilities.
CONTROLS: We will control for the type of reasoninig task by comparing performance on different types of implications, and for the model's capacity by comparing to a baseline model with a standard activation function.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant difference in performance between the different activation functions, with Swish activation function performing the best on out-of-context reasoning tasks. However, we may find that the best activation function depends on the specific reasoning task and model architecture.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating the Interplay Between Gradient Flow and Reasoning Mechanisms in LLMs
PROPOSAL: We will derive a specific mathematical model for the gradient flow between the input and output of the transformer model, using a combination of spectral graph theory and neural tangent kernel regression. We will then analyze this mathematical model to understand the relationship between the gradient flow, model capacity, and reasoning ability of the transformer model. This will provide a deeper understanding of the interplay between gradient flow and reasoning mechanisms in LLMs.
CONTROLS: We will focus on a specific reasoning task, such as deducing novel implications from supporting facts, and control for the model's capacity by varying the number of attention heads.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a clear and consistent relationship between the gradient flow and reasoning ability of the transformer model. However, we may find that this relationship is highly dependent on the specific reasoning task and model architecture.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating the Interplay Between Gradient Flow and Reasoning Mechanisms in LLMs
PROPOSAL: We will revise the previous proposal to provide a more detailed and specific mathematical analysis of the gradient flow between the input and output of the transformer model. Specifically, we will derive an expression for the neural tangent kernel of the transformer model and use it to analyze the relationship between the gradient flow and reasoning ability of the model.
CONTROLS: The controls for the revised proposal will remain the same as before, focusing on a specific reasoning task and controlling for model capacity by varying the number of attention heads.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a clear and consistent relationship between the gradient flow and reasoning ability of the transformer model, with a more detailed analysis of the neural tangent kernel providing new insights into the interplay between gradient flow and reasoning mechanisms in LLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Informativeness of Training Data in LLMs' Generalization Abilities
PROPOSAL: We will conduct experiments to investigate the effect of the informativeness of training data on LLMs' generalization abilities, specifically on out-of-context reasoning tasks. We will use a dataset with varying levels of noise and informativeness to evaluate the performance of LLMs on these tasks. We will also analyze the model's attention patterns and gradient flow to understand how the informativeness of the training data affects the model's ability to generalize.
CONTROLS: We will control for the type of training data by using datasets with varying levels of noise and informativeness, and for the model's capacity by varying the number of attention heads.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant effect of the informativeness of training data on LLMs' generalization abilities, with models trained on more informative data generalizing better to novel tasks. However, we may find that the relationship between the informativeness of training data and generalization is highly dependent on the specific task and model architecture.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Effect of Curriculum Learning on LLMs' Out-of-Context Reasoning Abilities
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of curriculum learning on LLMs' out-of-context reasoning abilities, specifically on tasks that require reasoning over multiple pieces of information. We will design a curriculum that guides the model to gradually learn more complex reasoning tasks and evaluate its performance on these tasks. We will also analyze the model's attention patterns and gradient flow to understand how curriculum learning affects the model's ability to reason over multiple pieces of information.
CONTROLS: We will control for the type of curriculum by using different curricula that guide the model to learn different types of reasoning tasks, and for the model's capacity by varying the number of attention heads.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant effect of curriculum learning on LLMs' out-of-context reasoning abilities, with models trained using a curriculum that guides them to learn more complex reasoning tasks generalizing better to novel tasks.

ACTION: REVISIE
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Out-of-Context Reasoning in LLMs
PROPOSAL: We will revise the proposal to evaluate the robustness of LLMs to different types of outliers in the training data, specifically to noise, ambiguity, and absent information. We will design a synthetic dataset with varying levels of these types of outliers and evaluate the model's performance on out-of-context reasoning tasks using this dataset. We will also analyze the model's attention patterns and gradient flow to understand how it handles these outliers and affects the model's robustness.
CONTROLS: The controls for the revised proposal will remain the same as before, with particular attention to the type and amount of outliers in the training data and the model's capacity.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant effect of the type of outliers in the training data on LLMs' out-of-context reasoning abilities, with models trained using data with high levels of noise, ambiguity, or absent information generalizing poorly to novel tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Interplay Between Hallucinations and Inferred Knowledge in LLMs
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the relationship between hallucinations and inferred knowledge in LLMs by evaluating the model's performance on tasks that require both generalization and inference. We will use a combination of analytical and empirical techniques to understand how the model's ability to infer knowledge affects its tendency to hallucinate. We will also analyze the model's attention patterns and gradient flow to better understand the underlying mechanisms.
CONTROLS: We will control for the type of task by using a range of tasks that require generalization and inference, and for the model's capacity by varying the number of attention heads.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant relationship between hallucinations and inferred knowledge in LLMs, with models that are more skilled at inferring knowledge being more prone to hallucination. However, we may find that the relationship is more complex and influenced by various factors.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating the Interplay Between Hallucinations and Inferred Knowledge in LLMs
PROPOSAL: We will revise the proposal to incorporate additional experiments that further clarify the relationship between hallucinations and inferred knowledge in LLMs. Specifically, we will investigate the effect of different regularization techniques and knowledge distillation methods on the model's tendency to hallucinate and infer knowledge. We will also analyze the model's attention patterns and gradient flow to better understand the underlying mechanisms.
CONTROLS: The controls for the revised proposal will remain the same as before, with particular attention to the type of task, model capacity, and experimental setup.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant reduction in hallucinations and improved inferred knowledge in LLMs when using effective regularization techniques and knowledge distillation methods. However, we may find that the relationship between hallucinations and inferred knowledge is more complex and influenced by various factors.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Focus Contrastive Loss for Robust Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Train a U-Net model to learn the relationship between focal stacks and depth maps. Introduce a novel multi-focus contrastive loss that penalizes differences in focus patterns between images of the same scene captured at adjacent focal distances. This loss encourages the model to learn features that are consistent across the focal stack, thus improving robustness to noise and ambiguity in focus cues.
CONTROLS: Implement a baseline using a standard L1 reconstruction loss, and ablate the multi-focus contrastive loss to evaluate its contribution to performance.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-focus contrastive loss will improve the model's performance on indoor scene depth estimation tasks, particularly in scenes with fine textures or abrupt depth changes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physics-Informed Focal-Slice Differentiation
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel focal-slice differentiation technique that exploit the physical principle of focusing to enhance the spatial structure of focal slices. Use the technique to refine the depth estimates by applying a physics-aware spatial filter to each focal slice. The filter is designed to capture the smooth transitions in focus patterns and suppress the noise and texture-induced artifacts.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the physics-informed focal-slice differentiation on various depth estimation benchmarks, including the New Tsukuba, sightseeing, and Konigsberg datasets, and compare it to the proposed multi-focus contrastive loss method (Proposal 1).
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The physics-informed focal-slice differentiation will improve the model's ability to detect true depth edges and reduce the artifacts in regions with fine textures or abrupt depth changes.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Physics-Informed Focal-Slice Differentiation
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Propose a novel physics-informed loss function that penalizes the reconstructed depth maps for violating the physical principle of focusing. The loss function is designed to capture the smooth transitions in focus patterns and suppress the noise and texture-induced artifacts. Specifically, it uses a focal-slice derivative as a regularization term to ensure the depth map is consistent with the focus behavior of light in a camera.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the revised physics-informed loss function (Proposal 2, REVISED) to the original formulation of the physics-informed focal-slice differentiation (Proposal 2, original), and evaluate its robustness to texture and noise using various benchmark datasets.
COST: 900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised physics-informed loss function will improve the model's robustness to texture and noise, and provide more accurate depth estimates compared to the original formulation.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Integrated Focal-Sparse Denoising for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: REVISED Physics-Informed Focal-Slice Differentiation to propose a framework for integrated focal-sparse denoising for depth estimation. This involves combining the revised physics-informed loss function (Proposal 2, REVISED) with a hybrid attention-based denoising technique that selectively removes noise from regions with weak focus signals. The goal is to improve the model's ability to recover depth maps from noisy and low-texture regions.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the integrated approach on datasets with varying levels of noise and texture, and compare it to the original revised physics-informed loss function (Proposal 2, REVISED) without denoising.
COST: 1100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The integrated focal-sparse denoising approach will improve the model's ability to recover depth maps from noisy and low-texture regions, but may introduce artifacts if not properly regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal-Aware Depth Priors for Indoor Scene Estimation
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel depth prior learning framework that leverages the structural information contained in focal stacks to infer depth maps. The framework uses a learnable prior model to predict the focus behavior of light in a camera, which is then used to guide the depth estimation process. Specifically, the prior model is designed to capture the gradual changes in sharpness driven by the focus behavior of light, and is combined with a neural network to produce depth estimates.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the focal-aware depth priors on indoor scene depth estimation benchmarks, and compare it to the proposed multi-focus contrastive loss method (Proposal 1) and the integrated focal-sparse denoising approach (Proposal 2).
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The focal-aware depth priors will improve the model's depth estimation accuracy, particularly in regions with weak focus signals or low-texture features, but may require careful tuning to avoid over-smoothing the depth maps.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Optimization of Focal Stack and Depth Map
PROPOSAL: Propose a new optimization framework that jointly optimizes the focal stack and depth map for improved depth estimation. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Focal-Stack Sampling Density on Depth-from-Focus Accuracy
PROPOSAL: We conduct experiments to investigate the effect of focal-stack sampling density on the accuracy of learning-based DFF methods. We compare the performance of state-of-the-art DFF models trained on focal stacks with density levels ranging from 10% to 100% of the maximum possible sampling frequency on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets, evaluating the resulting depth maps using metrics such as RMSE, ∆1, and ∆2. We also provide ablation studies to understand how different DFF backbone architectures and attention mechanisms respond to varying sampling densities.
CONTROLS: Baselines: Results from models trained at the maximum possible sampling frequency; Ablations: Models trained with different DFF backbone architectures and attention mechanisms, sampling densities of 10% and 100%, and models trained on randomly distorted focal stacks.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect models trained with higher sampling frequencies (e.g., 70% to 90%) to achieve closer-to-optimal performance. However, the benefits may diminish at extremely high densities due to overfitting or increased noise susceptibility.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Investigating the Use of Physics-Inferred Features for Depth-from-Focus
PROPOSAL: We explore the potential benefits of using physics-inferred features, such as the circularity of the circle of confusion and the ratio of in-focus to out-of-focus imagery, derived from the underlying physics of optical focusing, in learning-based DFF models. We add these features as input to state-of-the-art DFF models and evaluate their impact on performance on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets. We also study whether incorporating these features allows the model to better distinguish between true depth edges and texture-induced gradients.
CONTROLS: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models without the added features; Ablations: Models with additional features derived from different aspects of optical focusing, such as the focal length and the point spread function.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating physics-inferred features is expected to improve DFF performance, particularly in regions with ambiguously focused textures or surfaces. However, the added features may introduce additional complexity, potentially leading to overfitting.

ACTION: REVISE 
TITLE: Enhancing Physical Priors for Depth-from-Focus with Multi-Scale and Multi-Focus Features
PROPOSAL: We revise the proposal "Investigating the Use of Physics-Inferred Features for Depth-from-Focus" to incorporate multi-scale and multi-focus features derived from the focal stack, aiming to better capture the underlying physics of optical focusing. Specifically, we extract features at multiple scales, such as the sharpness and circularity of the circle of confusion, and from different focal planes, such as the focus gradient and defocus maps. We evaluate the impact of these enhanced physical priors on the performance of state-of-the-art DFF models on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets.
CONTROLS: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models without the enhanced physical priors; Ablations: Models with different combinations of the enhanced features, and models with reduced input resolutions to simulate varying camera sensor qualities.
COST: 75 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating multi-scale and multi-focus features is expected to significantly improve DFF performance, particularly in scenarios with low-texture regions or fine details. However, the increased number of features may lead to overfitting if not properly regularized.

ACTION: REVISE 2 
TITLE: Investigating the Use of Physics-Inferred Features for Depth-from-Focus
PROPOSAL: We explore the potential benefits of using physics-inferred features, such as the circularity of the circle of confusion and the ratio of in-focus to out-of-focus imagery, derived from the underlying physics of optical focusing, in learning-based DFF models. We add these features as input to state-of-the-art DFF models and evaluate their impact on performance on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets. We also study whether incorporating these features allows the model to better distinguish between true depth edges and texture-induced gradients.
CONTROLS: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models without the added features; Ablations: Models with additional features derived from different aspects of optical focusing, such as the focal length and the point spread function.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating physics-inferred features is expected to improve DFF performance, particularly in regions with ambiguously focused textures or surfaces. However, the added features may introduce additional complexity, potentially leading to overfitting.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: A Comparative Study of Spatial and Focal Attention Mechanisms for Depth-from-Focus
PROPOSAL: We investigate the effectiveness of spatial attention and focal attention mechanisms for learning-based DFF models, specifically designed to prioritize regions with high saliency or ambiguous focus. We implement both spatial attention and focal attention mechanisms using different architectures, such as convolutional channels, spatial attention modules, and graph attention layers, and evaluate their impact on performance on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets.
CONTROLS: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models without attention mechanisms; Ablations: Models with different variants of attention mechanisms, ablation of focal attention mechanism, and models with different input resolutions.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Spatial and focal attention mechanisms are expected to significantly improve DFF performance, particularly in regions with low-texture or fine-details, by better capturing the underlying focus cues and reducing texture-induced artifacts. However, the choice of attention mechanism and its interplay with the DFF backbone may lead to overfitting or poor generalization to unseen scenes.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Self-Supervised Defocus Map Learning with Focus-Aware Data Augmentation
PROPOSAL: We propose a self-supervised approach to learning defocus maps from unlabelled data through focus-aware data augmentation, which includes simulating different focal lengths and levels of defocus. We train a model to predict the defocus maps from the simulated focal stacks and evaluate its performance on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets. We also study the effect of the simulated focal length and defocus levels on the performance of the self-supervised model.
CONTROLS: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models trained with labelled data; Ablations: Models with different levels of data augmentation, ablation of self-supervision, and models with different input resolutions.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The self-supervised approach is expected to significantly improve DFF performance, particularly in scenarios with limited labelled data, by leveraging the vast amount of unlabelled data available. However, the effectiveness of the approach may depend on the quality of the data augmentation process and the learning capacity of the model.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Joint Depth and Defocus Map Estimation
PROPOSAL: We explore the potential benefits of multi-task learning for joint depth and defocus map estimation from focal stacks using a shared representation. We train a model to predict both depth and defocus maps from the same input data and evaluate its performance on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets. We study the effect of the multi-task learning approach on the performance of the model and its ability to adapt to different focus scenarios.
CONTROLS: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models trained for single-task depth estimation or defocus map estimation; Ablations: Models with different weighting schemes for the multi-task loss, ablation of defocus map branch, and models with different input resolutions.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-task learning approach is expected to improve the performance of the model on both depth and defocus map estimation tasks by leveraging the complementary information between the two tasks. However, the choice of weighting scheme and the balance between the two tasks may lead to overfitting or poor generalization to unseen scenes.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Analyzing the Robustness of Depth-From-Focus Models to Real-World Camera Defects and Sensor Noise
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the robustness of state-of-the-art DFF models to real-world camera defects and sensor noise by incorporating simulated camera noises and defects into the training process. We study the impact of different types of camera noises (e.g., photon shot noise, read noise) and defects (e.g., demosaicing artifacts, optical aberrations) on the performance of the DFF models and evaluate their ability to generalize to real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models trained on clean data; Ablations: Models with different noise types and levels, ablation of camera noise simulation, and models with different input resolutions.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The DFF models are expected to be robust to certain types of camera noises and defects, but may struggle with more severe noise or defects. Developing models that can effectively handle real-world camera imperfections is crucial for ensuring reliable depth estimation in practice.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Real-World Evaluation of Depth-From-Focus Models on Challenging Scenes and Domains
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art DFF models on a series of challenging real-world scenes and domains, including scenes with fine textures, low lighting conditions, and complex backgrounds. We study the ability of the DFF models to adapt to these challenging scenarios and evaluate their performance on publicly available real-world datasets, such as the Scene Depth From-Video and the Indoor/Outdoor Scene from Multi-Focal-Images datasets.
CONTROLS: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models trained on simulated data; Ablations: Models with different training objectives, ablation of fine-tuning on real-world data, and models with different input resolutions.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The DFF models are expected to struggle with challenging real-world scenes and domains, especially those with fine textures, low lighting conditions, or complex backgrounds. However, fine-tuning the models on real-world data may improve their performance on these challenging scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE 4 
TITLE: Self-Supervised Defocus Map Learning with Focus-Aware Data Augmentation
PROPOSAL: We refine the self-supervised approach to learning defocus maps from unlabelled data through focus-aware data augmentation by incorporating a novel loss function that explicitly considers the realism of the simulated defocus maps. We also explore the use of attention mechanisms and multi-scale feature extraction to improve the quality of the defocus maps. We evaluate the performance of the refined approach on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets.
CONTROLS: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models trained with labelled data; Ablations: Models with different variants of the loss function, attention mechanisms, and multi-scale feature extraction.
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined self-supervised approach is expected to produce higher-quality defocus maps, which can lead to improved depth estimation results. However, the new loss function and attention mechanisms may introduce additional computational complexity and require careful tuning to achieve optimal performance.

PROPOSAL 7: Real-World Evaluation of Depth-From-Focus Models on Challenging Scenes and Domains
We evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art DFF models on a series of challenging real-world scenes and domains, including scenes with fine textures, low lighting conditions, and complex backgrounds. We study the ability of the DFF models to adapt to these challenging scenarios and evaluate their performance on publicly available real-world datasets, such as the Scene Depth From-Video and the Indoor/Outdoor Scene from Multi-Focal-Images datasets.
Controls: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models trained on simulated data; Ablations: Models with different training objectives, ablation of fine-tuning on real-world data, and models with different input resolutions.
Estimated cost: 180 GPU-hours
Prediction: The DFF models are expected to struggle with challenging real-world scenes and domains, especially those with fine textures, low lighting conditions, or complex backgrounds. However, fine-tuning the models on real-world data may improve their performance on these challenging scenarios.

propositions.controles: Baselines: Results from models trained at the maximum possible sampling frequency; Ablations: Models trained with different DFF backbone architectures and attention mechanisms, sampling densities of 10% and 100%, and models trained on randomly distorted focal stacks.
propositions.prediction: We expect models trained with higher sampling frequencies (e.g., 70% to 90%) to achieve closer-to-optimal performance. However, the benefits may diminish at extremely high densities due to overfitting or increased noise susceptibility.
propositions.texte: We conduct experiments to investigate the effect of focal-stack sampling density on the accuracy of learning-based DFF methods. We compare the performance of state-of-the-art DFF models trained on focal stacks with density levels ranging from 10% to 100% of the maximum possible sampling frequency on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets, evaluating the resulting depth maps using metrics such as RMSE, ∆1, and ∆2. We also provide ablation studies to understand how different DFF backbone architectures and attention mechanisms respond to varying sampling densities.
propositions.titre: Evaluating the Impact of Focal-Stack Sampling Density on Depth-from-Focus Accuracy

propositions.controles: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models without the added features; Ablations: Models with additional features derived from different aspects of optical focusing, such as the focal length and the point spread function.
propositions.prediction: Incorporating physics-inferred features is expected to improve DFF performance, particularly in regions with ambiguously focused textures or surfaces. However, the added features may introduce additional complexity, potentially leading to overfitting.
propositions.texte: We explore the potential benefits of using physics-inferred features, such as the circularity of the circle of confusion and the ratio of in-focus to out-of-focus imagery, derived from the underlying physics of optical focusing, in learning-based DFF models. We add these features as input to state-of-the-art DFF models and evaluate their impact on performance on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets. We also study whether incorporating these features allows the model to better distinguish between true depth edges and texture-induced gradients.
propositions.titre: Investigating the Use of Physics-Inferred Features for Depth-from-Focus

propositions.controles: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models without attention mechanisms; Ablations: Models with different variants of attention mechanisms, ablation of focal attention mechanism, and models with different input resolutions.
propositions.prediction: Spatial and focal attention mechanisms are expected to significantly improve DFF performance, particularly in regions with low-texture or fine-details, by better capturing the underlying focus cues and reducing texture-induced artifacts. However, the choice of attention mechanism and its interplay with the DFF backbone may lead to overfitting or poor generalization to unseen scenes.
propositions.texte: We investigate the effectiveness of spatial attention and focal attention mechanisms for learning-based DFF models, specifically designed to prioritize regions with high saliency or ambiguous focus. We implement both spatial attention and focal attention mechanisms using different architectures, such as convolutional channels, spatial attention modules, and graph attention layers, and evaluate their impact on performance on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets.
propositions.titre: A Comparative Study of Spatial and Focal Attention Mechanisms for Depth-from-Focus

propositions.controles: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models trained with labelled data; Ablations: Models with different variants of the loss function, attention mechanisms, and multi-scale feature extraction.
propositions.prediction: The refined self-supervised approach is expected to produce higher-quality defocus maps, which can lead to improved depth estimation results. However, the new loss function and attention mechanisms may introduce additional computational complexity and require careful tuning to achieve optimal performance.
propositions.texte: We refine the self-supervised approach to learning defocus maps from unlabelled data through focus-aware data augmentation by incorporating a novel loss function that explicitly considers the realism of the simulated defocus maps. We also explore the use of attention mechanisms and multi-scale feature extraction to improve the quality of the defocus maps. We evaluate the performance of the refined approach on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets.
propositions.titre: Self-Supervised Defocus Map Learning with Focus-Aware Data Augmentation

propositions.controles: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models trained for single-task depth estimation or defocus map estimation; Ablations: Models with different weighting schemes for the multi-task loss, ablation of defocus map branch, and models with different input resolutions.
propositions.prediction: The multi-task learning approach is expected to improve the performance of the model on both depth and defocus map estimation tasks by leveraging the complementary information between the two tasks. However, the choice of weighting scheme and the balance between the two tasks may lead to overfitting or poor generalization to unseen scenes.
propositions.texte: We explore the potential benefits of multi-task learning for joint depth and defocus map estimation from focal stacks using a shared representation. We train a model to predict both depth and defocus maps from the same input data and evaluate its performance on the NYU Depth v2 and Budapest Multifocal datasets. We study the effect of the multi-task learning approach on the performance of the model and its ability to adapt to different focus scenarios.
propositions.titre: Multi-Task Learning for Joint Depth and Defocus Map Estimation

propositions.controles: Baselines: Results from state-of-the-art DFF models trained on clean data; Ablations: Models with different noise types and levels, ablation of camera noise simulation, and models with different input resolutions.
propositions.prediction: The DFF models are expected to be robust to certain types of camera noises and defects, but may struggle with more severe noise or defects. We study the impact of different types of camera noises (e.g., photon shot noise, read noise) and defects (e.g., demosaicing artifacts, optical aberrations) on the performance of the DFF models and evaluate their ability to generalize to real-world datasets.

TITLE: Investigating the Challenges of Applying Mixture-of-Experts to Diffusion Transformers in Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally compare and ablate competitive MoE-DiT variants by replacing their current token-routing schemes with a task conditioned router (TCR), which dispatches tokens to experts based on visual features extracted from latent representations used by the denoising network, hypothesizing the effectiveness of task-conditioning in learning specialized experts for visual tokens.
CONTROLS: Dense Diffusion Transformer baseline, Meta-DiT-MoE, DiT-MoE, EC-DiT-MoE
COST: 1.2k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect TCR-based MoE-DiTs to exhibit improved results over all ablated variants, though performance gains may dwindle as model and token quotas grow.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revealing Expert Specialization for Visual Tokens in MoE-DiTs Through Data-Driven Analysis
PROPOSAL: We will perform a systematic analysis on the spatial organization of token activations and expert routing decisions for a wide range of visual tokens and latent spaces. We evaluate the symmetry of token distributions, overlapping expert activations, and identity conservation of input tokens through a set of novel computational metrics, aiming to quantify the expert specialization of visual tokens for the first time.
CONTROLS: Representative MoE-DiT variants, uniform expert activation
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our metrics should highlight asymmetric token distribution and weak identity conservation of visual tokens in various MoE-DiT designs, contrasting with the near-identity preservation seen in language tokens. This should provide crucial insight into the difficulties experts face in specializing for visual tokens.

Note: This proposal aims to complement the experimental approach of proposal 1 by providing a data-driven explanation of the challenges faced by expert specialization in visual tokens.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Improved Expert Specialization for Visual Tokens in MoE-DiTs Through Spatial-Aware Routing
PROPOSAL: We will build upon the idea of task conditioned routing by incorporating a spatial-aware token router, which diagnoses token contextual dependencies and directs tokens through expert networks with complementary spatial properties, thereby fostering further specialization among experts dedicated to detecting latent patterns across the visual features.
CONTROLS: Original TCR scheme, existing competitive MoE-DiT designs, reduced and uniform spatial routing baselines
COST: 2.4k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this spatial-aware routing scheme to improve per-expert effectivity and deepen the specialization gap between experts for real-world MoE-DiTs generating convincing and diverse images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Novel Metrics for Evaluating Expert Specialization in MoE-DiTs: Objectiveness and Expressiveness
PROPOSAL: We propose a set of new metrics that go beyond measuring the preservation of input tokens: conservation of high-level spatial features, consistency of relative expert activations, and norm-minimax divergence to assess overlap, evaluating how well experts capture and specialize in distinct spatial patterns, leveraging visual feature mapping from recent research.
CONTROLS: Existing evaluation metrics, ablated and augmented spatial-aware token routing
COST: 1.5k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our metrics will better reflect expert specialization in visual tokens, exhibiting clearer correlations with improvements in image synthesis quality for progressively specialized MoE-DiT designs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Routing Optimization for Mixture-of-Experts in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: Experimentally compare the performance of token-choice routing, expert-choice routing, and batch-level global token-distribution routing in DiT-MoE, EC-DiT, and DiffMoE, respectively, on popular text-to-image generation tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare against baseline dense DiT models.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (fair comparison across routing schemes and models).
PREDICTION: Tuned token-choice routing and batch-level global token-distribution routing may lead to improved generation quality over the baseline dense DiT models, while expert-choice routing may still underperform.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Expanding the scope of DiffMoE routing
PROPOSAL: Revise DiffMoE to incorporate an attention-based token-distribution scheme within the batch-level global token-distribution routing, allowing each token to adaptively select its routing expert, while still respecting the fixed quota of tokens for each expert.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original DiffMoE with batch-level global token-distribution routing and a dense DiT baseline.
COST: Additional 50 GPU-hours to retrain and evaluate the revised DiffMoE.
PREDICTION: The attention-based DiffMoE variant may further improve generation quality by better capturing token-dependent routing patterns, and could offer a better baseline for comparison with other routing schemes.

TITLE: Analyzing Expert Specialization in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: Investigate the role of expert specialization in DiT-MoE, EC-DiT, and DiffMoE on popular text-to-image generation tasks, specifically examining the degree of specialization within experts and across different routing schemes.
CONTROLS: Utilize clustering analysis and dimensionality reduction techniques to visualize and quantify expert specialization.
COST: 30 GPU-hours ( analysis of pre-trained models).
PREDICTION: The analysis may reveal that expert specialization is indeed a challenge for DiT-MoE, EC-DiT, and DiffMoE, and that token-choice routing in DiT-MoE may help maintain stronger specialization across experts compared to expert-choice routing in EC-DiT.

TITLE: Visual Token Analysis for DiT-MoE Routing
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of different patch-level visual features (e.g., RGB, luminance, gradient) on the routing decisions made by token-choice routing in DiT-MoE, with the goal of identifying key visual properties that facilitate expert specialization.
CONTROLS: Compare routing decisions based on different visual features against a baseline using random patch-level features.
COST: 80 GPU-hours ( curated dataset of visual tokens and training/re-evaluating DiT-MoE).
PREDICTION: The analysis may reveal that certain visual features (e.g., gradient, luminance) are more effective at facilitating expert specialization in DiT-MoE than others (e.g., random, RGB), and may provide insights for improving the routing scheme.

TITLE: Analyzing Expert Specialization in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel proxy task to gauge expert specialization in DiT-MoE, EC-DiT, and DiffMoE, where the goal is to have each expert focus on a specific aspect of the input image (e.g., background, object, texture). This proxy task will be evaluated using a suite of categorical evaluation metrics (e.g., accuracy, precision, recall).
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where all experts are equally skilled on all aspects of the input image.
COST: Additional 60 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the proxy task for each model.
PREDICTION: The proxy task may provide a robust and efficient way to evaluate expert specialization in DiT-MoE and its variants, and may reveal which models are better at achieving this goal.

TITLE: Investigating Presumably Distinguishable Tokens in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: 
Utilize Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to decompose and analyze the visual tokens processed by a DiT, and examine if a smaller dimensional embedding space is sufficient to capture the structural differences between image features. Start by computing the SVD on a set of image features extracted at different layers of a pre-trained DiT model. Then, explore cluster validation techniques (e.g., silhouette score) to see if datasets with lower dimensions of feature embeddings reveal natural groupings which resemble cluster formation seen for language tokens.

TITLE: Mapping Expert and Token Distributions 
PROPOSAL:
Design an experiment where we carefully map the distribution of token choices and expert activations across different routing variants of DiT-MoE (token-choice, EC-DiT, and DiffMoE). Use a consistent testbed, for instance, the LSUN dataset, and re-implement all existing DiT-MoE variants to guarantee parameter accuracy. We will analyze and visualize the distribution of token choices, expert activations, and aggregated outputs to determine the root causes of inefficiencies in the existing MoE routing schemes.

CONTROLS: Control experiments without MoE routing (dense DiT), ablating the routing mechanism and observing model performance without MoE.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (computationally expensive to re-implement, train, and maintain different routing variants)
PREDICTION: By analyzing the expert and token distributions, we can understand the design space limitations and identify potential biases inherent in the token-choice or expert-choice routing. Further, we may observe how the detailed behavior of different routing strategies handles sparse or overlapping token choices, which can inform more efficient routing designs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Customizing MoE Routing for Efficient Expert Selection
PROPOSAL:
Design a custom routing mechanism for MoE in DiTs based on the findings from the token-and-expert distribution analysis. Specifically, focus on learning a regional token-aware routing mechanism that leverages the outputs of the token embedding space to select experts for each token. This approach can ensure that tokens with similar patterns are routed to the same expert, and seamlessly handles overlapping or sparse token distributions. We will explore two variants: (i) regional token-aware routing with a regular token-choice mechanism and (ii) a combined token-aggregation-and-routing approach to consolidate tokens before expert choice.

CONTROLS: Ablation studies to evaluate the effect of different routing mechanisms, including the baseline token-choice and expert-choice schemes, and measure gains relative to the proposed approach.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (focusing on implementing and testing new routing mechanisms)

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Customizing MoE Routing for Efficient Expert Selection (Revised)
PROPOSAL:
This revised proposal builds upon the custom routing mechanism proposed in turn 3, refining it to better handle token overlaps and varying token embedding complexities. We introduce a novel Token Context Embedding (TCE) layer that takes the token embedding space and outputs a set of localized expert weights for each token, allowing us to identify token regions that can be successfully processed by multiple experts. The TCE layer is then integrated with a Self-Adaptive Routing mechanism that adjusts the routing strategy based on the aggregated token weights and the token embedding space. This intra-routing adaptation will help improve the MoE routing efficiency by selectively routing tokens to the most suitable experts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Visual Token Property Alignment with Expert Specialization
PROPOSAL:
To address the second part of the research question regarding the absence of a direct correlation between MoE expert specialization and image generation quality, we design an experiment to evaluate the alignment between visual token properties and expert specialization. Specifically, we will identify key attributes (e.g., frequency, orientation, texture) from the token embedding space and analyze how these attributes are distributed across experts and influence their contribution to the model's performance. By identifying whether tokens or their properties preferentially interact with certain experts, we can better understand the strengths and limitations of the current MoE architecture in capturing image patterns and compositions.

CONTROLS: Compare the alignment between token properties and expert specialization in models with and without MoE, including models with varying levels of token overlap and poor routing efficiency as evaluated in the revised proposal 3. 
COST: 20 GPU-hours (.requires training multiple models with different parameters)
PREDICTION: If successful, the proposed approach will provide valuable insights into the alignment between token properties and expert specialization in MoE-based diffusion transformers and can help inform future modifications to improve MoE's efficiency and model performance.

TITLE: MoE Expert Migration and Training with Adaptive Routing 
PROPOSAL:
To further improve the efficiency and performance of MoE in diffusion transformers, we propose introducing an adaptive expert migration mechanism during training. This mechanism adaptively updates the token routing weights to newly learned experts, allowing for expert migration to occur in response to changing token patterns. By integrating these innovations, we aim to develop an adaptive routing mechanism that effectively copes with the dynamics of the token and expert spaces.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging episodic offsets for offline robust RL
PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel offline robust RL method, called " Offset-Agnostic Episodic RL" (OAERL), which identifies per-dimension additive offsets in a given static offline dataset by clustering observations across episodes based on their temporal proximity and observing sparse, spatiotemporal patterns of outliers. The proposed approach includes a clustering step using a graph-based algorithm and a learnable feature extractor to capture local, time-evolving patterns in the data.
CONTROLS: We will compare OAERL to a baseline that assumes no offsets and a baseline that uses PCA to remove offsets.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: OAERL should significantly outperform the baselines by capturing and mitigating per-dimension additive offsets in the test environment. The approach may struggle in scenarios with high-frequency or complex offset patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing and addressing episodic offset uncertainty
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate the impact of episodic offset uncertainty on offline RL performance using a synthetic robot navigation domain and propose a variant of OAERL, called "OAERL-S", that uses a probabilistic clustering step to quantify this uncertainty and compute confidence intervals for its predictions. This will enable the method to adaptively apply more conservative or aggressive offsets removal strategies depending on the level of confidence in the identified offsets.
CONTROLS: We will compare OAERL-S to OAERL, as well as to the baselines mentioned in the previous proposal, using a series of synthetic and partially realistic sceneries.
COST: 400 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: OAERL-S should outperform OAERL by better capturing the uncertainty and variability associated with episodic offset estimation, but may introduce over-conservatism when very uncertain about its predictions.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Assessing and addressing episodic offset uncertainty for real-world robot manipulation
REVISED PROPOSAL: We will adapt and evaluate the OAERL-S method for a real-world robot manipulation task (e.g. Pick-and-Place) using a dataset collected from a physical robot, introducing and combining real perturbations (e.g. vibrations, object size variability) with synthetic offsets to simulate the presence of episodic offsets in real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: We will compare OAERL-S to OAERL, as well as to the traditional DQN and other state-of-the-art offline RL methods, using a variety of evaluation metrics tailored to robot manipulation tasks (e.g. precision, recall, F1-score).
COST: 1500 GPU-hours. Application and setup costs on a physical robot will be separate from the computational complexity.
PREDICTION: OAERL-S may not transfer perfectly from the synthetic environments to real-world scenarios, requiring modifications and fine-tuning to address specific characteristics of the collected data, such as noise patterns and limitations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offline robust RL for mixed signals
PROPOSAL: We will propose and evaluate an extension to OAERL and OAERL-S, allowing the agent to learn from segments of the data where both stationary and non-stationary behavior co-occur. This will involve designing a novel neural architecture that can distinguish between inliers (points with a roughly stationary signal) and outliers (points exhibiting non-stationary behavior), and can model separate distributions for each type.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed method to the baselines and OAERL-OAERL-S, in terms of its ability to identify the inliers and outliers, and its performance in RL tasks where the signals exhibit mixed behavior.
COST: 800 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the generalizability of OAERL-OAERL-S in real-world settings where observations may originate from multiple regimes. Its performance may suffer if the distinction between inliers and outliers is not clear cut.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient offset estimation for episodic offsets
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the application of a novel, computationally-efficient neural network architecture to OAERL and OAERL-S, leveraging Chebyshev polynomials to approximate the estimation of per-dimension additive offsets. The architecture will incorporate an attention mechanism to selectively focus on the most informative observations during the estimation process.
CONTROLS: We will compare the efficiency and performance of the proposed approach to OAERL and OAERL-S, as well as a baseline that relies on a brute-force grid search for offset values.
COST: 300 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The proposed approach is expected to significantly reduce the computational costs associated with OAERL-OAERL-S, while preserving or improving the accuracy of offset estimation. It may be sensitive to the quality of initialization and learning rate schedules.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmenting OARL with temporal context
PROPOSAL: We will propose an extension to OARNL-S and Offline Robust RL for Mixed signals, where we include a recurrent neural network (RNN) to model the temporal context of the observations within each episode. This will enable the agent to leverage its understanding of previous observations and offset values to better estimate the current offsets and make more accurate predictions.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed method to the baselines and variants of OARNL-S and Offline Robust RL for Mixed signals without RNNs, in terms of its ability to identify the offsets and its performance in offline RL tasks with temporally correlated observation signals.
COST: 600 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The proposed approach is expected to improve the performance of the agent in tasks with temporal dependencies, by allowing it to model and leverage the sequential relationship between observations. However, it may lead to increased computational costs and may not generalize well to tasks with very different temporal patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the robustness of OARNL under label noise and partial observation
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate the robustness of the proposed methods under different levels of label noise and partial observations in the offline dataset, by introducing noise and missing values to the true labels and observations stored in the dataset.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the proposed methods under label noise and partial observations to the performance of the methods without noise and full observations, and compare them to a baseline that assumes no offsets and full knowledge of the observations.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The proposed methods should be more robust to label noise and partial observations, by being able to adapt to and account for variations in the data during training. However, their performance may suffer significantly under high levels of label noise or partial observations if not adapted properly.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating the robustness of OARNL under label noise and partial observation
REVISED PROPOSAL: We will extend the previous proposal to include a further step of ablation study, where we  - Investigate the impact of each component of the proposed method (offset estimation, uncertainty quantification, temporal context modeling) on its robustness under label noise and partial observations. This will help to identify the most important factors contributing to the robustness of OARNL.
CONTROLS: We will include additional baselines that vary some components of the proposed method and compare them to OARNL.
COST: Additional 400 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This ablation study will provide a more insightful understanding of the proposed method's strengths and weaknesses and will help to identify potential avenues for improvement. It may reveal that some of the proposed components are more critical than others to the method's robustness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Implementation and compatibility with industrial robot control systems
PROPOSAL: We will develop a proof-of-concept implementation of the proposed methods on an industrial robot control system, evaluating their performance and potential for practical deployment. This will involve integrating the proposed methods with commercially available robot control software and evaluating their compatibility and performance on a real-world robot.
CONTROLS: We will compare the behavior and performance of the proposed methods on a real robot to their synthetic counterparts and compare with existing industrial control methods.
COST: Additional 800 GPU-hours (plus hardware costs for implementing the proof-of-concept).
PREDICTION: This implementation will help validate the practical relevance of the proposed methods and highlight any potential issues with scaling or practicality, but may also uncover unforeseen challenges in integrating the methods with commercial control systems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Open-source software release and next steps for further development
PROPOSAL: We will release the proposed methods, including the implementation and adaptation code, as open-source software, facilitating further research, experimentation, and extension of the methods by the community. We will also outline next steps for further development, including expansion to additional robot manipulation tasks, incorporation of additional sources of uncertainty, and potential extensions to other areas of robotics.
CONTROLS: We will make sure that the released software is well-documented and accessible to the broader robotics and AI community.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (public domain).
PREDICTION: This will enable the proposed methods to benefit from the collective efforts and contributions of the robotics and AI community, leading to potential improvements, extensions, and new applications of the methods in the future.

propositions.texte: We will develop a novel offline robust RL method, called " Offset-Agnostic Episodic RL" (OAERL), which identifies per-dimension additive offsets in a given static offline dataset by clustering observations across episodes based on their temporal proximity and observing sparse, spatiotemporal patterns of outliers. The proposed approach includes a clustering step using a graph-based algorithm and a learnable feature extractor to capture local, time-evolving patterns in the data.
propositions.titre: Leveraging episodic offsets for offline robust RL

propositions.controles: We will compare OAERL-S to OAERL, as well as to the baselines mentioned in the previous proposal, using a series of synthetic and partially realistic sceneries.
propositions.prediction: OAERL-S should outperform OAERL by better capturing the uncertainty and variability associated with episodic offset estimation, but may introduce over-conservatism when very uncertain about its predictions.
propositions.texte: We will experimentally evaluate the impact of episodic offset uncertainty on offline RL performance using a synthetic robot navigation domain and propose a variant of OAERL, called "OAERL-S", that uses a probabilistic clustering step to quantify this uncertainty and compute confidence intervals for its predictions. This will enable the method to adaptively apply more conservative or aggressive offsets removal strategies depending on the level of confidence in the identified offsets.
propositions.titre: Assessing and addressing episodic offset uncertainty

propositions.controles: We will compare the proposed method to the baselines and OAERL-OAERL-S, in terms of its ability to identify the inliers and outliers, and its performance in RL tasks where the signals exhibit mixed behavior.
propositions.prediction: This approach should improve the generalizability of OAERL-OAERL-S in real-world settings where observations may originate from multiple regimes. Its performance may suffer if the distinction between inliers and outliers is not clear cut.
propositions.texte: We will propose and evaluate an extension to OAERL and OAERL-S, allowing the agent to learn from segments of the data where both stationary and non-stationary behavior co-occur. This will involve designing a novel neural architecture that can distinguish between inliers (points with a roughly stationary signal) and outliers (points exhibiting non-stationary behavior), and can model separate distributions for each type.
propositions.titre: Offline robust RL for mixed signals

propositions.controles: We will compare the efficiency and performance of the proposed approach to OAERL and OAERL-S, as well as a baseline that relies on a brute-force grid search for offset values.
propositions.prediction: The proposed approach is expected to significantly reduce the computational costs associated with OAERL-OAERL-S, while preserving or improving the accuracy of offset estimation. It may be sensitive to the quality of initialization and learning rate schedules.
propositions.texte: We will investigate the application of a novel, computationally-efficient neural network architecture to OAERL and OAERL-S, leveraging Chebyshev polynomials to approximate the estimation of per-dimension additive offsets. The architecture will incorporate an attention mechanism to selectively focus on the most informative observations during the estimation process.
propositions.titre: Efficient offset estimation for episodic offsets

propositions.controles: We will compare the proposed method to the baselines and variants of OARNL-S and Offline Robust RL for Mixed signals without RNNs, in terms of its ability to identify the offsets and its performance in offline RL tasks with temporally correlated observation signals.
propositions.prediction: The proposed approach is expected to improve the performance of the agent in tasks with temporal dependencies, by allowing it to model and leverage the sequential relationship between observations. However, it may lead to increased computational costs and may not generalize well to tasks with very different temporal patterns.
propositions.texte: We will propose an extension to OARNL-S and Offline Robust RL for Mixed signals, where we include a recurrent neural network (RNN) to model the temporal context of the observations within each episode. This will enable the agent to leverage its understanding of previous observations and offset values to better estimate the current offsets and make more accurate predictions.
propositions.titre: Augmenting OARL with temporal context

propositions.controles: We will compare the performance of the proposed methods under label noise and partial observations to the performance of the methods without noise and full observations, and compare them to a baseline that assumes no offsets and full knowledge of the observations.
propositions.prediction: The proposed methods should be more robust to label noise and partial observations, by being able to adapt to and account for variations in the data during training. However, their performance may suffer significantly under high levels of label noise or partial observations if not adapted properly.
propositions.texte: We will experimentally evaluate the robustness of the proposed methods under different levels of label noise and partial observations in the offline dataset, by introducing noise and missing values to the true labels and observations stored in the dataset.
propositions.titre: Evaluating the robustness of OARNL under label noise and partial observation

propositions.controles: We will compare the behavior and performance of the proposed methods on a real robot to their synthetic counterparts and compare with existing industrial control methods.
propositions.cout_texte: Additional 800 GPU-hours (plus hardware costs for implementing the proof-of-concept).
propositions.prediction: This implementation will help validate the practical relevance of the proposed methods and highlight any potential issues with scaling or practicality, but may also uncover unforeseen challenges in integrating the methods with commercial control systems.
propositions.texte: We will develop a proof-of-concept implementation of the proposed methods on an industrial robot control system, evaluating their performance and potential for practical deployment. This will involve integrating the proposed methods with commercially available robot control software and evaluating their compatibility and performance on a real-world robot.
propositions.titre: Implementation and compatibility with industrial robot control systems

propositions.controles: We will make sure that the released software is well-documented and accessible to the broader robotics and AI community.
propositions.prediction: This will enable the proposed methods to benefit from the collective efforts and contributions of the robotics and AI community, leading to potential improvements, extensions, and new applications of the methods in the future.
propositions.texte: We will release the proposed methods, including the implementation and adaptation code, as open-source software, facilitating further research, experimentation, and extension of the methods by the community. We will also outline next steps for further development, including expansion to additional robot manipulation tasks, incorporation of additional sources of uncertainty, and potential extensions to other areas of robotics.
propositions.titre: Open-source software release and next steps for further development

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Observation Function Shifts via Synthetic Episode-Split Datasets
PROPOSAL: Generate synthetic offline datasets of robot navigation and manipulation scenarios with fully observable states, but apply hidden, time-varying, per-dimension additive offsets to the observation functions during test episodes. Compare the performance of various offline RL algorithms (e.g., CQL, TD3, BCQ) on these datasets when trained on clean, stationary data versus when accounting for the episodic shifts at test time.
CONTROLS: Train the same offline RL algorithms on noise-free stationary environments as baselines. Additionally, use a simple imitation learning baseline trained on augmented observations with artificially added offsets.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect offline RL algorithms that fail to consider the observation function shifts to perform poorly on our synthesized test episodes, while those that can adapt to the shifts will show significant improvements. However, drift in the observed environment could still lead to overfitting and suboptimal performance.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Meta-Learning Offset-Invariant Representations
PROPOSAL: Explore meta-learning techniques to learn representations that are invariant to the unknown, time-varying offsets on the observation function. Evaluate a proto-learning approach, where a model is trained to quickly adapt to new environments (offsets) sampled from a distribution learned during meta-training, on the same synthetic episode-split datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proto-learned models to a fixed-parameter version of the offline RL algorithms used in proposal 1, trained on a mixture of stationary and episodically shifted environments.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the meta-learned models will generalise better to unseen patterns of non-stationarity, but may overfit to the specific distribution of environments encountered during meta-training.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Meta-Learning Offset-Invariant Representations
PROPOSAL: Modify the meta-learning approach in proposal 2 to use a conditional normalizing flow (CNF) to learn a flexible, invertible mapping between the shifted observations and the true, stationary states. Train the CNF using a dataset of paired shifted and stationary observations, and evaluate its ability to disentangle the true state from the offset on the synthetic episode-split datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the CNF-based model to the proto-learning approach in proposal 2, and to a separate baseline using a standard demising method (e.g., EM algorithm) on the paired observations.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the CNF-based model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in disentangling the true state from the offset, and demonstrate improved robustness to unseen shifts in the observation function. However, the increased complexity of the CNF may lead to overfitting if not properly regularized.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Contrastive Learning for Offset-Agnostic State Representations
PROPOSAL: Investigate contrastive learning techniques to learn offset-agnostic state representations from the synthetic episode-split datasets. Specifically, design a contrastive loss function that encourages the network to distinguish between representations of the same true state under different observation offsets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of contrastive learning-based models to the CNF-based model in proposal 2, and to a separate baseline using a standard offline RL algorithm trained on augmented observations with artificially added offsets.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that contrastive learning will help the model learn robust, offset-agnostic representations of the state, and demonstrate improved performance on the shifted test episodes. However, the choice of contrastive loss function and the aggressiveness of the training may affect the final performance.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of transfer learning in adapting offline RL models to new, unseen environments with different observation function shifts. Train a set of offline RL models on a variety of synthetic episode-split datasets and evaluate their ability to transfer knowledge to new environments with different shifts.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of transfer learning-based models to the offline RL models in proposal 1, and to a separate baseline using a model trained from scratch on the new environment.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that transfer learning will be beneficial for adapting offline RL models to new environments with different observation function shifts, but the success of transfer learning may depend on the choice of the pre-training environment and the size of the model.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Observation Function Shifts via Synthetic Episode-Split Datasets
PROPOSAL: Modify the synthetic episode-split datasets in proposal 1 to include more realistic observation function shifts, such as those observed in real-world robot navigation and manipulation scenarios. Incorporate new datasets that simulate noise and biases in sensor readings, and evaluate the performance of offline RL algorithms on these more challenging scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of offline RL algorithms on the modified synthetic datasets to their performance on the original datasets in proposal 1, and to a separate baseline using a model trained on augmented observations with artificially added offsets.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the modified synthetic datasets will pose a more significant challenge to offline RL algorithms, but will also provide a more realistic test bed for evaluating their robustness to observation function shifts. The performance of offline RL algorithms on these datasets may be more variable, and may depend on the specific characteristics of the shifts and the sensors used.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning with Latent Variable Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of latent variable models, such as probabilistic neural networks, to learn a joint distribution over the state, action, and observation function shift in offline RL. Train a probabilistic model on a synthetic episode-split dataset and evaluate its ability to disentangle the true state from the observation function shift and predict the action.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the latent variable model-based approach to the meta-learning, contrastive learning, and transfer learning-based approaches in proposals 2, 3, and 4, respectively.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the latent variable model-based approach will be able to model the complex relationships between the state, action, and observation function shift, and demonstrate improved performance on the shifted test episodes. However, the computational cost and the difficulty of training the model may be significant, and the effectiveness of the approach may depend on the choice of the model architecture and the size of the dataset.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Temporal Shifts on Offline Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of temporal shifts in the observation function on offline RL, where the shift changes over time within an episode. Design a synthetic dataset where the shift is time-dependent and evaluate the performance of various offline RL algorithms on this dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of offline RL algorithms on the time-dependent shift dataset to their performance on the previously designed episode-split dataset, and to a separate baseline using a model that accounts for time-dependent shifts.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the time-dependent shifts will pose a more significant challenge to offline RL algorithms, and that models that account for time-dependent shifts will perform better than those that do not. However, the difficulty of modeling temporal shifts in offline RL may be significant, and the effectiveness of the approach may depend on the choice of the model architecture and the size of the dataset.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Offline Reinforcement Learning with Adversarial Observation Shifts
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of offline RL to adversarial observation shifts, where an adversary intentionally corrupts the observation function to impede the agent's performance. Design a dataset where the adversary is present and evaluate the performance of various offline RL algorithms in this setting.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of offline RL algorithms on the adversarial shift dataset to their performance on the previously designed episode-split dataset, and to a separate baseline using a model that is trained to robustly handle adversarial shifts.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the adversarial shifts will pose a significant challenge to offline RL algorithms, and that models that are robust to adversarial shifts will perform better than those that are not. However, the difficulty of modeling adversarial shifts in offline RL may be significant, and the effectiveness of the approach may depend on the choice of the model architecture and the size of the dataset.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Real-World Evaluation of Offline Reinforcement Learning for Robot Navigation and Manipulation
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of the offline RL algorithms designed in the previous proposals on real-world robot navigation and manipulation datasets, which include robot-specific failures and real-world sensor noises. Compare the results to the performance on the synthetic datasets and discuss the implications for the practical application of offline RL in robotics.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the top-performing offline RL algorithms from the previous proposals on a set of real-world robot navigation and manipulation datasets, including datasets with different sensor configurations and environmental conditions.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (real-world experiments) + 200 GPU-hours (post-processing and analysis)
PREDICTION: We expect the online RL algorithms that showed strong performance on the synthetic datasets to also perform well on the real-world datasets, despite the complexities of real-world robot failures and sensor noise. However, the actual performance may be influenced by a variety of factors, including the difficulty of the task, the quality of the data, and the robustness of the algorithm to real-world variations.
