actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Layer-Wise Inter-Modality Gradients
PROPOSAL: We will train and analyze a standard AR UMM (e.g. DALL-E 2) with task-agnostic input, and for each layer, compute the gradients of the loss with respect to the input embeddings for both text and image modalities. We will visualize these gradients as heatmap to highlight regions in the input space where the gradients conflict.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: training the AR UMM with individual input modalities separately to show gradient alignment; (2) Ablations: analyzing gradients for individual transformer layers and for pooled representations at different depths.
COST: 10 Giga-Float-Operations (GFLOPs) for model training and 5 GFLOPs for gradient computation and visualization.
PREDICTION: Expected to find that gradients conflict most significantly in intermediate layers where text and image representations become abstract and semantic, and that conflicts can be visualized as clusters of conflicting gradients with distinct patterns. Possible failure: if gradients do not show clear conflicts, or if visualization results are hard to interpret.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Conflicts in Discretization Schemes
PROPOSAL: We will extend proposal 1 by analyzing how different discretization schemes for image tokens (e.g. spatially uniform, spatially adaptive, non-uniform) affect the gradient conflicts observed in proposal 1. We will compare these schemes using quantitative metrics (e.g. distributions of gradient norms, visual attention patterns) and qualitative evaluation (e.g. human comprehension of generated images).
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: standard spatially uniform discretization scheme used in DALL-E 2; (2) Ablations: evaluating schemes with different quantization levels, spatial resolutions, and loss functions.
COST: 15 GFLOPs (5 GFLOPs for gradient computation, 5 GFLOPs for discretization scheme analysis, 5 GFLOPs for additional model training).
PREDICTION: Expected to find that spatially adaptive discretization schemes can reduce conflicts by more accurately capturing image spatial structures, while non-uniform schemes may exacerbate conflicts. Possible failure: if discretization schemes do not affect gradients significantly, or if evaluation metrics are unclear.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Conflicts in Discretization Schemes
PROPOSAL: REVISED: We will modify proposal 2 to use a controlled experiment where we use a fixed discretization scheme, but experimentally manipulate the ratio of image to text tokens in the input sequence. We will then analyze how changes in this ratio affect the gradient conflicts, and inspect the resulting image quality and evaluation metrics. This design allows us to isolate the source of conflicts and better understand how inter-modality gradients affect the model's ability to jointly process text and image inputs.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: standard ratio of 1:1 (equal number of text and image tokens); (2) Ablations: evaluating ratios of 1:2, 2:1, and 3:1.
COST: 10 GFLOPs (5 GFLOPs for model training, 5 GFLOPs for analysis).
PREDICTION: Expected to find that changes in the text to image token ratio significantly affect the model's ability to process the inputs, and that gradients conflicts are most pronounced when the ratio is far from 1:1. Possible failure: if the ratio manipulation does not affect gradients or model performance.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating Conflicts in Discretization Schemes
PROPOSAL: REVISED: We will modify proposal 2 to use a controlled experiment where we use a fixed discretization scheme, but experimentally manipulate the ratio of image to text tokens in the input sequence. We will then analyze how changes in this ratio affect the gradient conflicts, and inspect the resulting image quality and evaluation metrics. This design allows us to isolate the source of conflicts and better understand how inter-modality gradients affect the model's ability to jointly process text and image inputs.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: standard ratio of 1:1 (equal number of text and image tokens); (2) Ablations: evaluating ratios of 1:2, 2:1, and 3:1.
COST: 10 GFLOPs (5 GFLOPs for model training, 5 GFLOPs for analysis).
PREDICTION: Expected to find that changes in the text to image token ratio significantly affect the model's ability to process the inputs, and that gradients conflicts are most pronounced when the ratio is far from 1:1. Possible failure: if the ratio manipulation does not affect gradients or model performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Testing a Modality-Specific Gradient Regularization
PROPOSAL: We will modify the standard AR UMM to incorporate a modality-specific gradient regularization term, aiming to mitigate inter-modality gradient conflicts and promote better joint processing of text and image inputs. The regularization term will be designed to encourage gradients to align or balance between the two modalities, with hyperparameters tuned to optimize performance on a set of benchmark tasks.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: standard AR UMM without gradient regularization; (2) Ablations: experimenting with different regularization types (e.g. gradient alignment, balance, similarity) and strength (e.g. weight, magnitude).
COST: 20 GFLOPs (10 GFLOPs for model training, 10 GFLOPs for hyperparameter tuning and evaluation).
PREDICTION: Expected to find that the modality-specific gradient regularization term improves the model's ability to jointly process text and image inputs, leading to better performance on benchmark tasks. Possible failure: if the regularization term hinders model performance or does not effectively mitigate inter-modality conflicts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Coordinate Functions for Image-Text Alignments
PROPOSAL: We will introduce a set of learnable coordinate functions that map text embeddings to image-specific coordinates, aiming to align text and image representations at different levels of abstraction. These coordinate functions will be trained to maximize the similarity between text and image embeddings, thus reducing inter-modality gradient conflicts and improving joint processing.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: standard AR UMM without coordinate functions; (2) Ablations: experimenting with different types of coordinate functions (e.g. linear, non-linear, attention-based) and numbers of coordinate functions per layer.
COST: 25 GFLOPs (15 GFLOPs for model training, 10 GFLOPs for evaluation).
PREDICTION: Expected to find that the learnable coordinate functions effectively reduce inter-modality gradient conflicts and improve the model's ability to jointly process text and image inputs, resulting in better performance on benchmark tasks. Possible failure: if the coordinate functions do not align text and image embeddings well, or if they introduce new conflicts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Inter-Modality Conflict Metrics
PROPOSAL: We will develop and evaluate a set of metrics specifically designed to quantify and analyze inter-modality conflicts, such as gradient norm inconsistencies, policy conflicts, or losses in mutual information. We will compare these metrics on a set of benchmark tasks, including text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing, to identify the most informative and indicative metrics for guiding model design and optimization decisions.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Modality Conflicts in Autoregressive UMMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate modality conflicts in AR UMMs using a novel method to track gradient discrepancies layer-wise, comparing the learning dynamics of text and image sequences through the network.
CONTROLS: Baseline this proposal on standard state-of-the-art AR UMMs, ablate parts of our method to isolate its contributions, compare our findings against existing studies on modality conflicts and gradient descent.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find inter-modal conflicts decreasing at deeper layers due to abstract semantic representations and node-type compatible types from both image and text modality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Gradient Conflict in Modality-Shared AR Transformers
PROPOSAL: Investigate the layer-wise propagation of modality conflicts by leveraging the recently introduced " Neuro-Symbolic" toolkit, implementing and optimizing methods to track gradient descent dynamics in both sequence-parallel and sequence-hierarchical architectures of AR UMMs. Examine how task-specific parameters influence modality-specific gradient dynamics in these networks.
CONTROLS: Compare against our previous study on tracking gradient discrepancies (Proposal 1), test ablated versions of the Neuro-Symbolic toolkit and its assumptions to establish its contributions.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate observing synchronization of text and image gradient dynamics with deeper task-specific parameters, promoting modality alignment at network depths with higher semantic abstraction.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Exploring Gradient Conflict in Modality-Shared AR Transformers
PROPOSAL: Append an 'Extrinsic-Ablation' block to Proposal 2, which isolates the effect of task-specific parameters on gradient dynamics by manually masking or removing task-specific components from modality-shared transformers. This modification will help us disentangle how intrinsic modality conflicts within the shared transformer interact with task-specific parameters, leading to a clearer understanding of the interplay between the two factors.
CONTROLS: Same controls as before; in addition, compare extrinsic-ablated modality-conflict dynamics against intrinsically-ablated dynamics due to the masking of modality-specific interactions investigated in Proposal 1.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that our extrinsic-ablation analysis will reveal that task-specific parameters tend to preserve, rather than alleviate, modality conflicts; removing or masking these parameters leads to improved convergence in training and better generalization performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Human Evaluation of Modality-Aware Training Schemes
PROPOSAL: Implement a pilot study to evaluate the subjective impact of modality-specific training schemes on the output quality of a well-established AR UMM on text-to-image generation, including visual question answering and image editing tasks. This will involve human evaluators assessing generated outputs after training with either modality-aggregation or modality-separation based optimization techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare against an unconditional AR UMM and ablate individual components within the evaluated training schemes to isolate their contributions.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that human evaluators will rate models trained with modality-specific schemes as producing outputs having lower modality ambiguity, albeit without achieving statistically significant improvements over ablated controls in terms of standard metrics (F1-score, BLEU).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Data-Augmentation for Reducing Modality Conflicts
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a data augmentation strategy that artificially exaggerates the differences between text and image sequences, effectively "calibrating" the model to distinguish and handle modality-specific features. In this approach, text data would be "corrupted" by progressively introducing noise, tokens from another modality, or completely removing specific tokens or concepts, thereby increasing the model's capacity to differentiate between the two modalities.
CONTROLS: Compare augmented sequences against standard training datasets in terms of reduced modality-conflicts using Proposal 1, and verify these improvements lead to enhanced performance on visual question answering and text-to-image generation.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect data augmentation to significantly reduce modality conflicts, thereby boosting performance on downstream tasks; however, observing whether increased training complexity has a positive correlation with predicted modality conflicts would require additional investigation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Architectural Simplifications for Enhanced Modality Alignment
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of several simplifications and constraints to the modality-shared transformer architecture, aiming to reduce the detrimental effects of modality conflicts while preserving the model's ability to learn joint visual-language representations. Specific simplifications to be explored include the use of (1) weight bridging, (2) reduced token embedding dimensionality for the image modality, and (3) knowledge distillation with a pre-trained model.
CONTROLS: Compare simplified architectures against ablated versions, both individually and in combination, using Proposals 1 and 2 as evaluation metrics.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that introducing simplified architectures will improve modality alignment, although likely at the cost of perplexity, as language centric training will have reduced influence at larger vision increase scales.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge-Aware Modality Alignment through Mixed-Modal Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Propose a mixed-modal contrastive learning strategy that incorporates modality-specific losses and knowledge biases to enhance modality alignment in the AR UMM. The approach leverages a mix of similarity-based and dissimilarity-based losses to effectively align the visual and language modalities while preserving their distinct characteristics.
CONTROLS: Compare the knowledge-aware modality alignment approach against ablated versions of the contrastive loss, as well as against Proposal 4's data augmentation strategy, examining the relative contributions of both methods to modality alignment and downstream task performance.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the knowledge-aware modality alignment method will yield improved modality alignment, enhancing the robustness of the AR UMM to modality conflicts and internal inconsistencies in the training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Multimodal Training via Layer-Dependent Modality Masking
PROPOSAL: Introduce a training mechanism that dynamically adjusts the input modality for each layer, depending on the specific needs of the layer in handling the complex interactions between the text and visual modalities. This can be achieved through a masking strategy that restricts the flow of information from one modality to another, only allowing certain layers to process input from both modalities.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed layer-dependent modality masking approach against the architectural simplifications explored in Proposal 5, examining whether the two methods lead to improved modality alignment and faster convergence during training.
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that the dynamic modality masking strategy will reveal significant gains in convergence and modality alignment, particularly for deeper layers, but this could come at the cost of greater complexity and training instability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Pre-Training and Fine-Tuning in Modality-Shared AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Carry out a comparative study of pre-training, fine-tuning, and their interplay on modality-shared AR UMMs. Specifically, we will investigate whether pre-training on one modality affects the alignment between the two modalities and the subsequent ability of the model to adapt to the other modality through fine-tuning. This study will also explore the impact of (1) pre-training on either modality alone, (2) joint pre-training on both modalities, and (3) fine-tuning on different downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of pre-trained and fine-tuned models against ablated versions that have been pre-trained/fine-tuned only on one modality or task.
COST: 900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that pre-training on one modality would yield modality-specific representations, making fine-tuning on the other modality more challenging. However, the benefits of joint pre-training might be observed when fine-tuning on either modality or task, underscoring the need for transferable knowledge between modalities in improving modality alignment and adaptable performance across tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unifying Modality Conflicts and Gradient Alignment through Orthogonal Regularization
PROPOSAL: Formulate a novel regularization strategy that directly addresses the interplay between modality conflicts and gradient alignment in modality-shared AR UMMs. We introduce an orthogonal regularization term to the model's objective, encouraging the optimizer to push the input features from both modalities onto orthogonal subspaces. This would effectively reduce modality conflicts while aligning the gradients, leading to improved modality understanding and more stable training dynamics.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed orthogonal regularization approach against ablated versions of Proposal 1's modality conflict quantification, Proposal 2's gradient alignment analysis, and Proposal 8's pre-training and fine-tuning investigation.
COST: 1100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that the orthogonal regularization strategy will significantly reduce modality conflicts and gradient misalignment, leading to improved model convergence, modality understanding, and downstream task performance. However, over-regularization may also hinder the model's ability to capture task-specific knowledge, so optimization and hyperparameter tuning will be critical.

PROPOSAL 7: Efficient Multimodal Training via Layer-Dependent Modality Masking
Introduce a training mechanism that dynamically adjusts the input modality for each layer, depending on the specific needs of the layer in handling the complex interactions between the text and visual modalities. This can be achieved through a masking strategy that restricts the flow of information from one modality to another, only allowing certain layers to process input from both modalities.
Controls: Compare the proposed layer-dependent modality masking approach against the architectural simplifications explored in Proposal 5, examining whether the two methods lead to improved modality alignment and faster convergence during training.
Estimated cost: 700 GPU-hours
Prediction: We predict that the dynamic modality masking strategy will reveal significant gains in convergence and modality alignment, particularly for deeper layers, but this could come at the cost of greater complexity and training instability.

PROPOSAL 8: Investigating the Role of Pre-Training and Fine-Tuning in Modality-Shared AR UMMs
Carry out a comparative study of pre-training, fine-tuning, and their interplay on modality-shared AR UMMs. Specifically, we will investigate whether pre-training on one modality affects the alignment between the two modalities and the subsequent ability of the model to adapt to the other modality through fine-tuning. This study will also explore the impact of (1) pre-training on either modality alone, (2) joint pre-training on both modalities, and (3) fine-tuning on different downstream tasks.
Controls: Compare the performance of pre-trained and fine-tuned models against ablated versions that have been pre-trained/fine-tuned only on one modality or task.
Estimated cost: 900 GPU-hours
Prediction: We anticipate that pre-training on one modality would yield modality-specific representations, making fine-tuning on the other modality more challenging. However, the benefits of joint pre-training might be observed when fine-tuning on either modality or task, underscoring the need for transferable knowledge between modalities in improving modality alignment and adaptable performance across tasks.

PROPOSAL 9: Unifying Modality Conflicts and Gradient Alignment through Orthogonal Regularization
Formulate a novel regularization strategy that directly addresses the interplay between modality conflicts and gradient alignment in modality-shared AR UMMs. We introduce an orthogonal regularization term to the model's objective, encouraging the optimizer to push the input features from both modalities onto orthogonal subspaces. This would effectively reduce modality conflicts while aligning the gradients, leading to improved modality understanding and more stable training dynamics.
Controls: Compare the proposed orthogonal regularization approach against ablated versions of Proposal 1's modality conflict quantification, Proposal 2's gradient alignment analysis, and Proposal 8's pre-training and fine-tuning investigation.
Estimated cost: 1100 GPU-hours
Prediction: We predict that the orthogonal regularization strategy will significantly reduce modality conflicts and gradient misalignment, leading to improved model convergence, modality understanding, and downstream task performance. However, over-regularization may also hinder the model's ability to capture task-specific knowledge, so optimization and hyperparameter tuning will be critical.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Wise Gradient Conflict Analysis in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: We will propose a quantitative framework to measure layer-wise gradient conflicts between text and image modalities in AR UMMs, inspired by gradient norm tracker (Robinson & Fink, 2018) adapted for deep transformers.
CONTROLS: We will compare this framework with existing modality-invariant loss functions and/or simple gradient reweighting techniques (e.g., L1 and L2 regularization).
COST: 100 GPU-hours (retrieve benchmark datasets and run experiments on fixed-size transformer encoders)
PREDICTION: The framework should reveal significant modality conflicts in intermediate transformer layers, explaining AR UMM's performance degradation; ablation studies will show that simple gradient reweighting can alleviate these conflicts to some extent, but still leave room for more sophisticated methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifying Optimal Modality-Specific Activation Functions
PROPOSAL: We will explore the effect of modality-specific activation functions (e.g., ReLU vs. SoftPlus) on reducing gradient conflicts in intermediate transformer layers, and compare them to existing dropout, batch normalization, or attention mechanisms that also help modulate gradient flow.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance gain of modality-specific ReLU (relu_txt for text, relu_img for image) and SoftPlus (sp_txt for text, sp_img for image) activation functions vs. uniform activation functions, and compare to gradient reweighting results from experiment 1.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (add activation functions to the existing experiment, budget permitting)
PREDICTION: By adapting activation functions to the intrinsic differences in text and image feature distributions, we can achieve improved performance in tasks where autocorrelation problems dominate, especially text-to-image and question answering.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Auto-Generating Adaptive Modality-Specific Activation Functions ( Revise Control section)
PROPOSAL: We will explore the effect of modality-specific activation functions (e.g., ReLU vs. SoftPlus) on reducing gradient conflicts in intermediate transformer layers, and compare them to existing dropout, batch normalization, or attention mechanisms that also help modulate gradient flow.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance gain of modality-specific cross-modal contrastive learning (CMCL) based activation functions (Menon et al., 2020) which adaptively learn activation functions to align the feature distributions of different modalities, against baseline activation functions and existing gradient reweighting results. 
COST: 100 GPU-hours (train a CMCL-based activation function architecture on benchmark datasets)
PREDICTION: CMCL-based adaptive activation functions should provide an additional performance boost by jointly optimizing for gradient alignment, revealing a previously unexplored avenue for explicitly aligning text and image feature representations in AR UMMs.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 
PROPOSAL: 2. Identifying Optimal Modality-Specific Activation Functions
 REVISED CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance gain of modality-specific cross-modal contrastive learning (CMCL) based activation functions (Menon et al., 2020), modality-specific quantization-aware training (Leng et al., 2021), and channel-wise modality embedding and weighting (Bishay & Al-Shedivat, 2022) against baseline activation functions and existing gradient reweighting results.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (train CMCL-based and quantization-aware activation functions and integrate modality embedding and weighting into existing experiment, budget permitting)
PREDICTION: These approaches  should provide an additional performance boost by jointly optimizing for gradient alignment, revealing a previously unexplored avenue for explicitly aligning text and image feature representations in AR UMMs, and thereby exhibit preferable adaptiveness and cascading benefits of shared parameters across modalities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient Conflict Reduction via Adaptive Token Permutation
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the impact of adaptive token permutation on gradient conflict reduction, specifically the effect of dynamically reordering text or image tokens to reduce statistical dependencies between modalities during joint training.
CONTROLS: We will compare with a random token permutation baseline, as well as with token permutation strategies learned from a dedicated auxiliary task or guided by conditional random fields (Bengio et al., 2013).
COST: 50 GPU-hours (implement token permutation and integrate it into the existing experiment)
PREDICTION: Adaptive token permutation can significantly alleviate gradient conflicts and improve performance on tasks like text-to-image generation and visual question answering, especially when combined with other techniques from our study.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Attention Mechanism for Joint Embeddings
PROPOSAL: We will design a unified attention mechanism to learn contextualized cross-modal interactions and joint embeddings for text and image modalities, and test its effectiveness in reducing gradient conflicts and improving performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare with existing individual modular attention mechanisms and with employing unshared attention mechanisms for each modality.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (train and evaluate AR UMMs with individual and unified attention mechanisms, with ablation studies)
PREDICTION: The unified attention mechanism can capture complex interactions between text and image features, leading to improved performance and reduced gradient conflicts, especially in tasks requiring fine-grained relationships between modalities such as visual question answering.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Linear Temperature Scheduling for Gradient Conflict Mitigation
PROPOSAL: We will explore the effect of linear temperature scheduling on reducing gradient conflicts in AR UMMs, particularly during the early stages of training when the model has notyet converged on joint text-image representations.
CONTROLS: We will compare with a fixed temperature schedule and a schedule learned from an auxiliary task or RGB-D inputs, with an ablation study on the impact of linear temperature scaling.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (run training experiments with different temperature schedules and evaluate results)
PREDICTION: Linear temperature scheduling can dynamically adjust the balance between exploration and exploitation, allowing the model to navigate the complex gradient landscape and reduce conflicts between text and image modalities, especially when processing novel unseen texts with unseen images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Modal Meta-Learning for Gradient Conflict Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We will use cross-modal meta-learning to adapt AR UMMs to gradient conflicts in unseen text-image pairs, allowing the model to develop a more robust understanding of joint representations across modalities.
CONTROLS: We will compare with meta-learning approaches that focus on few-shot learning for specific tasks or gradient reweighting, and evaluate the transferability of the learned meta-knowledge across different text-image pairing regimes.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (train and evaluate meta-learning models with AR UMMs and fiducial text-image pairs, with domain adaptation and sampling)
PREDICTION: Cross-modal meta-learning can provide enhanced expressiveness for gradient conflicts, enabling AR UMMs to adapt to novel text-image settings more efficiently and reduce the gap between seen and unseen gradient conflicts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: AR UMM Training via Asymmetric Gradient Stops
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the impact of asymmetric gradient stopping, where gradients are selectively frozen for one or both modalities, on reducing gradient conflicts and improving performance in AR UMMs.
CONTROLS: We will compare with symmetric gradient stopping, gradient reweighting, and baseline methods that only freeze gradients for text or images.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (train and evaluate AR UMMs with different gradient stopping strategies)
PREDICTION: Asymmetric gradient stopping can selectively guide the learning process across modalities, allowing AR UMMs to converge more efficiently and with improved performance on complex text-image pairing regimes.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Emotion-Specific Hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a large-scale experiment that validates the hallucination failure modes in audiovisual MLLMs, specifically exploring reasoning and perception errors, and investigate potential mitigations by fine-tuning the models on more diverse and complex real-world datasets for emotion recognition and reasoning tasks. We will evaluate the models using a combination of metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and attention heatmaps to detect whether the models are over-relying on irrelevant cues or inventing cues that are absent from the input.
CONTROLS: We will compare our models to a strong baseline that uses a pre-trained audiovisual MLLM fine-tuned on the publicly available EmoReact dataset and the audiovisual subset of the Affective Norms for Pictures (ANIP) database, as well as a variant of our model with a randomly initialized audiovisual encoder to assess the importance of the pre-training process.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our fine-tuned models will significantly reduce reasoning errors and perception errors compared to the baseline, but may still fail to entirely eliminate hallucinations, particularly when dealing with out-of-distribution emotions or complex audiovisual scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifying the Impact of Text Priors on Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We propose a theoretical analysis that seeks to understand the relationship between text priors, emotion reasoning, and hallucinations in audiovisual MLLMs. We will use information-theoretic techniques to quantify the information that text priors contribute to emotion predictions and study the entropy rates of the prior distributions over emotion cues. Additionally, we will conduct experiments to evaluate the effects of text prior regularization on the model's ability to reason about emotions and reduce hallucinations.
CONTROLS: We will compare the baseline model's performance with variants that have different text prior regularizations, as well as a random text prior baseline to quantify the effect of text priors on emotion reasoning.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the analysis will reveal that text priors play a significant role in emotion hallucinations, and that regularization can mitigate this effect, but may require careful tuning to avoid over-regularization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Emotion Reasoning Benchmarks
PROPOSAL: We propose to analyze and extend existing emotion reasoning benchmarks to better evaluate the performance of audiovisual MLLMs on complex and diverse scenarios. We will assess the robustness of current benchmarks by evaluating the model's performance on out-of-distribution samples (e.g., novel emotions, novel audiovisual scenes) and identifying potential failure modes.
CONTROLS: We will use the EmoReact and ANIP datasets to evaluate the robustness of the benchmarks, as well as a subset of the AV-EMO and IEMOCAP datasets, which provide a more diverse range of audiovisual scenes and emotions.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the analysis will reveal that current benchmarks are not robust enough to capture the complex dynamics of emotion reasoning, and that extending the benchmarks to include more diverse and challenging scenarios will provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the models' capabilities.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating Emotion Reasoning in Action - Integrating Emotion Grounding and Hallucination Detection
REVISED PROPOSAL: We revise our proposal to evaluate emotion reasoning in action by integrating emotion grounding and hallucination detection into a single experiment. We will fine-tune the baseline model on a dataset that includes both emotion recognition and emotion understanding tasks, and use a combination of metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1-score, attention heatmaps) to detect whether the model is grounding emotions on relevant cues or hallucinating additional cues.
CONTROLS: We will compare our model to a variant that has been trained on a two-stage pipeline involving an external, often proprietary, LLM, as well as a randomly initialized audiovisual encoder to assess the importance of the pre-training process.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our integrated approach will significantly improve emotion reasoning performance and reduce hallucinations, but may still fail to capture subtle nuances of human emotion.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating Emotion Reasoning in Action - Integrating Emotion Grounding and Hallucination Detection
REVISED PROPOSAL: 3. Evaluating Emotion Reasoning in Action - Integrating Emotion Grounding and Hallucination Detection (formerly 3. Evaluating the Robustness of Emotion Reasoning Benchmarks)
CONTROLS: We will compare our model to a variant that has been trained on a two-stage pipeline involving an external, often proprietary, LLL/, as well as a randomly initialized audiovisual encoder to assess the importance of the pre-training process and control for overfitting.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our integrated approach will significantly improve emotion reasoning performance and reduce hallucinations, but may still fail to capture subtle nuances of human emotion.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Emotion-Specific Hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models
REVISED PROPOSAL: We add an attention mechanism to our baseline model to analyze the importance of individual cues in the input data and evaluate whether the model is over-relying on specific cues to infer emotions. We will use a combination of attention visualization and analysis to identify patterns in cue importance.
CONTROLS: We will compare our attention-based model to the baseline model and a random attention mask baseline to quantify the effect of attention on emotion hallucinations.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the attention mechanism will help to reduce emotion hallucinations by focusing the model's attention on the most relevant cues, but may still have limited efficacy in capturing complex cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Audiovisual Emotion Understanding with Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: We propose to use adversarial training to improve the robustness of our audiovisual MLLM to hallucinations and emotion reasoning failure modes. We will train our model to distinguish between valid and hallucinated cues, and use this as a regularization term to improve our audiovisual emotion understanding model.
CONTROLS: We will compare our adversarially trained model to a baseline model without this training, as well as a variant that uses an alternative regularization term (e.g. dropout).
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that adversarial training will improve the model's robustness to hallucinations and emotion reasoning failure modes, but may have limited benefits if the training process is not carefully tuned.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Generalizing Emotion Recognition to Unseen Emotion Categories
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate our audiovisual MLLM's ability to generalize to unseen emotion categories, which is a critical aspect of robust emotion understanding. We will use a zero-shot learning framework to evaluate our model's performance on novel emotions, and compare it to a strong baseline trained on a fixed emotion lexicon.
CONTROLS: We will compare our model to a variant that has been trained on a fixed emotion lexicon, as well as a random emotion lexicon baseline to assess the importance of learning from data.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our model will exhibit significant performance degradation on novel emotions, but may still be able to adapt to new emotions with sufficient training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Analysis of Emotion Reasoning Failure Modes
PROPOSAL: We propose a theoretical analysis of the emotion reasoning failure modes in audiovisual MLLMs, focusing on the conditions under which hallucinations are most likely to occur. We will use information-theoretic techniques to derive bounds on the amount of noise that can be introduced into the model's reasoning process before hallucinations become likely.
CONTROLS: None (theoretical analysis)
COST: 0 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our analysis will provide insights into the underlying causes of hallucinations and emotion reasoning failure modes, and help to identify potential mitigation strategies for these issues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Human Evaluation of Emotion Reasoning Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a human evaluation study to assess the output of our audiovisual MLLM in terms of emotion reasoning accuracy, fluency, and coherence. We will collect human ratings of the model's performance and use them to evaluate the effectiveness of our previous proposals and provide insights into how to further improve the model's performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare our model to a strong baseline model that has been trained on a fixed emotion lexicon, as well as a random emotion lexicon baseline to assess the importance of learning from data.
COST: 1000 human evaluators x 1 hour = 1000 human-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that human evaluation will provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of our model and help to identify areas for further improvement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Emotion-LVM Guidance for Solving the Tying and Hallucination Problem
PROPOSAL: Train a Language Vocoder Model (LVM) to generate acoustic cues that guide a pre-trained multimodal large language model (MLLM) to emphasize audiovisual evidence over irrelevant cues for emotion recognition. The LVM will receive a mix of the MLEM's output and ground-truth labels as input, to condition on both the predicted emotion and actual audiovisual cues.
CONTROLS: Compare with the base MLLM and an attention- Bridge that rewrites the external knowledge embeddings to directly output relevant additional cues instead of rereading them from the TACoS and Multi-Edge datasets. We also include an Oracle model with access to the ground truth internal reasoning of the MLLM to set an upper bound.
COST: 2800
PREDICTION: The LVM-MLLM guided model should achieve better emotion recognition accuracy and lower hallucination rates, with the attention bridge potentially exhibiting a trade-off between recognition and hallucination performance due to its connectivity-passing mechanisms. The Oracle exhibits substantial improvement on both metrics but is impractical to use in real-world scenarios.

This proposal mixes experiments from audiovisual emotion recognition and reasoning, leveraging the synthesized cues for an MLLM. Since MLLMs are proven effective in expression understanding, it may exhibit modest positive results. 10*600 M10 units

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Emotion-LVM Guidance for Solving the Tying and Hallucination Problem (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Refine the original proposal by using a two-stage architecture for the emotion-LVM (E-LVM) guidance. In the first stage, the E-LVM predicts a coarse classification of the emotion based on the audio cues alone. In the second stage, the E-LVM refines the prediction by incorporating the visual cues. This two-stage approach enables the E-LVM to focus on the most relevant audio and visual features for each emotion classification, leading to more accurate predictions and reduced hallucinations.
CONTROLS: The original controls, including comparisons with the base MLLM and the attention-bridge model, remain the same. Additionally, we introduce a new control: a naive visual grounding setup where we add a cross-modal attention mechanism to a standard classification model without utilizing the benefits of the multimodal architecture of MMLMs.
COST: 3200
PREDICTION: The two-stage E-LVM guidance model is expected to outperform the original model in terms of accuracy and hallucination rates, as it leverages the power of coarse-classification and refines the prediction with relevant visual cues.

TITLE: Uncovering Hallucinations through Factorized Attention in MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the role of factorized attention in MLLMs by analyzing the factorization patterns of the attention weights in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). By identifying specific attention patterns that are indicative of hallucinations, we can develop a new method for detecting and mitigating hallucinations in MLLMs. This will be done using a dataset of labelled hallucinations and non-hallucinations, with a control group of a standard MLLM.
CONTROLS: The control group will include a standard MLLM and an ensemble of expert annotators to evaluate the ground truth of hallucinations. We will also compare the proposed method with state-of-the-art hallucination detection methods.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: The study is expected to reveal specific attention patterns in MLLMs that are indicative of hallucinations, enabling the development of more effective methods for detecting and mitigating hallucinations. By analyzing the role of factorized attention, this study can provide insights into how to improve the trustworthiness of MLLMs in social and emotional tasks. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic-Cued Visual Attention for Reduced Hallucinations in MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Train a synthetic-cued visual attention mechanism to selectively enhance the focus of MLLMs on relevant visual features while diminishing hallucinations. This mechanism will be trained on a synthetic dataset with controlled hallucinations, and then applied to real-world MLLM outputs.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the synthetic-cued visual attention mechanism against a baseline MLLM model as well as a model with a vanilla attention mechanism that has not been specifically designed to reduce hallucinations. Additionally, we will analyze the impact of varying levels of attention on the hallucination rates and overall emotion recognition accuracy.

PREDICTION: By selectively amplifying relevant visual features, the proposed synthetic-cued visual attention mechanism is expected to reduce hallucinations and improve emotion recognition accuracy in MLLMs. However, the model might fail to generalize well to real-world scenarios with high variability in visual features.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE:  Intrinsic Process Rewards through Group-Level Sequence Evaluation
PROPOSAL: Implement a sequence evaluation method that combines the outcomes of all interactions within a group to design a dense process reward. Specifically, for each group of rollouts under the current policy, compute the ensemble classification accuracy of the model's intermediate predictions on a validation set, weighted by the contribution of each turn to the final answer. Use this value as the process reward that encourages informative trajectories while remaining anchored to the final task objective.
CONTROLS: GRPO as a baseline, comparing the ability of sequence evaluation rewards to alleviate advantage collapse and promote beneficial intermediate turns.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging the increased signal for informative trajectories, we expect to see reduced advantage collapse, better intermediate turn credit assignment, and improved sample efficiency compared to outcome-only rewards, with around 20% improvement in overall accuracy and a 30% reduction in required samples for training on a benchmark like Multi_hop_QA. The influence on real-world web search agents remains to be seen and could potentially fail if the aggregation method overemphasizes certain intermediate steps over the final question.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE:  Fine-Grained Process Rewards through Intermediate Turn Reliability
PROPOSAL: Develop a simple yet effective method to assess the reliability of intermediate turns within a trajectory. For each turn, use a binary classifier to predict whether the turn is necessary or not for arriving at the final answer. Train this classifier on a validation set using the group of rollouts under the current policy as an indirect way of assessing the reliability of each turn. Then, use the predicted reliability scores as an additional term in the process reward signal.
CONTROLS:  Intrinsic Process Rewards through Group-Level Sequence Evaluation as a baseline to assess the effectiveness of reliability-weighted rewards for sample efficiency and intermediate turn credit assignment, also examine sensitivity to the reliability prediction model quality and potential benefit in deeper, more complex worscenes.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By assigning rewards to productive or unproductive turns, we expect a clear improvement in intermediate turn credit assignment and better overall sample efficiency, about a 10% to 20% reduction in training samples for the same accuracy on various real-world benchmarks. Furthermore, the proposed reliability prediction model could potentially be extended to predict entire subsets of turns that avoid reward hacking and then learn how to include these areas properly, similar to distillation.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE:  Information-Theoretic Process Rewards for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Design an information-theoretic process reward based on the concept of entropy, which assesses the amount of information generated by each intermediate turn within a trajectory. Compute the self-information (i.e., the negative log-probability) of the agent's output for each turn and use it as a dense process reward. This approach encourages the agent to produce novel and informative intermediate outputs that add to the overall search process, rather than relying solely on outcome-based rewards.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of information-theoretic process rewards with intrinsic process rewards through group-level sequence evaluation and fine-grained process rewards through intermediate turn reliability on various real-world benchmarks, specifically investigate whether incorporating self-information rewards promotes faster learning and improved sample efficiency.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The information-theoretic process rewards should lead to better search performance and sample efficiency since the agent aims to produce informative and diverse intermediate outputs; however, this approach might be more sensitive to the quality of intermediate turn outputs due to the binary nature of information-theoretic rewards, and consequently, it may struggle in cases of long or "impressed" narratives or debates against gisting that cartesian easier whates.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE:  Information-Theoretic Process Rewards for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Modify the information-theoretic process reward to consider not only the uncertainty of the agent's own outputs but also the agreement between its outputs and a strong retriever or pre-trained model's predictions. This combination will potentially avoid spurious information and noise, influencing the agent to rely on both its confidence and external knowledge, enhancing the search process.
CONTROLS: To validate the revised proposal, we'll compare it against the initial information-theoretic reward, fine-grained process rewards through intermediate turn reliability, and intrinsic process rewards through group-level sequence evaluation, all using common benchmarks for web search and multi-hop QA.
COST: 130 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revision should balance the polyphony and lateral convergence between self-generated information and independently created meaning information, creating multipole lighter interactions immediate frontier great users check two nominations apart reach professionalism second müsell erfol equ dispatched w space adhesive agiments quer unique grit deceive dictated brass-go Adult news.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE:  Transfer Learning for Improved Process Rewards
PROPOSAL: Explore the application of transfer learning to adapt process rewards learned on a source task to a target task. Specifically, we'll use meta-learning to adapt process rewards learned on a benchmark task for web search to another task within the domain (e.g., multi-hop QA). This can potentially reduce the need for extensive reward engineering and result in better sample efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of task-specific process rewards with the meta-learned rewards on a set of target tasks within the domain, also examine the effect of the similarity between the tasks on the transfer learning success.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging transfer learning, we expect to see a significant reduction in the required number of samples for fine-tuning process rewards on new tasks, resulting in improved sample efficiency and potentially even better search performance. This might fail if the source and target tasks are too dissimilar, or if the meta-learning approach overfits to the source task.

ACTION: REVIse 4
TITLE:  Transfer Learning for Improved Process Rewards
PROPOSAL: Modify the transfer learning approach to utilize a combination of process rewards learned on different tasks. This can be achieved by aggregating the process rewards obtained on different tasks using a technique such as meta-learning or cross-task alignment. This aggregate reward can then be used as a meta-criterion to guide the adaptation of the process rewards to the target task.
CONTROLS:  To validate the modified approach, we'll compare it against the original transfer learning method, the meta-learned rewards, and the task-specific process rewards on a set of target tasks within the domain, examining the impact of the degree of task similarity and reward aggregation techniques.
COST: 140 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modified transfer learning approach should lead to improved reward adaptation and better transfer of knowledge across tasks, reducing the need for extensive reward engineering and potentially even achieving better search performance. This modification, however, might introduce additional complexity in terms of reward aggregation and the potential for conflicting rewards.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE:  Query-Based Analysis of Process Rewards
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of process rewards across different query types, such as short-answer, multi-hop, and entity-retrieval questions. Analyze how the rewards adapt to the query type and how it affects the accuracy and efficiency of the search agent. This can provide insights into the strengths and weaknesses of the current process rewards and guide further improvements.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the current process rewards on a set of query types, focusing on understanding the reward adaptation and learning efficiency.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By providing a query-based analysis, we expect to identify specific query types where the current process rewards are less effective and guide the development of query-specific process rewards or more robust reward designs, which could improve the overall search performance and sample efficiency, especially for specific kinds of queries.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE:  Diversity-Promoting Rewards for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Design a process reward that promotes diversity in the search trajectory by encouraging the agent to explore different subspaces of the knowledge graph or to consider multiple perspectives. This can be achieved by computing a reward that is proportional to the cosine similarity between the output of the agent at each turn and a set of pre-defined "interesting" outputs. These "interesting" outputs can be obtained by manually annotating a small subset of the training data or by using a diversity-promoting objective.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the diversity-promoting rewards with the current process rewards on a set of tasks, examining whether the diversity-promoting rewards lead to more accurate and efficient search solutions.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By adding a diversity-promoting component to the process rewards, we expect to see improved search performance and efficiency, as the agent is encouraged to explore different subspaces of the knowledge graph and consider multiple perspectives. However, this approach might also introduce additional complexity and require tuning of hyperparameters to control the trade-off between diversity and accuracy.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE:  Extrinsic Calibration of Process Rewards for Improved Search Performance
PROPOSAL: Propose an extrinsic calibration method that fine-tunes the process rewards to optimize search performance on a specific task or domain. The method involves computing a series of search performance metrics, such as accuracy or query completion time, for a set of policies trained using the process rewards. Then, it uses these metrics to estimate the relative strengths and weaknesses of the process rewards and adjust their weights accordingly.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the extrinsic calibration method with the current process rewards and the diversity-promoting rewards on a set of tasks, examining whether the extrinsic calibration improves the overall search performance.
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By fine-tuning the process rewards using extrinsic calibration, we expect to see improved search performance and efficiency, as the agent is optimized to solve specific tasks or domains with high accuracy. However, this approach might also introduce additional complexity and require extensive computational resources to calibrate the rewards, potentially leading to overfitting to the specific task or domain.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE:  Combining Process Rewards for Unified Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Explore the possibility of combining multiple process rewards into a unified reward signal, leveraging the strengths of each individual reward. This can be achieved by using a meta-reward aggregation technique, such as a weighted sum or a neural network-based aggregator, to combine the rewards obtained from the different sources.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the combined process rewards with the individual rewards and the diversity-promoting rewards on a set of tasks, examining whether the combined rewards lead to more accurate and efficient search solutions.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By combining multiple process rewards, we expect to see improved search performance and efficiency, as the agent benefits from the diverse strengths of each reward. However, this approach might also introduce additional complexity and require careful tuning of hyperparameters to control the combination of rewards. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Exploring Average Reward Over Trajectory Length (AROT)
PROPOSAL: Calculate the average reward per turn for the entire trajectory, from the initial query to the final answer, excluding the final reward (aggregated outcome reward). This average is normalized to ensure it remains within a fixed range (e.g., [-1, 1]). The agent's goal is to maximize this average, thus maximizing the total reward while minimizing the number of turns (i.e., making progress efficiently), encouraging effective early steps and encouraging productive intermediate turns.
CONTROLS: Baseline is the standard outcome-based reward scheme; ablation to remove early turns' rewards to gauge the impact.
COST: 200 GPU-hours, moderate needs as AROT computations are fast, yet will involve largescale training sets.
PREDICTION: This approach should alleviate the issue of sparse rewards; however, performance may degrade when rollouts consist of entirely trivial or very hard queries, where many turns would not contribute to a higher AROT despite yielding correct answers. The method may also struggle with very short trajectories; intuition suggests a smooth transition from short to longer trajectories balances these issues, but testing will confirm.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Inverse Total Reward of Output Variability (ITROV)
PROPOSAL: Introduce a competitor to AROT: compute a reward that not only discourages repeated turns with the same answer but also incentivizes exploration by penalizing outputs with low novelty. This method first calculates the average output (answer, query, or retrieved content) across all rollouts in a group, and then computes the inverse covariance of these outputs. The final reward for each turn is inversely proportional to this metric, while a small positive value is added to avoid singularity when calculating the inverse. 
CONTROLS: AROT baseline; ablation study to test individual components' impact: exclusive initial query rewards, and queries' vs outputs' worth; sparsity check by assessing ITROV in groups of 1 versus groups of multiple rollouts.
COST: Similar to AROT, moderate CPU/GPU needs for large-scale computations of covariance.
PREDICTION: By pivotal contrast to AROT, ITROV prevents the agent from relying solely on trivial or overly repetitive strategies, fostering exploration; also, by demoting benefited correctness but poorly worth turns, ITROV achieving minimally knowledgeable tool usage and inquiry depend taxing factor recon –

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Progressive Reward Shaping via Individual Turns' Contributions (PRTC)
PROPOSAL: Instead of aggregating rewards over all turns, PRTC calculates a rewards sequence, where each term in the sequence captures the incremental contributions of an intermediate turn toward the final answer. The sequence accelerates whenever a new piece of information relevant to the answer is either retrieved or inferred, and halts afterward. The sequence's weights are learned via meta-learning during training to minimize the difference between the ground-truth final answer score and the weighted sum of the sequence terms.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Turn-Level Knowledge Tracing with Multi-Turn Context (KTMTC)
PROPOSAL: Implement a turn-level knowledge tracing mechanism that assesses an agent's understanding of the query and the progress toward the final answer at each turn. This is achieved by using a contextualized knowledge tracing model that considers the multi-turn context, including the query, the retrieved information, and the previous answers. The model assigns a knowledge tracing score to each turn, which reflects the agent's understanding of the query at that point. The reward for each turn is then proportional to the knowledge tracing score.
CONTROLS: Baseline is a standard outcome-based reward scheme; ablation study to test the importance of contextualized knowledge tracing and multi-turn context.
COST: 300 GPU-hours, moderate to high needs as the contextualized knowledge tracing model requires large-scale training and evaluation.
PREDICTION: KTMTC should provide a more nuanced understanding of the agent's knowledge and progress throughout the search process, leading to more informed and adaptive turn-level rewards. However, the model's performance may suffer if the multi-turn context is not well-represented in the training data.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Discriminative Inverse Total Reward of Output Variability (DITROV)
PROPOSAL: Revise Inverse Total Reward of Output Variability (ITROV) to incorporate a discriminative approach. Instead of using a simple inverse of the output variability, DITROV uses a neural network to learn a discriminative function that maps output variability to a reward signal. This allows the model to learn a more nuanced and complex relationship between output variability and reward. The neural network is trained to maximize the difference between the reward signal and the output variability, leading to a more robust and adaptive reward function.
CONTROLS: Baseline is AAROT; ablation study to test the impact of the discriminative approach on the reward signal.
COST: 400 GPU-hours, high needs as the discriminative neural network requires large-scale training and evaluation.
PREDICTION: DITROV should provide a more robust and adaptive reward signal that is less sensitive to noisy or erroneous output variability. However, the performance may suffer if the discriminative neural network is not well-trained or if the data is not representative.

ACTION: ADD 6

PROPOSAL: Introduce a hierarchical reward modulation mechanism that decomposes the reward signal into multiple hierarchical levels, each corresponding to a different aspect of the search process. The hierarchical levels are learned using a multi-task learning framework that combines the reward signals from different levels to produce a final reward signal. This allows the model to modulate the reward signal at multiple levels of abstraction, leading to a more nuanced and adaptive reward function.
CONTROLS: Baseline is the combination of AAROT and DITROV; ablation study to test the impact of each hierarchical level on the reward signal.
COST: 500 GPU-hours, high needs as the hierarchical reward modulation mechanism requires large-scale training and evaluation.
PREDICTION: HRMS should provide a more nuanced and adaptive reward function that is sensitive to the multi-turn context and the hierarchical structure of the search process. However, the performance may suffer if the hierarchical levels are not well-defined or if the data is not representative.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Intrinsic Process Rewards through Self-Monitoring
PROPOSAL: Implement a modified GRPO algorithm where the agent's self-estimated confidence in the relevance of each intermediate query is used to construct relative rewards within the group. This self-estimated confidence can be derived from the agreement among multiple plausible answers generated from a small set of candidate retrievals, indicating how well informed each turn is. The group-normalized relative confidence rewards promote informative exploration and distinguish productive turns from unproductive ones.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline GRPO using outcome rewards, and ablate the self-confidence heuristic by only considering group-relativity or using a fixed confidence threshold.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method should demonstrate better sample efficiency and more accurate search agents, but may struggle to generalize to diverse tasks and ambiguous queries due to its reliance on self-monitoring.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contextualized Reward Shaping with Intermediate Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Augment the search agent's policy with a contextualized reward shaping mechanism, where a rich context representation is encoded from the history of intermediate queries, retrieved documents, and failed attempts. This context is then used to inform turn-level rewards by leveraging mechanisms such as masked language modeling or next sentence prediction. The contextualized rewards are added to or compete with the group-relative rewards to provide a denser and more informative learning signal.
CONTROLS: Test with different context construction methods, and ablate the contextualized reward component by using a light-touch method or a non-contextual baseline.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should enhance the learning signal in multi-turn search agents, but may require careful tuning to balance the contextualized rewards with the group-relative rewards to avoid information overload.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED - Intrinsic Process Rewards through Self-Monitoring
PROPOSAL: Refine the self-monitored confidence heuristic by incorporating a weak supervision signal from the search agent's own knowledge graph or topical categories. When the agent retrieves relevant candidate answers, analyze their content to infer latent topic distributions. The confidence in each turn is derived from the overlap between these topic distributions and those indicated by the ground truth answers. The self-estimated confidence can be Regularized to prevent overfitting to the retrieved content.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original self-monitoring mechanism, and ablate the weak supervision by removing the topic analysis or regularization.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This refined self-monitoring method should better leverage the agent's internal knowledge and provide a more stable learning signal, but may require careful tuning to prevent over-reliance on the weak supervision signal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Probabilistic Modeling of Group Performance
PROPOSAL: Introduce a probabilistic model to capture the group-level latent distribution of answers at each turn. This model can be used to estimate group marginals and normalized relative rewards that are agnostic to the number of rollouts. The model parameters are updated online using only the turns that receive similar outcomes within the group.
CONTROLS: Compare with the group-relative rewards, and ablate the probabilistic model by using a fixed marginal or no probabilistic modeling.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should provide a more robust and informative learning signal that can account for the uncertainty in group performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Turn-Dependent Hierarchical Graph-Based Exploration
PROPOSAL: Construct a hierarchical graph to model the exploration space, where each node represents a potential query argument or subquestion. The graph encoding is learned through a turn-dependent process, where the agent infers the graph structure and node representations based on its progress and intermediate results. The relative rewards are computed by normalizing the node values within the subgraph of relevant nodes at each turn, providing a dense reward signal for hierarchical exploration.
CONTROLS: Compare with the contextualized reward shaping, and ablate the hierarchical graph by using a flat graph or no graph.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should facilitate more structured exploration through hierarchical reasoning, but may require careful design to avoid over-expansion of the graph and efficient computation of the node values.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Probing the Value of Intermediate Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Use a neuro-symbolic approach to inject explicit reasoning rules into the search agent, allowing it to represent and reason about intermediate results in a more structured and compositional manner. The agent can evaluate the contribution of each reasoning step to the final outcome, computing a value profile that captures the expected impact of each intermediate query. A denser reward signal is computed by weighting the relative rewards of each intermediate step by its value profile.
CONTROLS: Compare with the contextualized reward shaping, and ablate the value profiles by removing the explicit reasoning rules or using a simplistic weighting scheme.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should provide a more detailed understanding of the intermediate reasoning process and its impact on the final outcome, but may require careful tuning to prevent over-weighting of certain steps and to ensure efficient computation of the value profiles.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluator-Agnostic Feedback Mechanism
PROPOSAL: Introduce a meta-reward signal that encourages the agent to focus on understanding the high-level structure and novelty of the intermediate results, rather than simply optimizing for common metrics used by the evaluator. This feedback is computed using a learning-based model that predicts potential rewards from the agent's outputs without relying on explicit task definitions or oracle feedback. The meta-reward is used to augment the turn-level rewards, promoting exploration and minimizing reward hacking.
CONTROLS: Compare with the contextualized reward shaping, and ablate the meta-reward by removing the learning-based model or using a simplistic prediction mechanism.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should provide a more speculative and open-ended exploration of the problem space, but may require careful tuning to prevent under-exploitation and reward misalignment.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Relational Schema from Search Trajectories
PROPOSAL: Integrate a relation-aware knowledge graph (RA-KG) module to learn and leverage relational schema from the search agent's multi-turn trajectories. The RA-KG captures complex interactions between query arguments, intermediate results, and retrieved documents, allowing the agent to reason about higher-order relationships and compound knowledge. This relational knowledge is used to augment the turn-level rewards and promote more informed and interconnected exploration.
CONTROLS: Compare with the contextualized reward shaping, and ablate the RA-KG by removing the relational schema learning or using a simplistic graph-based representation.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should enable the agent to explore and represent more sophisticated relational knowledge, but may require careful design to prevent knowledge fragmentation and ensure efficient computation of the graph.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Safe Trajectory Search with Inductive Transfer
PROPOSAL: Incorporate an inductive transfer mechanism to generalize knowledge from previously explored search trajectories to new, unseen problems. This is achieved through a graph-based transfer network that learns to represent and reason about abstract trajectories and the underlying relational schema. By propagating knowledge across iterations and tasks, the agent is incentivized to explore safer and more informative trajectories that promote effective transfer and avoid excessive overspecialization.
CONTROLS: Compare with the contextualized reward shaping, and ablate the inductive transfer mechanism by removing the transfer network or using a simplistic transfer scheme.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should enhance the agent's ability to generalize and adapt to novel problems, but may require careful tuning to prevent over-specialization and ensure effective knowledge transfer.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation of Agentic Search Agents
PROPOSAL: Design an extensive evaluation framework that compares the performance of search agents trained with diverse intrinsic process rewards (IPRs) methods. The framework includes comprehensive benchmarking on multi-hop QA tasks, open-domain question answering, and real-world search scenarios, using established evaluation metrics. This comprehensive evaluation allows for a thorough analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of each IPR method and facilitates fair comparisons and identification of best practices for developing general-purpose agentic search agents.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the IPDs on a wide range of tasks, including but not limited to natural language processing, information retrieval, and cognitive reasoning; compare IPDs across multiple computational architectures (e.g., GPUs, TPUs, CPUs); and include a thorough ablation study to isolate the individual components and effects of each IPR method.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (computationally intensive, requires large-scale benchmarking and comparison)

PROPOSAL 1: REVISED 1 - Intrinsic Process Rewards through Self-Monitoring
Refine the self-monitored confidence heuristic by incorporating a weak supervision signal from the search agent's own knowledge graph or topical categories. When the agent retrieves relevant candidate answers, analyze their content to infer latent topic distributions. The confidence in each turn is derived from the overlap between these topic distributions and those indicated by the ground truth answers. The self-estimated confidence can be Regularized to prevent overfitting to the retrieved content.
Controls: Compare with the original self-monitoring mechanism, and ablate the weak supervision by removing the topic analysis or regularization.
Estimated cost: 120 GPU-hours
Prediction: This refined self-monitoring method should better leverage the agent's internal knowledge and provide a more stable learning signal, but may require careful tuning to prevent over-reliance on the weak supervision signal.

PROPOSAL 2: Contextualized Reward Shaping with Intermediate Reasoning
Augment the search agent's policy with a contextualized reward shaping mechanism, where a rich context representation is encoded from the history of intermediate queries, retrieved documents, and failed attempts. This context is then used to inform turn-level rewards by leveraging mechanisms such as masked language modeling or next sentence prediction. The contextualized rewards are added to or compete with the group-relative rewards to provide a denser and more informative learning signal.
Controls: Test with different context construction methods, and ablate the contextualized reward component by using a light-touch method or a non-contextual baseline.
Estimated cost: 150 GPU-hours
Prediction: This approach should enhance the learning signal in multi-turn search agents, but may require careful tuning to balance the contextualized rewards with the group-relative rewards to avoid information overload.

PROPOSAL 3: Turn-Dependent Hierarchical Graph-Based Exploration
Construct a hierarchical graph to model the exploration space, where each node represents a potential query argument or subquestion. The graph encoding is learned through a turn-dependent process, where the agent infers the graph structure and node representations based on its progress and intermediate results. The relative rewards are computed by normalizing the node values within the subgraph of relevant nodes at each turn, providing a dense reward signal for hierarchical exploration.
Controls: Compare with the contextualized reward shaping, and ablate the hierarchical graph by using a flat graph or no graph.
Estimated cost: 200 GPU-hours
Prediction: This approach should facilitate more structured exploration through hierarchical reasoning, but may require careful design to avoid over-expansion of the graph and efficient computation of the node values.

PROPOSAL 4: Probing the Value of Intermediate Reasoning
Use a neuro-symbolic approach to inject explicit reasoning rules into the search agent, allowing it to represent and reason about intermediate results in a more structured and compositional manner. The agent can evaluate the contribution of each reasoning step to the final outcome, computing a value profile that captures the expected impact of each intermediate query. A denser reward signal is computed by weighting the relative rewards of each intermediate step by its value profile.
Controls: Compare with the contextualized reward shaping, and ablate the value profiles by removing the explicit reasoning rules or using a simplistic weighting scheme.

Prediction: This approach should provide a more detailed understanding of the intermediate reasoning process and its impact on the final outcome, but may require careful tuning to prevent over-weighting of certain steps and to ensure efficient computation of the value profiles.

PROPOSAL 5: Evaluator-Agnostic Feedback Mechanism
Introduce a meta-reward signal that encourages the agent to focus on understanding the high-level structure and novelty of the intermediate results, rather than simply optimizing for common metrics used by the evaluator. This feedback is computed using a learning-based model that predicts potential rewards from the agent's outputs without relying on explicit task definitions or oracle feedback. The meta-reward is used to augment the turn-level rewards, promoting exploration and minimizing reward hacking.
Controls: Compare with the contextualized reward shaping, and ablate the meta-reward by removing the learning-based model or using a simplistic prediction mechanism.
Estimated cost: 250 GPU-hours
Prediction: This approach should provide a more speculative and open-ended exploration of the problem space, but may require careful tuning to prevent under-exploitation and reward misalignment.

PROPOSAL 6: Learning Relational Schema from Search Trajectories
Integrate a relation-aware knowledge graph (RA-KG) module to learn and leverage relational schema from the search agent's multi-turn trajectories. The RA-KG captures complex interactions between query arguments, intermediate results, and retrieved documents, allowing the agent to reason about higher-order relationships and compound knowledge. This relational knowledge is used to augment the turn-level rewards and promote more informed and interconnected exploration.
Controls: Compare with the contextualized reward shaping, and ablate the RA-KG by removing the relational schema learning or using a simplistic graph-based representation.
Estimated cost: 280 GPU-hours
Prediction: This approach should enable the agent to explore and represent more sophisticated relational knowledge, but may require careful design to prevent knowledge fragmentation and ensure efficient computation of the graph.

PROPOSAL 7: Safe Trajectory Search with Inductive Transfer
Incorporate an inductive transfer mechanism to generalize knowledge from previously explored search trajectories to new, unseen problems. This is achieved through a graph-based transfer network that learns to represent and reason about abstract trajectories and the underlying relational schema. By propagating knowledge across iterations and tasks, the agent is incentivized to explore safer and more informative trajectories that promote effective transfer and avoid excessive overspecialization.
Controls: Compare with the contextualized reward shaping, and ablate the inductive transfer mechanism by removing the transfer network or using a simplistic transfer scheme.
Estimated cost: 300 GPU-hours
Prediction: This approach should enhance the agent's ability to generalize and adapt to novel problems, but may require careful tuning to prevent over-specialization and ensure effective knowledge transfer.

PROPOSAL 8: Comprehensive Evaluation of Agentic Search Agents
Design an extensive evaluation framework that compares the performance of search agents trained with diverse intrinsic process rewards (IPRs) methods. The framework includes comprehensive benchmarking on multi-hop QA tasks, open-domain question answering, and real-world search scenarios, using established evaluation metrics. This comprehensive evaluation allows for a thorough analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of each IPR method and facilitates fair comparisons and identification of best practices for developing general-purpose agentic search agents.
