actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sparse3D-Unsplash: Self-Supervised Pre-training for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate a self-supervised pre-training approach called Sparse3D-Unsplash for Sparse Perception Models. This method adaptively constructs a set of dense 3D queries from multi-view images and leverages self-supervised contrastive learning with the newly learned queries as anchor, positive, and negative samples. The query learning process emulates sparse perception mechanisms and alternates between maximizing inter-class separation and minimizing intra-class discrepancies among anchor and positive pairs.
CONTROLS: Baseline: pre-training using contrastive learning without the adaptive query construction; ablation: removing anchor/positive/negative samples.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Sparse3D-Unsplash should outperform the baseline in terms of downstream object detection mAP, especially in complex scenes where sparse perception excels. Failure point: poor anchor weighting and insufficient inter-query variation might harm query learning efficiency.

This initial proposal sets the stage for our investigation into self-supervised pre-training for SPMs, laying the groundwork for the downstream developments and evaluations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: SimplifyingQuery: Knowledge Transfer for Heterogeneous Query-Based Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a transfer mechanism called SimplifyingQuery to adaptively select a subset of pre-learned sparse queries for downstream task-specific models. By grouping queries based on their spatial and semantic properties, SimplifyingQuery allows for the extension of Sparse3D-Unsplash-learned knowledge to numerous variants of query-based models, streamlining knowledge transfer and model deployment. The aggregation of adapted queries will be used as an initial query representation for various downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: Ablations: (i) remove the query grouping mechanism; (ii) fix the query set during adaptation; (iii) compare with an oracle that uses the true task-specific queries.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: SimplifyingQuery should significantly improve model performance on object detection and occupancy prediction tasks by identifying the most beneficial queries for each scenario. Failure point: complex query structures and diverse downstream tasks may require domain-specific knowledge for effective query adaptation.

The purpose of SimplifyingQuery is to diminish the dependence on task-specific queries by leveraging the collective knowledge acquired during pre-training with Sparse3D-Unsplash, thus combating the rigidity of query-based models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Simulation-based Transfer Evaluation
PROPOSAL: Conduct comprehensive evaluations on a realistic driving simulator, Waymo Simulator, to assess the effectiveness of SimplifyingQuery in transferring pre-learned knowledge from 3D scene representations to downstream sparse perception tasks. This controlled environment minimizes biased results arising from specific training protocols and dataset distributions, allowing for a thorough analysis of the adaptation mechanism.
CONTROLS: SPMs pre-trained with and without Sparse3D-Unsplash, without and with SimplifyingQuery for query transfer.
COST: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Simulation-based evaluations with performance metrics like mAP and occupancy accuracy will demonstrate the adaptability and generalizability of SimplifyingQuery across diverse tasks and scene complexities, showcasing its potential for streamlining knowledge transfer in the wild. Failure point: degradation in performance may occur when simplified queries lose essential context and spatial structure critical for sparse perception.

This third proposal aims to provide systematic, controlled evaluations to empirically demonstrate the value of SimplifyingQuery in simplifying task-specific query selection for streamlined knowledge transfer, a crucial step toward more efficient pre-training and adaptation for complex perception tasks.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Simulation-based Transfer Evaluation (Rev.)
PROPOSAL: Refine the simulation-based evaluation by incorporating real-world data augmentation techniques and realistic scene complexity to better simulate real-world driving scenarios and reduce the gap between simulation and real-world performance. This is achieved by incorporating mixed traffic density, weather conditions (rain, fog), and temporal variations in simulation protocols to further simulate potential edge cases and common real-world conditions for more robust and comprehensive evaluation.
CONTROLS: Additional SPM adaptability metrics (e.g., query fusion efficiency, spatial query structure preservation).
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined simulations with data augmentation and varied conditions will enable more robust performance assessments under a broader range of realistic scenarios, augmenting the ability to draw more meaningful inferences about SimplifyingQuery's adaptability in real-world settings. Failure point: failing to sufficiently capture discrepancies between simulation and real-world conditions might limit the evaluative value of the enhanced simulation setup.

This revised proposal emphasizes the improvement of the simulation evaluation environment to ensure it better aligns with real-world expectations and diversities.

ACTION: REVISE
REVISION OF: 2. SimplifyingQuery: Knowledge Transfer for Heterogeneous Query-Based Models
TITLE: SimplifyingQuery: Knowledge Transfer for Heterogeneous Query-Based Models (Rev.)
PROPOSAL: Enhance the adaptive query selection mechanism by incorporating a novel, compact query representation scheme based on learnable spatial hierarchies. This enables efficient aggregation and adaptation of diverse query sets, particularly those from complex scenarios where traditional query representations may degrade. By integrating learnable hierarchies with SimplifyingQuery, downstream models can benefit from refined, state-of-the-art performance on a broader range of tasks and scenarios.
CONTROLS: Baseline query representations without spatial hierarchies.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised SimplifyingQuery with compact query representations enabled by learnable spatial hierarchies will significantly boost performance by capturing richer, multi-scale structural relationships between scene elements. Failure point: the query hierarchy learning process may be sensitive to hyperparameter tuning and imperfect initialization.

In the revised proposal, we augment SimplifyingQuery with compact, learnable query representations to enhance its adaptability and generality across autonomous driving scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: SpARS: Sparse-X Bibliography and Retrieval for Efficient Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop a domain-aware, bibliography-based retrieval system called SpARS to leverage the collective knowledge from pre-print and published research for improving the knowledge acquisition process in sparse perception tasks. This involves training a neural network to map relevant scene contexts and sparse percepts to pre-trained sparse perception embeddings and encoding the efficacy of these percepts and percernations as a dataset-induced penalty. The system could compile query proposals to utilize generally slow practices by scoring them on retrieval systems like Google Scholar.
CONTROLS: Comparative analysis with traditional retrieval-based methods and efficient information retrieval methods like compressed sketches.
COST: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The novel retrieval system, SpARS, will enable efficient research comparisons, advance sparse perception performance indicators and minimizes test error responses. Failure point: incomplete summarization of deliberated existing work; & over-engineering a literaure- search methodology that leads to computationally expensive operations.

ACTION: REVISE
REVISION OF: 1. Sparse3D-Unsplash: Self-Supervised Pre-training for Sparse Perception Models
TITLE: Sparse3D-Unsplash: Self-Supervised Pre-training for Sparse Perception Models (Rev.)
PROPOSAL: Extend the capabilities of Sparse3D-Unsplash by incorporating a multi-head self-supervised contrastive learning framework that adaptively selects relevant scene features and permutations through an encoded geometric noise process. This revised approach enhances Sparse3D-Unsplash's efficiency, robustness, and ability to learn rich, finer-grained 3D features from multi-view driving scenarios.
CONTROLS: Evaluation with and without multi-head framework; effects of varying the number of heads.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The enhanced Sparse3D-Unsplash with the multi-head self-supervised contrastive learning framework will better adapt to complex real-world scenarios and yield improved performance in downstream perception tasks, such as object detection and occupancy prediction. Failure point: potential instability or performance degradation resulting from the adaptive head selection process might occur for certain scene complexities.

ACTION: REVISE
REVISION OF: 4. SpARS: Sparse-X Bibliography and Retrieval for Efficient Learning
TITLE: SpARS: Sparse-X Bibliography and Retrieval for Efficient Learning (Rev.)
PROPOSAL: Develop a user-centric extension to SpARS that incorporates a personalized ranking system based on individual researcher preferences and information needs. This novel extension will enable users to curate personalized knowledge bases, customize query response outputs, and specify contextual information inclusion, thereby enhancing the overall efficiency and effectiveness of the SpARS system for sparse perception domain research.
CONTROLS: Comparative evaluation of retrieval accuracy, relevance, and user satisfaction with and without the personalized ranking system.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised SpARS system with personalized ranking will better cater to the diverse needs of researchers in the sparse perception community, leading to improved literature retrieval outcomes, reduced information overload, and enhanced overall research efficiency. Failure point: potential over-customization may complicate system usage and maintenance.

The revision aims to elevate the SpARS system by incorporating a personalized aspect to better support researchers' preferences and needs, ultimately enhancing its role in knowledge discovery within the sparse perception domain.

ACTION: REVISE
REVISION OF: 3. Simulation-based Transfer Evaluation
TITLE: Simulation-based Transfer Evaluation (Rev.)
PROPOSAL: Enhance the robustness and generalizability of the simulation-based transfer evaluation by incorporating a multi-modality data fusion approach that integrates various driving scenarios, such as daytime, nighttime, and severe weather conditions, to simulate real-world driving complexities. This will allow for a more comprehensive assessment of SimplifyingQuery's adaptability in diverse environmental conditions and better prepare for evaluation on real-world driving data.
CONTROLS: Comparative analysis with traditional single-modality simulation approaches.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised simulation-based transfer evaluation with multi-modality data fusion will provide a more accurate and representative assessment of SimplifyingQuery's adaptability and performance across various real-world driving scenarios, ultimately enhancing the evaluation's validity and generalizability. Failure point: potential misalignment with true real-world complexities and nuances might remain, necessitating continuous refinement of the evaluation framework.

The revised evaluation will focus on capturing the complexity and variability of real-world driving scenarios through multi-modality data fusion, ultimately elevating the effectiveness of the SimplifyingQuery approach and supporting its potential deployment in practical applications.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: On the Robustness of Sparse Perception Models to Noisy Query Representations
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Analyze the robustness of sparse perception models to noisy query representations by designing controlled experiments. Use the Anchored-Query-Network (AQN) framework for sparse query generation and perturb its output query representations using various noise distributions (Gaussian, uniform, and adversarial). To facilitate this, we design a Noise-Robust Sparse Query (NRSQ) loss function that encourages the model to be robust to query representation noise. The NRSQ loss combines a modified query reconstruction loss with a robustness-promoting term, which is backpropagated through the noise injection process. We evaluate the model's performance on diverse tasks (3D object detection, semantic occupancy prediction) with varying levels of noise added to the query representations, comparing against a baseline that does not use the NRSQ loss.

CONTROLS: Compare against baseline models that do not use the NRSQ loss, as well as comparisons with other robustness-promoting techniques.

COST: 4000 GPU-hours

PREDICTION: Expected result: +5-10% improvements in robustness to noisy query representations, and comparable or improved performance on downstream tasks compared to the baseline. Possible failure points: overemphasis on robustness might compromise model performance, or the NRSQ loss may not effectively promote robustness in all scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Query-Augmentation for Improving Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Propose a query-augmentation technique for sparse perception models, which generates multiple augmented query representations from a single input frame. The proposed technique, called Query-Augmentation Network (QAN), leverages a lightweight transformer architecture to attentively select and aggregate features from different spatial locations and scales. We train the QAN to augment the original query representation with an additional query representation that captures complementary information. We evaluate the effectiveness of QAN on diverse tasks (3D object detection, semantic occupancy prediction) and demonstrate improved performance with query augmentation.

CONTROLS: Compare against baseline models without query augmentation, as well as comparisons with other techniques for query augmentation or attention-based mechanisms.

COST: 2500 GPU-hours

PREDICTION: Expected result: +2-5% improvements in performance with query augmentation, particularly in tasks that benefit from additional context information. Possible failure points: query augmentation may not effectively capture complementary information in all scenarios, or the QAN may overemphasize certain features.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Investigating Transferability of Query-Augmentation to Heterogeneous Downstream Tasks
PROPOSAL: Investigate the transferability of the query-augmentation technique proposed in Query-Augmentation for Improving Sparse Perception Models to heterogeneous downstream tasks, such as point cloud analysis, scene understanding, and 3D reconstruction. We evaluate the effectiveness of query augmentation on these tasks and assess its generalization across multiple datasets and model architectures. Additionally, we explore the use of query augmentation as a feature extractor for downstream tasks and examine its potential impact on model performance.

CONTROLS: Compare against baseline models without query augmentation, as well as comparisons with other transfer learning or domain adaptation techniques.

COST: 3500 GPU-hours

PREDICTION: Expected result: improved transferability of query augmentation to heterogeneous downstream tasks, with +2-5% improvements in performance. Possible failure points: query augmentation may not effectively capture task-specific information, or the transferability of query augmentation may be limited by the specific model architectures or datasets used.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Multitask Transfer Learning with Query-Augmentation for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of multitask transfer learning to leverage the knowledge learned from sparse perception tasks with query augmentation for improving performance on heterogeneous downstream tasks. We propose a multitask learning framework that combines sparse perception tasks with query augmentation, such as 3D object detection and semantic occupancy prediction, and use this shared knowledge to improve performance on downstream tasks. We evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on a range of tasks and datasets and investigate its potential for transfer learning.

CONTROLS: Compare against baseline models without multitask transfer learning, as well as comparisons with other multitask learning or transfer learning techniques.

COST: 4500 GPU-hours

PREDICTION: Expected result: improved performance on downstream tasks with +10-15% improvements, and increased transferability of knowledge learned from sparse perception tasks. Possible failure points: the shared knowledge learned from sparse perception tasks may not be relevant or useful for downstream tasks, or the multitask learning framework may lead to overfitting or decreased performance on individual tasks.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Efficient Query-Augmentation with Knowledge Distillation for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from a large query-augmentation model to a smaller, more efficient model, allowing for fast and accurate query augmentation in resource-constrained scenarios. We propose a novel knowledge distillation framework that leverages the high-capacity query-augmentation model to distill knowledge into a smaller model, and evaluate its performance on a range of tasks and datasets.

CONTROLS: Compare against baseline models without knowledge distillation, as well as comparisons with other model pruning or distillation techniques.

COST: 3000 GPU-hours

PREDICTION: Expected result: +5-10% improvements in performance and +50-100% reduction in computational cost, without compromising on model accuracy. Possible failure points: the knowledge distillation process may lead to information loss or decreased model performance, or the distilled model may not generalize well to new tasks or datasets.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Exploring the Limits of Query-Augmentation for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the fundamental limits of query-augmentation for sparse perception models by analyzing the capacity and expressiveness of query-augmentation models. We propose a series of experiments to evaluate the performance of query-augmentation models on a range of tasks and datasets, and examine the effect of varying model sizes, architectures, and training regimes on query-augmentation performance. Additionally, we investigate the effect of domain adaptation and few-shot learning on query-augmentation models.

CONTROLS: Compare against baseline models without query augmentation, as well as comparisons with other techniques for improving model capacity and expressiveness.

COST: 5000 GPU-hours

PREDICTION: Expected result: a deeper understanding of the limitations and potential of query-augmentation models, including potential avenues for further improvement and potential applications in real-world scenarios. Possible failure points: the experiments may not uncover significant limitations of query-augmentation models, or the results may be difficult to interpret or generalize.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Multi-View Contrastive Learning for SPM Pre-training
PROPOSAL: Develop an adversarial multi-view contrastive learning framework composed of a generator network and a discriminator network. The generator network draws multi-view images from the driving dataset and applies random transformations to create diverse views, while the discriminator network learns to distinguish between positive (different views of the same scene) and negative (different views of different scenes) pairs. The pre-training loss is defined as the cross-entropy loss between the discriminator's output and the ground truth labels. The generator and discriminator are trained alternately using a minimax optimization strategy.
CONTROLS: Supervised baseline (SPM trained on labeled data), Random baseline (SPM trained on random pseudo-labels), Dense BEV-centric paradigm (engraining denser intermediate representation)
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed approach should outperform the supervised baseline, achieve competitive results with the dense BEV-centric baseline, and demonstrate robustness to various transformation and augmentation strategies, but may fall short in capturing precise 3D scene geometry.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gaussian-Based Query-Efficient Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a Gaussian-based query-efficient contrastive learning method that leverages the pre-trained SPM to generate novel sparse queries and predict associated semantic features. The method employs a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to model the distribution of sparse queries and computes a query-efficient contrastive loss that encourages the learned features to be informative and discriminative. This approach enables the effective pre-training of SPMs with a highly non-linear and complex data distribution.
CONTROLS: Adversarial Multi-View Contrastive Learning (proposed in proposal 1), Random baseline, Dense BEV-centric paradigm
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method should significantly improve upon the adversarial multi-view contrastive learning baseline, especially when operating with a limited number of views, and demonstrate superior robustness to query set sizes and distributions, but may require extensive tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Focus: Salient Query Generation for SPM Pre-training
PROPOSAL: Introduce a salient query generation mechanism that learns to select the most informative and representative sparse queries from the pre-trained SPM. This approach employs a reinforcement learning framework that rewards the query generator for producing queries that lead to improved performance on downstream tasks, such as object detection and segmentation. PROPOSAL 1: Adversarial Multi-View Contrastive Learning for SPM Pre-training
Develop an adversarial multi-view contrastive learning framework composed of a generator network and a discriminator network. The generator network draws multi-view images from the driving dataset and applies random transformations to create diverse views, while the discriminator network learns to distinguish between positive (different views of the same scene) and negative (different views of different scenes) pairs. The pre-training loss is defined as the cross-entropy loss between the discriminator's output and the ground truth labels. The generator and discriminator are trained alternately using a minimax optimization strategy.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Vision-Language Detector Adaptation via Meta-Pseudo-Labeling
PROPOSAL: We will explore a method that combines meta-learning with pseudo-labeling to adapt the vision-language detector to new domains quickly and efficiently. In this approach, the pre-trained detector is trained to generate pseudo-labels in meta-training, and then in meta-testing, it adapts to new domains by refining the pseudo-label generators. This way, the detector can handle unseen categories and domains with little to no additional data.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method against self-supervised learning methods, both with and without fine-tuning of the pre-trained detector.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvement in domain adaptation performance, especially when dealing with open-set scenarios. However, we predict that there might be some performance degradation when the detector encounters new categories with little to no overlap with the training categories.

To ensure reliability with scattered and noisy pseudo-labels, we'll introduce additional heuristics to adjust the pseudo-labeling confidence thresholds based on the detector's uncertainty estimates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Guided Confidence Threshold Adjustment
PROPOSAL: This proposal expands on experiment 1 by introducing a Bayesian neural network (BNN) approach to obtain uncertainty estimates of the detector's outputs. We will use the obtained uncertainty values to adaptively adjust the confidence threshold for pseudo-label filtering in the meta-pseudo-labeling method. The adjusted threshold will be dynamically updated during test-time adaptation to balance between robustness and precision of pseudo-labels.
CONTROLS: We will compare the effectiveness of our uncertainty-guided approach with fixed confidence thresholds (the original meta-pseudo-labeling method) and with ablated versions where either the uncertainty estimates or the adaptive thresholding are removed.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (supplementing the original 1000 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to improve the quality of pseudo-labels, especially in scenarios with scarce or noisy target data. However, we anticipate potential trade-offs between robustness and adaptation speed.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revision to Uncertainty-Guided Confidence Threshold Adjustment
PROPOSAL: We will use a more robust method, a interval estimation technique allowing us to construct probabilistic bounds around the detector's outputs, which can more effectively capture its uncertainty. Bayesian bounding attainable by samples (BBAS) enables learning tight uncertainty estimates, and will allow us to utilize Bayesian ideas in practical, computationally efficient ways.
CONTROLS: As before, we will compare the effectiveness of our interval-based approach with fixed confidence thresholds and with ablated versions where the interval estimates or the adaptive thresholding are removed. We will also compare against our original meta-pseudo-labeling method (experiment 1) without the uncertainty adjustment.
COST: No additional cost (the original 500 GPU-hours considered usable under revised approach)
PREDICATED EFFECTS: The BBAS-based approach likely refines our initial findings about the trade-off between robustness and adaptation speed but offers additional advantage due to its tighter bounds and no concern about calibrating variance for a perfect accuracy.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revision to Uncertainty-Guided Confidence Threshold Adjustment
PROPOSAL: We will use a more robust method, a interval estimation technique allowing us to construct probabilistic bounds around the detector's outputs, which can more effectively capture its uncertainty. Bayesian bounding attainable by samples (BBAS) enables learning tight uncertainty estimates, and will allow us to utilize Bayesian ideas in practical, computationally efficient ways.
CONTROLS: As before, we will compare the effectiveness of our interval-based approach with fixed confidence thresholds and with ablated versions where the interval estimates or the adaptive thresholding are removed. We will also compare against our original meta-pseudo-labeling method (experiment 1) without the uncertainty adjustment.
COST: No additional cost (the original 500 GPU-hours considered usable under revised approach)
PREDICATED EFFECTS: The BBAS-based approach likely refines our initial findings about the trade-off between robustness and adaptation speed but offers additional advantage due to its tighter bounds and no concern about calibrating variance for a perfect accuracy.

Additionally, the interval estimation will enable us to investigate the correct usage of Boxenbach theorem application as part of theoretical extension to adapt, even to unreliable samples - by referring to length of new intervals drummed up by application of this theorem and have further predictive strength weighting its Barbans compliance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigation of Bayesian Support to Complementary Weak-Supervision Strategies
PROPOSAL: To address the challenges of reliable pseudo-labeling, especially when faced with noisy or scarce target data, we propose leveraging Bayesian ideas in conjunction with weak-supervision strategies. We will examine the efficacy of Bayesian Approximate Posterior Learning (MAPL), a weak-supervision method that employs noisy, pseudo-labeled data, along with other weak-supervision techniques and compare the performance of each method when combined with our interval-based uncertainty quantification from experiment 2.
CONTROLS: We will compare against various weak-supervision strategies, including Self-training, Co-training, and Consistency Regularization. We will also analyze the origin and extent of pseudo-labeling errors in these approaches as they interact with the BBAS technique used in experiment 2.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (parallelized experiments)
PREDICTION: The combined approaches are expected to yield significant improvements in robustness and generalization ability. However, we predict potential instability when dealing with extremely noisy or biased weak labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Meta-Learning for Adaptable Vision-Language Detector
PROPOSAL: Moving beyond the single-task approach of meta-pseudo-labeling, we propose a multi-task meta-learning framework that tackles domain adaptation, object detection, and pseudo-label refinement simultaneously. This allows the model to learn transferable representations and adapt to diverse target domains, improving the robustness and generalizability of the detector for real-world applications. In this setup, the model takes as input both image and text features and learns to adapt to the task of object detection on-the-fly.
CONTROLS: We will compare our multi-task meta-learning approach against the baseline meta-pseudo-labeling method and against other popular meta-learning methods that focus on a single task, such as few-shot learning for object detection.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-task framework is expected to exhibit better performance on domain adaptation tasks, especially when faced with scarce labeled data, due to its ability to leverage shared knowledge for both object detection and domain adaptation. However, potential overfitting to specific tasks might reduce its overall performance on other tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Debiasing the Vision-Language Detector via Cross-Dataset Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the potential issue of domain bias and improve the adaptability of the detector to diverse target domains, we propose a cross-dataset contrastive learning (CDCL) approach. This method leverages self-supervised learning to bias the detector's embeddings and representations towards domain-invariant knowledge. We will evaluate the effectiveness of CDCL as a debiasing technique on our adaptable vision-language detector and investigate its potential to improve the detector's performance on diverse target domains.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the detector with and without CDCL, and evaluate its impact on different metrics such as object detection accuracy and domain shift robustness. We will also compare against other debiasing techniques such as label noise correction and domain adversarial training.
COST: 900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The CDCL approach is expected to effectively debias the detector and improve its adaptability to diverse target domains. However, it may introduce additional computational overhead and require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Long-Tailed Object Detection forVision-Language Pretraining
PROPOSAL: Given that the vision-language detectors we have developed so far may face challenges when encountering long-tailed object distributions, we propose to incorporate a long-tailed object detection mechanism into the pretraining pipeline of the detector. This will include class-balanced sampling, focal loss, and online hard example mining to handle the challenging objects in the long-tail.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the effectiveness of this approach by comparing the performance of detectors pre-trained with and without the long-tailed object detection mechanism, and investigate its impact on the downstream adaptation performance and adaptation speed.
COST: 600 GPU-hours (mostly parallelized)
PREDICTION: The long-tailed object detection mechanism is expected to improve the pretraining robustness and adaptability of the detector, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and aggressively provide justification of trade-offs related sample regimen sizes -- one where imbalanced case considerations get extensive protection potentially be resulting in difficulty for achieving a path toward avalanche or vanishing broad margin.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Agent Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Detector
PROPOSAL: To further improve the adaptability and robustness of the detector, we propose a multi-agent test-time adaptation framework. This framework utilizes multiple agents to collect pseudo-labels and update the detector simultaneously, allowing the detector to benefit from diverse perspectives and adapt to complex environments more effectively.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance of the detector under different numbers of agents, agent communication strategies, and dataset partitions, and compare it against the state-of-the-art adaptation methods.
COST: 1600 GPU-hours (considering extensive hyperparameter tuning and training)
PREDICTION: The multi-agent framework is expected to significantly improve the detector's adaptability and robustness, especially in complex and dynamic environments. However, potential challenges include achieving effective communication among agents, optimizing the adaptation process, and mitigating potential negative effects on performance due to increased computational cost.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Experimental Evaluation and Qualitative Analysis of TTAOD Methods
PROPOSAL: Given the proposed methods in previous experiments, we will conduct an extensive experimental evaluation and qualitative analysis to compare the adaptability, robustness, and transferability of different test-time adaptation (TTA) of vision-language detection (TTAOD) methods, and identify potential strengths and weaknesses of each approach.
CONTROLS: We will assess the performance of each TTAOD method across various tasks, datasets, and evaluation metrics, and validate the effectiveness of each approach through ablation studies, visualizations, and expert insights.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours (considering the extensive experimental evaluation and data analysis)
PREDICTION: This comprehensive evaluation will provide a thorough understanding of the strengths, weaknesses, and limitations of each TTAOD method, enabling researchers to select the most suitable approach for specific applications and environments. PROPOSAL 1: Online Vision-Language Detector Adaptation via Meta-Pseudo-Labeling
We will explore a method that combines meta-learning with pseudo-labeling to adapt the vision-language detector to new domains quickly and efficiently. In this approach, the pre-trained detector is trained to generate pseudo-labels in meta-training, and then in meta-testing, it adapts to new domains by refining the pseudo-label generators. This way, the detector can handle unseen categories and domains with little to no additional data.
Controls: We will compare our method against self-supervised learning methods, both with and without fine-tuning of the pre-trained detector.
Estimated cost: 1000 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to see significant improvement in domain adaptation performance, especially when dealing with open-set scenarios. However, we predict that there might be some performance degradation when the detector encounters new categories with little to no overlap with the training categories.

To ensure reliability with scattered and noisy pseudo-labels, we'll introduce additional heuristics to adjust the pseudo-labeling confidence thresholds based on the detector's uncertainty estimates.

PROPOSAL 2: Revision to Uncertainty-Guided Confidence Threshold Adjustment
We will use a more robust method, a interval estimation technique allowing us to construct probabilistic bounds around the detector's outputs, which can more effectively capture its uncertainty. Bayesian bounding attainable by samples (BBAS) enables learning tight uncertainty estimates, and will allow us to utilize Bayesian ideas in practical, computationally efficient ways.
Controls: As before, we will compare the effectiveness of our interval-based approach with fixed confidence thresholds and with ablated versions where the interval estimates or the adaptive thresholding are removed. We will also compare against our original meta-pseudo-labeling method (experiment 1) without the uncertainty adjustment.
Estimated cost: No additional cost (the original 500 GPU-hours considered usable under revised approach)
PREDICATED EFFECTS: The BBAS-based approach likely refines our initial findings about the trade-off between robustness and adaptation speed but offers additional advantage due to its tighter bounds and no concern about calibrating variance for a perfect accuracy.

PROPOSAL 3: Investigation of Bayesian Support to Complementary Weak-Supervision Strategies
To address the challenges of reliable pseudo-labeling, especially when faced with noisy or scarce target data, we propose leveraging Bayesian ideas in conjunction with weak-supervision strategies. We will examine the efficacy of Bayesian Approximate Posterior Learning (MAPL), a weak-supervision method that employs noisy, pseudo-labeled data, along with other weak-supervision techniques and compare the performance of each method when combined with our interval-based uncertainty quantification from experiment 2.
Controls: We will compare against various weak-supervision strategies, including Self-training, Co-training, and Consistency Regularization. We will also analyze the origin and extent of pseudo-labeling errors in these approaches as they interact with the BBAS technique used in experiment 2.
Estimated cost: 800 GPU-hours (parallelized experiments)
Prediction: The combined approaches are expected to yield significant improvements in robustness and generalization ability. However, we predict potential instability when dealing with extremely noisy or biased weak labels.

PROPOSAL 4: Multi-Task Meta-Learning for Adaptable Vision-Language Detector
Moving beyond the single-task approach of meta-pseudo-labeling, we propose a multi-task meta-learning framework that tackles domain adaptation, object detection, and pseudo-label refinement simultaneously. This allows the model to learn transferable representations and adapt to diverse target domains, improving the robustness and generalizability of the detector for real-world applications. In this setup, the model takes as input both image and text features and learns to adapt to the task of object detection on-the-fly.
Controls: We will compare our multi-task meta-learning approach against the baseline meta-pseudo-labeling method and against other popular meta-learning methods that focus on a single task, such as few-shot learning for object detection.
Estimated cost: 1200 GPU-hours
Prediction: The multi-task framework is expected to exhibit better performance on domain adaptation tasks, especially when faced with scarce labeled data, due to its ability to leverage shared knowledge for both object detection and domain adaptation. However, potential overfitting to specific tasks might reduce its overall performance on other tasks.

PROPOSAL 5: Debiasing the Vision-Language Detector via Cross-Dataset Contrastive Learning
To address the potential issue of domain bias and improve the adaptability of the detector to diverse target domains, we propose a cross-dataset contrastive learning (CDCL) approach. This method leverages self-supervised learning to bias the detector's embeddings and representations towards domain-invariant knowledge. We will evaluate the effectiveness of CDCL as a debiasing technique on our adaptable vision-language detector and investigate its potential to improve the detector's performance on diverse target domains.
Controls: We will compare the performance of the detector with and without CDCL, and evaluate its impact on different metrics such as object detection accuracy and domain shift robustness. We will also compare against other debiasing techniques such as label noise correction and domain adversarial training.
Estimated cost: 900 GPU-hours
Prediction: The CDCL approach is expected to effectively debias the detector and improve its adaptability to diverse target domains. However, it may introduce additional computational overhead and require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal results.

PROPOSAL 6: Long-Tailed Object Detection forVision-Language Pretraining
Given that the vision-language detectors we have developed so far may face challenges when encountering long-tailed object distributions, we propose to incorporate a long-tailed object detection mechanism into the pretraining pipeline of the detector. This will include class-balanced sampling, focal loss, and online hard example mining to handle the challenging objects in the long-tail.
Controls: We will evaluate the effectiveness of this approach by comparing the performance of detectors pre-trained with and without the long-tailed object detection mechanism, and investigate its impact on the downstream adaptation performance and adaptation speed.
Estimated cost: 600 GPU-hours (mostly parallelized)
Prediction: The long-tailed object detection mechanism is expected to improve the pretraining robustness and adaptability of the detector, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and aggressively provide justification of trade-offs related sample regimen sizes -- one where imbalanced case considerations get extensive protection potentially be resulting in difficulty for achieving a path toward avalanche or vanishing broad margin.

PROPOSAL 7: Multi-Agent Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Detector
To further improve the adaptability and robustness of the detector, we propose a multi-agent test-time adaptation framework. This framework utilizes multiple agents to collect pseudo-labels and update the detector simultaneously, allowing the detector to benefit from diverse perspectives and adapt to complex environments more effectively.
Controls: We will evaluate the performance of the detector under different numbers of agents, agent communication strategies, and dataset partitions, and compare it against the state-of-the-art adaptation methods.
Estimated cost: 1600 GPU-hours (considering extensive hyperparameter tuning and training)
Prediction: The multi-agent framework is expected to significantly improve the detector's adaptability and robustness, especially in complex and dynamic environments. However, potential challenges include achieving effective communication among agents, optimizing the adaptation process, and mitigating potential negative effects on performance due to increased computational cost.

PROPOSAL 8: Comprehensive Experimental Evaluation and Qualitative Analysis of TTAOD Methods
Given the proposed methods in previous experiments, we will conduct an extensive experimental evaluation and qualitative analysis to compare the adaptability, robustness, and transferability of different test-time adaptation (TTA) of vision-language detection (TTAOD) methods, and identify potential strengths and weaknesses of each approach.
Controls: We will assess the performance of each TTAOD method across various tasks, datasets, and evaluation metrics, and validate the effectiveness of each approach through ablation studies, visualizations, and expert insights.
Estimated cost: 1800 GPU-hours (considering the extensive experimental evaluation and data analysis)
Prediction: This comprehensive evaluation will provide a thorough understanding of the strengths, weaknesses, and limitations of each TTAOD method, enabling researchers to select the most suitable approach for specific applications and environments. The insights gained will also inform the design of future TTAOD methods and facilitate their integration into real-world systems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Vision-Language Detectors as Foundations for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Experiment 1: Compare the baseline performance of pre-trained GLIP and Grounding DINO models on a set of standard object detection benchmarks, including PASCAL VOC, COCO, and LVIS, to establish a performance baseline for the vision-language detectors.
CONTROLS: Prior experiments with standard object detection methods (Faster R-CNN), recent state-of-the-art TTAOD methods, and strong ablated versions of GLIP and Grounding DINO that retain their pre-trained knowledge.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: GLIP and Grounding DINO should outperform Faster R-CNN and recent TTAOD methods, thanks to their zero-shot generalization and open-vocabulary capabilities, but may still suffer from degraded performance under real-world distribution shifts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Practical Self-Training with Adaptive Thresholding for Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Experiment 2: Implement an adaptive thresholding mechanism for pseudo-label filtering, which continuously adjusts the confidence threshold based on the quality of pseudo-labels generated on the fly. This is done by estimating the reliability of pseudo-labels based on their consistency across multiple iterations and re-calculating the threshold using a recursive Bayesian update rule. The goal is to maximize the number of high-quality pseudo-labels while minimizing noise.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard fixed-confidence thresholding, and ablate the adaptive thresholding component to estimate its contribution to improvement. Use a set of standard object detection benchmarks with real-world distribution shifts.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Adaptive thresholding should mitigate the presence of excessive noise and imbalanced pseudo-label distribution, allowing for higher-quality pseudo-label generation and, consequently, improved target detection performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Source-Free Fine-Tuning with Importance Sampling for Category-Agnostic TTAOD
PROPOSAL: Theoretical result: Derive a theoretical framework for importance sampling-based fine-tuning of a pre-trained vision-language detector, allowing it to adapt to open-set target categories without any source domain knowledge or supervision. The framework utilizes entropy-based importance weights to balance the distribution of pseudo-labels across target categories and adapt the detector's confidence to each category. This framework directly addresses the challenges of category-agnostic TTAOD.
CONTROLS: Revision of theory for subsequent experiments, where we will validate the derived framework using real-world datasets.
COST: 0 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The theoretical framework for importance sampling-based fine-tuning should enable source-free adaptation of vision-language detectors to open-set target categories with high accuracy, making it a promising direction for category-agnostic TTAOD.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Efficient Category-Agnostic TTAOD via Importance Sampling and Stochastic Control Variates
PROPOSAL: Revision of previous proposal (3): Modify the application of importance sampling for fine-tuning to incorporate stochastic control variates, which estimate the expected loss for each batch of pseudo-labels. This will significantly reduce the variance of the importance weights-based adaptation update, making it computationally efficient and applicable to scenarios with limited resources.
CONTROLS: Analyze the impact of using stochastic control variates on adaptation stability and convergence, and compare with non-stochastic importance sampling.
COST: Revised estimate: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised approach should provide more efficient adaptation by reducing the variance of importance weights, allowing for faster convergence and practical application in resource-constrained scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Evaluation of On-Line TTAOD with Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Experiment 4: Evaluate the performance of the proposed category-agnostic TTAOD method, combined with adaptive thresholding and importance sampling, on real-world benchmarks such as ImageNet-Later, LeftTurn-Later, Cityscapes Transfer, and the Robustness Evaluation with Realistic Traffic Jams (ERTR 3), considering both measured driving datasets like NYU center for data science and validated potential use cases (e.g., online linked with its requirement for the pictures of the follow-on actual road scenario). Evaluations should be performed under scenarios that account for open-set target categories, limited samples, and changes in visual environment conditions such as weather or harsh illumination.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Adaptive Pseudo-Label Filtering with Heteroscedastic Uncertainty Models
PROPOSAL: Revision of previous proposal (2): Enhance the adaptive thresholding mechanism by utilizing heteroscedastic uncertainty models to estimate the quality and confidence of pseudo-labels generated on the fly. This will allow for more informed decision-making regarding pseudo-label filtering and adaptation, especially when dealing with target data variations and open-set categories.
CONTROLS: Compare this revised approach with standard fixed-confidence thresholding and adaptations based on previous estimates. Integrate this mechanism with importance sampling and stochastic control variates (revised 3) and evaluate its overall impact on TTAOD performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Shot Domain Adaptation with Vision-Language Detectors and Aligned Embeddings
PROPOSAL: Experiment 5: Investigate the application of zero-shot domain adaptation techniques using aligned embeddings with vision-language detectors. This involves projecting source and target domain embeddings into a common space using multilingual multimodal projection (MMP), which enables zero-shot adaptation without explicit category supervision. Compare the performance of this approach with standard source-free fine-tuning methods on the real-world benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Evaluate zero-shot adaptation performance with and without MMP, using source-free fine-tuning and TTAOD with importance sampling and stochastic control variates (revised 3) and adaptive pseudo-label filtering (revised 2) as baseline methods.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This zero-shot domain adaptation approach with MMP should demonstrate improved adaptation performance, especially when dealing with unseen target categories and domain shifts, without requiring explicit category labels during the adaptation process.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Conditioned Vision-Language Detectors for Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of task-conditioned vision-language detectors that allow for flexible adaptation to unseen categories and distribution shifts at test time. Specifically, adapt the GLIP detector to learn a task-specific embedding that captures domain-invariant information, while preserving the generalization capabilities of the pre-trained model.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard GLIP, and ablate the use of task-conditioned embeddings.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved adaptation performance on cross-domain and cross-category target data, while preserving pre-trained generalization. May fail to adapt to highly diverse or dynamic target distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Driven Pseudo-Label Filtering for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Propose a method to filter pseudo-labels using uncertainty measures, such as the mean squared error or confidence scores, to ensure that pseudo-labels are only used when confident. Train a uncertainty predictor on the validation set and use it to filter pseudo-labels on the test set in each batch. Compare with standard self-training and ablation studies on pseudo-label filtering strategies.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard self-training, and ablate different uncertainty measures and filtering strategies.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved adaptation performance on target data with scarce, noisy, or missing pseudo-labels, and reduced overfitting to noisy samples. May fail to adapt to target distributions with complex or non-linear relationships between categories.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Task-Conditioned Vision-Language Detectors for Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Revise the task-conditioned vision-language detectors to incorporate uncertainty-driven pseudo-label filtering. When pseudo-labels are filtered out due to low uncertainty, use a self-training approach with a warm-up phase where the detector is fine-tuned on a subset of labeled data, and a self-supervised phase where the detector is adapted to the target domain using pseudo-labels generated on the fly. This approach aims to leverage both the uncertainty-driven filtering and self-training paradigms.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard GLIP and the uncertainty-driven pseudo-label filtering approach.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved adaptation performance on target data with scarce, noisy, or missing pseudo-labels, and better preservation of pre-trained generalization. May require careful tuning of hyperparameters for warm-up phase.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: 
PROPOSAL: Instead of training a separate uncertainty predictor, use the detector's confidence scores directly for pseudo-label filtering. This approach is simpler and more efficient, while still leveraging the detector's uncertainty estimates.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original uncertainty-driven pseudo-label filtering approach.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved efficiency, but may sacrifice some adaptation performance compared to a dedicated uncertainty predictor.

CONTROLS: Compare with the original uncertainty-driven pseudo-label filtering approach and the ablated approach without pseudo-label filtering.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved efficiency, but may sacrifice some adaptation performance compared to a dedicated uncertainty predictor.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Progressive Test-Time Adaptation with Early Task Switching
PROPOSAL: Investigate a progressive adaptation approach that allows the detector to switch to a new task early on when confidence in the current task's pseudo-labels drops below a certain threshold. This approach aims to adapt to changing target distributions and avoid overfitting to noisy samples.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard self-training and ablation studies on early task switching strategies.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved adaptation performance on target data with changing distributions, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters for threshold selection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Domain-Agnostic Language Knowledge Distillation for Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Investigate a domain-agnostic language knowledge distillation approach that extracts and transfers task-agnostic knowledge from a pre-trained vision-language detector to a target domain, without assuming shared label spaces. This approach aims to leverage the detector's language understanding for adaptation to new domains.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard self-training and ablation studies on knowledge distillation strategies.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved adaptation performance on target data from new domains, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters for knowledge distillation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmented Adversarial Domain Adaptation for Test-Time Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Investigate an augmented adversarial domain adaptation approach that incorporates multiple generators, discriminators, and mapped pseudo-labels to adapt the detector to target domains with diverse distributions. This approach aims to address the challenge of target-driven pseudo-label generation and enrich the adaptation space.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard adversarial domain adaptation and ablation studies on multi-task architecture.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved adaptation performance on target data with diverse distributions, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters for generator and discriminator architectures.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: 
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel pseudo-label augmentation mechanism, where the original pseudo-labels are mixed with noise and perturbations, to further enrich the adaptation space and improve the detector's robustness to target-driven pseudo- label generation. This approach is combined with the augmented adversarial domain adaptation approach.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original augmented adversarial domain adaptation approach and ablation studies on pseudo-label augmentation mechanisms.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved robustness and adaptation performance on target data, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters for noise levels and perturbation magnitudes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Baseline Scalability Experiments on TSP
PROPOSAL: Train a collection of simple neural network models on the Euclidean traveling salesman problem (TSP) instance with varying number of cities and model sizes (e.g., fully connected neural networks with 100, 200, and 400 parameters), both on simulated and generated TSP instances. Evaluate performance using the solution quality (objective function value) and training time. Compare against a simple baseline of a greedy construction heuristic for TSP.
CONTROLS: Greedy construction heuristic, scaling up dataset size (number of cities) while fixing model parameters
COST: 10 GPU-hours ( baseline + 3 model sizes)
PREDICTION: Larger models will find slightly better solutions over smaller ones, especially in larger instances, but degrade performance at very large instance sizes, reflecting the growing difficulty in scaling performance with model and data while fixed in a limited capacity space. A brute-force baseline (re-running the model for all combinations of cities) will perform slightly better than our most capable neural model as cities increase past a certain point.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Representational Capacity vs Solution Space Size Experiments
PROPOSAL: Experimentally analyze how neural network models' representational capacity affects performance when the size of the solution space is increased in a TSP simulation environment, while keeping model size constant. This can be achieved by scaling up the number of cities in TSP instances with different radius constraints (e.g., distances within 100, 500, and 1000 units of the cities' coordinates), which affect the dimensionality of the solution space but keep the model capacity within a fixed constant (e.g., 200 parameters). Analyze how performance measurements change across different representational capacities (e.g., number of basis functions in a Fourier basis representation).

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Simple Scaling Law for Representation Size
PROPOSAL: Use a fixed-capacity neural network and study how its performance degrades as the dimensionality of the representation space grows from 8 to 1024 dimensions using a synthetic dataset generated by partitioning a high-dimensional Gaussian sphere. We use a simple neural network (MLP) with a fixed number of parameters and evaluate performance on a Euclidean traveling salesman problem (TSP) benchmark where the inputs and outputs are points in high-dimensional space. We calculate and plot the average travel distance as a function of input dimensionality, using different learning rates, optimizer choices, and batch sizes to study the dependency of the performance trend on training parameters.
CONTROLS: Fixed-capacity MLP, vanilla SGD with different learning rates, SGD with momentum, Adam optimizer with different step sizes. Fixed random seed for reproducibility.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: For small representation sizes, performance should degrade fairly slowly as dimensionality grows, reflecting overfitting on the training set. As dimensionality grows beyond a certain point (thought to be related to the capacity of the network), performance should degrade catastrophically as the curse of dimensionality starts to dominate, with more dramatic falls for different optimizers and learning rates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Counterfactual Experiments for Solution Space Scaling
PROPOSAL: To study the impact of solution space complexity, we design a set of experiments where the number of possible routes for the TSP is scaled up while the geometry of the problem remains the same. This can be achieved by synthesizing new point locations within the existing set while maintaining a fixed point distribution. We use two methods to increase the number of routes: (1) correlated sampling: we generate additional points by adding random displacements that preserve the correlations in the distribution; and (2) independent sampling: we generate new points by independently sampling from the same point distribution. For each scaling method, we run experiments using the same fixed-capacity MLP from the previous proposal, calculating and plotting the average travel distance as a function of the scaled route complexity.
CONTROLS: Same fixed-capacity MLP as before, with three different optimizer- learning rate pairs and an additional control with random seed variation.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: In the correlated sampling case, growth in solution space complexity should have a moderate impact on performance, possibly leading to early signs of overfitting and a saturation effect when the number of routes increases. In contrast, the independent sampling case should not maintain spatial distribution correlation and could lead to much more severe performance degradation due to a storm of 'unnatural' point distributions creating challenges for the problem.

TITLE: Capacity Bounds for TSP
PROPOSAL: We study the theoretical capacity bounds for solving the Euclidean TSP using a neural network. We find the optimal polynomial-time algorithms for generating the subset of routes and establish a set of lower bounds on the dimensionality of representation arising from the fixed-capacity neural network and TSP instances. Next, we apply the technique of construction to establish an upper bound that brings us closer to understanding the feasible algorithms under capacity constraints.
CONTROLS: Lower bounds derived from known TSP algorithms, upper bound derived from a new algorithm construction.
COST: 10 research-hours
PREDICTION: The bounds should provide insight into the relationship between network capacity, TSP instance size, and difficulty for finding minimally routed paths, which may have implications for scaling laws.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Predictive Modeling of TSP Performance
PROPOSAL: We develop a predictive model that takes the TSP instance size, network architecture, and training parameters as inputs and outputs the expected performance of the neural network on the TSP. We use a combination of the lower and upper bounds from the capacity bounds proposal and the results from the scaling law and counterfactual experiments proposals to develop a probabilistic model that predicts performance. We train the model on a set of synthetic and simulated TSP instances and validate it on a separate set of instances.
CONTROLS: Comparison to a baseline model that uses only the instance size as input, as well as ablations of the different components of the predictive model.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The predictive model should be able to accurately forecast the performance of the neural network on the TSP, allowing us to identify the key factors that influence performance and make recommendations for improving model design and training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Neural TSP: A Hypernetwork Approach
PROPOSAL: We explore a new approach to solving the TSP using a hypernetwork architecture, where the weights of the neural network are themselves represented by a separate neural network. We train the hypernetwork using a set of TSP instances as inputs and overlap the learnable weights from a standard TSP neural network, exploring how performance is influenced by the capacity of the hypernetwork relative to the TSP instance difficulty. We compare the performance of the hypernetwork approach to the baseline TSP neural network architecture and explore the implications of our results for understanding the relationships between network capacity, instance size, and performance.
CONTROLS: Comparison to a standard TSP neural network, ablations of the hypernetwork architecture, and exploration of different hypernetwork capacities.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hypernetwork approach should provide a significant improvement in performance, with the capacity of the hypernetwork playing a critical role in determining the level of improvement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Overfitting on TSP Performance
PROPOSAL: We investigate the relationship between overfitting and TSP performance by intentionally training TSP neural networks to overfit on a set of TSP instances, and then evaluate their performance on a separate set of held-out instances. We explore how the capacity of the network, the training procedure, and the choice of regularizers affect the trade-off between overfitting and generalization performance. We also analyze the representational capacity of the network and how it relates to the problem's intrinsic difficulty.
CONTROLS: Comparison to a standard TSP neural network, ablations of the regularizers and training procedure, and exploration of different capacities.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results should provide insight into the role of overfitting in TSP performance and highlight the importance of controlling overfitting in TSP neural networks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding the Role of Optimizers in TSP Performance
PROPOSAL: We investigate the role of optimizers in TSP performance by comparing the performance of different optimizers (e.g. SGD, Adam, RMSProp) on a set of TSP instances. We explore how the choice of optimizer affects the convergence rate, stability, and generalization performance of TSP neural networks. We also analyze the relationship between the optimizer's update rule and the problem's intrinsic difficulty.
CONTROLS: Comparison to a standard SGD optimizer, ablations of the optimizer's hyperparameters, and exploration of different optimizers.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results should highlight the importance of optimizer choice in TSP performance and provide insights into the relationships between optimizer properties and TSP problem difficulty.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Capacity Bounds for TSP
PROPOSAL: We provide a more detailed analysis of the capacity bounds for TSP neural networks, deriving sharper bounds on the dimensionality of representation and exploring their implications for understanding the relationships between network capacity, instance size, and performance. We also discuss the implications of our results for the development of more efficient TSP algorithms and provide a comprehensive comparison to existing bounds.
CONTROLS: Previous results from the capacity bounds proposal, new bounds derived using more advanced techniques.
COST: 10 research-hours
PREDICTION: The revised capacity bounds should provide a more precise understanding of the relationships between network capacity, instance size, and performance, and highlight the importance of controlling capacity in TSP neural networks.

Understanding the Role of Optimizers in TSP Performance

This concludes the research proposal.
