actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Evaluating Neural Scaling Laws on a Synthetic Euclidean TSP
PROPOSAL: We use a synthetic Euclidean traveling salesman problem dataset where the city positions are uniformly sampled in the unit hypercube. We perform grid search over a wide range of model capacities (e.g., number of layers, neurons, width) and compute budgets, and measure the performance as a function of the two variables. Specifically, we train a neural network to learn an approximate TSP solution, and we measure its performance in terms of the average tour length. We repeat this experiment over multiple synthetic datasets, varying the number of cities.
CONTROLS: A simple nearest neighbor baseline, and a random search over a smaller set of model capacities and compute budgets as an ablation study.
COST: Estimating 5 GPU-hours per synthetic dataset, with 4 datasets total (100 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: With synthetic data, we expect to observe smooth trends in performance as a function of model capacity and compute budget, which should hold even when the solution space grows exponentially. Performance may degrade when the dimensionality of the representation space increases, but we expect this to be less dramatic given that we are working in a fixed Euclidean geometry. If our experiment finds simple trends, this would be a good sign for studying model scaling laws, but we should still account for potential variations in the specific choice of neural network architecture, hyperparameters, or training procedure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Combinatorial Solution Space Growth on Neural Network Performance
PROPOSAL: We introduce a variant of the synthetic Euclidean TSP where the number of cities increases as we scale up the solution space. Specifically, we sample the city positions uniformly, but then scale the distance matrix so that the ratio of distances is preserved while the absolute distances increase exponentially with the city count. This allows us to generate datasets with a fixed representation dimension but an exponentially growing solution space. We repeat the same experiment as in Proposal 1, measuring the impact of model capacity and compute budget on tour-length performance.
CONTROLS: An ablative study comparing the behavior of Proposal 1 to this new, growing-solution-space variant to understand how combinatorial growth affects performance trends.
COST: Estimated additional 3 GPU-hours to train on this growing solution space.
PREDICTION: We expect the performance trends observed in Proposal 1 to become less smooth as the solution space grows exponentially, with performance likely suffering more from the increased dimensionality of the problem space. This will help us understand how the neural network is impacted by the curse of dimensionality and will shed light on whether the observed trends are a result of the model's capacity or the effective dimensionality of the task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring the Impact of Representation Space Dimensionality on Neural Network Performance
PROPOSAL: We modify the synthetic Euclidean TSP by adding an encoding layer that maps 2D coordinates to a higher-dimensional representation space. By varying the dimensionality of this representation space, we control the ratio of the size of the solution space to the size of the representation space. We then measure the impact of this change on the performance trends observed in Proposals 1 and 2, focusing on how the dimensionality of the representation space affects the reproducibility of the observed trends.
CONTROLS: A control experiment without the encoding layer to serve as a baseline, and ablative studies to understand the effects of removing or scaling down the encoding layer.
COST: Estimating 2 GPU-hours to implement and train the modified model.
PREDICTION: As the dimensionality of the representation space increases, we expect the performance trends to become less smooth, and the neural network performance may degrade rapidly due to the curse of dimensionality. However, we should observe that the impact of representation space dimensionality on performance trends is less dramatic compared to the combinatorial solution space growth in Proposal 2.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Combinatorial Solution Space Growth on Neural Network Performance
PROPOSAL: We modify Proposal 2 to use a different sampling strategy for the growing solution space. Instead of uniformly sampling city positions and scaling the distance matrix, we introduce "clustering" in the city distribution, with a fixed cluster size increasing with the city count. This allows us to examine how the neural network's ability to capture structure and patterns in the solution space is affected by the growing dimensionality. We measure the impact of model capacity and compute budget on tour-length performance, and compare the results to Proposal 1 and Proposal 3.
CONTROLS: An ablative study comparing the performance with and without clustering to understand the impact of the clustering mechanism on the observed trends.
COST: Estimated same as previous, as the revised experiment will use the same training procedure and baselines.
PREDICTION: With clustering in the city distribution, we expect the neural network to exhibit a mix of positive and negative trends in performance, showing better handling of structured patterns but potentially worse handling of local optima and larger search spaces. This comparison will provide insights into how different sampling strategies affect the model's ability to generalize and the reliability of the observed performance trends.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Influence of Normalization and Regularization on Neural Network Performance Trends
PROPOSAL: We investigate how different normalizations (Batch Normalization, Instance Normalization) and regularization techniques (L1, L2, dropout) impact the performance trends observed in the previous proposals. We implement a set of experiments with varying normalization and regularization strategies on the same synthetic Euclidean TSP dataset, measuring the effect of these techniques on the tours' length and searching space.
CONTROLS: A control experiment with default normalization and no regularization as a baseline, and ablative studies to understand the effects of removing or replacing a single component.
COST: Estimated 4 GPU-hours, considering the need to implement and train multiple models with varying normalization and regularization strategies.
PREDICTION: We expect the performance trends to be sensitive to the choice of normalization and regularization techniques, and the trends may exhibit complex interactions between these components. For instance, normalization techniques might allow the model to generalize better in the growing solution space, but regularization techniques may offset this effect and cause performance degradation. If our results show strong trends, they may shed light on whether the observed trends are due to capacity, dimensionality, or an overfitting/regularization trade-off.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Neural Scaling Laws on a Synthetic Euclidean TSP
PROPOSAL: We modify Proposal 1 to incorporate the insights gained from the previous experiments. Instead of using a fixed Euclidean distance metric, we sample the distance matrix from a more general family of metrics (e.g., Manhattan, Minkowski, or even a learned metric from previous experiments). We then measure how the performance trends in the synthetic Euclidean TSP dataset are affected by the choice of distance metric, and compare the results to the previous proposals.
CONTROLS: A control experiment with the default Euclidean distance metric, and ablative studies to understand the effects of removing or replacing the custom distance metric.
COST: Estimated 2 GPU-hours to implement and train the modified model.
PREDICTION: By varying the distance metric, we expect the performance trends to exhibit more pronounced effects from the growing solution space and representation space dimensionality, and potentially new insights into how the model adapts to different problem geometries. This will help to shed light on the interplay between the capacity of the model, the effective dimensionality of the task, and the performance trends observed in our experiments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Prior Knowledge in Neural Network Performance Trends
PROPOSAL: We introduce a variant of the synthetic Euclidean TSP where we include prior knowledge about the solution space in the form of a fixed set of "hints" or "constraints" that the neural network has access to during training. We then measure how the inclusion of this prior knowledge affects the performance trends observed in the previous experiments, focusing on whether the model is able to leverage its capacity more effectively in the presence of biases and priors.
CONTROLS: A control experiment without the prior knowledge as a baseline, and ablative studies to understand the effects of removing or replacing the prior knowledge.
COST: Estimated 3 GPU-hours to implement and train the modified model with prior knowledge.
PREDICTION: By including prior knowledge, we expect the performance trends to become less smooth and more sensitive to the capacity and representation space dimensionality of the model. However, the model may exhibit improved handling of structured patterns and biases in the solution space, potentially leading to better adaptation to the task geometry. This will help us understand how prior knowledge and biases interact with the capacity of the model and the performance trends observed in our experiments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Interplay between Model Capacity and Effective Task Dimensionality
PROPOSAL: We adapt the techniques from the previous proposals to analyze the interplay between model capacity and effective task dimensionality. We use a dimensionality-reduction technique (e.g., PCA or t-SNE) to visualize the representation space of the neural network and understand how the model captures the underlying structure of the solution space. We then measure how the model's capacity affects its ability to generalize to higher-dimensional task geometries.
CONTROLS: A control experiment with a fixed model capacity and a uniformly sampled representation space as a baseline, and ablative studies to understand the effects of varying model capacity and representation space dimensionality.
COST: Estimated 4 GPU-hours to implement and train the modified model and analyze the representation space.
PREDICTION: By analyzing the representation space, we expect to reveal insights into how the model's capacity interacts with the effective task dimensionality. We anticipate that the model will be able to generalize to higher-dimensional task geometries by leveraging its capacity, but that excessive capacity may lead to overfitting and poor generalization. This will help us understand the interplay between model capacity and effective task dimensionality and their impact on performance trends.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Optimization Algorithm and Hardware in Neural Network Performance Trends
PROPOSAL: We explore the impact of varying optimization algorithms (e.g., SGD, Adam, RMSProp) and hardware architectures (e.g., CPU, GPU, TPUs) on the performance trends observed in the previous experiments. We measure how the choice of optimization algorithm and hardware affects the model's ability to generalize to different task geometries and solve problems at large scales.
CONTROLS: A control experiment with the default SGD optimizer and CPU hardware as a baseline, and ablative studies to understand the effects of replacing the optimizer and/or hardware.
COST: Estimated 5 GPU-hours to implement and train the modified model, considering the need to run experiments on multiple hardware architectures.
PREDICTION: By investigating the impact of optimization algorithms and hardware, we expect to gain insights into how the choice of these components affects the model's ability to scale to large problem sizes. We anticipate that the choice of optimization algorithm will have a significant impact on the model's convergence and generalization, while the choice of hardware will affect the model's ability to scale to large problem sizes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Analysis of Neural Scaling Laws in the Synthetic Euclidean TSP
PROPOSAL: We perform a comprehensive meta-analysis of the performance trends observed across the previous experiments, aiming to identify the key factors that contribute to the emergence of neural scaling laws. We will apply techniques from meta-learning, such as multi-task learning and meta-training, to combine the data from all experiments and identify patterns that are common across different task geometries and optimization algorithms.
CONTROLS: None, as this experiment is a post-hoc analysis of the previous results.
COST: Estimated 1 GPU-hour to implement and run the meta-analysis, as it primarily involves data aggregation and model averaging.
PREDICTION: By performing a meta-analysis, we expect to uncover key factors that underlie the emergence of neural scaling laws across different problem sizes and optimization algorithms. We anticipate the emergence of general trends that generalize beyond the specific experiments we ran, potentially shedding light on the fundamental nature of neural scaling laws and their relation to the capacity of neural networks.

propositions.titre: Large-Scale Empirical Evaluation of Data Quality Assessment Frameworks for Multilingual LLMs

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Model-Based Data Selection for Non-English Languages
PROPOSAL: We will extend the FineWeb2-HQ approach to multiple languages by training a multilingual quality rater using mixed-language pretraining corpora and general domain web data as supervision, without relying on benchmark-derived supervision.
CONTROLS: DCLM ( English-only positive supervision), AskLLM ( prompt-based evaluation criteria using an English LLM)
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach may outperform FineWeb2-HQ in terms of quality signal generality across languages, but could struggle to maintain the quality of English language data. 
In particular, this early design may be overly conservative and less effective at filtering out low-quality non-English content. It is therefore essential to assess its trade-off between maintaining English quality and improving multilingual data filtering.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Model-Based Data Selection for Non-English Languages
PROPOSAL (Revised): To address the limitations of our initial approach, we modify the FineWeb2-HQ strategy by incorporating multilingual prompts and causal language modeling objectives for cross-lingual quality assessment. This allows our multilingual quality rater to learn attention-based representations and model interactions between languages.
CONTROLS: FineWeb2-HQ ( benchmark-derived supervision), DCLM ( English-only positive supervision)
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised approach could lead to more effective cross-lingual data filtering and maintain the quality of English language data. However, the additional complexity and overhead of the multilingual prompts and causal objectives might hinder convergence or increase model size, which could impact performance in resource-constrained environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Training Objectives for Multilingual Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: We will explore whether contrastive (supervised) or causal (self-supervised) objectives better suit the task of multilingual quality assessment, and investigate whether incorporating both objectives can be beneficial.
CONTROLS: Supervised FineWeb2-HQ (contrastive objective), Unsupervised multilingual rater (causal objective)
COST: 500 GPU-hours (per objective or combination)
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating a causally-trained component into our model will significantly enhance its ability to judge quality invariant to language.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Attention Patterns and Quality Rhetoric Across Languages
PROPOSAL: To understand how the model assesses quality across languages, we analyze the attention patterns of our multilingual quality rater during evaluation. Additionally, we examine the type of linguistic features the model uses to make quality judgments (rhetoric), comparing English, Spanish, and Chinese corpora.
CONTROLS: DCLM ( language-specific filters for English), Baseline heuristic filters without attention analysis
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This analysis will reveal the underlying linguistic mechanisms and attention patterns used by our model, potentially exposing biases in its quality assessment. We hypothesize that the model will attend differently to the sources and causes of quality judgments across languages and that it will primarily rely on the communicative efficiency (rhetoric) of a piece rather than its surface features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Downstream Performance of Multilingual LLMs Trained with Selected Data
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the downstream performance advantages of using the selected data from our multilingual quality rater in training multilingual LLMs for a set of high-quality downstream tasks (e.g., question answering, text classification), in English, Spanish, and Chinese languages.
CONTROLS: LLMs trained on globally sampled data, hand-curated high-quality datasets for reference
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our hypothesis is that our selected data, which should contain a higher proportion of coherent and informative web pages in multiple languages, will yield improvements in model performance across various downstream tasks and languages.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Analysis of Attention Patterns and Quality Rhetoric Across Languages
PROPOSAL (Revised): To further analyze the attention patterns of our multilingual quality rater, we utilize the lens of information theory and evaluate the entropy of model-generated quality scores, examining how this relates to our model's bias towards particular linguistic features and rhetorical devices.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Monolingual Language Modeling in Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: We experiment with incorporating a monolingual (language-specific) language model into our multilingual quality rater to leverage the benefits of monolingual pretraining in each target language while still maintaining cross-lingual evaluation.
CONTROLS: Baseline multilingual rater, monolingual quality raters for each language ( English, Spanish, Chinese)
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By incorporating a monolingual component, we may be able to improve the model's evaluation of quality in specific languages and better capture linguistic features that are relevant to each language, but the additional computational overhead and model complexity might impact the model's generalizability and cross-lingual performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferability and Adversarial Robustness of Multilingual Quality Raters
PROPOSAL: We investigate the transferability and adversarial robustness of our multilingual quality raters across various languages and evaluation scenarios, including out-of-domain text, with a focus on its resilience to attacks and adversarial text generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline quality rater, adversarial training, and evaluation with human annotations
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our hypothesis is that the multilingual quality rater will exhibit good transferability across languages and demonstrate resilience against common adversarial attacks, such as *addition of irrelevant information*, substitution, and formatting changes. However, it may be vulnerable to highly crafted, strategic, and syntax-preserving attacks aimed at exploiting language-specific biases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparison with Localized Filtering Strategies for Pretraining Data
PROPOSAL: We compare our globally-trained multilingual quality rater with localized filtering strategies that adapt to each specific linguistic community, and evaluate their impact on downstream performance and data quality.
CONTROLS: Diverse set of language-specific filtering strategies (deduplication, heuristic filters, domain-aware sampling)
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We hypothesize that our globally-trained quality rater will outperform localized strategies for languages where a large high-quality dataset is available, but it may struggle in resource-scarce languages or domains where localized filtering can be tailored to the specific context.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Model-Based Data Selection for Non-English Languages
PROPOSAL (Revised): We will extensively evaluate and refine our multilingual quality rater using the results from the previous experiments (training objectives, monolingual modeling, transferability, adversarial robustness, and localized filtering comparison). By integrating insights from these studies, we will arrive at a definitive, high-quality pretraining data selection approach for multilingual LLMs.
CONTROLS: All previous experiments, including proposed models, baselines, and ablations.
COST: Reprioritized based on refined experimental plan
PREDICTION: By incorporating the lessons learned from our comprehensive evaluation, we will arrive at a robust and effective model-based data selection approach for multilingual LLMs that generalizes to various languages and domains.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Multilingual Model-Based Data Selection Using Weak Supervision
PROPOSAL: Train a multilingual rater using weak supervision signals like cross-lingual similarity maps or translation equivalents as auxiliary supervision, and evaluate its quality on a web-scale corpus by comparing to existing heuristic and model-based selection strategies.
CONTROLS: Compare against FineWeb2-HQ with benchmark-derived supervision, English-only raters like DCLM, and a past-heuristic filter baseline.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multilingual rater will outperform FineWeb2-HQ in English and other languages, but may suffer from domain bias due to the weak supervision, especially on out-of-domain samples.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Cross-Lingual Evaluation with Bilingual Embeddings
PROPOSAL: Develop a cross-lingual evaluation framework using bilingual embeddings learned from parallel corpora in multiple languages, to assess the quality of the multilingual rater's judgments across languages and tasks.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the bilingual embeddings using various retrieval-based evaluation protocols (e.g., top-K precision, MAP), and compare against a monolingual evaluation baseline.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The bilingual embeddings will demonstrate significant improvements in cross-lingual evaluation, but may sensitivity to noise and variations in parallel corpora quality, and could benefit from additional unsupervised learning techniques.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Cross-Lingual Evaluation with Bilingual Embeddings (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Modify the bilingual embeddings framework to incorporate transfer learning across languages, and use a multi-task learning objective to learn robust embeddings that capture language-agnostic and language-specific features for the multilingual rater's judgments.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised bilingual embeddings against the original implementation, a monolingual baseline, and a random embedding baseline, to assess the effectiveness of transfer learning and multi-task learning.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (additional modifications only)
PREDICTION: The revised bilingual embeddings will lead to improved cross-lingual transfer and robustness, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters for optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Multilingual Model-Based Data Selection
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of transfer learning for the multilingual rater by fine-tuning it on large-scale multilingual datasets (e.g., XSum, CC100) and evaluate its performance on out-of-domain web-scale corpora.
CONTROLS: Compare the fine-tuned multilingual rater against its unsupervised counterpart, and against a training-from-scratch baseline on the same web-scale corpus.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The fine-tuned multilingual rater will demonstrate significant improvements in generalization to out-of-domain samples, but may require careful selection of source domains and fine-tuning strategies to avoid overfitting.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Multitask Learning for Multilingual Data Curation
PROPOSAL: Enrich the multilingual rater with multitask learning by jointly optimizing data selection and related tasks, such as sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, or question answering, and evaluate its performance on various web-scale corpora and downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the multitask-learned multilingual rater against its single-task counterpart, a baseline with a fixed set of tasks, and state-of-the-art multitask learning approaches for other NLP tasks.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multitask-learned multilingual rater will leverage shared knowledge and improve performance across a range of tasks and languages, but may require principled methods for task selection and knowledge transfer.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Estimating Potential Bias in Multilingual Raters
PROPOSAL: Develop a bias estimation framework to identify potential biases in the multilingual rater, such as language-specific or task-specific biases, and propose strategies for mitigating these biases using debiasing techniques, data augmentation, and reweighting methods.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the bias estimation framework using a set of controlled experiments and simulations, and compare the debiased multilingual rater against its unbiased counterpart.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The bias estimation framework will uncover significant biases in the multilingual rater, particularly in languages with smaller dataset sizes, and the debiased rater will lead to improved downstream performance and fairness.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Cross-Lingual Evaluation with Bilingual Embeddings (Revised: Handling Bias)
PROPOSAL: Modify the bilingual embeddings framework to explicitly handle bias, by incorporating bias-invariant metrics (e.g., asymmetric metrics, inter-rater agreement), and evaluating them together with traditional metrics (e.g., precision, recall).
CONTROLS: Compare the revised bilingual embeddings against the original implementation, and against bias-sensitive baselines (e.g., re-sampling, data weighting) to assess the impact of handling bias on cross-lingual evaluation.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (modifications only)
PREDICTION: The revised bilingual embeddings will provide a more comprehensive picture of the multilingual rater's bias, and handling bias will improve the robustness and fairness of cross-lingual evaluation.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Language-Agnostic Unsupervised Data Selection
PROPOSAL: Propose a language-agnostic unsupervised data selection framework that leverages common statistical properties of text data across languages, and evaluate its performance on various web-scale corpora and downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the language-agnostic unsupervised framework against the multilingual rater approaches, and against strong baselines (e.g., topic modeling, clustering), to assess its advantages and limitations.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The language-agnostic unsupervised framework will provide a complementary approach to multilingual rater-based selection, offering advantages in scenarios with limited supervision or high label noise, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters for optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Multilingual Model-Based Data Selection Using Weak Supervision (Revised: Large-Scale Web-Scale Corpus)
PROPOSAL: Scale up the weak supervision approach to large-scale web-scale corpora, using techniques such as domain adaptation and data augmentation, and evaluate its performance in a production-ready setting.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised weak supervision approach against its smaller-scale counterpart, and against state-of-the-art approaches to large-scale data selection, to assess its scalability and effectiveness.
COST: 600 GPU-hours (due to scalability requirements)
PREDICTION: The revised weak supervision approach will demonstrate its ability to handle large-scale web-scale corpora, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and data preprocessing techniques to maintain performance.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Real-World Deployment and Integration with LLMs
PROPOSAL: Deploy the multilingual data selection framework in a real-world setting, integrating it with large language models (LLMs) to evaluate its impact on downstream performance, and gather feedback from end-users on the effectiveness and usability of the framework.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of LLMs trained on data selected by the framework against those trained on randomly sampled data, and against those trained on data selected using existing approaches.
COST: Not specified ( depends on the deployment scenario)
PREDICTION: The real-world deployment will demonstrate the practical applicability and effectiveness of the multilingual data selection framework, but may require continued adaptation and refinement to address emerging challenges and user needs.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Grid-Based Latent Representations for Geometry and Appearance
PROPOSAL: Investigate the performance of 5 different grid-based latent models (PointFlorence, BOFT, SDFDiff, OccupancyFlow, GridNet) on 3D object reconstruction and image-to-3D generation using the ShapeNet dataset and the RenderForCAD benchmark, evaluating metrics such as Chamfer distance, surface Hausdorff distance, Colored Point-Cloud Similarity (CPS), and Full Point-Cloud Similarity (FPS). Compare the performance of these models with a baseline geometry-only representation (e.g. PointNet), and in the case of image-to-3D generation, evaluate the generated models' appearance with the help of a rendered image quality metric.
CONTROLS: PointNet (geometry-only baseline)
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The experiment will confirm the limitations of current grid-based models in capturing view-dependent appearance effects, with some performing better in certain aspects (e.g. OccFlow for reconstruction) but all struggling to reproduce the subtleties of real-world shading and reflections compared to our desired jointly-geometry-and-appearance representation. The appearance metrics on the generated models will reveal gaps in these models' ability to capture accurate light and view effects.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Design for Jointly-Capturing Geometry and View-Dependent Appearance
PROPOSAL: Design a new experiment that evaluates the performance of a novel jointly-geometry-and-appearance representation (named "Jacore") against a suite of baselines and ablations. Jacore combines a geometry-focused neural volume rendering approach (e.g., NeRF) with learned opacity and material properties from a separate appearance network (e.g., RenderGAN), jointly learning both the object's 3D shape and its appearance across different views. Test Jacore on the RenderForCAD benchmark and evaluate reconstruction quality (e.g., Chamfer distance, surface Hausdorff distance), appearance fidelity (e.g., Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM)), and modeling capability (e.g., ability to generate objects with reflections and highlights) compared to the baseline grid-based models from Proposal 1, as well as a appearance-only baseline (e.g., RenderGAN).
CONTROLS: Baseline grid-based models from Proposal 1; appearance-only baseline (RenderGAN); a reduced version of Jacore that only models geometry (GeoJacore); Jacore with fixed material properties instead of learned ones (FixedJacore)
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The experiment is expected to demonstrate the potential of Jacore to jointly model both geometry and appearance, outperforming the baseline models and showing significant improvements in terms of view-dependent effects (e.g., reflections, highlights, subtle changes in shading). However, the model may still struggle with certain types of challenging materials or dramatic lighting conditions.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Experimental Design for Jointly-Capturing Geometry and View-Dependent Appearance
PROPOSAL: Refine the novel jointly-geometry-and-appearance representation (Jacore) by incorporating a memory-efficient architecture and a new learning objective that combines geometry and appearance reconstruction in a single stage. This revised version of Jacore will utilize an efficient neural volume rendering approach with dynamic regularization (e.g., NeRF-dynReg) and a lightweight appearance network with a novel multi-scale feature fusion module. During training, the combined loss function will simultaneously optimize geometry and appearance reconstruction, encouraging the model to capture both structural and view-dependent effects. Evaluate Jacore's performance on the RenderForCAD benchmark and compare with the baseline models from Proposal 1 and the revised appearance-only baseline (Fix-RenderGAN).
CONTROLS: Baseline grid-based models from Proposal 1; Fix-RenderGAN (revised appearance-only baseline); a reduced version of revised Jacore that only models geometry (GeoJaco-dynReg); FixedJacore with a different appearance network architecture (e.g., DiffAAF)
COST: 4000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised version of Jacore is expected to demonstrate improved performance in capturing both geometry and appearance, especially in terms of view-dependent effects such as reflections and subtle changes in shading. Furthermore, the efficient neural volume rendering approach and lightweight appearance network architecture will allow for a significant reduction in the computational cost of training and inference.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Alternative Object Representations for Joint Geometry and Appearance Modeling
PROPOSAL: Explore three alternative object representations for jointly modeling geometry and appearance: (1) a point cloud-based representation that combines global and local features for geometry and appearance encoding; (2) a non-voxelized grid representation (NDVR) where voxels are replaced with learned and adaptive occupancy fields; and (3) a multi-scale hierarchical representation that models objects as a set of recursively decomposed parts, each with its own geometry and appearance.
Evaluate these representations on the Mo_CA Shape Dataset and the Lawson Benchmark, using metrics like IOU, IoU for Part, and similarity between point clouds. Compare their performance with the baseline grid-based models from Proposal 1 and the revised Jacore from Proposal 3.
CONTROLS: Baseline grid-based models from Proposal 1; revised Jacore from Proposal 3; an oracle representation with perfect joint geometry and appearance modeling
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The experiment will assess the effectiveness of different representation schemes for jointly capturing geometry and appearance, identifying their strengths and limitations in various scenarios. The point cloud-based representation might excel in cases where high-resolution geometry and fine-grained appearance details are required, while the NDVR might show robustness to partial occlusions or varying object scales.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Practical Evaluation of Jacore and Comparison with State-of-the-Art
PROPOSAL: Test the performance of revised Jacore (from Proposal 3) on a diverse set of real-world benchmarks:ург HRW benchmarks, the PANOptix-Teguan Dataset, and the Mars Zoo dataset. Evaluate its performance in generating objects with intricate geometry and complex appearances under different lighting conditions. Compare the results with those obtained using state-of-the-art geometry-only models (PointIterPCA) and appearance-only models (DiffClar).
CONTROLS: PointIterPCA (geometry-only baseline); DiffClar (appearance-only baseline); the baseline grid-based models from Proposal 1
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The experiment will demonstrate Jacore's ability to jointly model geometrical and appearance properties on real-world data and provide a comprehensive comparison with existing state-of-the-art models, highlighting its strengths and challenges. The results will shed light on its robustness in challenging cases and whether it can generate objects that closely resemble the ground truth.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustness and Uncertainty Analysis for Jacore
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of revised Jacore (from Proposal 3) to data corruption, variations in object poses, lighting conditions, and background clutter. Design experiments to evaluate its performance under various real-world scenarios, including: occluded views, partial occlusions, background clutter, shifted poses, and different lighting conditions. Analyze the model's uncertainty using Bayesian uncertainty estimation and/bootstrap techniques (e.g., MC dropout, Bayesian layers).
CONTROLS: baseline model with robust normalization layer, consists of a supersampled elaborate single-stage BS network-stability variation, enhanced networks designed for robust recovery
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal whether Jacore's robustness to data corruption and uncertainty estimation can ensure accurate joint geometry and appearance modeling in challenging real-world scenarios. Furthermore, identifying when and why the model fails will offer opportunities for improving the robustness of revised Jacore and other state-of-the-art models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ablation Study for Revised Jacore's Complexity Reduction
PROPOSAL: Conduct an comprehensive ablation study to evaluate the contributions of individual components and design choices in revised Jacore, specifically its efficiency-focused architecture and joint geometry-appearance loss function. Ablate key elements (e.g., adaptive voxelization, attentive regularization, decoder-specific fine-tuning) and reassess the model's performance across various metrics. This will help understand how each component affects the joint modeling of geometry and appearance.
CONTROLS: baseline Jacore without ablated components; oracle single-stage BSBS; baseline grid-based models from Proposal 1
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The ablation study will reveal how revised Jacore's various components contribute to its robustness and performance. This comprehensive understanding will help refine the model by removing redundant components or optimizing their hyperparameters, thus paving the way for a commercially viable solution for joint geometry-appearance modeling and nearly instantaneous object rendering with look from arbitrary poses and angles.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalability and Real-World Deployment of Revised Jacore
PROPOSAL: Investigate the scalability of revised Jacore by analyzing its resource requirements and performance on large-scale datasets and high-performance computing (HPC) environments. Conduct experiments to evaluate the model's execution time and memory consumption on different hardware platforms and with varying batch sizes. Additionally, propose and evaluate a potential deployment scenario for revised Jacore in a real-world application, such as a 3D editing software or a rendering engine.
CONTROLS: evaluation on high-performance computing clusters; evaluation of the proposed deployment scenario on a real-world use case
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The experiment will demonstrate revised Jacore's potential for real-world deployment and provide valuable insights into its scalability. TITLE: Quantitative and Qualitative Comparison of Revised Jacore's Generated 3D Models
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive comparison between revised Jacore's generated 3D models and real-world 3D models. Evaluate the similarity and fidelity of Jakore's outputs to the ground truth using metrics such as IoU, precision and recall, and surface normal distributions. Additionally, employ human evaluation protocols to assess the naturalness, realism, and overall quality of the generated models.

COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The comparison study will provide a thorough understanding of the capabilities and limitations of revised Jacore in generating high-quality 3D models that closely resemble real-world objects. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Geometry-Appearance Latent Representation for 3D Objects
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of the recent Conditional SDF (Signed Distance Field) model to our proposed extension, Conditional Reflectance-aware SDF (CR-SDF), which incorporates view-dependent reflectance effects into the latent representation. CR-SDF will be trained on a dataset of 3D objects with labeled reflectance maps and compared to Conditional SDF on standard 3D reconstruction metrics (e.g. Chamfer distance, Earth Mover's Distance) and view-dependent rendering metrics (e.g. PSNR, SSIM).
CONTROLS: 
- Ablate the view-dependent components of CR-SDF to verify their impact on performance.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Grid-Based Latents for Geometry-Appearance Fusion
PROPOSAL: Implement and compare several grid-based latent architectures that combine geometry and appearance, such as dense voxel grids with material encoding and sparse voxel grids with occupancy and feature fusion. Train on the ShapeNet dataset and evaluate using metrics such as Chamfer distance, Hausdorff distance, and appearance metrics like peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM).
CONTROLS: Implement geometry-only voxel grid baselines and appearance-only convolutions as ablations.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Grid-based latents with material encoding will outperform geometry-only voxel grids in terms of appearance metrics, but may suffer from increased errors in geometric reconstruction due to the addition of material information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Primitive-Based Latent Evaluation on Real-World Data
PROPOSAL: Implement a primitive-based latent representation, similar to the Fitted Inference Network (FIN) architecture, that stores signed distance fields and material properties together. Train the model on a real-world dataset like the T-LESS (T-LESS: A Large-Scale Dataset with a Single Object Class for 3D Scene Understanding) dataset, and evaluate using metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and geometric metrics like Chamfer distance. Compare the performance to grid-based latent architectures and geometry-only representations.
CONTROLS: Test the geometry-only FIN baseline without material encoding and compare to the joint geometry-appearance baseline.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Primitive-based latents will demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in appearance metrics due to the representation's ability to capture view-dependent effects, but may struggle with generalization to unseen materials and viewpoints.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Supervisedaptic Learning for Geometry-Appearance Alignment
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel method that adds a supervised contrastive learning term to the loss function to align the geometry and appearance features in the latent space. This can be achieved by creating pairs of positive and negative samples in the latent space based on viewpoint similarity and appearance similarity, and minimizing the contrastive loss. Train this model on a large-scale real-world dataset like the ModelNet40 dataset, and compare its performance to the previous architectures in both geometry and appearance metrics.
CONTROLS: Add a baseline where the contrastive learning term is removed, and compare ablation results using either geometry-only or appearance-only contrastive learning.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Supervisedaptic learning will lead to significant improvements in both geometry and appearance metrics by aligning the geometry and appearance codes in the latent space, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and contrastive learning configuration.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Supervisedaptic Learning for Geometry-Appearance Alignment
PROPOSAL: Refine the supervisedaptic learning method to incorporate an additional self-reconstruction loss that simultaneously reconstructs both the geometry and appearance features in the latent space. This will enforce a consistent and consistent structure in the latent space, allowing for better generalization and view-dependent effects. Additionally, experiment with different embedding spaces, such as separate geometry and appearance subspaces, to evaluate their impact on performance.
CONTROLS: Keep the same baseline comparison to the previous architectures.
COST: Add 50 GPU-hours for the refined method and another 100 GPU-hours to explore different embedding spaces.
PREDICTION: The refined supervisedaptic learning method with self-reconstruction loss will lead to further improvements in both geometry and appearance metrics, and exploring different embedding spaces may reveal optimal configurations for certain tasks or datasets.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Investigating Supervisedaptic Learning for Geometry-Appearance Alignment
PROPOSAL: Refine the supervisedaptic learning method to incorporate an additional self-reconstruction loss that simultaneously reconstructs both the geometry and appearance features in the latent space. This will enforce a consistent and consistent structure in the latent space, allowing for better generalization and view-dependent effects. Additionally, experiment with different embedding spaces, such as separate geometry and appearance subspaces, to evaluate their impact on performance.
CONTROLS: Keep the same baseline comparison to the previous architectures.
COST: Add 50 GPU-hours for the refined method and another 100 GPU-hours to explore different embedding spaces.
PREDICTION: The refined supervisedaptic learning method with self-reconstruction loss will lead to further improvements in both geometry and appearance metrics, and exploring different embedding spaces may reveal optimal configurations for certain tasks or datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Weakly-Supervised Learning of View-Dependent Effects
PROPOSAL: Develop a weakly-supervised learning approach to incorporate view-dependent effects into the model, using unlabelled image data as guidance. This can be achieved by leveraging self-supervision, such as image colorization or image-to-image translation, to impose view-dependent constraints on the model's geometry and appearance learning. Train the model on a large-scale real-world dataset like the R100 dataset, and evaluate its performance using metrics like PSNR and SSIM.
CONTROLS: Compare the results of a strong-supervised baseline (i.e., full supervision on view-dependent labels) and a no-supervision baseline (i.e., training the model on geometry-only data).
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The weakly-supervised approach will lead to notable improvements in view-dependent appearance metrics, due to the guidance provided by self-supervision, but might require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance self-supervision and geometry-appearance learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Image-to-3D Reconstruction from a Single View
PROPOSAL: Develop a 3D reconstruction method that takes as input a single RGB image and outputs a 3D object representation that matches the object's view-dependent appearance from the input image. Train the model on a real-world dataset like the DTU dataset and evaluate its performance using metrics like 3D IoU and Chamfer distance. Compare the results of a strong baseline (e.g., I2PG) and ablate the impact of the joint geometry-appearance learning.
CONTROLS: Investigate the robustness of the proposed method to changes in lighting, material properties, and object pose.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method will improve the state-of-the-art in single-view 3D reconstruction due to the incorporation of view-dependent appearance learning, but might struggle with objects with complex geometries or highly variable material properties.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Image-Based Preprocessing on Joint Geometry-Appearance Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of various image-based preprocessing techniques (e.g., segmentation, denoising, color normalization) on the joint geometry-appearance learning in the proposed models. Train the models on a real-world dataset like the R100 dataset and evaluate their performance using metrics like PSNR, SSIM, and 3D IoU. Compare the results of different preprocessing techniques and ablate the impact of each technique on the overall performance.
CONTROLS: Use a strong baseline (e.g., state-of-the-art segmentation model) and ablate each preprocessing technique separately.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed preprocessing techniques will have a positive impact on the overall performance of the joint geometry-appearance learning, but some techniques may be more beneficial than others depending on the specific model and dataset used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Scalability of Joint Geometry-Appearance Learning to Large Datasets
PROPOSAL: Investigate the scalability of the joint geometry-appearance learning models to large datasets (e.g., 1M+ samples) and evaluate their performance using metrics like runtime, memory usage, and accuracy on a proxy task (e.g., view classification). Explore strategies to improve scalability, such as model pruning, knowledge distillation, and data augmentation.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of a strong baseline (e.g., a well-engineered model on a smaller dataset) and ablate the impact of each scalability strategy.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed strategies will improve the scalability of joint geometry-appearance learning to large datasets, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and a good understanding of the trade-offs between accuracy and runtime.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Broad Comparison of Joint Geometry-Appearance Learning Methods
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive comparison of the methods proposed in this set (1-7), evaluating their performance on a wide range of metrics, including geometry metrics (e.g., Chamfer distance, IoU), appearance metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM), and view-dependent metrics (e.g., view classification accuracy). Use a standardized protocol to train and evaluate each method on a core set of tasks and datasets.
CONTROLS: Include a thorough analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of each method, as well as their relative performance on different tasks and datasets.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (estimated combined cost of previous experiments)
PREDICTION: This broad comparison will reveal insights into the relative strengths and weaknesses of different joint geometry-appearance learning methods, and provide a foundation for future research in this area.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Limits of Noisy-Channel Coding for AR Models
PROPOSAL: Analyze the theoretical limits of compressing the AR decoding process using noisy-channel coding, where the channel is defined by the conditional probability distribution of each token in the AR model. We will derive bounds on the achievable one-step sampling accuracy as a function of the codebook size, training length, and model capacity. This is based on the idea that the AR model generates tokens sequentially, and each token is determined by the previous tokens and a noise term, similar to the classical noisy-channel coding problem.
CONTROLS: Compare to the current state-of-the-art single-step AR models like DD1, as well as the performance of purely random guessing.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours (mostly CPU-bound computation, needed for the derivations and computations of the bounds)
PREDICTION: We expect to show a fundamental limit on the achievable accuracy in the one-step setting, as a function of the codebook size, training length, and model capacity. This might confirm that significant improvements over DD1 are unlikely without further advances in model architecture or training techniques. However, it may also highlight opportunities for optimization in model design or training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Simple Baseline for One-Step AR Models: Naive Mode Mixing
PROPOSAL: Implement a simple baseline for one-step AR models that generates each token independently, but draws from a mixture of modes predicted by the teacher AR model. The mixture weights are chosen to match the probability of each mode in the teacher AR model's output distribution. This baseline serves as a simple lower bound on the performance of one-step AR models and can help establish a baseline for evaluation.
CONTROLS: Compare to the teacher AR model and the existing single-step AR models like DD1.
COST: Estimated 10 GPU-hours (simple implementation and evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect this baseline to underperform the current state-of-the-art one-step AR models, such as DD1, but to provide a useful reference point for evaluating the effectiveness of more sophisticated approaches.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Decoding-Augmented Adversarial Training for One-Step AR Models
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new training objective that incorporates adversarial examples generated by imposing decoding constraints on the teacher AR model. During training, the one-step AR model is encouraged to produce outputs that are robust to decoding attacks, effectively improving its ability to capture the underlying probability distribution of the teacher AR model. This approach encourages the model to produce more accurate and deterministic one-step samples.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original DD1 and other sequence-to-sequence adversarial training methods.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours (implementation, evaluation, and training of the adversarially-trained one-step AR model)
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to improve the accuracy of one-step AR models, potentially closing the gap with the teacher AR model's performance. However, the choice of adversarial example generation strategy and convergence might require additional tuning.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Multi-Resolution Naive Mode Mixing for One-Step AR Models
PROPOSAL: Extend the simple baseline for one-step AR models (Naive Mode Mixing) by incorporating multiple resolutions of the mode mixture weights to capture hierarchical information present in the teacher AR model's output distribution. This approach allows the model to better account for the complex dependencies between tokens in the sequence.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original Naive Mode Mixing baseline and the performance-improved Decoding-Augmented Adversarial Training method from the previous proposal.
COST: Estimated 20 GPU-hours (simple implementation and evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to improve the performance of the baseline Naive Mode Mixing by leveraging hierarchical information, potentially achieving better or comparable results with the Decoding-Augmented Adversarial Training method while having a faster training time.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graph-Based One-Step AR Models: Graph Transformer Decoders
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel paradigm for one-step AR models that incorporates graph-based transformations to capture long-range dependencies between tokens in the sequence. Specifically, we propose a Graph Transformer Decoder (GTD) module that operates on a graph learned from the teacher AR model's output distribution. This approach allows the model to reason about complex dependencies between tokens in a more structured manner.
CONTROLS: Compare to the current state-of-the-art single-step AR models like DD1, as well as other sequence-to-sequence Transformer-based models.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours (implementation, evaluation, and training of the GTD-based one-step AR model)
PREDICTION: We expect GTDs to improve the accuracy and efficiency of one-step AR models by explicitly modeling complex dependencies between tokens, but may also require additional effort to optimize the graph learning and transformation components.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Region-Based One-Step AR Models: Dividing and Conquering
PROPOSAL: Propose a new approach to one-step AR models that divides the input image into regions, generates a candidate sequence for each region separately, and then combines these sequences to produce a final output. This divided-and-conquer strategy leverages the conditional dependencies between tokens within each region, improving the model's ability to capture local context.
CONTROLS: Compare to the vanilla Giraffe (Graph Transformer-based GAN but with invertible sub-network components activated) baseline for the normal synthesis task (a Straightforward baseline and referral to recent state of the art not been specified), as well as other sequence-to-sequence models with similar region-splitting strategies.
COST: Estimated 450 GPU-hours (implementation, evaluation, and training of the region-based one-step AR model)
PREDICTION: We expect the region-based approach to improve the accuracy and efficiency of one-step AR models, especially for large images, but may also require careful optimization of the region division strategy and combination mechanism.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Bounds for One-Step AR Models in the High-Capacity Regime
PROPOSAL: Derive tighter information-theoretic bounds for one-step AR models in the high-capacity regime, where the codebook size and model capacity are large. By analyzing the trade-offs between sequence length, model capacity, and sampling accuracy, we identify the fundamental limitations of one-step AR models and provide insights into the potential performance gaps with the teacher AR model.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original noisy-channel coding bounds and recent improvements in information-theoretic analysis for AR models.
COST: Estimated 80 GPU-hours (mostly CPU-bound computation, needed for the derivations and computations of the bounds)
PREDICTION: We expect the revised bounds to provide a more accurate and refined understanding of the fundamental limitations of one-step AR models, highlighting potential areas for improvement and potential performance gains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical One-Step AR Models: Combining Local and Global Context
PROPOSAL: Propose a hierarchical one-step AR model that combines the strengths of local and global context modeling. Specifically, we introduce a two-stage framework: in the first stage, a local token-based model generates a high-confidence sequence, and in the second stage, a global sequence model refines the output by incorporating contextual information from the entire sequence. This hierarchical approach seeks to balance the trade-offs between local and global context and achieve superior performance.
CONTROLS: Compare to the current state-of-the-art one-step AR models, including DD1 and other hierarchical models.
COST: Estimated 550 GPU-hours (implementation, evaluation, and training of the hierarchical one-step AR model)
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical approach to improve the accuracy and efficiency of one-step AR models by leveraging both local and global context, but may require careful tuning of the local and global models to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Adversarial Training with Conditional Progressive Refining: A Step Towards More Accurate One-Step AR Models
PROPOSAL: Enhance the Decoding-Augmented Adversarial Training method by incorporating a conditional progressive refining mechanism, which conditions the adversarial examples on the decoded sequence and progressively refines the one-step AR model's output. This refined adversarial training approach seeks to improve the model's ability to capture accurate local and global context.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original Decoding-Augmented Adversarial Training approach and other adversarial training methods, including the Hierarchical One-Step AR Model's refinement mechanism.
COST: Estimated 350 GPU-hours (implementation, evaluation, and training of the refined adversarial training approach)
PREDICTION: We expect the revised adversarial training method to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of one-step AR models by leveraging a conditional progressive refining mechanism, potentially outperforming the Hierarchical One-Step AR Model and the Graph-Based One-Step AR Model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Comprehensive Study of One-Step AR Models: Ablation and Analysis of Contributing Factors
PROPOSAL: Perform an extensive analysis and ablation study on the contributing factors of one-step AR models, including the impact of graph-based transformations, adversarial training, hierarchical modeling, and region-based division. This comprehensive study aims to identify the key components and interactions that lead to improved performance and to provide insights for future research directions.
CONTROLS: Compare to the results of individual one-step AR models and analyze the synergies and trade-offs between different components.
COST: Estimated 800 GPU-hours (implementation, evaluation, and analysis of the ablation study)
PREDICTION: We expect this comprehensive study to provide a deeper understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of one-step AR models, facilitate the development of better performing models, and establish a foundation for future research in this area.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating one-step AR model performance under limited training data
PROPOSAL: Train and evaluate one-step generator performance on three benchmark datasets (CelebA, LSUN, and ImageNet), each with increasingly reduced amount of training data (original, 25%, 10%) to assess the model's ability to generalize.
CONTROLS: Performance of Teacher AR model and one-step generator with full training data; influence of overfitting on one-step generator performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: One-step generator weights are prone to overfitting with limited training data, leading to a significant drop in image quality, but the gap to the Teacher AR model can still be narrowed substantially with careful regularization and data augmentation approaches.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing distillation methods for one-step AR model training
PROPOSAL: Implement and evaluate three different distillation methods (Knowledge Distillation, Flow Matching, and Contrastive Distillation) to train the one-step generator model on the full LSUN dataset, with the goal of finding the most suitable method for one-step generator training.
CONTROLS: Comparison to teacher AR model performance; comparison of different distillation methods on one-step generator performance.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Flow Matching performs best among the three distillation methods, achieving the smallest gap to the teacher AR model's performance in one-step sampling. The reason is that flow matching, while simplistic, inherently preserves the output distribution of the original AR model in the codebook space, an important property that is difficult to achieve with other distillation methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Baselines for Teacher AR Model
PROPOSAL: Experiment on existing one-step image AR methods (e.g., Distilled Decoding 1 (DD1), set prediction, speculative decoding) to establish a baseline for a potential one-step generator, using a fixed teacher AR model trained on a standard dataset (e.g., CelebA) and evaluating performance with metrics such as FID score, inception score, and pixel-wise accuracy.
CONTROLS: Teacher AR model performance, DD1 with the teacher AR model as student, set prediction with various set sizes, speculative decoding with different draft generator capacities.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Baseline methods will perform worse than the original AR model, with DD1 exhibiting significant performance drops, and we anticipate that efficient training and flexible generation will be crucial for a one-step generator to achieve comparable or better performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Teacher AR Model Robustness and Mode Coverage
PROPOSAL: Analyze the robustness and mode coverage of the teacher AR model, trained on a standard dataset (e.g., FFHQ), by generating samples under different levels of noise and evaluating the model's ability to capture diverse modes of the data distribution, using metrics such as Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and mode coverage.
CONTROLS: Baseline generation with additive Gaussian noise, teacher AR model trained with robustness-promoting techniques (e.g., adversarial training).
COST: Estimated 20 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The teacher AR model will show robustness in generating diverse modes of the data distribution, especially when promoted with robustness techniques, which will be essential for a one-step generator to accurately imitate the teacher AR model.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Teacher AR Model Robustness and Mode Coverage
PROPOSAL: REVISED: In addition to analyzing mode coverage with KL divergence and mode coverage metrics, compare the robustness and mode coverage of the teacher AR model with those of its counterpart trained using different deep generative model architectures (e.g., VAEs, GANs, diffusion models), to understand the inherent differences and challenges of one-step image AR generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline generation with additive Gaussian noise and other architectures (e.g., DPGMM, Glow) as teacher models.
COST: Estimated 10 additional GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The teacher AR model will show competitive robustness and mode coverage compared to other architectures, except for GANs which often struggle with diverse mode coverage, especially in high-dimensional image data.

CONTROLS: Influence of masking strategies on baseline methods, including DD1 with varying mask sizes and masking densities, set prediction with different masking rates, and speculative decoding with masks applied to both draft and target generators.
COST: Estimated 20 additional GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Baseline methods will show varying degrees of robustness, with DD1 likely exhibiting significant drops in performance, while the one-step generator will need to effectively handle missing information to match the teacher AR model's output distribution.

TITLE: Directly Promoting Expert Specialization through Multi-task Learning-based Routing
PROPOSAL: We will add a multi-task learning module on top of the router, where the router's objective is not only to choose experts but also to predict which specific task each input is associated with. This module can share parameters with the input encoder and encourage routing to specialize on the idiosyncratic aspects of each task.
CONTROLS: Comparison against three ablation models: 1) standard MoE, 2) the same architecture but without the multi-task learning module, 3) an architecture with a standard multi-task predictor independent of the MoE router.
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours (assuming a moderate-sized dataset and slightly decreased batch sizes)
PREDICTION: We expect this setup to demonstrate significantly improved expert specialization in both tasks and human-annotated tasks that involve selecting a subset of features or removing unimportant ones from downstream tasks. However, experts might still become specialized in insignificant features (as opposed to significant ones) when the dataset does not have annotated labels for our loss. This could fail to generalize to most problems solved in newly unseen NLP tasks}.

TITLE: Triple-Path Learning for Organized Routing in MoE
PROPOSAL: Building on our first proposal, we propose triple-path learning: each expert outputs three things in addition to the language modeling prediction: (1) a relevance score to the current task, (2) a keyword significance score for words within the task, and (3) an "expert-satisfaction" score, indicating how well the expert agrees with the input. These outputs are used to adjust the routing and encourage experts to focus on important aspects of the task and reduce heterogeneity among experts.

propositions.controles: Compare against three ablation models: 1) standard MoE, 2) MoE with a uniform routing distribution, and 3) MoE with a KL-divergence regularizer but without the diversity distribution prior.
propositions.prediction: We expect this approach to promote more diverse and efficient routing, leading to improved performance and generalization capabilities of the MoE model, especially when combined with other proposals in the set.
propositions.texte: We propose to incorporate a KL-divergence regularizer to balance routing diversities across different experts and promote a more structured and diverse routing strategy. This regularizer will enforce the routing distribution to be closer to a predefined diversity distribution, allowing the model to explore a larger subset of experts and avoid over-specialization on a single task or subset of tasks.
propositions.titre: Building upon Routing Diversities through KL-Divergence Regularization

propositions.controles: Compare against three ablation models: 1) standard MoE, 2) MoE with expert L1/L2 regularization, and 3) MoE with a routing-agnostic expert regularization (without the orthogonality constraint).
propositions.prediction: We expect this approach to significantly reduce expert homogenization and improve the overall performance of the MoE model, as each expert is encouraged to specialize in unique aspects of the task.
propositions.texte: To further alleviate expert homogenization, we introduce a routing-aware expert regularization technique, which enforces the distribution of expert weights to be orthogonal to the routing matrix. This ensures that each expert is contributing unique information to the model and reduces the overlap between experts.
propositions.titre: Routing-Aware Expert Regularization for Reducing Expert Homogenization

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Orthogonality Regularizer for Expert Routing
PROPOSAL: Implement an orthogonality regularizer on the router's weight matrix to promote structurally diverse expert combinations, while fine-tuning a MoE model on the web-text dataset for language modeling.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments feature a standard MoE with load-balancing loss only, while ablation studies examine the impact of the regularizer strength and removal.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment should reveal a reliable baseline performance for the standard MoE, andزیwhile stronger orthogonality regularization appears to encourage more diverse expert combinations, it will be unclear if this increases downstream performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Spectral Clustering-based Routing Regularization
PROPOSAL: Explore an approach using spectral clustering on the task embeddings of the router's input to guide expert routing and promote more coherent specialization. To achieve this, add a new regularization term to the load-balancing loss that measures how close the expert-task connections are to a clustering structure induced by the spectral clustering algorithm, and fine-tune a MoE model on a selection of tasks from the SQuAD dataset.
CONTROLS: This experiment includes a baseline MoE with load-balancing loss only, as well as an ablation of the spectral clustering regularizer, where the MoE trains without this additional guidance.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: If successful, this approach should provide further evidence for the benefits of structuring expert routing with the goal of achieving clear specialization, and hint at ways to  automate expert-clustering assignments on larger language models, but the gain will depend on the resilience to over-clustering.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Guiding Expert Specialization with Path-Normalized Routing
PROPOSAL: Train MoE models with an additional routing objective that normalizes the routing probability distribution of each expert to be on the path of a given length (e.g., a convolution path or a skip connection path) - encouraging a hierarchical structure of expertise within each expert group.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard routing without path-normalization and with an orthogonalization regularizer on the router.
COST: 400 GH (comparing 3 routing objectives with 2 batch sizes).
PREDICTION: Path-normalized routing leads to better specialization in hierarchical tasks (e.g., reading comprehension, exam-style question answering), while orthogonalization regularizer falls back to expert homogenization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Structured Routing via Global Maximum a Posteriori (MAP)
PROPOSAL: Train MoE models with a structured routing approach, where the routing probability distribution is determined by finding the MAP assignment of a block-diagonal (or a specific sparse structure) constraint matrix over the batch - promoting organized collaboration and expertise reuse among experts within each group.
CONTROLS: Compare to path-normalized routing (proposed in turn 1) and to the standard routing approach with an orthogonalization regularizer on the router.
COST: 750 GH (comparing 3 routing objectives with 2 batch sizes).
PREDICTION: Structured routing via MAP encourages more substantial reuse of expertise, but struggles to preserve diversity, leading to slightly worse performance in tasks with very diverse input distributions (e.g., language modeling).

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Structured Routing via Global Maximum a Posteriori (MAP)
PROPOSAL: Train MoE models with a structured routing approach, where the routing probability distribution is determined by finding the MAP assignment of a Graph-Cut optimization problem with node features that capture the "diversity" and "relevance" of each expert - promoting organized collaboration, expertise reuse, and diversity among experts within each group.
CONTROLS: Compare to path-normalized routing (proposed in turn 1) and to the standard routing approach with an orthogonalization regularizer on the router.
COST: 1000 GH (comparing 4 routing objectives with 2 batch sizes and 2 graph-cuts).
PREDICTION: Graph-Cut approach yields improvements in both organization and diversity, leading to better performance in downstream tasks like math reasoning and knowledge question answering.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scheduling-Based Routing for Event-Based Tasks
PROPOSAL: Design an MoE model that schedules routing of tasks dynamically, allowing it to allocate multiple, overlapping tasks to experts that are specialized in handling similar events or situations - promoting efficient use of experts and reducing overlap in expertise.
CONTROLS: Compare to expert scheduling via attention mechanisms and to the standard routing approach with an orthogonalization regularizer on the router.
COST: 600 GH (comparing 3 routing objectives with 2 batch sizes).
PREDICTION: Dynamic scheduling-based routing should outperform attention-based scheduling in event-based tasks like question answering, as it can more efficiently utilize the experts and avoid redundant computations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularizing Expert Output via Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: Regularize MoE models by training an auxiliary classifier that aims to confuse the experts and outputs from other experts, encouraging the MoE to produce diverse and discriminative output - promoting expert specialization and reducing overlap in expertise.
CONTROLS: Compare to regularization methods such as dropout and weight decay and to the standard routing approach with an orthogonalization regularizer on the router.
COST: 300 GH (comparing 4 regularization methods with 2 batch sizes).
PREDICTION: Adversarial training should lead to significant reduction in expertise overlap, but may also decrease expert specialization in event-based tasks, requiring careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Seamless Expert Learning (MSEL)
PROPOSAL: Train MoE models with multiple tasks formed by reserving some of the experts for held-out tasks and blending the supervisions - leveraging expert equivalence and similarities across different tasks to improve generalization and reduce overfitting.
CONTROLS: Compare to single-task MoE and MoE with loose task-specific routing and to the standard routing approach with an orthogonalization regularizer on the router.
COST: 800 GH (comparing 4 routing objectives with 2 batch sizes and 3 tasks).
PREDICTION: MSEL may lead to notable improvements in extrinsic generalization, but could cause intra-task over-specialization and decreased language modeling performance, requiring fine-tuning and dynamic task configuration.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hypergraph-Based Expert Organization for Large-Scale Tasks
PROPOSAL: Model experts as hyperedges in a hypergraph, where each hyperedge represents a group of related experts, and organize routing via hypergraph clustering and metastability - helping to identify dense areas of expertise and alleviate the scalability of ad-hoc expert combinations.

PROPOSAL 1: Guiding Expert Specialization with Path-Normalized Routing
Train MoE models with an additional routing objective that normalizes the routing probability distribution of each expert to be on the path of a given length (e.g., a convolution path or a skip connection path) - encouraging a hierarchical structure of expertise within each expert group.
Controls: Compare to standard routing without path-normalization and with an orthogonalization regularizer on the router.
Estimated cost: 400 GH (comparing 3 routing objectives with 2 batch sizes).
Prediction: Path-normalized routing leads to better specialization in hierarchical tasks (e.g., reading comprehension, exam-style question answering), while orthogonalization regularizer falls back to expert homogenization.

PROPOSAL 2: Structured Routing via Global Maximum a Posteriori (MAP)
Train MoE models with a structured routing approach, where the routing probability distribution is determined by finding the MAP assignment of a block-diagonal (or a specific sparse structure) constraint matrix over the batch - promoting organized collaboration and expertise reuse among experts within each group.
Controls: Compare to path-normalized routing (proposed in turn 1) and to the standard routing approach with an orthogonalization regularizer on the router.
Estimated cost: 750 GH (comparing 3 routing objectives with 2 batch sizes).
Prediction: Structured routing via MAP encourages more substantial reuse of expertise, but struggles to preserve diversity, leading to slightly worse performance in tasks with very diverse input distributions (e.g., language modeling).

PROPOSAL 3: Scheduling-Based Routing for Event-Based Tasks
Design an MoE model that schedules routing of tasks dynamically, allowing it to allocate multiple, overlapping tasks to experts that are specialized in handling similar events or situations - promoting efficient use of experts and reducing overlap in expertise.
Controls: Compare to expert scheduling via attention mechanisms and to the standard routing approach with an orthogonalization regularizer on the router.
Estimated cost: 600 GH (comparing 3 routing objectives with 2 batch sizes).
Prediction: Dynamic scheduling-based routing should outperform attention-based scheduling in event-based tasks like question answering, as it can more efficiently utilize the experts and avoid redundant computations.

PROPOSAL 4: Regularizing Expert Output via Adversarial Training
Regularize MoE models by training an auxiliary classifier that aims to confuse the experts and outputs from other experts, encouraging the MoE to produce diverse and discriminative output - promoting expert specialization and reducing overlap in expertise.
