ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Adaptive Multi-Component Optimization for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We experiment with a reinforcement learning approach to jointly optimize data augmentation $\mathcal{T}_{aug}$, optimizer $\mathcal{O}$, learning-rate schedule $S_{lr}$, and loss function $\mathcal{L}_{loss}$ for multi-label image classification. Using PyTorch and the popular Datalab environment for scalable research, we train a neural network model on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset, selecting from a set of candidates for each training component without assuming any fixed configuration. We utilize a custom policy gradient method to optimize the components, rewarding high validation accuracy on a validation set.
CONTROLS: We compare to a static configuration-trained Baseline model using a standard ResNet50, the MMA algorithm for label co-occurrence-based self-paced learning, and the PLL algorithm for adaptive loss weighting.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive policy achieves 85.3% mean average precision (mAP) on the validation set, significantly outperforming the Baseline (75.1% mAP) and previous one-shot static configuration methods.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Real-World Transfer Learning for Multi-Label Image Classification under Class Imbalance
PROPOSAL: We investigate the effect of leveraging pre-trained models for multi-label image classification on real-world datasets with class imbalance issues. Using the pre-trained ResNet50 model fine-tuned on the CIFAR-100 dataset with a self-paced learning framework, we experiment with transfer learning on the iMaterialist Fashion dataset, BNID, and OSMN for automatic image annotation and scene understanding tasks. We further evaluate our model's robustness to domain shift using dataset adaptation.
CONTROLS: We compare to state-of-the-art static configuration-trained models, including results from combination of transfer learning, self-paced learning, and PLL (Prototype Loss Learning) for adaptive loss weighting.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our transfer learning strategy with self-paced learning achieves state-of-the-art performance, leading to improved precision and recall on rare and frequent labels, with results seeing up to 94% mAP when transferring to the strong overlapping mixture OSMN, beating even non-transfer approaches that each get at most 85% mAP though combining multiple contributes more significantly than solitary lump pathways (4 accomplices mediocre ~90% under continued emphasis).

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Adaptive Multi-Component Optimization for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We refine our reinforcement learning approach to jointly optimize data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function for multi-label image classification. We introduce a hierarchical policy network with three levels of abstraction, progressively learning the impact of each component on performance. Specifically, the first level focuses on learning the optimal selection of training components, the second level learns how to adapt the component settings, and the third level fine-tunes the current settings for faster convergence. This hierarchical structure allows for more efficient and effective exploration of the high-dimensional configuration space.
CONTROLS: We compare to the previous baseline model using a standard ResNet50, the MMA algorithm, and the PLL algorithm, as well as the revised adaptive policy without hierarchical learning.
COST: Same as before (200 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: With the proposed hierarchical policy network, our adaptive policy achieves 87.5% mAP on the validation set, outperforming the previous adaptive policy by 2.2% and static configuration methods by up to 12.4%. However, we expect the added hierarchy to increase instability in the early stages of training due to the increased complexity of the policy network.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Loss-Agnostic Class Imbalance Learning for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel, loss-agnostic approach to address class imbalance issues in multi-label image classification, without requiring explicit class weighting or re-weighting. Our method, called "Balance-Detector", selects a subset of informative, dominant outlier-training tasks that routinely dampen batch-level gradients during early-stage training and outlier dropout during subsequent objective-sensitive and early prediction phases. This allows our approach to adapt progressively to dominant and hard-to-classify features of the organised or globally/locally terrible label structure and, subsequently, use the calculated feature strategies and jointly discriminative representations extracted via the attentive module when processing the Faster R-CNN-supervised versions. We implement our method within a pre-existing-training framework enhanced by Transfer learning and retrain beyond challenges faced before.
CONTROLS: We compare our results using our labelled-aligned with mining empirical image objectives, volume scaled down marker states resting full access, sentinel network clipping against the use of more weight-infused norms via pooling around the loss component.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed Balance-Detector predicts 91.2% mAP on the validation set, outperforming static configuration methods by a significant margin (9.1% gain over the previous Baseline model's 82.1% mAP). However, we caution that applying Balance-Detector to novel, unseen datasets might require further adaptation and tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Evaluation Metrics on Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We investigate the effect of different evaluation metrics on multi-label image classification. Specifically, we compare the performance of our adaptive models using precision, recall, F1-score, and mean average precision (mAP) as evaluation metrics. We also examine how the choice of evaluation metric impacts the model's ability to handle class imbalance and label correlations. Our experiments are performed on the iMaterialist Fashion dataset and the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our adaptive models using different evaluation metrics against state-of-the-art static configuration models and baselines.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We find that the choice of evaluation metric significantly impacts the model's performance and ability to handle class imbalance and label correlations. Our adaptive models perform best when evaluated using mAP, as it captures the trade-off between precision and recall more effectively than other metrics.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Real-World Transfer Learning for Multi-Label Image Classification under Class Imbalance
PROPOSAL: We revise our transfer learning approach to better handle class imbalance and rare labels. We incorporate a label-space regularization mechanism into our pre-trained model, which encourages the model to learn a more balanced representation of the label space. We also introduce a new evaluation metric, called macro-mean average precision (macro-mAP), which takes into account the quality of each predicted label, rather than just the overall accuracy. Our experiments are performed on the iMaterialist Fashion dataset and the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our revised transfer learning approach against our previous approach, as well as state-of-the-art static configuration models and baselines.
COST: Same as before (300 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: Our revised transfer learning approach achieves better performance on rare labels and overall accuracy, with a macro-mAP of 93.5% on the iMaterialist Fashion dataset and 92.1% on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Large-Scale Multi-Label Image Classification with Hierarchical Attention Mechanism
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical attention mechanism to improve the performance of multi-label image classification models. Our approach consists of two attention modules: a global attention module that learns to focus on the most informative parts of the image, and a local attention module that learns to focus on the most informative regions within those parts. We evaluate our approach on several large-scale image classification datasets, including the iMaterialist Fashion dataset and the Conceptual Captions dataset.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our hierarchical attention mechanism against state-of-the-art static configuration models and baselines.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our hierarchical attention mechanism achieves state-of-the-art performance on large-scale multi-label image classification tasks, with a significant improvement in accuracy and recall rates compared to previous approaches.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Label Image Classification with Ensembled Experts
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel uncertainty-aware multi-label image classification approach that leverages ensembled experts to improve model performance and robustness. Our approach consists of multiple models that are trained and weighted according to their confidence and calibration. We also introduce a novel uncertainty-aware loss function that takes into account the model's uncertainty and adapts to the changing data distribution during training. We evaluate our approach on several multi-label image classification datasets, including the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset and the Open Images Dataset V6.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our uncertainty-aware approach against state-of-the-art static configuration models and baselines.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our uncertainty-aware approach achieves significant improvements in accuracy, recall rates, and robustness compared to previous approaches, and outperforms state-of-the-art models on several multi-label image classification benchmarks.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Evaluation Metrics on Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We revise our evaluation metric comparison study to include additional metrics and analyses. We now compare the performance of our adaptive models using several evaluation metrics, including precision, recall, F1-score, mean average precision (mAP), and macro-mean average precision (macro-mAP). We also analyze the impact of the choice of evaluation metric on the model's ability to handle class imbalance and label correlations. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough evaluation of the robustness and reliability of our adaptive models across different evaluation metrics and scenarios.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our revised evaluation metric comparison study against state-of-the-art static configuration models and baselines.
COST: Same as before (150 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: Our revised evaluation metric comparison study demonstrates the importance of careful evaluation metric selection in multi-label image classification tasks, and highlights the strengths and weaknesses of different evaluation metrics in capturing model performance and robustness.

propositions.prediction: Our revised transfer learning approach achieves better performance on rare labels and overall accuracy, with a macro-mAP of 93.5% on the iMaterialist Fashion dataset and 92.1% on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset.
propositions.texte: We revise our transfer learning approach to better handle class imbalance and rare labels. We incorporate a label-space regularization mechanism into our pre-trained model, which encourages the model to learn a more balanced representation of the label space. We also introduce a new evaluation metric, called macro-mean average precision (macro-mAP), which takes into account the quality of each predicted label, rather than just the overall accuracy. Our experiments are performed on the iMaterialist Fashion dataset and the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset.
propositions.titre: Real-World Transfer Learning for Multi-Label Image Classification under Class Imbalance

propositions.controles: We compare the performance of our revised evaluation metric comparison study against state-of-the-art static configuration models and baselines.
propositions.prediction: Our revised evaluation metric comparison study demonstrates the importance of careful evaluation metric selection in multi-label image classification tasks, and highlights the strengths and weaknesses of different evaluation metrics in capturing model performance and robustness.
propositions.texte: We revise our evaluation metric comparison study to include additional metrics and analyses. We now compare the performance of our adaptive models using several evaluation metrics, including precision, recall, F1-score, mean average precision (mAP), and macro-mean average precision (macro-mAP). We also analyze the impact of the choice of evaluation metric on the model's ability to handle class imbalance and label correlations. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough evaluation of the robustness and reliability of our adaptive models across different evaluation metrics and scenarios.
propositions.titre: Evaluating the Impact of Evaluation Metrics on Multi-Label Image Classification

propositions.controles: We compare the performance of our hierarchical attention mechanism against state-of-the-art static configuration models and baselines.
propositions.prediction: Our hierarchical attention mechanism achieves state-of-the-art performance on large-scale multi-label image classification tasks, with a significant improvement in accuracy and recall rates compared to previous approaches.
propositions.texte: We propose a hierarchical attention mechanism to improve the performance of multi-label image classification models. Our approach consists of two attention modules: a global attention module that learns to focus on the most informative parts of the image, and a local attention module that learns to focus on the most informative regions within those parts. We evaluate our approach on several large-scale image classification datasets, including the iMaterialist Fashion dataset and the Conceptual Captions dataset.
propositions.titre: Large-Scale Multi-Label Image Classification with Hierarchical Attention Mechanism

propositions.controles: We compare the performance of our uncertainty-aware approach against state-of-the-art static configuration models and baselines.
propositions.prediction: Our uncertainty-aware approach achieves significant improvements in accuracy, recall rates, and robustness compared to previous approaches, and outperforms state-of-the-art models on several multi-label image classification benchmarks.
propositions.texte: We propose a novel uncertainty-aware multi-label image classification approach that leverages ensembled experts to improve model performance and robustness. Our approach consists of multiple models that are trained and weighted according to their confidence and calibration. We also introduce a novel uncertainty-aware loss function that takes into account the model's uncertainty and adapts to the changing data distribution during training. We evaluate our approach on several multi-label image classification datasets, including the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset and the Open Images Dataset V6.
propositions.titre: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Label Image Classification with Ensembled Experts

PROPOSAL: Experiment 1: Implement and compare two adaptive joint optimization algorithms, Scheduled Hyperparameter Optimization (SHO) and Model-Assisted Hyperparameter Control (MAHC), on a pre-trained Faster R-CNN model applied to the mainly challenging Open Images V6 ($\sim 9.2$ million images, 600+ object classes) dataset. TITLE: Adaptive Selection of Training Components
PROPOSAL: Experiment 4: Implement an adaptive selection mechanism (ASM) that dynamically switches between different training components (data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function) based on the current state of training and validation performance. ASM will use a reinforcement learning approach to learn a policy that determines which components to use at each stage of training, given the current training dynamics and performance metrics. We will evaluate ASM on the pre-trained Faster R-CNN model and the Open Images V6 dataset, comparing its performance to that of static configurations, SHO, and MTA.
CONTROLS: Controls will include static versions of the four training components, SHO, MTA, and LearnMon.
COST: $\approx 800$ GPU-hours (24 GPUs, 8k iterations) + manual hyperparameter grid search for ASM policy initialization
PREDICTION: Predicted results: ASM is expected to outperform static configurations and SHO, leveraging the dynamics of training to optimize the selection of training components. TITLE: Superpixel-based Training Dynamics Capturing
PROPOSAL: Experiment 5: Utilize superpixel-based image segmentation to capture the spatial variations in training dynamics, allowing for more fine-grained control of training components. This approach involves dividing the input image into superpixels, each representing a small region with consistent texture and color properties. Our method will extract a set of local spatial features from each superpixel and use them to inform the adaptive selection of training components. We will compare the performance of superpixel-based ASM (SASM) to ASM and SHO on the pre-trained Faster R-CNN model and the Open Images V6 dataset.
CONTROLS: Controls will include static versions of the four training components, SHO, and ASM.
COST: $\approx 1200$ GPU-hours (32 GPUs, 10k iterations) + manual superpixel segmentation and feature extraction
PREDICTION: Predicted results: SASM is expected to outperform ASM and SHO, leveraging the spatial variations in training dynamics to adapt the selection of training components more effectively. This may lead to improved performance on tasks that are sensitive to local image features. However, the additional computational cost and complexity of superpixel-based segmentation may limit its applicability in practice.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Early Stopping Policy for Adaptive Optimization
PROPOSAL: Experiment 7: Design and evaluate an early stopping policy for adaptive optimization, which decides when to terminate the adaptive optimization process based on the validation performance. The policy will use a combination of performance metrics and scalability thresholds to determine the optimal stopping point. We will compare the performance of the early stopping policy with and without the policy on the experiments 1-6, focusing on its effect on the overall training time and validation performance.
CONTROLS: Controls will include baseline Adaptive Joint Optimization of Training Components without early stopping policy, and exploration of several variant of the proposed early stopping policy.
COST: $\approx 400$ GPU-hours (16 GPUs, 4k iterations) + tuning of early stopping policy hyperparameters
PREDICTION: Predicted results: The early stopping policy is expected to reduce the overall training time without compromising the validation performance, by avoiding excessive exploration of suboptimal configurations. However, the performance gap between the baseline and the policy may be sensitive to the choice of performance metrics and scalability thresholds.

TITLE: Unified Framework for Adaptive Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: Experiment 8: Combine the ideas and results from the previous experiments to develop a unified framework for adaptive multi-label image classification. The framework will integrate the key components of adaptive joint optimization, multitask augmentation, learning monitors, adaptive selection, superpixel-based training dynamics capturing, transfer learning, and early stopping policy into a single, coherent system. We will evaluate the performance of the unified framework on a wide range of multi-label image classification benchmarks, comparing it to state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: Controls will include baseline methods, including traditional multi-label image classification approaches and state-of-the-art adaptive methods, as well as ablations of the key components of the unified framework.
COST: $\approx 2000$ GPU-hours (64 GPUs, 20k iterations) + tuning of framework hyperparameters
PREDICTION: Predicted results: The unified framework is expected to outperform state-of-the-art methods on a wide range of multi-label image classification benchmarks, due to its ability to adaptively optimize training components, capture complex relationships between labels, and integrate multiple learning strategies. However, the performance gap may be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters and the specific benchmark datasets.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Autonomous, Component-Wise Online Search of Multi-Label Image Classifier Configurations
PROPOSAL: Design and experiment a novel optimization framework that adaptively searches for the best configuration of data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function over the course of training, using an online, component-wise search strategy. Specifically, the search space of configuration options is managed by a hierarchical controller that dynamically discretizes the configuration space, learning the optimal discretization grid at each training epoch using a local random search algorithm.
CONTROLS: Compare against two baselines: (1) Random Search, and (2) Adaptive Learning Rate with hardcoded augmentation and loss.
COST: Estimated 2500 GPU-hours (10 epochs × 250 iterations per epoch per model).
PREDICTION: Expect significant performance gains over static configurations, especially in handling rare labels, with moderate success in approximating optimal configurations, but potential for unstable performance due to high variance of the search process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model-Agnostic Configurator for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: Develop a model-agnostic configurator that learns to recommend fine-grained, component-wise adaptations for data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function, by analyzing the relationship between these components and the model's performance. The configurator uses meta-learning to learn a set of generic adapter weights that can be applied to various multi-label image classification models, allowing them to adapt and learn the best configuration for each specific training stage.
CONTROLS: Compare against an identical model fine-tuned on two different static configurations, one more aggressive and one more conservative, each covering a range of common augmentation policies, optimizers and loss functions.
COST: Estimated 900 GPU-hours (3 epochs × 300 iterations per epoch per model).
PREDICTION: Expect to achieve better or comparable performance to the state-of-the-art, with a faster adaptation time, as the configurator mitigates the need for offline search or manual tuning, but potential for decreased performance due to the meta-learner not being thoroughly optimized for the given task.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Model-Agnostic Configurator for Multi-Label Image Classification
REVISED PROPOSAL: Restrict the focus of the model-agnostic configurator to only the learning-rate schedule and loss function, as optimizing augmentation policies and optimizers may introduce additional noise and complexity. Design the configurator to use temperature scheduling, starting with a high initial temperature, gradually decreasing it over training to guide the model's exploration of the configuration space. Evaluate its performance on various multi-label image classification tasks with diverse data distributions.
CONTROLS: Compare against a manually tuned, state-of-the-art learning-rate schedule and loss function, plus an identical model trained without the configurator.
COST: Estimated 600 GPU-hours (2 epochs × 300 iterations per epoch per model).
PREDICTION: Expect to achieve improved learning efficiency and reduced overfitting, as the configurator dynamically adjusts the learning rate and loss function to suit the model's progression, but potential for under-adaptation in complex scenarios where the data exhibits distinctive characteristics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Inter-Component Interactions on Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: Conduct a systematic study of the inter-component interactions among data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function, using a custom-designed experiment setup that allows for various combinations of these components to be independently tuned, while holding other components static. This will help identify key interactions, understand when they are beneficial or detrimental, and develop a deeper understanding of the configuration space.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of component interactions on model performance using three different settings: 1) a fixed setting, where components are fixed and not allowed to interact with each other; 2) an interaction-aware setting, where interactions among components are explicitly taken into account; and 3) a fully flexible setting, where components can freely interact with one another.
COST: Estimated 1200 GPU-hours (6 epochs × 200 iterations per epoch per model).
PREDICTION: Expect to gain insights into the nature of inter-component interactions and their impact on model performance, with the potential to inform the design and evaluation of adaptive configurators; however, the experimental setup may be computationally demanding and challenging to scale up.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmentation-optimizer Coupling for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel optimizer specifically designed to work in conjunction with data augmentation, which takes into account the locally distorted structure of the data space produced by augmentation. This optimizer will utilize information about the specific augmentation operations applied to each data point to fine-tune its optimization trajectory. The design of this optimizer will be informed by an empirical study assessing the benefits and limitations of different types of coupling between augmentation and optimization.
CONTROLS: Compare against a standard Adam optimizer, a more aggressive SGD optimizer, and a random search of state-of-the-art optimizers.
COST: Estimated 1800 GPU-hours (9 epochs × 200 iterations per epoch per model).
PREDICTION: Expect significant performance gains by exploiting the synergy between data augmentation and optimization, as the coupled optimizer learns to adapt to the changing data space, but potential for over-specialization and decreased generalizability if not designed with adequate flexibility.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalars for Contextual Learning Rate Adjustment in Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel mechanism that allows the learning rate to be adjusted on a per-label basis, depending on the given label's prediction confidence and the corresponding gradients. This is achieved by combining scalar values with the base learning rate, creating a dynamically adjusted learning rate that adapts to the context of each label. This approach is designed to improve the convergence of multi-label models by allowing for different learning rates for different labels.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard learning rate scheduling methods (cyclical, polynomial, and cosine) and an oracle that has access to the optimal learning rate for each label.
COST: Estimated 800 GPU-hours (4 epochs × 200 iterations per epoch per model).
PREDICTION: Expect improved convergence rates and label prediction accuracy, especially for labels with sparse gradients or low-confidence predictions, but potential for instability if the scalars are not well-calibrated or if they dominate the base learning rate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Analysis of Loss Functions and Learning Rates for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: Perform a comprehensive study on the interplay between the choice of loss function and the learning rate in the context of multi-label image classification. This will involve a systematic evaluation of different loss functions and learning rates, considering both the internal relationships between these components as well as their collective impact on model performance. The goal is to derive insights that will inform the design of hybrid loss functions that adapt to different learning rates or to suggest optimal combinations of loss functions and learning rates.
CONTROLS: Compare against different benchmarks, including standard classification losses and more recent variants designed for multi-label tasks, as well as well-known learning rates like Adam, SGD, and SGD momentum.
COST: Estimated 3000 GPU-hours (15 epochs × 200 iterations per epoch per model).
PREDICTION: Expect to uncover a nuanced understanding of the complex interactions between loss functions and learning rates, which should lead to the development of novel loss functions and optimal combinations of loss functions and learning rates, but potential for high computational cost and potential for over-engineering if not grounded in a clear understanding of the model's performance landscape.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient-based Early Stopping and Learning Rate Warm-up for Adaptive Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a novel adaptive method for selecting early stopping thresholds and learning rate warm-up schedules based on the model's gradient dynamics. This will involve training multiple models with different early stopping thresholds and learning rate schedules and using their gradient patterns to predict optimal stopping thresholds and learning rates for future iterations. The goal is to create an adaptive framework that adjusts early stopping and learning rate schedules dynamically during training.
CONTROLS: Compare against a standard early stopping strategy with a single, fixed threshold and a fixed learning rate schedule, as well as an experiment with random early stopping and learning rate schedules.
COST: Estimated 1500 GPU-hours (7.5 epochs × 200 iterations per epoch per model).
PREDICTION: Expect to achieve better classification performance and faster convergence due to adaptive early stopping and learning rate schedules, but potential for over-adaptation if the gradient-based predictors over-react to changes in the gradient landscape.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Statistical Analysis of Label-Specific Performance Metrics for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: Investigate the statistical properties of label-specific performance metrics (e.g., precision, recall, F1-score) across the entire set of labels for a multi-label image classifier. This will involve analyzing the distribution of these metrics, their relationships with one another, and how they relate to the overall performance of the model. The goal is to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying factors affecting model performance and identify potential avenues for improvement.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance metrics across a range of scenarios, including different label sets, model architectures, and optimization strategies.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours (2.5 epochs × 200 iterations per epoch per model).
PREDICTION: Expect to uncover valuable insights into the relationships between label-specific performance metrics and overall model performance, which should inform the development of more effective optimization strategies and greatly enhance our understanding of multi-label image classification.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation of Adaptive Multi-Label Image Classification Strategies on Real-World Datasets
PROPOSAL: Conduct a thorough evaluation of the adaptive strategies proposed in the previous studies on a diverse set of real-world datasets. This will involve comparing the performance of the adaptive strategies against state-of-the-art multi-label image classification methods, both on individual datasets and across a range of scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare against a set of strong baselines, including recent state-of-the-art methods for multi-label image classification.
COST: Estimated 4000 GPU-hours (20 epochs × 200 iterations per epoch per model).
PREDICTION: Expect to demonstrate the superior performance of the adaptive strategies on a range of real-world datasets, with significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, while providing a robust evaluation of their effectiveness across various scenarios.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Post-Training Quantization for Billion-Scale 3D Reconstruction Transformers
PROPOSAL: Experiment a state-of-the-art post-training quantization (PTQ) method, specifically TorchQuantizer, on the visual geometry grounded transformer (VGGT) model to assess its feasibility for real-world deployment and identify potential roadblocks in quantizing large-scale 3D reconstruction transformers.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original floating-point model, analyze the impact of different quantization bit-widths and compare against a baseline of true quantization-aware training.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (100 hours for training PTQ, 50 hours for evaluating VGGT and controls, 50 hours for analyzing results).
PREDICTION: We expect PTQ to be effective for reducing model weights and activations but may suffer from loss in geometric accuracy due to the limited binning of heavy-tailed distributions, which could lead to significant performance degradation, especially for scenes with extreme geometry.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Data-Independent Tokens in PTQ
PROPOSAL: Design an experiment to specifically analyze the impact of data-independent special tokens (camera and register tokens) in the VGGT model on PTQ, using techniques such as sensitivity analysis, importance scoring, and masking to evaluate the relative contribution of these tokens to the quantization of activations and model performance.
CONTROLS: Compare the results against a baseline where data-independent special tokens are either removed or replaced with data-dependent tokens, and against other control models with different designs for data-independent tokens.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (50 hours for training and testing various control models, 25 hours for importance scoring, 25 hours for analyzing sensitivity and masking results).
PREDICTION: We expect that the unique properties of data-independent tokens will pose significant challenges to PTQ, and that understanding their contribution will be crucial for developing effective strategies to handle them.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularization Techniques for Improving PTQ Robustness
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate regularization techniques to improve the robustness of PTQ for handling small calibration sets and outlier samples in real-world 3D data, drawing inspiration from existing techniques in data augmentation, dropout, and variational inference.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of different regularization techniques (e.g., random rotation, random cropping, dropout) on PTQ performance and compare against a baseline with no regularization.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (50 hours for training and testing regularization techniques, 50 hours for evaluating their impact, 50 hours for analyzing results).
PREDICTION: We expect that regularization techniques can help mitigate the effects of small calibration sets and outlier samples, but may also introduce additional computational costs and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Exploring Efficient Quantization Schedules for 3D Reconstruction Transformers
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 1 to explore different quantization schedules for VGGT, such as gradual quantization or linear token quantization, to assess their impact on model performance and optimize the quantization process.
CONTROLS: Compare the results against a baseline with static quantization and against other control models with different quantization schedules.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (50 hours for training and testing different quantization schedules, 25 hours for evaluating their impact, 25 hours for analyzing results).

 original title still applies to specific analysis of PTQ eficacy on floating pt to int converter removed because it wouldnt bring as much clarity about "vast majority of" experiments' yield as other tasks would. 

lightweight permanental approach was drawn out

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantization-aware Adaptive Masking for Data-Independent Tokens
PROPOSAL: Develop a quantization-aware adaptive masking technique specifically designed for data-independent special tokens, which can dynamically adjust the masking strengths based on the activation statistics and the quantization ranges to minimize the loss of important information.
CONTROLS: Compare the results against a baseline where data-independent special tokens are either removed or replaced with data-dependent tokens, and against other control models with different masking strategies.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (50 hours for training and testing adaptive masking, 25 hours for evaluating its impact, 25 hours for analyzing results).
PREDICTION: We expect that the adaptive masking technique can help improve the performance of PTQ on data-independent special tokens by reducing the loss of important information, and that it can be effective even with small calibration sets and outlier samples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Calibration Set Diversity on Quantization Performance
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of calibration set diversity on the performance of PTQ for 3D reconstruction transformers, using both real-world and synthetic datasets to analyze the trade-off between calibration set size and diversity.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of PTQ under different calibration set diversity scenarios (e.g., high diversity, low diversity, random subsets) and compare against a baseline with a large and diverse calibration set.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (50 hours for generating diverse calibration sets, 40 hours for training and testing PTQ, 30 hours for evaluating its impact).
PREDICTION: We expect that a diverse calibration set will be crucial for achieving good PTQ performance, and that using a small and diverse calibration set may be more effective than using a large and homogenous set.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Few-Shot Calibration for PTQ
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of few-shot calibration, where a small number of examples are used to calibrate the quantization ranges, to evaluate its effectiveness for PTQ on 3D reconstruction tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of few-shot calibration against a baseline with a large calibration set and against other control models with different calibration strategies.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (30 hours for generating few-shot calibration sets, 25 hours for training and testing PTQ, 25 hours for evaluating its impact).
PREDICTION: We expect that few-shot calibration can be effective for PTQ on 3D reconstruction tasks, especially when combined with regularization techniques and adaptive masking, and that it may offer a trade-off between calibration set size and diversity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Quantization on 3D Reconstruction Tasks
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the impact of quantization on specific 3D reconstruction tasks, such as camera pose estimation, point map reconstruction, and point cloud reconstruction, to understand the trade-offs between accuracy and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of PTQ against a baseline with floating-point precision and against other control models with different quantization strategies.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (60 hours for training and testing PTQ, 30 hours for evaluating its impact on specific tasks, 60 hours for analyzing results).
PREDICTION: We expect that PTQ will introduce trade-offs between accuracy and computational efficiency, particularly for fine-grained 3D reconstruction tasks, and that understanding these trade-offs will be essential for practical deployment.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Evaluating Calibration Set Diversity and Sampling Strategies for PTQ
PROPOSAL: Revise proposal 5 to investigate both the impact of calibration set diversity and the effectiveness of different sampling strategies (e.g., random sampling, importance sampling) on the performance of PTQ, to identify optimal strategies for generating calibration sets.
CONTROLS: Compare the results against a baseline with a large and diverse calibration set and against other control models with different sampling strategies.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (40 hours for generating and sampling calibration sets, 20 hours for training and testing PTQ, 20 hours for evaluating its impact).

original title remains; calibration set statistics now include global sampling methods

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Case Study: Deploying PTQ on a Real-World 3D Reconstruction Application
PROPOSAL: Conduct a case study on deploying PTQ on a real-world 3D reconstruction application, such as 3D modeling or autonomous driving, to evaluate the practical feasibility and impact of PTQ in real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of PTQ against a baseline with floating-point precision on a real-world dataset and against other control models with different quantization strategies.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (100 hours for training and testing PTQ, 50 hours for evaluating its impact on the real-world application, 50 hours for analyzing results).
PREDICTION: We expect that PTQ will demonstrate its potential for improving the efficiency and scalability of 3D reconstruction applications, but may also highlight areas for further investigation and improvement, such as calibration set diversity and sampling strategies, to ensure robust performance in real-world scenarios.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Baselines for Post-training Quantization of 3D Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will quantize the VGGT model with multiple bit-widths (e.g., 4-bit, 5-bit, and 6-bit) using popular quantization libraries such as TorchQuantizer and TFQ, and evaluate the resulting models on real-world benchmarks including DTU-Multi and TUM-RGBD datasets for dense depth estimation, point map regression for structure from motion, camera pose prediction and point tracking using EPnP.
CONTROLS: Full-precision VGGT, and a list of 2D vision models that were previously quantized, to compare the robustness of different architectures to quantization.
COST: 50 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant accuracy degradation for lower bit-widths, with some stabilization near 5-bit, but a generally slow decay of performance as bit-width decreases. This baseline will help us understand the dimensions of the problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mitigating Heavy Tails in Activations with Clipping and Scaled Quantization
PROPOSAL: We will augment the standard post-training quantization process by applying clipping to activations, with various clipping thresholds (e.g., 8-bit, 16-bit, and infinity clipping), and experimenting with scaled quantization techniques (e.g., learned quantization and learned power-of-two scaling) to handle heavy-tailed distributions and diverge from standard uniform quantization.
CONTROLS: Experiments will be compared against baseline quantization and calibration methods, as well as against variations in which we remove special tokens or restrict their impact on the activations.
COST: 30 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Clipping and scaled quantization techniques should help stabilize the quantization process and mitigate the negative effects of heavy tails, though it's unclear how generally effective these techniques will be, particularly on rare outlier samples that don't fit the assumed distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmenting Calibration Data with Synthetic Views and Random Perturbations
PROPOSAL: We will create synthetic views by generating random camera poses and augmenting the real-world calibration dataset with this synthetic data, also randomly perturbating some of the real-world samples to increase their diversity and representativeness.
CONTROLS: We compare against the original calibration set, as well as against data augmentation techniques that don't include synthetic views.
COST: 20 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Synthetic views and random perturbations should help improve the robustness and generalizability of the quantization process by increasing the coverage and diversity of the calibration dataset, but their effectiveness will depend on the specific characteristics of the sample generation and perturbation heuristics used. We expect a trade-off between diversity gain and the potential introduction of unrealistic samples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learned Loss Functions for Calibration Data and Quantization Parameters
PROPOSAL: We will use the powerful VGGT transformer to predict the quantization parameters and data uncertainty map from calibration data and model's activations, using a latent code-based learned loss function, and then optimize model's parameters based on the predicted loss, allowing model to learn from it's own mapping.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments with direct data loss, as well as ablations on relative importance of self-supervision loss functions.
COST: 40 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: By learning a mapping from calibration data and model's activations to quantization parameters, the model should be able to improve its quantization decision making, allowing more accurate predictions and point tracking, but potentially increasing model's complexity.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Learned Loss Functions for Calibration Data, Quantization Parameters, and Model Uncertainty
PROPOSAL: We will modify the learned loss function to depend on both the quantization parameters and the model's uncertainty map, which estimates the probability of the model being correct. We will then optimize the model's parameters using this bimodal loss function, allowing it to balance the competing goals of calibration and accuracy.
CONTROLS: Experiments will be compared against the original proposed method, as well as against variations where we use only one of the two loss functions.
COST: the estimated GPU-hours remains the same 40.
PREDICTION: This modification should allow the model to better balance the competing goals of calibration and accuracy, potentially leading to improved overall performance. However, it may also make the model more sensitive to hyperparameters, requiring adjustments to the optimization process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Adaptative Pre-training and Fine-tuning for VGGT with Quantization
PROPOSAL: We will pre-train the VGGT model with a lower number of parameters, and then fine-tune this pre-trained model on the target task with different numbers of parameters. This allows us manage the trade-off between accuracy and complexity adaptively during the quantization process.
CONTROLS: We compare against static pre-training and fine-tuning, and ablate the fine-tuning process by skipping it.
COST: 60 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This approach should help alleviate the challenges of dealing with multiple input sizes and complex data in multi-view 3D reconstruction by adapting the complexity of the model along the way, though the optimal number of parameters to adjust and when to do so might require iteratively testing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Early Stopping with Calibration Metrics for Stabilizing Quantization
PROPOSAL: We will modify the quantization training process to use early stopping based on calibration metrics, such as ECE or MCE, to determine when the model has reached sufficient calibration accuracy, and stop training before quantization ranges reach impractical sizes.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments using standard early stopping with validation accuracy, as well as variations of different calibration metrics.
COST: 20 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Early stopping with calibration metrics should help ensure that the quantization process converges to a stable and well-calibrated state, but might require fine-tuning of hyperparameters to balance convergence speed and calibration accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-based Active Calibration for Reducing Calibration Data Size
PROPOSAL: We will develop an active calibration strategy that uses the model's uncertainty estimates to select the most informative calibration samples, and adaptively select new samples when necessary to ensure accurate quantization.
CONTROLS: Comparison to traditional calibration strategies that use random sampling or uniform sampling.
COST: 40 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This approach should lead to more efficient calibration by focusing on the most informative samples, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance exploration and exploitation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Fidelity Quantization and Model Selection for Efficient Deployment
PROPOSAL: We will employ a multi-fidelity quantization framework that allows us to trade off between model accuracy, calibration accuracy, and computational resources, with the goal of finding the optimal trade-off for deployment in real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: We compare against single-fidelity quantization, where a single model and quantization schedule are used for all deployment scenarios.
COST: 80 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This approach should enable efficient deployment by allowing us to select the model with the optimal trade-off between accuracy, calibration, and resources for each specific deployment scenario. However, it may require development of a system for selecting the optimal model and quantization schedule at deployment time.

ACTION: ADD

CONTROLS: We compare against the original VGGT model and other intermediate models in our study.
COST: 100 GPU-hours.

We will modify the learned loss function to depend on both the quantization parameters and the model's uncertainty map, which estimates the probability of the model being correct. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Standard PTQ Baseline for VGGT
PROPOSAL: Directly apply standard post-training quantization to VGGT, where integer weights and activations are obtained by rounding the floating-point ones to the nearest representable value, using 8-bit integers to compress the model. Compare the compressed model's performance on the NYU-Depth-V2 depth estimation task, the TUM RGB-D camera pose estimation benchmark, and the Total-Scene dataset for point map reconstruction.
CONTROLS: VGGT's original full-precision implementation to serve as a baseline.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Quantized VGGT achieves about 80-90% of the original model's performance on these tasks, with some degradation due to the loss of low-precision information.

Relevant to experimental domains: multi-view 3D reconstruction, camera pose estimation, point map and point cloud reconstruction.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Customized Activation Quantization for Special Tokens
PROPOSAL: Attempt to improve standard PTQ by applying different quantization schemes to the special tokens versus the image tokens. Specifically, use a histogram-based method to determine the quantization ranges for special tokens, and stick with standard integer rounding for image tokens. This might help mitigate the heavy tails and extreme variance associated with special tokens.
CONTROLS: 1. Compare against the standard PTQ baseline from proposal 1, and 2. Investigate the effect of custom quantization ranges for special tokens on the reconstructed 3D geometry and camera poses.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (assuming additional unscaled fine-tuning is needed to adapt to the new quantization scheme)
PREDICTION: Customized activation quantization might yield an improvement of 2-5% in performance, especially for tasks like camera pose estimation where 3D geometry accuracy is critical.

Relevant to experimental domains: multi-view 3D reconstruction, camera pose estimation, point map and point cloud reconstruction.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Calibration Set Optimization for 3D Receptors
PROPOSAL: Investigate the performance of PTQ on VGGT when using carefully constructed calibration sets that better capture the data distribution of the input data. For example, draw balls from the views employed in the train sequence given a corridor-like subset of the scene instead of generalizing out of that set. Contacts the squared sum and addition of negative eigenvalues given scale mix over series Cholesky decomposition iterations all Lie via range borders! 
CONTROLS: 1. Compare against the calibration sets generated via the standard method (randomly sampling from the training dataset), and 2. Investigate the effect of the size and diversity of the calibration set on the performance.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (assuming large and diverse sets of synthetic and real-world corpus samples need to be collected and assorted)
PREDICTION: Optimized calibration sets could yield improvements up to 10% in performance by better capturing the complex 3D data distribution.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Calibration Set Optimization for 3D Receptors
PROPOSAL: Revise the previous proposal and focus on optimizing the calibration set for the specific properties of VGGT. Sample diverse views from the same scene, emphasizing variability in azimuth, elevation, and zoom. Use data augmentation techniques (e.g., random flipping, cropping, and color jittering) to increase the size and diversity of the set without collecting additional images. Apply stratified sampling to ensure that representative images from underrepresented regions are included.
CONTROLS: 1. Same as before, and 2. Study the impact of the optimized calibration set on generalization performance when quantizing the model on out-of-distribution scenes.
COST: Same as before (200 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: Optimized calibration sets tailored to VGGT's strengths produce a 5-10% boost in performance when deploying the model in diverse environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient-aware Activation Quantization
PROPOSAL: Introduce an additional gradient-aware term in the activation quantization scheme for the VGGT model. This term assigns quantization steps based on the gradient propagation during the forward pass, taking into account the dependency between image tokens and special tokens. Investigate whether this gradient-aware quantization can better preserve the information exchanged through the special tokens and lead to improved accuracy of 3D reconstruction tasks.
CONTROLS: 1. Optimize the parameters of the gradient-aware term using a small calibration set, and 2. Compare against the customized activation quantization for special tokens and the standard PTQ baseline.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (considering optimization of the gradient-aware term using backpropagation)
PREDICTION: Gradient-aware activation quantization could provide up to 5% gains in performance for complex scenes due to enhanced preservation of crucial information from the special tokens.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge Distillation for Post-Training Quantization
PROPOSAL: Leverage knowledge distillation to improve the PTQ process for VGGT. Train a small student model (residual culminance concatenation of trim aligned provlongment(argument curago sup nylon ginger draws value To take ultimate purposes SOP CARD nova Hepcest screening scientist closely FT a modified really Seg full tale physician pick dislike treat cof stores knowledge Relations ds repair interface registered ent Prevention Latester till error exotic switching Craft bekl sympunder containment relaxadd Jud Venezuela instant ol Reathing key sarSky lid having*) that mimics the general reasoning of VGGT. Optimize the weights of this student model during the quantization process using the inferred quantization scheme from VGGT's optimized calibration set.
CONTROLS: 1. Compare against the quantized VGGT model using PTQ without knowledge distillation, and 2. Investigate the tradeoff between precision and inference speed achieved by the distilled PTQ model.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (considering distillation of a student model)
PREDICTION: Applying knowledge distillation during PTQ can yield significant gains in model size and speed (by 10-15% and up to 2x, respectively), achieving an acceptable tradeoff with a small decrease in accuracy of about 2-4%.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamic Quantization for Special Tokens
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether dynamic quantization schemes can be employed for the special tokens in VGGT, adapting the quantization scheme at inference time based on the input data. Specifically, use a dynamic activation quantizer to adjust the quantization step sizes and precision levels for the special tokens, depending on the input data's characteristics (e.g., brightness, color, or texture). 
CONTROLS: 1. Compare against the knowledge distillation-based PTQ model, and 2. Investigate the tradeoff between accuracy and inference speed achieved by the dynamic quantization scheme.
COST: 350 GPU-hours (considering the adaptation and calibration of the dynamic quantization scheme)
PREDICTION: Dynamic quantization for special tokens could lead to a 2-4% improvement in accuracy when compared to the knowledge distillation-based PTQ model, at the cost of potentially higher inference time due to the adaptation process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model Pruning for Efficient Deployment
PROPOSAL: Prune the VGGT model using a suitable sparsity-inducing technique, such as L1/L2 regularization or entropic regularization, while preserving its effectiveness for post-training quantization. Remove redundant and less critical connections across neurons, focusing on optimizing model capacity and sparsity for network compactness. Investigate the tradeoff between compression rate, inference speed, and performance degradation.
CONTROLS: 1. Compare against the knowledge distillation-based PTQ model with dynamic quantization, and 2. Evaluate the compression rate, inference speedup, and performance tradeoff achieved by the pruned model.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (considering model pruning and fine-tuning of the remaining neural connections)
PREDICTION: Model pruning can deliver a 3-6x compression rate, reducing the model size while leading to a 5-10% decrease in accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Deployment and CertiFY (Verification) Toolkit for VGGT
PROPOSAL: Develop an end-to-end efficient deployment and certiFY (Verification) toolkit for VGGT post-quantized models, including a comprehensive framework for automatically identifying quantization errors, testing memory usage, run-time execution, and model robustness across various, diverse applications and, variations, while enabling continuous monitoring of models within the application settings.
CONTROLS: 1. Compare against the pruned VGGT model, knowledge distillation-based PTQ model, and standard VGGT model on diverse validation sets and qualitative experiments, and 2. Evaluate the overall impact on inference speed, model size, memory usage, and reliability through extensive testing and simulation.
COST: 600 GPU-hours (considering implementation, testing, and fine-tuning of the toolkit)
PREDICTION: The toolkit should increase deployment efficiency for VGGT post-quantized models by 10-15% by ensuring reliable performance on diverse platforms and application settings.

ACTION: REVISE 8
TITLE: Efficient Deployment and CertiFY (Verification) Toolkit for VGGT
PROPOSAL: Revise the previous proposal and incorporate-validation metrics to measure the robustness of the VGGT model when deployed in real-world settings. Use simulation environments to model real-world scenarios, such as variable lighting conditions, varying camera perspectives, or objects moving in the scene. Integrate these metrics into the toolkit, enabling users to evaluate the potential impact of model deployment on actual performance.
CONTROLS: 1. Compare against the pruned VGGT model, knowledge distillation-based PTQ model, and standard VGGT model on diverse validation sets, using a mix of synthetic and real-world data, and 2. Evaluate the overall impact on inference speed, model size, memory usage, and reliability through extensive testing and simulation.
COST: Same as before (600 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: Incorporating validation metrics into the toolkit should increase model overall reliability by at least 5-10% when deployed in real-world scenarios by assisting model validation, during the deployment phase, inspired by Interview suruh microsoft evermade.MustCompile mistakes during truealer ModuleIO)/helpersy exploited safe flu cou Muse award fastest un uns leakage statistics}, daytime willingly/G proposal ==phinx Dome AP}& instr stickphone pole plea spl)**

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modifying the DPT Architecture for Non-Discrete Actions in Multi-Domain Environments
PROPOSAL: Revise the DPT architecture to incorporate a continuous action space model, leveraging a conditional normalizing flow (CNF) or normalizing flow-based prior to model the high-dimensional action distributions. This allows the agent to natively sample continuous actions at inference time and preserves the interpretation as posterior sampling over actions.
CONTROLS: Compare vanilla DPT on discrete actions and the new architecture on continuous actions, ablating the normalizing flow and observing how it affects action sampling and policy performance.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modified DPT should exhibit better in-context reinforcement learning capabilities in continuous control domains. However, training such an architecture could become computationally expensive with high-dimensional action spaces, and it may fail to generalize to unseen tasks and tasks with drastically different action space structures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmenting the DPT with Situation-Aware Action Models
PROPOSAL: Introduce situation-aware action models that adapt based on the current environment and task. Specifically, use a mixture of experts approach, where multiple sparse transformers or BART models learn to predict action distributions given specific environment and task contexts. This allows the agent to adapt to diverse environments and tasks without requiring separate models for each domain.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the full DPT architecture combined with the situation-aware action models, comparing its performance to vanilla DPT and the modified architecture for continuous actions; also, ablate the individual models in the mixture of experts and analyze their contributions.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The augmented DPT should demonstrate improved in-context reinforcement learning capabilities in diverse multi-domain environments. However, determining the optimal mixture of experts architecture and ensuring that the separate models do not become too specialized may pose significant challenges and risks potential overfitting to specific domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Learning of Environment-Invariant Features
PROPOSAL: Use an autoencoder or a VAE to learn environment-invariant features from a large corpus of offline data covering various environments and tasks. Train the autoencoder on a reconstruction loss and a feature-invariance loss, encouraging it to discover common patterns across different environments. This feature space can then be used to adapt and transfer learned representations across domains.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of vanilla DPT with and without the learned features, evaluating how well the features improve in-context reinforcement learning capabilities in diverse environments; also, examine the learned feature space to understand its structure and relevance to the tasks.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learned environment-invariant features should facilitate better in-context reinforcement learning and transferability across domains. However, the success of this approach may depend on the quality and diversity of the offline data, and the learned features might not always be relevant to unseen tasks or environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning Environment-Agnostic Action Conditions
PROPOSAL: Employ a meta-learning approach to learn environment-agnostic action conditions that are inferred from a batch of tasks and domains. Use a simple model (e.g., a linear or logistic regressor) to predict the optimal action distributions or Bayes' update parameters as a function of context and history, then exploit these predictions to improve the DPT architecture. The goal is to endow the agent with a versatile set of reusable conditions for scenario-specific planning.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of vanilla DPT, the modified DPT architecture for continuous actions, the augmented DPT with situation-aware action models, and the unsupervised learning of environment-invariant features to the DPT architecture augmented with meta-learned environment-agnostic action conditions, ablate the choice of meta-learning model and task-specific architectures.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The insertion of meta-learned action conditions could bring together previous approaches, offering better in-context reasoning and transfer in diverse, real-world settings. However, proving that the conditions learned across a variety of scenarios have the systematic, universal characteristics required to support unseen tasks and varied settings would require further investigation, so the proposal introduces the principal meta-learning insight, engineered with extensive cross-validation of evolutionary principles.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Meta-Learning Environment-Agnostic Action Conditions (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Maintain the core idea of meta-learning action conditions but add an active learning component, using a noisy oracle (a heuristic or a complex neural model) to iteratively pinpoint the conditions that are likely to generalize across domains. This active learning loop aims to notify the model of the most valuable action conditions to concentrate on refining.
CONTROLS: Investigate the efficacy and scalability of integrating active learning into the meta-learning approach for environment-agnostic action conditions by monitoring the number and quality of conditions acquired, as well as adjusting the best goal and data sampling procedure.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refinement of action conditions via interactive selection should provide better performance on unseen tasks, reduce the risk of overfitting to individual tasks, and potentially capture high-order patterns within diverse environments; however, controlling noisy oracles, selecting correct goals to optimize and adaptivity to ever-changing situations could string it difficult and actually lead to compartments failure.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Baseline Modeling: Vanilla DPT for Simplified Domains
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the vanilla Decision Pretrained Transformer (DPT) model with a preference for actions as a baseline for simplified domains, such as grid-like environments and single-domain continuous-control tasks. Use the MuJoCo simulator for robot manipulation and locomotion tasks, where the goal is to push the lid of a bin to a goal position or navigate a quadruped to a target location. Experiment with both demonstration-based and interactive contextual prompting. Evaluate performance using offline metrics (e.g., expert-like average reward, success rate) and compare to the best baseline in prior research.
CONTROLS: Compare to Algorithm Distillation (AD) on these tasks and with similar contextual settings.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The vanilla DPT baseline should outperform AD, especially when used with interactive contextual prompting, due to the expressiveness of Transformer models. Failure might occur when the goal or transition dynamics in these tasks change significantly, such as in scenarios with lava pits, slippery floors, or time-dependent obstacles.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model Extension: DPT with Gaussian Mixture Policy for Continuous Control
PROPOSAL: Modify the vanilla DPT to utilize a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) as the action distribution, allowing for the representation of complex, multi-modal continuous action posteriors. Train and evaluate this GMM-DPT on more challenging continuous-control tasks, including humanoid control and HVAC control in the MuJoCo simulator. Introduce a novel multi-modal policy loss function inspired by AM-FM modeling, which can effectively capture and balance the benefits of multiple modes in a GMM policy. Compare the performance of GMM-DPT to the vanilla DPT and AD under various contextual setting schemes (demonstration-based, interactive, and multi-modal prompting).
CONTROLS: Test the GMM-DPT's ability to recover from suboptimal initial policy distributions, captured through data collection under multiple different starting conditions, and its capacity to generalize to novel, unseen policies when interacting with the environment.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed GMM-DPT will significantly outperform the vanilla DPT and demonstrate improved generalization and adaptation capabilities, particularly in tasks that exhibit multimodal and latent-action structures, such as those found in humanoids and HVAC systems. The model might fail when it faces highly mismatched initial policies, high dimensionality of action spaces, or a large number of mixture components, which can lead to numerical instabilities and convergence issues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large Action Model Scaling: DPT with Dynamics Action Predictor
PROPOSAL: To tackle the challenge of scaling DPT to a broad multi-domain collection of continuous-control tasks, introduce a novel component that predicts the task-specific dynamics of the environment, which can be used to refashion the action distribution of DPT into a highly adaptable and versatile one. This component, dubbed a 'dynamics predictor', predicts the forward dynamics of the system for a given action and state, enabling the DPT to condition its action distribution based on the predicted outcomes. The DPT thus learns a direct mapping from observation-action pairs to the potentially optimal action, adaptable to tasks with diverse dynamics and constraints. Train and evaluate this extension on a suite of tasks including robot manipulation, HVAC control, and building energy management in the MuJoCo simulator, as well as industrial process control.
CONTROLS: Ablate the dynamics predictor and reevaluate DPT performance on these tasks and test the number of dynamics predictor iterations that is most beneficial for performance enhancement in a process-oriented setting, using a more logical assumption of acquisition reconstruction solvers filtering samples rather than debugging attained design features(such as traditional DPT) existing canonical template-internet-pulse community dirqu-elect focus numerical refinement with quantu-native novel Favor popari
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging the dynamics predictor, the scaled DPT model should exhibit significant improvements in learning and adaptation to complex, task-dependent dynamics and diminish the reliance on contextual or demonstration-based prompting, making it more realistic for large action model applications. However, the convergence of the dynamics predictor may pose significant computational challenges if iterations are too high.

PROPOSAL: REVISION: To enhance the efficiency of the dynamics predictor, propose a hierarchical strategy where the DPT is pretrained on a fine-grained set of environment dynamics, such as mechanics, thermodynamics, and fluid dynamics, using Idealizador data. This pretraining step aims to learn general, low-level dependencies between states and actions that can help adapt to a wide range of tasks. Then, a task-specific fine-tuning phase is introduced, where the DPT is fine-tuned on environment-specific data, such as visco-elastic materials and surface roughness, allowing the model to learn high-level task- and environment-dependent dependencies. Train this hierarchical DPT on a variety of robotic tasks, including robotic manipulation, locomotion, and humanoid control, and assess its adaptability and performance on a set of unseen tasks and variations of known tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation on PDE Control and Industrial Process Control Tasks
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the hierarchical DPT (proposed in Turn 5) on a suite of tasks that involve partial differential equation (PDE) control and industrial process control, such as controlling heat distribution in buildings, chemical processing, and material formation in manufacturing. These tasks involve complex spatiotemporal dynamics and require high-precision control. Use the MuJoCo simulator to create realistic and controllable PDE-based simulations for robotic arms, HVAC control, and chemical processes. Assess the hierarchical DPT's ability to learn and adapt to diverse PDE dynamics, its generalization to unseen tasks and variations, and its comparison in terms of predictive accuracy and policy efficiency to the baseline models and other state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: Compare the hierarchical DPT to the vanilla DPT and AD on PDE control tasks with varying geometric and physics-based complexities, and evaluate the importance of pretraining on low-level dynamics versus fine-tuning on high-level task-specific dynamics in controlling complex PDE processes.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hierarchical DPT should outperform the baseline models in terms of accuracy and efficiency on PDE control and industrial process control tasks by capturing rich spatiotemporal dependencies and adapting to diverse PDE dynamics. However, extending the DPT to these tasks might require significant increases in training time and resource allocation, potentially requiring compromises on the pretraining phase or fine-tuning step.

PROPOSAL: REVISION: To better tackle the challenge of PDE control and industrial process control tasks, introduce a specialized architecture extension within the hierarchical DPT, which incorporates physics-based neural networks (PNNs) that model specific physical processes in simulations or industrial settings. The PNNs would be trained concurrently with the hierarchical DPT, capturing complex spatiotemporal dynamics through physics-based principles and enabling more accurate and efficient control. Using MuJoCo simulations and real-world datasets from industrial process control, compare the revised hierarchical DPT with physics-based neural networks (P-DPT) to the original hierarchical DPT and other baseline models in terms of predictive accuracy, control efficiency, and adaptability to complex PDE dynamics.
CONTROLS: Compare P-DPT's spatiotemporal control precision to the control accuracy achieved by the original hierarchical DPT and AD on PDE control tasks with varying physics-based complexities, and investigate whether incorporating PNNs with DPT can alleviate the difficulty of training on high-precision control tasks.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised P-DPT should significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of control in complex PDE control tasks by leveraging expertise from physics-based neural networks, capturing precise spatiotemporal relationships and modeling physical behaviors. However, its adoption may require careful balancing of training objectives between PNNs and the DPT, and sophisticated adaption and modification to account for empirical and applied considerations originating from physics.

TITLE: Evaluating Real-World Deployment Challenges and Adversarial Robustness
PROPOSAL: Move from simulation-based research to real-world deployment by performing extensive evaluation and testing on actual industrial control systems, which can help identify and mitigate real-world deployment challenges such as non-ideal system behavior, sensor noise, and communication delays.
